ROBERT BRAINERD GAYLOllD, the sixty-fifth Most Worshipful Grand
Master of the Jurisdiction of the State of California, completed his duties
as Grand Master on Friday, the 14th day of October, 1932, after a long
and useful service to the Fraternity; deserving and worthy of the Ion,
respect and admiration of his Brethren.
While he was honored by being exalted to the dignified office of Most
Worshipful Grand Master, the Grand Lodge of California was equally
honored by the nobili:ty of character ever exemplified by their Grand
Master. Brother Gaylord received 'the degrees in, and is at present a
member of, Oakland Lodge No. 188, was initiated February 11th, 1899,
passed to the degree of Fellowcraft February 23rd, 1899, and raised to
the degree of Master Mason March 18th, 1899. He served in the several
stations of the Lodge, being Master in 1906. He is a member of Oakland
Chapter No. 36, Royal A'rch Masons, having received the degrees in Sa.id
Chapter as follows: Mark Master, September 17, 1902; Past Master,
October 1, 1902; Most Excellent Master, October 8, 1902; and Royal
Arch Mason, October 22, 1902. He is a member of Oakland Commandery
No. 11, Knights Templar, having received the Order of Knighthood
there on November 17, 1903. He served as Eminent Commander in 1923,
after passing in the several subordinate chairs. He is a member of the
Oakland Scottish ~ite Bodies, his record being as follows: Received
the 14th Degree, March 25, 1907; the 32nd Degree, June 14, 1909;
K. C. C.H., October 22, 1929. He served as Orator of Oakland Scottish
Rite Bodies, 1910-11. He is a member of Islam Temple A. A. 0. N. M. S.,
having joined the Shrine April 25, 1910; is a member of St. Philip Conclave Red Cross of Constantine, and was Sovereign in 1929. He served
as Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge in 1917, and Right Eminent Grand
Commander of the Grand Commandery of California in 1930.

Throughout his long and active Masonic career, Brother Gaylord has
ever exemplified ·the principles and tenets of Masonry, and practiced the
virtues of_Christian Knighthood as promulgated by the Commandery of
Knights Templar. By the sterling qualities of his character as daily

exemplified in his service in the Grand Lodge and Grand Conunandery
of the jurisdiction of the State of California, he has endeared himself to
the entire Masonic Family of our Grand Jurisdiction.

.

Brother Gaylord was born at River Falls, Wisconsin, November 24,
1876, the son of Titus Brainerd Gaylord and Annie Phimelia Parker
Gaylord. On his mother's side, he traces his New York Colonial ancestry,
while he is a descendant, on his father's side, of the Pioneer. William
Gaylord, who settled in Massach?setts in 1631. He came to California in
1883 and lived in San Jose until 1894, when he moved to Oakland with
his family. He attended our pablic schools and received a diploma from
the University of California in 1897, having been graduated from Hastings
Law School. He has followed the profession of the law, and at present
.
has his offices in the Russ Building in San Francisco.

Brother Gaylord's success in life was made certain wh~" Ql1 July 17, "
1901, he was united in marriage with Harriet Brown Lumley," who took .: . ' .
her place as a loving companion and the heart of an inspiring family
life, a place which she has held with true womanly grace and charm.
They have been blessed with a son, Robert Brainerd Gaylord Jr., and a
daughter, Rachel C. Gaylord, who are successful in their chosen prO:
fessions.
· Tt may be truthfully said of Robert Brainerd Gaylord that in his
Ma'sonic as well as in his civic life, his character has ·been such as to
induce emulation by his fellow men. He is courageous, fearless and outstanding in his decisions of right, truth and justice, as well as kind,
courteous and charitable in his relationship with his fellow men in· thought
as well as in deed.

clares that the seat and spring of religion are in the head. Heresy trials
in the name of religion are always trials for heresy of the head. Heresy
is wrong thinking; it is never predicated ort wrong behavior. And we
must not have less thinking in religion-we need clearer thinking. As a
man thinketh in his heart, so is he.
Another view is that religion is emotion-a fine emotion. This is
religion of the heart and not of the head. It converts it into a fine glow.
It says, in effect, that if a man feels good, he may think as he pleases.
A great many people do right in order to feel right; it is better to do
right because' it is right, whether we feel good over it or not. Religion·
is not a matter of feeling; it is a matter of fact.
·Another view is that religion is an activity. It consists in doing
something. It is an answer to the cry, What shall I do to inherit eternal
life? It makes of religion a sort of a glorified fussiness. · It locates religion neither in the head nor in the heart, ~t in the hands and feet. It
makes religion a synonym for service. This is the popular view of religion, but it is an abortive view.
A fourth view is that religion is passivity-a sort of quiescent acquiescence in an inner working, wonder working God, who does it all,
while we lean back upon His waiting breast and allow Him to do it all .
This makes of religion a contemplation-a mere subjectivity.
There came a Man who spake as never man . spake, and He said,
"Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart and with all thy
soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength, and thy neighbor
as thyself." That is to say, religion is an idea. It grips the mind. Religion is an emotion-it grips the heart. Religion is an activity-it takes
the strength. Religion is a passivity-it commaI)ds the soul.

DEVOTIONAL SERVICE
The V. R. John Snape, Grand Chaplain, conducted a
brief but interesting and instructive devotional service, with
appropriate music by the Grand Organist. The Grand Chaplain's text was Religion, and his remarks thereon were substantially as follows:
Religion, t{ it means anything, means everything. It is not an accident, or an incident, or an expedient, .o r a commercial convenience. It is
not a method of moral behavior. It is life--God's life-in human life-expressing itself in human conduct.
Four great ideas, which have developed into four great philosophies
set forth the great facts of religion.
One view of religion is that religion is an idea. It is the philosophy
that if a man thinks correctly, he may do as he pleases. This view de-

TRIBUTE TO GEORGE WASHINGTON
Past Grand Master Albert E. Boynton then addressed
Grand Lodge as follows :
Throughout the length and breadth of the land, the 200th anniversary
of the birth of "the Father of his Country" is being observed this year~
George Washington, the first President of the United States, was
born at Wakefield, Virginia, February 22, 1732. At.the age of three, his
family moved to what later became known as Mount Vernon, a magnificent estate on the banks of the Potomac River. His father died when
he was eleven years of age. His elder half-brother secured for him an
appointment as midshipman in the British Navy, but his mother, described as a woman of · fine presence, intelligent, high-minded, resolute
Christian character, would not permit him to accept it.
He acquired all of his schooling before he was sixteen. His teacher
was a convict-a political prisoner sent over from England.

8

• t PROCEEDINGS OF THE

When seventeen, he was commissioned as a surveyor by William and
Mary College.
For two years, Washington pursued the vocation of surveyor, but
the encroachments of the French aroused the military spirit of the people
and, although he was only nineteen, he secured an appointment as a Major
in the Virginia militia, later acting in a similar capacity in Braddock's
campaign, where he played an outstanding part.
At the age of twenty-seven, he married Martha Custis, widow of
.Colonel Custis.
He was a member of the Virginia House of Burgesses for sixteen
years.
These were troublous times, and the mother country was bearing
down on the colonies. The period from the passage of the Stamp Act in
1765 to the outbreak of the Revolution was one of feverish excitement
throughout the colonies.
In 1774, the first Continental Congress met in Philadelphia. Washington was one of the seven delegates from Virginia. His position in
the gathering is best known through Patrick Henry's tribute: "If you
speak of eloquence, Mr. Rutledge of South Carolina is by far the greatest
orator, but if you speak of solid information and sound judgment, Colonel
Washington is unquestionably the greatest .man on the floor."
The next year, the secon°d Continental Congress assembled in Independence Hall, Philadelphi~, with John l!ancock as President. Blood
had already been shed on the soil of New En!Jland. Congress regularly
adopted the New England provincial army, and the pay of the Commander-in-Chief was fixed at $500 per month. Washington, at the age
of forty-three, was unanimously elected to take command. He accepted
the appointment but stipulated that he would accept no pay for his services.
He assumed command of the Continental Army under an elm tree
on the Cambridge Common adjoining Harvard University.
It is impossible to follow our national hero through his campaigns,
or dilate on Valley Forge, Trenton, Brandywine and Yorktown.
. The end of the Revolution came when Yorktown fell, and Washington received the sword of Cornwallis in surrender.
Thus closed the mighty struggle for American independence.
.As the Commander-in-Chief of the Continental Army, the services
and achievements of George Washington are unique in the world's history.
He was much more than the Commander-in-Chief. He was the one necessary person whose ability and calm, unswerving, determined sense of
patriotic duty to country put real backbone into the R~volution and kept
it from collapsing or merging into civil conflict under the hardships and
privations encountered during the eight years of war. Without General

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

9

Washington at . its head, it could never have succeeded. His faith in the
cause and his devotion to the ideals it embodied, made him the symbol of
America-the spirit of the Revolution.
Our wise and unselfish commander of tattered soldiery wrung victory
from the seasoned legions of Europe under discouragements that would
have crushed any save an indomitable spirit.
Of his leadership and skill, Von Moltke said in Berlin in 1874 :
"You have in American history one of the greatest captains
of all times. I t might be said of him, as it was of William the
Silent, that he seldom won a battle, but he never lost a campaign."
Washington's farewell t~ his officers at New York was an affecting
scene.
Not a word was spoken as he embraced his c'omrades. The deep
feeling and manly tenderness of these veterans in the parting moment
could find no utterance in words.
Arriving in Annapolis where Congress was in session,· he resigned
his commission and proceeded to Mount Vernon. Shortly after his arrival,
he wrote Lafayette, who had served with him :
"I have become a private citizen on the banks of the Potomac,
in the shadow of my own vine and my own fig tree, free from the
bustle of a camp, and the busy scenes of public life. I am solacing
myself with these tranquil enjoyments of which the soldier, who
is ever in pursuit of fame-the statesman, whose watchful days
and sleepless nights are spent in devising schemes to promote the
welfare of his own, p~rhaps the ruin of other countries, as if
this globe was insufficient for us all-and the courtier, who is always watching the countenance of his pri~ce in the hope of catching a gracious smile~an have very little conception. I have not
only retired from all public employment, but am retiring within
myself, and shall be able to view the solitary walk, and tread the
paths of private life, with heartfelt satisfaction. Envious of none,
I am determined to be pleased with all; and this, my dear friend, ,
being the order of my march, I will move gently down the stream
of life, until I sleep with my fathers."
But it was not to be. The Constitutional Convention drafted Washington as its President. It took four months to complete the document
and it was nearly a year before it was ratified by a sufficient number of
States to become effective.
Washington received the entire vote of the electoral college and
was unanimously chosen as the first President of the United States.
Two days after being notified of his election, he set out from Mount
Vernon on his journey to N ew York. This trip proved a veritable ovation from start to finish.

11

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

His approach and entry into New York was a perfect triumph and
beggars description.
On the balcony of Federal Hall, in the presence of a vast concourse
of citizens, and surrounded by intimate friends and former comrades,
he took the oath of office as President of the United States. This oath
was administered by Robert L1vingston, Chancellor of the State of New
York, and Grand Master of its · Grand Lodge. The Bible used for the
occasion was brought from the Lodge Room of St. John's Lodge.
His eight years as President were most trying. It could not have been
otherwise. A new nation was being organized and grave questions had
to be met and settled. Several times, Congress was on .the very verge of
dissolution. To pacify these warring elements and smooth the way for the
successful administration of the government's affairs, was not an easy
task and probably could not have been accomplished by a less resourceful
man than the President. Through his calm leadership, salutary advice and
consummate diplomacy, most of the vexed issues were satisfactorily adjusted.
·
Having determined to retire at the end of his 'second term, some six
months previous to its expiration, he published his Farewell Address or,
as it has been aptly termed, ''Washington's Legacy to the American
People." This marvelous document will be cherished as long as America
exists.
After leaving the Presidency, Washington returned to Mount Vernon.
The last year of his life was largel;r devoted to the settlement of his
private affairs and in arranging for the final distribution of his vast estate,
he being the richest man in the United "States.
And now, to digress, my Brethren,. may I .recall to your minds some
of the facts about Washington, the Mason?
He received the degrees of· ,Preemasonry in Fredericksburg Lodge at
Fredericksburg, Virginia; paid his initiation fee in November, 1752,
amounting to two pounds, three shillings (between ten and eleven dollars),
and was "brought to light" as
Entered Apprentice. He was passed as
a Fellow Craft in March, and raised as a Master Mason August 4, 1753.
He was not yet twenty-one when he became an Entered Apprentice which,
apparently, ·was allowable in Virginia. Washington remained a member
of Fredericksburg Lodge throughout his life.
In April, 1788, the Virginia Grand Lodge issued a charter to Alexandria Lodge No. 22, and Washington was designated as the first Master
of the Lodge. Dual membership was permissible in Virginia in those early
days, as it is today, the only inhibition being that a Mason could not be
a member of two Lodges in the same town. He served as ].laster for .two
y~ars. After his death, the name of the Lodge was changed to Alexandria
Washington Lodge, and the Lodge is so known today.

Washington was Master of his Lodge when elected and inaugurated
as President of the United States, he being the only President.to have that
distinction.
When the Grand Lodge of Virginia was organized in 1777, he was
offered the position of Grand Master but declined because, at that time, he
had never serv~d as Master or Warden of a chartered Lodge.
He was a frequent visitor to M;°sonic Lodges in the different colonies
and was an honorary member of several.
Upon invitation of the Grand Lodge of Maryland,. which' ha~ been
requested to lay the corner stone of the National Capitol, Wash1ng~on
officiated as Grand Master. The trowel used on that memorable occasion
is the property of Alexandria Washington Lodge. It has been used a. few
times since the last occasion being some three weeks ago when President
Hoover laid the comer stone of the new Post Office Building in Washington.
·
Many Masonic articles were found among his effects and listed in the
inventory of his estate:
The constitutions of four Grand Lodges-Pennsylvania, New York,
Virginia and Massachusetts-were dedicated to him.
More Masonic Lodges have been named after Washington than ~y
other person, there being nine such Lodges in the state of Pennsylvama,
alone.
Towns cities and states have been named in his honor. Monuments
have been :rected to his memory-the greatest of all being the magnifice!1t
memorial which the Masons of America have constructed at Alexandria,
Virginia, and which was dedicated on May 12th last.
Many of our groat Presidents, themselves members of the Craft, h~ve
paid tribute to Washington, the Mason. Theodore Roosevelt, addressing
the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania in 1902, said:
"One of the things that attracted me so greatly in Masonry,
that I hailed the chance of becoming a Mason, was that it really
did act up to what we, as a government, and as' a people, are
pledged to-of treating each man on his merits as a man. ~en
Brother George Washington went into a Lodge of the Fraternity,
he went into the one place in the United States where he stood
below or above his fellows, according to their official position in
the Lodge. He :went into the place where the ideal of our g~vern­
ment was realized as far as it is humanly possible for mankind to
realize a lofty ideal."
But to resume:
The curtain was about to fall around the greatest figure in history.
He was sick but two days, dying December 14, 1799, of pneumonia. On
his deathbed, after nearly twenty-four hours of struggle for breath, he

Shortly after his death, at the request of Congress, his 'comrade-inarms, Major General Henry Lee, delivered before that body a masterly
funeral oration, paraphrasing his life in the immortal words: "First in
war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen."
In summing up, it has been truly said that, "in the throes of war and
revolution, America had brought forth a man to be ranked with the greate_st and noblest of any age in all the world. There have been greater
generals in the field and 'statesmen in 'the Cabine't in our own and other
nations. There has been no greater character. When we 'think of Washington, it is not as a military leader, nor as an executive or diplomat. We t
think of the man who, by sheer force of character, held a divided and'
disorganized country together until victory was achieved, and who, after
peace was won, still held his disunited country by their love and respect
and admiration for himself, until a '·nation was }Velded into enduring
strength and unity. . .
.
..
· There were great patriots in America whose' names are inscribed in
the story of that time. There were many humble folk whose names have
faded from our histories and were never kn~wn outside their narrow village circle, who struggled and .suffer~d from the noblest motives. But war
bring's out the worst as well as the. best in men. It is a mistake to think
of the America of 1776-1783 as a nation.of patriots, pressing their services
to gain freedom. '. It was hard to get men into the army, and to keep them
there. Often Washington had. neither money, nor food, nor clothing to
offer them. But he always had an army, pitifully small as it was at times
which held the flag flying in _the field through love of him, and confidenc~
in the; character "'.hich they sensed in his dignifled presence.
Without him, the cause .would have been irretrievably lost, and the
~un~er . of the . orators would .have rumbled .long since into forgetfui
silence. When the days were blackest, men clung to his unfaltering courage as to the last firm ground in a rising flood. When, later the forces of
disunion in the new country seemed to ·threaten disrupti~n, men again
~allied to him as the solid bond of union. Legacy to America from these
troubled. years! he is, apart from independence itself, the noblest heritage
of all."

Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
For better or worse, another year in Masonry in this Jurisdiction
has become history. During this year general economic conditions
_h ave been precarious and unavoidably they have been reflected in
the experiences of our Lodges. For the first time in many years, if
not in the history of Grand Lodge, the repbrt of the Grand Secretary
shows a net loss in membership. A year ago we were one of only
eight jutisdictions in the country to report a net gain, and only' one
of t}le eight showed a larger net gain than our own; this year our net
loss approximates 1800. While such a report is depressing, our
Fraternity may well congratulate itself that under such extreme conditions our showing is as good as we find it. The spirit of our Lodges
is healthy; the needs of our Brethren have revivified our fraternal
spirit, our realization of human brotherhopd and interdependence has
been quickened, and time has been available for other than ritualistic
activities. I believe it safely can be said that Masonry is fundamentally stronger today than .during high water marks 'of membership
prosperity and financial affluence. During these times, as an organization, we may welt learn the lessons which most of us as individuals
have been compelled to study; the virtues of the simple life; the
interdependence of human relationships; the true relative values of
human aims and human accomplishments.
Much of the subject matter of this report already has been placed
before you. Approximately two months ago I forwarded to all
Lodges, all Inspectors and all interested committee men, the recommendations and decisions found in this report, so far as they were
available at that time. N ecessarity, additional decisions and recommendations have been made; nor was any attempt made to give
advance publicity to the general discussion of the events and problems of the year. Normally, the greater portion of Grand Lodge
action is grouped about the decisions and recommendations of the
Grand Master. Many of our members attend Grand Lodge at only
one communication. Even with previous experience, the large number present at any commu.nication prohibits adequate consideration
upon the floor of Grand Lodge, or during the four days of the commttnication. Much of the work is done in committee and advance
information is valuable to committee men themselves. To date I
have received much of commendation and,none of criticism for this
prqce.d ure; I hope that by reason of the plan the member s of Grand
Lodge will participate more intelligently in its deliberations and will
find greater pleasure and profit from their attendance; the results

Apportionment of Grand Lodge Work Among Grand Officers
The tremendous increase of members in our jurisdiction with
the corresponding multiplication of duties devolving upon the Grand
Master under the administratio·n of his office as heretofore conducted,
necessitates some radical revision of our executive system, and of the ·
relationship between the Grand officers and the constituent Lodges.
After consultation among the elective line officers, a solution of this
problem was attempted, which it is hoped will be found advantageous.
It relieves the situation, and if the plan meets the sympathetic cooperation of the Lodges, we believe that they will ultimately find
themselves better served through a division of labor than by an
ineffective attempt (at whatever personal sacrifice) on the part of
one man occupying the position of Grand Master to adequately
maintain contacts with all of the Lodges of the jurisdiction, while at
the same time attempting to adequately perform the executive duties
of his office. The following letter which was issued to the Lodges is
self explanatory.
"EXECUTIVE DISTRICTS FOR GRAND OFFICERS

To the Masters and Brethren of the Constituent Lodges
of This Jurisdiction:
The number of Lodges and Inspection Districts in the jurisdiction is now so large that it is impractical for any one man to establish
proper contacts with the officers and the Brethren. Even with his
entire time devoted to the office, the contacts are inadequate, nor is
it possible for every man who serves as Grand Master to wholly
neglect his personal affairs for a year. Changed conditions demand
development of our executive system; it is no longer advisable to
restrict the organization of our work to the forms which were sufficient in the early days of this Grand Lodge, nor is it to the interest
of the fraternity that the entire responsibility for executive work in
this jurisdiction between communications of Grand Lodge shall rest
upon one man.
Our Lodges come in immediate contact with their Inspectors,
and the organization and maintenance of Officers' Associations marks
substantial progress toward the development of a proper State-wide
organization; through this procedure the local work centers in the
Officers' Associations under the general direction of the Inspector,
who becomes responsible to the Lodges of his district not only for
ritualistic attainments but for guidance in the general conduct of
Masonic affairs.
The general situation has received the careful consideration of
th~ present Grand Lodge officers, and in line with the recommendation of Grand Master Ross at the 1931 communication, it has been
decided to sub-divide the State into three executive districts, one

Visitations
It has been a source of deep regret and personal loss that I have
been obliged to conform to the announcement, which I made a
year ago, that I could not hope to follow the example of several of
my predecessors in personally meeting the Brethren throughout the
jurisdiction. Whether I have found the executive duties of the position more exacting than they, oi: whether I have given to them undue
attention, I cannot say; I know that they have made far greater
demands for time than I anticipated or was forewarned. I have given
to the duties of the office the limit of time and strength, and it is my
only regret that more time could not have been found, and that the
duties of the office could not have been discharged more efficiently.
For reasons indicated elsewhere in this report, I firmly believe, however, that the loss through personal contact with the Brethren of
the jurisdiction is more a personal loss of the Grand Master than of
the Brethren; the greatest pleasure of the office is found in these
se.lf same personal contacts and friendships created or _renewed, but
I believe that the solution for effective administration is to be found
in a division of responsibility, and the dignifying of offices other than
that of the Grand Master. Except where conflicting engagements
prevented, I have endeavored to personally attend the more outstanding meetings of our Lodges, as well as the laying of cornerstones and other public ceremonies, and in addition to these occasions
I have made such additional visits as time· and circumstances permitted. A detailed enumeration would be neither of value nor of
interest to Grand Lodge.

Digest of Decisions
The questions which have been presented for consideration during
the past year have again demonstrated the value of the Digest which
was compiled by Past Grand Master Ross. Its comprehensive
. chara~er and facility for research materially lighten the labor of the
man who must answer a Masonic question. Independent investigation
for themselves by Lodge officers has been materially promoted, both
by ou.r Officers' Associations and by this pigest, but there remain
many officers who seem to be still unaware of its existence or wh.o,
if aware,' find it easier to write a letter than to consult an ind~x. The
duties of the executive officers of Grand Lodge ;tre exacting; perhaps
fifty per cent of the questions which are asked of the Grand Secretary
and the Grand Master are plainly covered by decisions in the Digest ;
fraternal courtesy demands that all letters receive a proper answer ;
a large amount of time is wasted in checking the citation for an answer
to questi~ns which should not be asked. Unfortunately, the Secretaries of our Lodges who, because of experience, should be the best
informed, and who are the natural custodians of the Constitution
and the Digest, are the most frequent offenders in this respect. There
have been several instances in which questions were asked .based
upon decisions appearing in antiquated editions of. the Constitution
and in complete disregard of both the later editions of the Constitution and the Digest which is now the authoritative recourse for Masonic law in California.

George Washington Bicentennial
Early in the year a committee was appointed to promote proper
participation by our Lodges in the fitting observance of the 200th
Anniversary of the Birth of George Washington. An independent
report will be filed by that committee, which speaks for itself. I believe that this anniversary has been very generally observed by our
Lodges, both directly and in co-operation with the general community
observance, and I feel that substantial credit is due to this committee
for the extent and mariner of its activities in this connection.
The dedication of the George Washington Memorial Monument
at. Washington, D. C., was attended by our Senior Grand Warden,
the Grand Secretary, Past Grand Master Boynton, who is a director
of the Association; Brother Jeffries, Chairman of the Finance Com-

Grand Masters' Conference
The dedication ~f the Me1J1orial was immediately preceded by
the annual conference of Grand Masters at Washington. The same
representatives from California were in attendance.' Gathering, as it
· did, representatives from all our jurisdictions, it was a most valuable
opportunity for exchange of views and discussion of problems, but
an even greater value lies in the personal contact with the officers
from the respec.tive jurisdictions, permitting not only fellowship and
common purpose, but ability to harmoniously and in a personal manner deal 'with the questions which arise among the jurisdictions.
Our Grand officers who have attended such a conference are unanipious in their recommendation of its desirability, and it is to be
hoped that no future Grand Master will fail to avail himself of the
opportunity to attend. The conference of Grand Secretaries, which
is held concurrently, is of equal advantage to our Grand Secretary,
and from the standpoint of personal contacts is of even greater
value than the conference of Grand Masters; a large proportion of
our interjurisdictional business is conducted through the Grand
Secretary, and normally these Grand Secretaries continue in office
from year to year. In this connection, I recommend that our own
Grand Secretary be requested to attend the 1933 conference, and that
a proper ~ppropriation be made to cover his expenses.

the services they rendered to mankind, have made their names an
ornament to our Order.

Washington was born in Virginia, who, through the greatness, the
splendour of his public action, and the virtue of his private life, is an
honour to his land, and has shown himself one of the greatest among
great men.
"As clever an administrator in peace time as he had been a brave
soldier during the war of Independence, he wisely and strongly
org:inized his country after he had liberated her from foreign dominat10n.
"His work once accomplished, as modest as he was distinguished,
he deliberately left the highest post in the Republic, to retire in the
simplest manner, among his family.
'

of abnegation, of d1smterestedness, of courage, of higher wisdom is to
be found?
"Therefore, we, Free Masons of the Gr~nd Orient de France
find our pride in the fact that one of the best who ever was among
us, the Brother Lafayette, has had the great honour to fight at his
side for the cause of Liberty.

3om the American Free Masons, m order to exalt our Illustrious

Public Schools Week
Our committee with its recurring efficiency has again promoted
the observance of Public Sch"ols Week. The detailed results will
appear in its own report. The efforts of this committee, ·and particularly of its chairman, and the time which is so generously given by
them to so worthy a purpose, deserve the deep appreciation of the
Fraternity throughout the jurisdiction; it is a ·public as well as a
~fasonic service.
In this connection consideration may well be given to the education which our children now receive. Education involves not only

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

21

the mental training which is afforded by a general school system,
but equally general preparation to meet the problems of life. It
has been well said that "an education is not worth very much which
teaches a child how to make a living but does not teach him how
to live." It is a well known fact that with the outstanding efficiency of
our public educational system, we nevertheless have in the United
States probably the highest percentage of juvenile crime found in
any country in the world. Nor are these juvenile criminals confined to
those of deficient education. An illustration of this is found in statistics recently issued by the Warden of Sing Sing Prison, in which
he states that 19%o/o of the 1931 admissions to the prison were high
school graduates, and that during the first fou; months in 1932 the
ratio rose to more than 25 o/o. It is obvious that these high school
graduates did not receive their training in a proper atmosphere, and
that their environment was not sufficiently conducive to the development of a proper attitude towards society. In our desire for the
separation of church and state, moral instruction has for practical
purposes been eliminated from the public schools; whether this
tendency is advantageous is a subject upon which there exists wide
diversity of opinion. There can, however, be no diversity of opinion
upon the fact that the combined means through which we give our
children an education, whether it be in the public school, at home
or through other existing channels for moral and religious training,
must be such as will inspire them with proper ideals, develop a
proper character and give to them the inherent integrity which will
make for upstanding manhood, good citizenship and the proper
relationship of man to his fellow-man. It is almost self-evident that
somewhere along the line we are inefficient ; a highly developed educational system and a maximum percentage of juvenile crime should not
go hand in hand. With our emphasis upon mental instruction in the
public schools and the maintenance of the public school system, we
may also well give earnest thought to the development of efficiency
and the proper channels for training for the denlopment of a high
type of character among the youth of today and the generations to
come. Whether in our own homes we maintain the proper example
and create the proper environment, whether the moral atmosphere
of our public schools and our higher educational institutions, is as it
should be, and whether our agencies for moral instruction are sufficiently fostered and emphasized, is a vital question for every man;
a question which calls for introspection as well as observation.
I have suggested that our present problems are not exclusively
material; neither are they solely local. We are prone to regard such
world movements as the Russian programs as primarily economic,
as a challenge to the primacy of the capitalistic system, and as of only
indirect and financial importance to ourselves. The standards of

2Z

men throughout the world and their effect upon human relationships
necessarily influence our own standards and both our moral and our
physical welfare. One illustration will suffice. The atheistic purposes
of the Soviet government are well known; many of us do not realize
that at this time Soviet atheistic propaganda is further reaching and
more effective than its commercial propaganda. The league of
fighting atheists is supported by the Soviet government. It has a
present membership of at least 5,000,000, and under a five-year plan
it is hoped to increase that membership to 17,000,000. Supporting
radio broadcasts are comprehensive and thirty-five anti-religious universities are furnishing instruction to active atheists. This league
supports kindred orgapizations in other countries; in Germany alone
it fosters leagues whose present membership is 850,000. The most
serious challenge from the movement is its effect upon the rising
generation. Neither argument nor illustration is required to demonstrate to any of us that all we have of human uplift, every decrease of
friction in the relationships among men and every step of permanent
mental and moral progress for the race, finds its source in belief in
an almighty a:nd all-wise God and in that progressive appreciation of
the will and purposes of the Divine Being which He has afforded to
us through diverse channels through the ages. Belief in God is the
bedrock upon which civilization rests, and systematic attack upon
that belief must be not lightly disregarded. An enlightened conception of the {:reator is as essential a part of the education of our youth
as the more direct form of mental instruction· for which we strive
today.
Unemployment · ·
All of our Lodges during the past year have felt the need for
assisting many of our members to obtain employment. It is not
necessary to recite the varying methods which have been pursued, nor
the varying degrees of success, depending partly upon conditions and
partly upon the energy which was devoted to the work. Through both
the efforts of Employment Bureaus and the efforts of individual
Lodge committees, much· has been done to relieve the situation.
Conditions and needs so greatly vary in different localities, that no
definite state program appeared advisable. Accordingly, the following
letter was issued to the Lodges upon the subject:
To the Masters and Brethren of the Constituent Lodges
of This Jurisdiction:
·
The most pressing and practical charity confronting our Lodges
today is the problem of unemployment. Our concern . is three-fold :
1. The need among our own number.
.2. General conditions in the community.
3. The effect upon both general business conditions and human
relationships.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

. 23

All Lodges are most strongly urged to appoint a competent and
energetic committee to undertake this responsibility if such a committee has not already been appointed.
Charitable purposes for which Lodge funds may be expended
are restricted to necessary relief for our own Brethren and their
families. ·Contributions from those funds cannot be made to general
community relief, nor should our members be solicited as Masons
for such general relief. Necessarily our primary effort is to be assured
that every member of the Lodge is adequately employed; to this end
a canvass should be made of the entire membership without waiting
for solicitation on behalf of a needy Brother. Both at Lodge meetings
and through individual contacts, an urgent appeal should be made to
members who are able to furnish or to assist in obtaining employment. A card index of the Lodge membership classifying the Brethren
in these respects will be of value.
As individuals, each Mason should discharge his responsibility
toward relieving the general unemployment situation. Particularly
in smaller communities, or.g anized general relief may well be conducted under the sponsorship of the Lodge if no general organization
already · has been effectel;l. In some instances our Lodge committees
have already successfully promoted one day a week and/or one day
a month employment movements, and this is only one illustration of
the manner in which a Lodge committee can properly foster relief
without expending Lodge funds and without solicitmg individual
contributions in the name of the Lodge.
The situation is urgent and promptness is imperative; it deserves
every Masonic effort; failure to meet it may bring appalling results;
pArticularly, it is our duty to assure every Mason reasonable employment if it can be made available through any source or by any effort.
Dated: February 10, 1932.
Fraternally yours,
.
.
ROBERT B. GAYLORD,
Grand Master.
Board of Control
As always, the report of the Board of Control will be of general
intere~t. Its work continues throughout the year and its efficiency
has been amply demonstrated. The adoption of uniform and businesslike procedure by our Boards of Relief is obviously desirable and the
Board of Control has contributed largely to present success. The
Boards of Relief cannot be too strongly urged to co-operate with the
Board of Control. It is also desirable that any delays in obtaining
reimbursement for expenses incurred should be promptly reported to
the Board of Control; delay always increases the difficulty of collection in any financial transaction and misunderstandings frequently
· are avoided by prompt action. Year by year since the organization
of the Board of Control there have been decreased requirements for
reimbursement by Grand Lodge, and it is a reasonable conclusion,
particularly at the present time, that this condition is due to the activities of the Board of Control. Insofar as these reductions are due to
more ltusiness-like methods and a larger percentage of direct reimbursement f ron'l other jurisdictions, too high praise cannot be given.

neither mechanical nor mercenary. Our charity funds are a trust and
must not be carelessly or extravagantly disbursed; conversely, no
worthy brother or his dependents should suffer by reason of technicalities, nor should worthy applicants to a Board of Relief be made
to feel that our charity is mechanical or grudgingly bestowed, or
that our sole purpose is to avoid the disbursement of charity funds.
The Board of Control in its activities necessarily emphasizes the
~ecessity for economy and business-like methods, particularly at a
time when demands are so numerous. Because of this function Boards
of Relief and other executive officers should not misconstrue the
purpose of the Board of Control or the ~xtent of Masonic charity.
Necessarily, cases will arise where immediate assistance in reasonable
amounts is essential to adequate relief of the situation, and good judgment must be exercised as well as business methods; this does not
me~n extravagance or carelessness, but it does mean the exemplification of brotherhood; our charity is brotherhood and not fraternal
insurance. In the face of adverse conditions and widespread want,
increased savings in reimbursement are, I am informed, shown this
year, while deficits normally would be expected. I have had no
opportunity to analyze the underlying occasion for such savi~s as
appear and, while praising without stint all increase in efficiency and
success in obtaining direct reimbursement, I feel that both the Boa.rd
of Control and our Boards of Relief should be sure during the coming
year that efficiency shall 'not degenerate. into niggardliness or evasion
of legitimate Masonic responsibility; if we must err, it should be on
t~e side of charity.
Issuance of Literature to Lodge Members
In the interest of tax reduction, petitions for three proposed
amendments to the San Francisco charter, providing for reductions
in salary of certain municipal employes, were recently circulated. A
number of the employes affected are members of the Order and in
several San Francisco Lodges circulars were issued, signed by members of the Lodge, and addressed officially to the members of the
Lodge generally. In the circ\llar it was stated that the adoption of
the amendments would result in salary reductions and would cause
direct financial loss to a specified number of the members of the
particular Lodge, the names of these members being listed in the
circular. This was followed by a statement that "aside from the injury
to these brothers" there were other objections to the amendments;
the circular then specifying three arguments against the amendments.
In conclusion the circular requested those to whom it was sent to
refrain from supporting the petitions and to withdraw their signatures if previously affixed. The letters were signed "Sincerely and
Fraternally Yours."

The highly improper character of these circulars is self evident,
but particular mention should be made of the following reasons:
1. The official Lodge roster was used as a mailing list. As elsewhere indicated in this report, the Lodge roster is not maintained for
such a purpose.
2. It is an appeal to Masons because of fraternal connection to
oppose pending political legislation upon the ground of the selfish
interest and financial loss of a few named members of the Lodge.
The attempt to use the Lodge roster and Lodge membership for
personal financial advantage is distinctly contrary to Masonic .principles. The circulars were inspired and issued through a group of
Masons in the Municipal employ who would be adversely affected
by the proposed legislation. ·
3. The appeal was an attempt to influence political action of
Lodge members because of Lodge affiliation, thereby endeavoring to
involve the Lodge in controversial politics. A sharp difference of
opinion existed among Lodge members as to the advisability of the
legislation and whether it was a legitimate measure for tax economy.
· Issuance of such a circular, with its misuse of Masonic affiliation
and Lodge rosters,' cannot be too strongly condemned. In some
instances the circulars were issued without the knowledge of Lodge
officers, while in others the Lodge officers either approved or participated, being themselves adversely affected by the proposed legislation.
Unfortunately, the issuance of the letter was not called to my
attention until too late to nullify its mischievous effect as applied to
the particular legislation. However, it is illustrative of repeated
attempts (sometimes thoughtless and sometimes intentional) to take
advantage of and misuse Lodge affiliations and Lodge rosters, and it
is not too late to call attention to the impropriety of such action. It
is a growing evil, and persistence in it necessarily will result in drastic
discipline if we are to maintain our ideals.

Masonic Homes Endowment
The ultimate goal for maintenance of our Homes is an adequate
endowment fund. The activities of past years have resulted in a substantial increase in endowment, and we are still reaping a harvest
of testamentary gifts. From a fund of $17,000.00 in 1910, the amount
grew to $718,000.00 in 1931, the greater portion of which accrued
from legacies. There are, however, tremendous future possibilities for
endowment which must not be neglected. While it is unlikely that,
in these times of stress, we can materially increase our endowment by
contributions of living donors, apd while in such a period it is almost
equally difficult to obtain additional testamentary provisions we
should at least seek to prevent loss of testamentary provisions already

Per Diem of Representatives
At the last communication of Grand Lodge, the question of revision of pay of members was deferred to the present communication.
It is inevitable that any satisfactory plan for revision will require
an increased appropriation by Grand Lodge. Whether it will reduce
the net cost to California Masonry through the elimination of direct
appropriations by our Lodges, is open to discussion. In any event,
the present condition of our treasury and our present sources of
revenue do not justify increased appropriations at this communication, and our policy should be retrenchment rather than increase. It
is to be hoped that the present stringency will further actuate our
Lodges to refrain from undue appropriations for expenses of attendance upon Grand Lodge; in any event, both the responsibility and the
remedy for excessive expense, if such there be, rests with the constituent Lodge. I feel that I have no alternative to recommending
that no action upon the subject be taken at this communication.
Reduction of Initiation Fees
Although no change in fees has been made by the great majo;ity
of our Lodges, nevertheless there has been a substantial tendency
to reduce the fees, evidenced by the number of Lodges which have
submitted amendments to l:iy-laws to that effect. While I have
uniformly approved these amendments, upon the theory that it is a
question which each Lodge must settle for itself, nevertheless unless
the circumstances are unusual, I believe it is a mistake for our Lodges
to reduce fees even during. the present financial stringency. The
reduction of fees tends to cheapen our Fraternity and in the long
run does not, I believe, result in any advantage to the particular
Lodge. Experience in the past in our own and its allied organizations
indicates that a reduction in fees tends to lower the stand'ard of
membership and ultimately has tended to even reduce the number
of petitioners. I do not believe that the man who will be deterred
from membership because of a small difference in initiation fee
sliould be encouraged to join the fraternity. In a modified sense
Masonic membership is ·a luxury, and no man should expend his

money for that purpose if the necessities of himself and his family
are such that a small difference in the original charge will prevent
his presenting a petition. Nor do I regard the present reduction in
the number of petitions as an evil. In our general average as an
organization in this jurisdiction we might better devote our attention
to digesting the membership which we already have, than to expend
our efforts to increase membership and devote our time to the mere
initiation of candidates. While the reduction in revenue may necessitate a corresponding reduction in expenditures, that also is not an
unmixed evil.
Nonpayment of Dues
The reports from Lodge~ indicate an alarming increase in the
number of suspensions for nonpayment of dues. As an illustration,
in one lodge having a membership of less than 250, the Secretary
rep.orted ten per cent of the membership suspended for this reason.
The seriousness of the situation is evident when we consider the
fact that the only brother who should be suspended is one who is
financially able to pay his dues but declines to do so. In the Lodge
in question three of those suspended were Past Masters. It is almost
inconceivable that, even under present conditions, ten per cent of
the membership fall. in the category of those who can but will not
pay their dues. Either proper efforts have not been made by the
committee on delinqu'ent dues or there is a woeful lack of Masonic
spirit in the membership of the Lodge, including its Past Masters.
I urge upon the brethren of the itJrisdiction their duty of loyalty to
our Fraternity in these times.. of stress, and I emphasize the importance
of the work of the committee on delinquent dues. No member should
be suspended until he has been personally interviewed by the comuiittee, and the situation presented to him in a fraternal spirit. Nor
should any brother be suspended unless, following an interview, the
committee is convinced that the delinquent brother is financially able
to pay. If a brother because of conditions or reverses is unable to
· pay either his dues should be remitted or he should be granted further
tim~, as circumstances dictate; he should not be suspended. Unless
there is the definite prospect within a reasonable time of ability to
pay, dues should be remitted rather than to grant extensions of time.
The difficulty with unreasonable extensions of time is that the
dues accumulate to such an amount that it is unlikely the brother
will ultimately pay the accumulated sum. The requirements of Sections 117 and 118 of the Constitution should be strictly observed,
but compliance with those sections does not necessarily result in
suspension for nonpayment. The sections grant the alternatives of
suspensions, remission of dues or extension of time for payment. I
particularly emphasize the further fact that under no circumstances
should the notice mentioned in Section 117 be sent to a brother untH

and in an earnest endeavor to arrange for the payment of his dues

Masonic Keys
From time to time through advertising circ;ulars and otherwise,
the attention of members of the craft is called to so-called keys or
books of instruction covering the secret work. It is self-evident that
the issuance of such publications is a violation of the oath and the
use of them is not only discountenanced, but prohibited.
Through lack of realization, our officers occasionally resort to
this assistance, for which reason I take this opportunity to remind
the craft in general that such use is prohibited and that all Masons
should discountenance any tendency to resort to, or encourage such
publications.

Decisions

I. Election by Ballot.
A question was presented. covering the rules governing election by
ballot in constituent Lodges and the form of the semi-annual report
of delinquencies which is to be made by the Secretary; a controversy
having arisen whether the Secretary by viva voce vote may be instructed
to cast the ballot and whether the Secretary's report of delinquents must
be publicly made known to the Lodge.
I replied that pursuant to decision of Grand Master Rucker (Ross'
Digest No. 593), Grand Lodge has ruled that the word "ballot" as
used in our constitution, means a secret vote by balls, cubes or slips of
paper; therefore, that when Section 135 prov·ides that officers of a Lodge
shall be·elected "by ballot," this must be a secret ballot and cannot be
by acclamation or by instructing the Secretary to cast the ballot pursuant
to a show of hands or a call for ayes and noes. In some instances this
procedure may appear cumbersome, but it appears to be the law.
As. to the Secretary's report of delinquents, I gave it as my opinion
that this report must be orally< announced to the Lodge unless by appro·
priate action of the Lodge the report is filed waiving oral presentation.
In common acceptation, a matter is not "reported" to a Lodge by merely
filing a written report which is in no way made known to the Lodge.
On the other hand, I call attention to the fact that under decision reported
in Section 143 of the Digest, this report may be presented orally without
a written report for permanent filing.

30

In this connection I call attention to the fact that the same language
regarding procedure for electing officers "by ballot" is found in Section
17, governing, the election of Grand Lodge officers, as appears in Section
135, relating to constituent Lodges. If the present ruling is approved
by Grand Lodge, either Section 17 should be so amended as to obviate
the necessity for secret ballot on the elective officers, or Grand Lodge
should hereafter be prepared to obey its own rules and modify its present
custom of dispensing with the secret ballot as applied to all officers
other than the Junior Grand Warden.
It is no answer to say that in the
absence of objection the secret ballot may be waived, unless we are willing to apply the same construction to the identical language governing
constituent Lodges, thereby giving them a similar right to waive the
secret ballot. The ruling of Past Grand Master Rucker appears to directly controvert such a rule.

The, Master elect of Delta Lodge No. 47i, received his certificate
of qualification but was unable to present himself for installation" because
of illness which apparently might prove chronic. In reply to questions

regarding the election and installation of a Master, I stated:
1. That under Section 135 of the Constitution the present Master
·
continues in office until his successor is elected and i~stalled.
2. That by analogy with Section 139 of the Constitution, the failure
of the Master to present himself for installation is the equiv.alent of
failure to obtain a certificate of qualification,' and that if he has not
presented himself for installation within sixty days from election, the
Lodge might declare the election vacated and petition for a dispensation
to elect a Master.
3. That in its discretion the Lodge might temporarily defer declaring
the office vacant and requesting the dispensation if it appeared that the
Master elect could and desired to assume his duties within a reasonable
time, "but that the Lodge should not contipue indefinitely vyithout a
regularly elected Master. '
4. In response to the question as to the status of the Wardens, I
stated that unless one of them were elected to the position of Master,
they would continue to serve in the offices in which they were installed
until the close of the year; all officers other than the Master · having
been regularly installed.

VI. Avouchment.

-AOne of our Officers Associations inquired whether for the purpose
of vouching for a brother or for coaching .a candidate at the request
of a Lodge of which the coaching brother was ~ot a member, a torn
letter of identification can be used, one part of the letter being given
to the party to whom the avouchment is given and the other to the
brother or candidate for whom the avouchment is made. The essence of this question is whether avouchment must be transmitted
orally or whether a written communication is sufficient. I have
been unable to find any decision upon the question in this jurisdiction.
In principle there is no essential necessity for an oral communication if the written avouchment is sufficiently identified. Necessarily,
the vouching brother must be personally known by and identified
to the brother to whom the assurance is given, and such means of
communication must be adopted as will insure against possibility
of mistake or fraud. Mere possession of a fragment of a letter of
itself necessarily is insufficient, as the letter may 'be lost or stolen
and used by some person other than the one to whom it was delivered. However, if the identity of the person bearing the portion
of the letter is established there is no inherent objection to vouching
for a brother by written communication as well as by word of mouth.
Under such circumstances the identity can be established through
any of the customary methods, including signature, place of residence, business affiliations or other proper means of identification,
although care must be exercised to establish identification beyond
possibility of mistake.
As concerns avouchment among Masons as individuals the question is settled by Section .125 of the Constitution, which permits
such avouchment by one brother to another for a third brother, "all
three being present." This language precludes transmitted written
communications. The language does not in terms, however, apply
to a written avouchment addressed to the Master of the Lodge.
Doubtless the constitutional provision was enacted because of the
danger of careless identification unless all three brethren are per-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

sonally present at the time of avouchment. The objection does not
apply with the same force to a written avouchment forwarded to the
Master of a Lodge, and the Constitution does not in terms prohibit
such written avouchment. I accordingly ruled:
1. That no avouchment is sufficient among Masons in their individual capacity unless all three parties concerned are present at the
time.
2. That if uncontrovertible evidence of identity is presented and
if the vouching brother is personally known to the Master of the
Lodge, a written communication by the vouching brother to the
Master of the Lodge is not prohibited by the Constitution and therefore is sufficient.
I am moved to rule formally and to this effect because of the
lack of discussion of the subject matter · in our decisions and the
frequency with which analogous questions are presented.

-BA brother received his first degree in a California Lodge and
subsequently received his second and third degrees in other Lodges
at the request of the California· Lodge. He subsequently dimitted to
another California Lodge and \n the meantime had never sat in
his own original Lodge as a Master Mason, although per the usual
certificate his name had been entered as a member of the Lodge, and
a dimit was issued to him in due course. He subsequently desired
to visit the original Lodge and the question arose whether his membership coupled with identification was a sufficient avouchment or
whether an examination was necessary.
I ruled that no examination was necessary if it appeared in the
usual manner that he was in good standing in the Lodge to which
he had dimitted. A Lodge should certainly take official notice of
its own membership if the identity of the member is established, even
though at the time no one is present who has sat in Lodge with the
brother. If the certificate that the degrees have been conferred by
request in another Lodge is sufficient to justify the entry of the
brother's name ·as a member of the original· Lodge, equally it should
be sufficient to establish his standing as a Master Mason as of that
date.

death of the Lodge in which he was elected. The law seems clear
that membership in his original Lodge terminated with the Issuance
of. the dimit (Ross Digest, 2d Ed., Section 102). It is true that
Section 161 of the Constitution recites that "at the stated meeting
at which the dimit is presented the Secretary shall enter the applicant's name as a member of the Lodge." On its face this implies
that membership is not acquired until the dimit is presented at the
stated meeting of the Lodge to which the brother is elected. However, he loses his membership in his original Lodge upon the issuance of the dimit and it is inconceivable that it is the purpose of
the section to leave a brother, who died under the circumstances
above recited, in a situation in which he is not a member of either
Lodge. The purpose of the section, is to permit a brother to maintain membership in one Lodge until he acquires membership in another. His connection with the original Lodge terminates with the
issuance of the dimit and he has been elected in another Lodge; the
only reasonable construction of the section in the light of its purpose
seems to be that notwithstanding the language of the section the
brother becomes a member of the Lodge to which he has been
elected coincidentally with the issuance of the dimit by the original
Lodge. While not necessary for the decision of the present question
apparently the change in membership occurs at the time the request
for dimit is presented to the original Lodge ; the rule being that membership terminates upon presentation of a request for a dimit. (See
Section 102 above cited from Ross Digest.)

VI II. Automatic Expulsion.

-ASection 192 of the Constitution conditionally provides for automatic expulsion of a brother who shall suffer a final judgment of
conviction of a felony "and be imprisoned in pursuance thereof."
The question has been raised whether conviction immediately followed by release on probation satisfies this requirement. In one
instance the brother was convicted in Nevada of bank robbery, which
carries capital punishment, and in another instance the brother was
convicted of embezzling county funds. In both cases probation immediately followed conviction.
·

38

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The provision of our law requiring imprisonment as a condition
to automatic expulsion indicates that the constructive confinement
incident to probation does not satisfy its requirements. Except.
in the remote contingency of a pardon concurrently with conviction
final conviction necessarily results in either release on bail, release
on probation or imprisonment. If it were intended that the constructive confinement incident to probation or release on bail shall
permit automatic expulsion, then the reference in the law to imprisonment is superfluous. It is a settled rule o.f construction that
unless necessary to do so, no provision will be disregarded as meanirigless; I therefore advised that in my opinion the phrase "imprisoned in pursuance . thereoP' must be literally construed and that
unless conviction is followed by actual imprisonment the provisions
for automatic expulsion do not applt.'

by the Junior Warden under instructions from the Master. Under
such circumstances I have designated a Past Master to preside, but
I call the attention of our Lodges to the fact that there is no occasion
for the Master to direct the filing of charges. Both under Section
192 and under Section 189 it is the official duty of ,the Junior Warden
to prefer charges and there should be no necessity for instructions
from the Master. Of course, if a Junior Warden neglects his duty
in this respect it is incumbent on the Master to direc·t the filing of
the charges; however, the Junior Warden should act without the
necessity for special instructions.

-BA member of one of our Lodges was convicted of a felony, whereupon the court made an order that the "proceedings be suspended
and the defendant granted probation for a period of six years" under
condition that the first three years of that period be spent at the
county road camp, a part of the county penal system. The question
was asked whether this constitutes imprisonment following conviction within the meaning of tne pro\risions of Section 192 of the Constitution governing automatic_expulsion.
I replied that in my opinion the brother is subject to automatic
expulsion. Section 192 does not in te;ms provide that time shall
be served as a part of the sentence following the conviction· the
requirement being that he shall be imprisoned "in pursuance" of the
conviction. I see no distinction between imprisonment as an incident to sentence following conviction and imprisonment for a shorter
period in the county institution as a ccindition to probation. In
both cases the imprisonment is pursuant to the conviction and incident to the conviction and arises from the conviction. Our courts
have held that confinement in a road camp is imprisonment within
the meaning of the penal sections governing escape, which seems
to settle the question that the work at the road camp constitutes
imprisonment. The court evidently regarded the . road camp confinement as imprisonment; the order recites that modification of the
probation will be considered if the defendant shows a good record
after serving twenty months in the county jail.

X. Criminal Conviction as Evidence at Masonic Trials.
On several occasions the question has been presented whether the
certified record of final conviction in a criminal proceeding is prima
facie evidence in a Masonic t r ia l of guilt of the offense covered by
the criminal proceedings. Section 202 of the Constitution provides
for the use of transcripts of court tes•t imony and Section 192 covers
automatic expulsion, but I find no provision dealing with the use
of the record of conviction alone as a prima facie case in an ordinary
Masonic trial. In the report of the Grievance Committee, found
in Section 527 of Ross' Digest, it is held that such a record is not
evidence prior to its becoming final, but the report, except through
possible implication, does not determine the question now presented.
As the review of trial records goes to the Grievance Committee
I did not feel that I had authority to officially express an opinion.
Common sense dictates that such a conviction should constitute
prima facie proof, but -there are technical reasons which throw doubt
upon the subject, accentuated by our rule that in Masonic trials we
are not concluded by the determination of courts of the land.
Accordingly, I recommend that the Jurisprudence Committee
.consider this question and, if after deliberation, doubt exists in the
minds of the Committee as to the sufficiency of such a record of final
conviction to establish a prima facie case, that the Committee frame
appropriate legislation making it prima facie evidence of the commission of the crime involved. Whether the commission of that
crime constitutes a Masonic offense necessarily is for consideration
by the Masonic tribunal and the prima facie case afforded by the
record of conviction is subject to rebuttal; but the establishment
of such a rule will frequently save unnecessary expense to our
Lodges and in the interest of certainty there should be a definite
ruling upon the point.
XI. Penal Jurisdiction Following Suspension.
A brother suspended for non-payment of dues by one of the Hawaiian Lodges is alleged to have defrauded other Lodges by obtain-

ing loans and cashing worthless checks. He is not within the
territorial jurisdiction of the Lodge and the question was asked
whether the Lodge retained jurisdiction to try him on charges which
might be preferred or whether under Section 188 penal jurisdiction
is limited to the Lodge within whose jurisdiction he now resides.
I replied that in my opinion the restriction upon penal jurisdiction of a Mason who has been suspended "for cause" does not apply
to a Mason who has been suspended for non-payment of dues and
that the Lodge from which he was suspended retains penal jurisdiction.
The decision of Grand Master Curtis reported as No. 505 in our
Digest of Decisions and Regulations differentiates between suspension for non-payment of dues and suspension for cause and implies
that a suspension for non-payment of dues is not a tuspension for
cause within the meaning of the law. Section 188, after referring
to suspension for non-payment of dues, refers specifically in the last
sentence to suspension for cause, indicating upon .t he face of the
section that there is a distinction between the two and that suspension for non-payment of dues is not a suspension for cause within
the meaning of the section.

XII. Master's Discretion in Proceeding to Trial of Charges.
Charges were presented to the Master of a Lodge which, although informally drawn, undoubtedly upon their face sufficiently
charged the character of the offense, namely, illicit relations with
the accuser's wife.
With commendable conscientiousness the Master investigated
the circumstances of the case at great length and from numerous
sources; his ultimate conclusion being that the accuser was mistaken
in believing that impropriety existed. Investigations indicated that
the accuser was somewhat erratic and that he had previously made
similar charges without due justification. Because of this the Master desired to disregard the charges. Independently of the possibility of a mistaken conclusion on the part of the Master in so
serious a situation it is my view that if charges are presented, which
upon their face are sufficient, no jurisdiction exists on the part of
the Master to investigate the supporting evidence or to reject the
charges because in his opinion they cannot or will not be proven.
If charges, which are sufficient upoh their face, are presented by a
Master Mason in good standing, he is entitled to a trial of the
charge regardless of the opinion of anyone, and neither the Master
nor any committee appointed by the Master is authorized to go
behind them. My attention has been called to several instances in
which the Master appointed investigating committees; this, I believe,

•

is wholly without authority and constitutes a disclosure by the Ma~­
ter which at least technically violates our law. The accuser is
en;itled to have a duly elected commission pass upon the sufficiency
of such evidence as he may present in support of the charges, and
neither the Master nor anyone else except the trial commission can
go behind the support which the signature of the accuser gives. to
the suffidency of the accuser's reasons and grounds for preferring
the particular charges.

XIII. Trial Postponement Pending Civil Action.
The Master of a Lodge handed me for consideration charges
which have been presented to him in which the accuser charged the
accused with seducing and over a considerable period of time violating the chastity of ·t he accuser's wife. The Master stated that
the accuser admittedly intends to make the subject matter of these
charges a subject also for civil action; that the Master suggest~d
the postponement of a Masonic trial pending the result of the trial
in the civil courts, but that the accuser objects to the postponeme?t
on the ground that "he did not consider he would be able to obtam
justice in a civil action prior to a Masonic trial." The Master inquired whether he is obligated to proceed wi·th the trial.
I re~lied that while the Master is undoubtedly. obligated to. accept
the charges and while our law does not specifically provide for
postponement of the Masonic trial under such circumstances, nevertheless that in my opinion the spirit of our law contemplates deferring of Masonic trials under such circumstances; that in view of the
avowed purpose of the accuser to institute civil proceedings the
Master is justified in postponing the calling of a meeting to elect
commissioners under Section 193 until the trial in the courts of the
land has been determined, or until it shalt appear that such a c~vil
trial is not contemplated. This conforms to the purpose which
underlies the provision of the first sentence in Section 192. I also
called the Master's attention to the fact that no Mason is entitled
to use Masonic trial procedure for the purpose of obtaining evidence
to be used in a subsequent civil action.

Particularly under present economic condition~ the question of

be revised.

that while disbursements for charity must be made in a spirit of

due regard for present and prospective requirements of other members of the Lodge. Accordingly I advised in this case that the
charity to be extended must be determined in the light of the resources of the Lodge and the present and prospective requirements

the Lodge to . determine for itself what can and should be done, having due regard to the fraternal spirit upon which our organization

unreasonable expenditures be made for his benefit, nor can he dictate
to the Lodge the amount of its charity r1or the manner in which

XX!. Delinquent Dues of Expelled Mason.

termination of membership. When the brother is restored to membership by action of Grand Lodge under Section 211, he is restored
"to the ·r ights and privileges of Masonry," except that his membership in the particular Lodge is not reinstated. The restoration operates as a new membership following a complete severance and I

XXII. Refreshment Fund.
One of our Lodges inquired whether in computing the amount
of the twenty per cent fund available for refreshment and the promotion of fraternal intercourse, under Section 89, Grand Lodge dues
or fees must first be deducted, or whether computation is made upon
the gross income.
I replied that in my opinion there is available for this fund twenty
per cent of the revenue without first deducting Grand Lodge per
capita, whether the per capita be paid for the Masonic Homes or
other G_rand Lodge purposes, but that in computing the revenue of
the Lodge the sum of $25 paid by each candidate for the benefit of
the Homes is not a part of the revenue of the Lodge. Section 89
prescribes that "twenty per cent of the total revenue" is available.
On the other hand, Subdivision · 1 of Section 41 prescribes that the
payment of $25 shall be collected directly from the petitioner for the
use and benefit of the Homes; in fact, the Lodge acts as an agent
for Grand Lodge in collecting this sum of $25 from the petitioner.
Apparently it is not contemplated tha·t the amount should be a part
of the revenue of the Lodge as such; on the other hand, the per
capita tax is paid from the general funds of the Lodge.

XX V . Corner Stones.
An invitation was extended to lay, during Public Schools Week,
the corner stone of a grammar school building. It appeared, however, that the building has been occupied as a school for several
months although the corner stone has n-0t been set, the statement
being made that "it was deemed advisable to wait for an auspicious
moment before so doing."
In the light of precedents established by previous Grand Masters
and in conformity with Masonic tradition, I felt obliged to decline
the invitation, although I did so with regret because of the appr?priateness of the occasion. Properly a corner stone should be laid
as a part of the foundation and before any portion of the walls has
been reared and this fact should be well known to the craft. Because of th~ recently increasing tendency to request the laying of
corner stones for buildings when the steel framework is up, or a substantial portion of the walls is in place, or even when the building
is substantially or entirely completed, I call the matter to the attention of Grand Lodge.
W hile Grand Masters in the past · have
sometimes shut their eyes to a partial erection of ·t he building I
know of no instance in which the corner stone of a completed and
occupied building has been laid by Grand Lodge. The ceremony
is far more significant if the corner stone is laid at the proper t ime,
when no portion ·of the building other than founda tion is in place,
and it is as easy to arrange for the laying of the corner stone at this
stage of the building instead of a later period in the construction.

XXVI. Degree Teams.
Substantial differences of opinion exist in the jurisdiction
to
the efficiency and advisability of so-called degree teams, and in . rde.r
that there may be some declaration of policy upon the part of Grand
Lodge, I shall as a ruling briefly outline my views upon the subject.
Ritualistic perfection is essential to successful Lodge activity, but
at best it is a means to an end, and the vital factor in all Lodge work
is the interest of the individual Mason. If, and to the extertt that a
degree team legitimately promotes general interest and increases
.
attendance, it is a valuable contribution, provided:
1. Work shall be conferred by a degree team at the request of •·
the Master and not at the solicitation of the team or its representative. I am told that there are instances in which teams have
practically insisted upon their right to confer the degree. The responsibility for the work of each Lodge rests upon the Master, and 1
whether a team shall serve or not rests in his arbitrary discretion.
Any team which presumes to dictate or to attem.pt to unduly influence a Master should be summarily disbanded.
Z. Conferring of degrees by a degree team should be an exceptional event; primarily it is the function of the officers of the Lodge
to fi 11 the chairs.
3. Only an efficient degree team should be permitted to act. In
this respect the responsibility rests with the Master, and he should
not request or permit a team to serve without first obtaining reliable
assurance of its efficiency. Because of the exceptional character of
the occasion on which the degree team is used, its work should be
more, rather than less, efficient than the work of the regular officers.
4. It is an indispensable condition that the work of the degree
team in both sections of the third degree shall be conducted in a
dignified manner consistent with the high purposes ef Masonry and
the impression which the degree is designed to create in the mind of
the candidate. Too frequently, on the part of both degree teams and
regular officers, there is a tendency to make light of one section of
this degree, thereby depriving the candidate of the noble teachings
which that section is designed to exemplify.
'XXVII. Uniform Code of By-Laws.

-AOne of our Lodges presented for approval an amendment to its
by-laws dispensing generally with affiliation fees, but providing that
the fee should be $50.00 if the application were based upon a dimit
from the Lodge in question. The letter accompanying the amend-

· GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
