ment disclosed that the dues of that Lodge are high and are found
burdensome under present financial conditions. Many of the members are taking dimits with the avowed intention of subsequently
reapplying for membership if the dues are reduced and/or when
financial conditions improve. The brethren of the Lodge regarded
this as an injustice to those who continued their membership in the
Lodge, notwithstanding present hardships. I felt obliged to rul~ that
the Uniform Code of By-Laws is inflexible, and that there 1s no

Because of my opinion that the Uniform Code of By-Laws is
inflexible, I similarly disapproved an amendment whereby one affiliation fee is charged for members from this jurisdiction and a different and larger fee for members affiliating from other jurisdictions.
Frequently, amendments have been presented in which there were
minor departures from the language of the Uniform Code, but without changing the meaning. In each instance I have required that the
amendment conform to the Code. It is my understanding that the
language of the Uniform Code is inflexible to the dotting of an "i"
and the crossing of a "t," and that the only discretion allowed to
Lodges is the literal one of making appropriate insertions in the
blanks found in the Uniform Code. In this connection, I call attention to the carelessness of many Secretaries. With few exceptions,
it was the evident intent of the Secretary to follow the language of
the Code, but I think it is a conservative estimate to say that in fifty
per cent of the amendments which were presented for approval, there
were departures from the Code either by paraphrasing expressions
or by omitting or adding words without changing the meaning. It
does not seem uncharitable to say that no brother is competent to
act as Secretary of a Lodge who is unable to at least copy without
mistakes ~ single paragraph from the Uniform Code.

dues quarterly in advance on the first day of January, April, July
and October, many of our Lodges formally amended their By-Laws
and forwarded a certificate of amendment for approval by the Grand
Master.

for subordinate Lodges. In 1911 Grand Master Weller held that it

One of our Boards of Relief, whose claim for a substantial amount

in California. The widow was over ninety years of age and, prior
to her death, expressed a wish that her remains be cremated and the
ashes deposited in her husband's grave. .Prior to her death, the
Eastern Lodge refused to authorize any charity, apparently because
she received a small pension and was able to live in a little home which
is mortgaged for its full value. Col!ditions immediately prior to her
death became so critical that the amount was insufficient and at the
last the local Board of Relief advanced approximately $75.00 for
necessary assistance, which the Eastern Lodge refused to either
authorize or reim.burse. That Lodge also declined to authorize funeral expenses. The Board of Relief was unwilling to bear the expense without assurance of reimbursement through the Board of
Control, although the amount was only about $75.00 above embalming
expense already incurred. I was unable to find any authority for the
payment of funeral expenses under these circumstances. The obligation to bury a Mason in good standing seems clear, although he
belongs in anoth'er jurisdiction and that jurisdiction refuses to pay;
equally, we are obligated to assist his widow during her lifetime.

XXIX. Conferring of Degrees in Nevada by a California Lodge Upon
Its Own Candidate.
One of our Lodges requested permission to confer a third degree
on one of its own members in the hall of a Nevada Lodge pursuant
to invitation from the latter Lodge. I replied that no Lodge can
meet outside of its own Lodge room, but that I saw no objection
to the officers, as individuals, attending a meeting of a recognized
Lodge in Nevada and, if requested by the Master of that Lodge to
act, conferring a degree in that Lodge; the meeting, however, being
a meeting of the Nevada Lodge. I also advised that the only procedure by which the degree at that meeting could be conferred on a
Fellow-Craft belonging to a California Lodge was through formal
action by the California Lodge requesting the Nevada Lodge to
confer the degree, that request to be transmitted through the Grand
Master or the Grand Secretary of this jurisdiction to the Grand
Master of Nevada. The language of Section 155 of the constitution
permitting the conferring of the third degree on a California candidate in "another Lodge" is not restricted to another Lodge in this
jurisdiction; being general in its form. I see no reason for not
applying it to a Lodge in another jurisdiction. Nor does the section
restrict the reasons for the request to residents in the other jurisdiction or other analogous causes. Whether the reason for the request
is sufficient is a question to be determined by the respective Grand
Masters when the situation is presented. While Section 155 does
not in terms require that the request from a Lodge of this jurisdiction
to a Lodge of another jurisdiction shall be transmitted through the
Grand Master . or the Grand Secretary of this jurisdiction, the fact
that requests from another jurisdiction must come through its Grand
Master or Grand Secretary to the Grand Master or Grand Secretary
of this jurisdiction, implies that this is the proper procedure.

Recommendations

I. Educational Committee.
The matter of Masonic education was left in the hands of the Grand
Master for investigation, a contingent appropriation being provided.
During the year no committee has been appointed, nor has active educational work been undertaken, except that a special committee has
been appointed to foster the celebration of the George Washington
Bicentennial in this jurisdiction, the expense of that committee being
borne by the appropriation last mentioned. I have refrained from
further action, partly from motives of economy and partly through
uncertainty as to a procedure whose results would justify further
investment of our funds.
Proper Masonic education is a critical question and a crying need,
but the means to be adopted and the educational lines to be followed
are subjects of widespread diversity of opinion. That through the
years gone by we have neglected the cultivation through education of
a fraternal and progressive spirit upon the part of our L\:idges, seems
self-evident. If we had expended upon these activities a tithe of the
money and energy which during my Masonic memory have been devoted to the perfection of the ritual, we would not today, I believe, be
concerned either with lack of interest in our Lodges or with a problem
of Masonic education. I have no criticism to offer for development of
the ritual, but the ritual at best is only a means to an end, and should
constitute only a minor consideration in our Masonic activities.
Lodges cannot live for ritual, nor will our membership attend for
ritual, nor will ritual alone accomplish the mission of Masonry. Unless we can retain the fraternal spirit and the lively interest which
characterized our early brethren and the meetings of our earlier
Lodges, then the usefulness of Masonry has terminated. While I have
given considerable thought to the subject, I do not feel justified in
making concrete recommendations. I am, however, convinced that
the only satisfactory procedure, if any, for Grand Lodge activity in
this respect, is the appointment of a salaried Grand Lodge representative who will devote his entire time to this work in the same manner
in which the ritual is so splendidly perfected and maintained by our
present Grand Lecturer. I am inclined to the view that it should be
the work of this representative not to lecture to our Lodges or to give
instruction, but to devote his time to the promotion of independent
efforts on the part of OU(' Lodges, in the same manner in which my
predecessor Grand Masters have cultivated interest in officers' associations. The man who can properly fill such a position is not easy to
find, and it would be better that Grand Lodge do nothing for five

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

53

years than that we should prematurely select a man who is not fitted
to the task; a task which I believe presents the greatest problem of
modern Masonry.
I recommend that a committee of not less than three nor more than
five be appointed by the incoming Grand Master to study this question,
and to report its conclusions at the next communication of Grand
Lodge, either in such general form or expressed in such con~rete
legislation as the committee may deem advisable. If the committee
reaches the conclusion that there should be a full time paid representative of Grand Lodge to handle this activity, and if through its investigations it has come in contact with a man whom it believes
competent to discharge that duty, I recommend that the committee,
in conjunction with its report, nominate the man of its choice. I feel
that the permanent work should be handled through some committee
and that flexibility of administration should be obtained by making
this position appointive through a committee rather than elective
through Grand Lodge. An elective official of normal personality, who
occupies office for a number of successive years, inevitably gains the
confidence and love of his brethren. It is conceivable that in the course
of years it would be to the interest of Grand Lodge that a change in
office be made. The difficulty of such a change in an elective office
is obvious and for that reason I believe that efficiency will be promoted thr~ugh an appointive officer coming under the jurisdiction of
a committee either appointed by the Grand Master or consisting of
the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master and the Grand Wardens.
My views in this respect are strengthened by the fact that for a few
years at least the work necessarily will be experimental, mistakes may
be made in the selection of a representative, and the greatest freedom
should be permitted during the experimental stage to obtain the best
man qualified for the undertaking.

III. Finl)ncial Conditions.
During the past year Grand Lodge itself has suffered from reduced
revenue and increased demands, and during the coming year there
should be such further retrenchment as is reasonably possible. · Retrenchment is desirable, not only because of our own financial situation, but as an object lesson to our Lodges. Many of them are in a
precarious situation, and at least some of them have not administered
their funds as carefully as they might. Expenses should be budgeted,
income should be conserved, and the present situation should be used
as an opportunity to place the administration of all our Lodges on a
sound financial basis. Notwithstanding Grand Loqge deficits, it is to
be hoped that it will not be necessary to increase our per capita tax.
Of all our work, our Homes have suffered the most severely from loss
of revenue; to relieve that situation, I recommend that the per capita
tax, which normally is credited to the building fund, be transferred at
least for the coming year to general maintenance o( the Homes, as I
feel that the avoidance of unnecessary hardsh~ upon the Lodges under
present conditions is more important than the addition to the building
fund. If, upon a review of the financial situation by the Finance Committee, it shall be found that the entire amount of this fifty cents per
capita is not required for this purpose, the amount withheld from the
building fund can be modified accordingly.

From time to time applications are made for Grand Lodge relief,

occasion the relief has been provided through the Masonic Homes, and
special provision has been made for the relief of tuberculosis cases.
Without formal authority, I appointed a committee which has handled

State, and in both sections linked it to both the work of the Masonic

V. Life Membership Funds
An attempt has been made through legislation to control the investment of life membership funds, but' there is an' ever present
danger of diversion or expenditure of these funds th~ough lax~tr or
ill advised investment or lack of proper records. Durmg my vlSlt to
the conference of Grand Masters at Washington, I learned from the
Grand Master of Oregon of legislation recently adopted in that State
at his suggestion, and which I believe might well be followed in California. Briefly stated, all life membership funds are held in custody
by Grand Lodge, investment being made through a special ~ommitt~e
appointed for that purpose. Each Lodge holds a pro rata interest m
the total fund, depending upon the amount of life membership moneys
held by Grand Lodge in trust for the particular Lodge. The Lodge
exercises no control over the fund, but regularly receives its proportion of the income. I can see no objection to this procedure, and it
possesses many obvious advantages. Through an investment of so
large a sum, distribution of investment is possible, which can not be
accomplished through investment by the individual Lodge. Investment being handled by a general committee of men experienced in
financial affairs there is greater assurance of secure investment than
if the investme~t is made directly by local Lodges whose officers in
many instances are not skilled in financial affairs. The plan eliminates
possibility of diversion of the fund ~y the ~o~al Lodge,. :Whether
through expenditure or investment m proh1b1ted securities, ~d
whether the possibility of diversion exists in carelessness, finan~ial
pressure upon the Lodge, lack of sufficient information or otherwise.
I recommend that legislation be enacted for the creation of such a
committee requiring that all life membership funds now held by
Lodges be' transmitted to the committee, and that all future life membership payments be forwarded immediately to the committee when
received. While not an essential part of the recommendation, it may
well be found advisable to provide for a special, adequately bonded
Treasurer for this committee so that no fear may exist of commingling
of these funds with other Grand Lodge funds. If the Treasurer of

Grand Lodge acts as Treasurer for these funds, they should be kept
scrupulously segregated from other funds, and fidelity in connection
with them should be covered by an independent bond.

VI. Investment of Life Membership Funds.
Section 129 of the Constituti~n provides that life membership funds
shall be "invested in securities legal for Savings Banks under the laws
of the State o.f California and the Territory of Hawaii." The history
of the provision is that an amendment was proposed which referred
to Savings Bank investments under California law; at the time the
amendment was adopted the point was raised that Hawaiian Lodges
should be authorized to invest in securities which are legal for Savings
Banks in the Hawaiian Islands and the amendment from the floor was
adopted in its present language. Undoubtedly it was the intent of
Grand Lodge that securities which are legal investments for Savings
Banks either in California or the Islands shall be acceptable, but a
literal construction of the existing language would limit investments
to securities which are legal in both jurisdictions, eliminating securities which are recognized under the laws of only one of the two named
jurisdictions.
For the purpo~e of practicaf results and because of the history of
the legislation, I have advised Lodges that they are justified in investing these funds in securities which are legal either under the laws of
California or under the laws of the Territory of Hawaii. In the interest
of future clarity, however, I recommend that the clause be amended
to read "invested in securities legal for Savings Banks under either the
laws of the State of California or the laws of the Territory of Hawaii."
If desired, the change can be so worded that Hawaiian Lodges are
regulated by the laws of Hawaii and California Lodges by the laws
of California, but such a provision is somewhat cumbersome and to my
mind is not essential.

One of the brothers who received a fifty year button during the
past year suggested that through action of Grand Lodge all brethren
who are .qualified to receive fifty year buttons be exempted from paying dues to their Lodge and be correspondingly omitted in computing
payments accruing from their Lodge to Grand Lodge.
He recited the fact that many Lodges remit the dues of older members who are unable to pay, but that such action savors of charity
which should be avoided. He feels that because of the advanced
years of such members no unreasonable burden would be imposed
upon our Lodges thereby.

VIII. Addresses on Stationery.
The stationery provided for Inspectors bears only the title of Grand
Lodge and the number of the Inspection District. Unless the Inspector in each instance is sufficiently thoughtful to append his address,
the party with whom he corresponds is obliged to locate the address
through other sources before replying. The expense of printing an
address is small !Ind I recommend that the Inspector's name and
address be supplied on his stationery.
In this connection I call the attention of the officers of Lodges to
the fact that a very substantial portion of the letters which are sent
to the Grand Master bear no address. In other instances, the stationery for many of our Lodges bears only the address of the Lodge room
which means delay in receipt by Master or Secretary of a reply which
is addressed to the ~odge room, and which normally is not received
until the next meeting night.
IX. Masonic Temple Associations.
In one of our Lodges a bitter controversy developed between the
Inspector (who was a member of the Lodge) and three Past Masters
who held the office of Trustees, and in which controversy most of the
Past Masters were involved. The situation was inexcusable and illustrated two evils. After exhaustive investigation, both personally and
by proxy, I was satisfied that the underlying cause of the friction was
the disposition of the Inspector on the one hand to exercise a controlling influence on the Lodge, and a similar disposition on the other
hand on the part of the Trustees. This paternalistic attitude on the
part of Trustees, and the inadvisability of the now unnecessary Trus·
tee system, is mentioned elsewhere in this report. I am equally of the
opinion that, while many Lodges take pride in the fact that their
Lodge is in the Inspection District of one of their number, nevertheless, this situation also contains inadvisable possibilities for friction
and paternalism. A Past Master who is also Inspector is no more than
human if he does not feel that more attention should be paid to his
recommendations than to the recommendations of other Past Masters,
and having the welfare of his Lodge at heart he is again no more than
human if he does not unconsciously develop a paternalistic attitude
and dominating influence. Attempts to change this situation meet
with determined opposition, but I believe the welfare of Masonry will
be promoted in the long run if our Lodges and our Inspectors will
jointly agree that, wherever practical, no Lodge shall have one of its
own number for Inspector. Notwithstanding vehement statements

58

69

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

that the dangers of the situation are magnified, the fact remains that
during the single year in which I have served as Grand Master several
pointed illustrations have come to my attention, and it is reasonable
to assume that an approximately equal number of other and similar
situations arise each year; naturally no Inspector will admit even to
himself that such a situation exists in his own ca·s e; nor is it likely
that the Lodge itself will concede the situation. The fact remains
that such situations which are obvious to third parties repeatedly
present themselves. This particular illustration is mentioned because
of another important point which was involved.
The Lodge holds all of the stock (except one share which cannot
be located) of the Temple Association whose building it occupies.
From time to time surplus funds of the Lodge have been advanced in
one form or another to the Temple Association untH all of its debts
have been discharged. Notwithstanding freedom from debt, and the
receipt of an adequate maintenance income, payments from the Lodge
have been continued as funds were available, so that practically the
entire surplus of the Lodge, amounting to some $5,000.00, is in the
hands of the Temple Association, and was deposited by the Temple
Association in a building and loan association from which it cannot
at present be withdrawn. A ~ote to cover the amount was issued by
the Temple Association to the Lodge. The Inspector insisted that
the Treasurer of the Lodge was the proper custodian for its funds,
and that if the amount could not be paid in cash, the deposit with the
Loan Association should be transferred from the Temple Association
to the Lodge, thereby cancelling the note and placing the funds under
the direct control of the Lodge and in the custody of its Treasurer.
Upon appeal to the Grand Master, the Trustees objected to this procedure, giving as a primary reason the fear that if the money were in
the custody of the treasurer the Lodge might be unduly tempted to
expend it, and that the further they could get the funds from the
direct control of the Lodge, the greater the security afforded against
dissipation of the money. I ruled that the Inspector was correct in
his contention, however praiseworthy the motives of the Trustees
might be. As, already stated, it was self-evident from the discussion
that underlying these opposing contentions was a struggle between
the Inspector and the Trustees for domination in the Lodge, notwithstanding the fact that, as members of the Lodge, neither the Inspector
nor the Trustees were entitled to any greater influence than any other
Past Master, and that, except as their advice is sought, Past Masters
themselves should remember that they are entitled only to the same
voice as any other member. In the discharge of his official duties the
Inspector should be treated as the representative of the Grand Master
but in his capacity of a member of the Lodge he is on a level with hi~

fellow members. The Trustees have no authority whatever; they are
mere naked custodians of title, whose duty it is to be governed exclusively by the instructions and wishes of the Lodge. In connection
with this particular situation, I feel that there is a weakness in our
law. The erection of temples is subject to control of Grand Lodge
through the supervision of the Committee on Financing Building
Projects. There is, however, no specific limitation upon the manner
in which Lodge funds shall be invested in the securities of Temple
Associations whose building is already erected. While I have informally ruled that the investment of funds in an existing Temple Asso ·
ciation should be submitted to this committee, the technical accuracy
of the ruling may be open to question. I recommend that by appropriate legislation our Lodges shall be definitely prohibited from hereafter
investing any of their funds in the securities of any Temple A11sociation without approval of this committee.

X. Lodge Trustees.
In the report of Grand Master Ross mention was made of the California statute which permits Lodges to hold title to real property
without incorporation (Statutes of 1911, p. 1093; General Laws No.
687) . He also commented upon the questionable right of Masonic
Lodges to take title because Section 87 of our Constitution provides
for the holding of title through Trustees, but does not in terms permit
a Lodge to hold title in its own name, and because of the provision of
the statute that the right of the Lodge to hold title is subject to the
regulations of the Grand Lodge. He recommended that the constitution in terms permit Lodges to take title in their own names, but
apparently no action was taken upon the recommendation, either in
committee or by Grand Lodge.
It is the policy of Grand Lodge, as evidenced in Section 87, that a
Lodge shall exerc.ise complete control of its own affairs, that it cannot
entrust any of its assets to a corporation, and that the Trustees who
are appointed shall be subject to its control. Vesting title in Trustees
is an indirect method of holding title which possesses no inherent
advantage in view of the policy of Grand Lodge law; the intervention
of Trustees, who must be merely dummies under the requirements of
Section 87, serves merely to complicate the situation where the statute
permits the Lodge to hold title. Moreover, too frequently a spirit of
paternalism develops on the part of Trustees. Holding title, they feel
that they can exercise a guardianship for the Lodge, notwithstanding
the provisions of the constitution. However good the motives of the
Trustees may be, this is not the law. During the past year friction
has developed in several instances because of the desire of the Trustees
to direct the financial policy of the Lodge and because of the practical

60

61

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

difficulty in controlling the action of the Trustees when differences of
opinion exist. I can see no useful purpose to be subserved by vesting
title in Trustees, and to promote both hai;mony and simplicity of
procedure I recommend that our law be changed by eliminating the
right of Lodges to elect Trustees and by squarely providing that title
to Lodge property shall vest in the Lodge. This can be accomplished
by changing the third sentence in Section 87 to read substantially as
follows:
Title to all of its assets, whether real or personal, shall vest
in the Lodge, and the acquisition and encumbrance of property and investment and re-investment of funds shall be determined solely by action of the Lodge.

Rite and the Scottish Rite, they represent the appeal which fellowship
and social intercourse make to the brethren who affiliate with them.
Of itself this may indicate a lack on the part of the average Lodge in
developing a well-rounded program. The spirit of fellowship and
brotherly cheer and intercourse are as important as ritualistic work.
If more of our time were given to activities beyond the conferring of
degrees, we might find less disposition to affiliate with collateral
organizations. Quality of candidates and membership, means far
more than numbers or the financial prosperity of the Lodge as an
organization. Cultivation of the social side of our fraternity may well
be accomplished on evenings when there is no degree work, and is far
better than to leave the Lodge room dark.
I am firmly convinced that our Ritual itself may be materially
shortened with profit to the Lodge, without injury to the work, and
with a result of increased attendance and the development of fellowship. Repetitions may be eliminated without loss of impressiveness.
The portion of the work at which there is the smallest attendance is
the lecture. Substantial portions of each lecture are mere repetitions
of preceding work, which add little to its value and which materially
discourage the attendance of the brethren. A knowledge of the work
is best obtained by attending subsequent meetings. Much of the explanation of the work and the philosophy of the lecture can better be .
imparted by instruction given to the candidate at a subsequent time.
I recommend:
1. That the committee on Ritual be directed to review the Ritual
and the lectures for the purpose of radically reducing their length
without loss of dignity and impressiveness, the findings to be reported
at the next communication of Grand Lodge.
2. That a special committee be appointed by the incoming Grand
Master to co-operate with the Committee on Ritual in the above
mentioned investigation, and that such special committee also investigate and, if deemed advisable, report a plan for instruction of candidates through intelligent explanation of the Ritual and our Masonic
philosophy, such instruction to be given privately at some time after
all of the degrees have been conferred upon the candidate, rather than
through the medium of the lecture in open Lodge.
3. That the giving of private instruction to candidates be made
obligatory and that appropriate legislation to that end be reported at
the next communicaion of Grand Lodge.
4. That Lodges be encouraged to use for purposes of fellowship
and the promotion of participation in current moral and civic activities, the time mad~ available through the abbreviation of Ritual or
lecture.

XI. Pioneer Masonry.
The Grand Secretary has made many valuable contributions in
varied fields to the welfare of both general Masonry and our own
jurisdiction in particular. In this connection I cannot refrain from
emphasizing his study of "Masonic Beginnings in California and
Hawaii" which has been issued in pamphlet form by Grand Lodge
during the present year. It is extremely interesting as a study and
most valuable as a part of the permanent record of our history. I
commend it to the attention of both Lodges and individual Masons.
With pleasure and profit it might well be made the subject for an
evening's entertainment and instruction by' every Lodge in the jurisdiction.
XII. Dedication Ceremonies.
An invitation was extended to me by local Lodges to dedicate a
Masonic Plot in the Cemetery. I was unable to personally attend, but
stated that while such a dedication is unusual, and any cheapening of
the dedication ceremony should be avoided, I can see no legitimate
objection to it; that the dedication of a resting place for deceased
brethren and their families is as appropriate as a dedication of a
meeting place for living brethren. The request emphasizes the fact
that no ceremonial is prescribed for such an event.
. If Grand Lodge approves the dedication of Masonic burial places,
or other dedications consistent with Masonic dignity, I recommend
that the Grand Secretary be directed to prepare and submit at the
next communication of Grand Lodge a modification of the ceremonial
for .dedicating halls which can appropriately be used for other dedications.

XVI. R efund of Unearne-d Dues.
Under our Uniform Code of By-Laws, dues are payable quarterly
in advance. Under the decision of Past Grand Master Ross, approved
by Grand Lodge in 1931 (Section 5-B of Digest of Decisions), a Lodge
cannot refund dues paid in advance, except dues paid in excess of
those for the current quarter. Giving the decision its full effect, if a
member dies during the first month of the quarter, the unearned dues
for the following two months cannot be refunded. Similarly, in the
case of a brother who is expelled or suspended for cause during the

64

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

quarter, I have felt 'obliged (see decision embodied in report) to rule
that no right of refund for the unearned dues accrues even when the
conviction is vacated by Grand Lodge. Another illustration is found
in the case of a California brother who applies for affiliation in November and is elected to membership in December. His petition for
affiliation must be accompanied by a receipt for not less than three
months' dues from his former Lodge. In the normal course his dimit
will be presented to the new Lodge at the February stated meet~ng
and his dues in the new Lodge commence March 1st under Section
161. His obligation for dues to his former Lodge does not terminate
until the dimit is issued, which under the illustration would be at" some
date following the January stated meeting of the new Lodge. In the
meantime, three months' dues to his former Lodge accrue on January
1st. Under the ruling no part of the dues for the January-March
quarter in the former Lodge can be refunded.
I see neither occasion for nor essential merit in a rule which prevents the refund of unearned dues merely because dues are payable
quarterly in advance. If the dues were payable annually in advance,
a man would lose the benefit of eleven months' dues although his
connection with the Lodge terminated in January. I therefore recommend the adoption of appropriate legislation requiring the refund of
unearned dues, whether for a current quarter or otherwise, and from
whatever cause the membership terminates. A financial penalty even
in the case of expulsion which becomes final, is not consistent with
Masonic principles, nor is there any occasion for the forfeiture of
unearned dues where membership terminates in the ordinary way,
merely because the by-laws re.quire the payment of dues in advance.

XVII. Commercial Activities of Lodges.
There is . an increasing tendency on the part of our Lodges to
directly or indirectly foster collateral financial undertakings. Most,
if not all, of these undertakings are meritorious in their purpose, but
the tendency is so strong that I believe there should be some declaration of policy on the part of Grand Lodge either discouraging such
activities or giving definite approval to these movements.
The danger is illustrated by a critical situation which arose in one
of our Lodges. In that instance the Lodge, by resolution, approved
the formation of an independent association among its members, denominated a Thrift Society, whose avowed purpose was to promote
thrift among the membership and to afford an opportunity for safe
and profitable investment. During a period of several years many
of the brethren joined the organization and it handled very substantial
sums of money under the management of an elected Board of Direc-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

66

tors. For a time the investments were profitable, but with the decline
in prices which preceded the present depression, the organization
suffered substantial losses, and at the time the matter came to my
attention its assets were insufficient at current market prices to pay
the amount of its deposits. This resulted in criticism of the management, charges that favored members were permitted to withdraw
funds in full while this condition existed, and threats of civil action
and criminal prosecution. Whether the charges were or were not
justified, whether the investments which were made were honestly
selected, and whether the membership tacitly, if not expressly, approved some of the more speculative investments, are all beside the
question. The essential fact is that under a resolution of approval and
authorization adopted by the Lodge, this collateral business activity
was inaugurated, resulting in dissension among the membership and
threatening serious injury both to the Lodge and to Masonry if
general publicity had resulted.
Following these developments, I had a census of the Lodges
taken to ascertain the extent and character of these collateral business
undertakings throughout the State. I found only one other organization similar to the Thrift Society above mentioned, but it appears
that a very substantial proportion of the Lodges of the State are
fostering what are known as "Widows and Orphans Funds." Some
of these funds have only nominal reserve, and depend largely upon
· the proceeds of an immediate assessment to pay death benefits. Others
have accumulated a substantial surplus which requires investment
and over whose investment at the present time neither the locai
Lodge nor Grand Lodge exercises control. While I know of no
instance to date in which friction has developed from these CO·
operative death benefit organizations, nevertheless it cannot be denied
that they hold inherent possibilities for future friction, particularly
in those cases in which a substantial reserve is maintained. There
is also the possibility that in the course of time some of them at least
will meet the difficulties which have confronted ordinary commercial
insurance societies operating upon the assessment plan.
I have neither approved nor attempted to discourage any of these
organizations, feeling that the question is too important for any
Grand Master to determine for himself. I do feel, however, that
the time has come when Grand Lodge should squarely face this
situation and directly either approve or disapprove these activities.
If they are to be continued, it should be with the approval of Grand
Lodge, and with a proper assumption of responsibility for direction
and control on the part of the Lodge which fosters the organization,
and with a corresponding responsibility if trouble or financial difficulty results. If these financial activities are to be curbed, the question is of sufficient importance to merit the action of Grand Lodge.

66

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Another illustration of a commercial activity was the action of
one of our Lodges in promoting a movement which has frequently
been attempted commercially and usually with an unsatisfactory
conclusion. A list of selected merchants in various lines of business
in San Francisco was collected by a committee, under an arrangement
whereby these merchants would pay to the committee an agreed
percentage of proceeds froi:µ sales made to members of the Lodge.
These proceeds were to be used by the committee for _unemployment
relief. Members of the Lodge were circularized and urged to patronize
these particular dealers; a "confidential list of dealers" accompanying
the circular. Criticism resulted that the tendency of this movement
was to temporarily divert to other channels business which was previously enjoyed by members of the Order, but that once diverted
the patronage was likely to remain with the new dealer after the
payment of commissions to the Lodge ceased. It was also contended
that the movement was a commercialization of Masonic membership.
Another suggestion was that the list contained the names of firms
whose prices were so high that they could well afford, to pay the
commission, leaving them still a net selling price equal to the prices
charged by other dealers, many of whom were members of the
Order. Whether the list of dealers was confined to members l:>f the
Order did not appear. It is self-evident that if any substantial number of Lodges in a commercial center adopted such a plan, it would
result in a network of competition for Masonic business, based
directly on an appeal to Masonry as an inducement to patronize a
particular group of men. I felt that the inherent dangers in such a
program were sufficiently obvious to justify me, without reporting
the matter to Grand Lodge, to direct a cessation of the activity.
It is impractical to detail all of the collateral commercial activities
which our Lodges are sponsoring, and the foregoing instances sufficiently illustrate the tendency. Masonry at all times has prided
itself that it was not a commercial institution and that mercenary
considerations shall not influence our members as Masons. While
the Widows and Orphans Funds are probably the least danger~us
illustration, and while the immediate relief of a brother's family
is most laudable, it is a serious question nevertheless whether we
are to embark upon the field of fraternal insurance and transform·
ourselves, at lea.st in part, into a mutual benefit society. It is my personal opinion that it does not conform to the purposes of Masonry,
and that in the long run it will prove disastrous, and I have no hesitancy whatsoever in disapproving the remaining commercial activities
which have come to my attention. However, if we are to become a
fraternal insurance society, it should not be done by indirection, with
the ultimate possibility of controversy as to the extent to which a

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

67

particular Lodge is legally or morally responsible for the collateral
organization which it has directly or tacitly sponsored, but over which
it exercises no control or supervision. I recommend that this Grand
Lodge adopt a definite policy upon the subject so that there may
hereafter be a definite rule for the guidance both of its officers
and its constituent Lodges.

XVIII. Lodge Rosters.
Grand Lodge has ruled (Digest, Sec. 22a) that Lodge rosters
should not be exploited for commercial purposes or other non-Masonic
use, and that Masters are obligated to prevent improper use of the
list. I believe experience has demonstrated that this is not sufficient
protection. Many of our Lodges publish rosters which include the
addresses of the members and when these are distributed it is physically impossible to prevent improper use and/or use by unauthorized
persons. Numerous instances have come to my attention during the
year, and these doubtless represent only a small percentage of the
infractions. In several cases such rosters were used as a mailing list
for political literature of a highly improper character. In other cases
the roster was used for commercial purposes. My attention was called
to the roster of one Lodge in which was listed not only the address
but the telephone number and occupa~ion of each brother, and the
roster also contained a classified business directory of the members
similar in form to the classified list appearing in the telephone book.
The inadvisability, if not the impropriety, of such a roster is obvious.
The only effective manner in which to prevent improper use of Lodge
roster is to omit all details other than the names. The Secretary is
the proper custodian of detailed information regarding the membership, and it may well be that the disadvantages overbalance the
benefits of issuing even a list of members without addresses or other
details. However, the glaring evil can be eliminated by restricting
rosters to a list of membership. I therefore recommend the adoption
of appropriate legislation to be framed by the Jurisprudence Committee prohibiting Lodges and their officers from issuing or permitting the issuance or distribution of any ,roster or other list of members
containing addresses, telephone numbers, occupation or other details
regarding the membership, except addresses and telephone numbers
of officers. By the legislation the Secretary should also be prohibited
without written permission of the Master from permitting the use or
transcription of all or any part of the Lodge's mailing list for ·any
purpose other than the issuance of communications from the Lodge
or its officers; such a requirement will fix responsibility for protection
of the roster.

XIX: Maintenance of Masonic Homes.
I believe that it is only a question of time when we shall be
obliged to depart from our present plan for the maintenance of the
Homes. The ideal source of revenue is an adequate endow.m ent fund,
and it is to be hoped that as the years progress we may larg:ly
increase our present endowment. It is interesting to note that dun~g
a period of approximately twenty years, from 1910 to 1931, we increased our endowment from $17,000.00 to over $700,000.00, and that
the greater portion of this amount has accru~d from te.stament~ry
gifts. This sum, however, must be largely increased during coming
years if it is to afford an adequate remedy. Such an. endowme~t
cannot be too strongly urged and I anticipate that. at th1~ comi:riunication of Grand Lodge a special report upon this subJect will be
presented for your consideration. It is self evident, however, that
a long period of time must elapse before we shall have an adequate
endowment.
In the meantime, there remains a question, which is incre~singly
discussed, whether we shall look for maintenance to a per capita tax
and the payments by initiates and affiliates, or whether to :" greater
or less extent the Lodges shall directly contribute to the maint~na~ce
of those who are admitted at Decoto and Covina upon t~e application
of the Lodge. Many jurisdictions have already determined that the
latter is the wiser course, and I believe that sooner or later we shall
find it advisable in California to require that at least a portion of
the expense be borne by the Lodge upon whose applic~tion th: a~­
mission is granted. A merited criticism _o f our Masonic .charity is
that it has become too mechanical, and t~at the. do~or ~s too f~r
removed from the recipient. Ideal Masonic charity is still that in
which each brother directly contributes to the need, temporary. or
permanent, of another brother o~ his depe?dents . . The increasing
size of our membership makes this method 1mpractical, and we use
the Lodge as an intermediate agency betwee~ the. contributor .and the
needy brother. When we rely upon a per capita :ax, we increase
once more the distance between donor and beneficiary, and to that
extent we lose still more the spirit of Masonic brotherhood and
charity. The inevitable result of the per capita system is a lack of
feeling of responsibility upon the part of the Lodge, and a tendency
upon the part of the Lodge to seek to shift responsibility to the stat~­
wide charity fund, and to scrutinize applications less closely than 1f
the immediate expense were imposed upon the treasury of the Lodge.
This tendency varies with circumstances and membership, and financial conditions, but it is ever present. Such a chang~ mu~t be made
gradually, but I believe it will be in the interest of California Masonry
and its charity that the change be made. It may be contended that

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

69

a temporary injustice will result to Lodges which have contributed
regularly, and which to date have presented only a limited number
of applications. The first answer to this contention is that if the
change is desirable, it should not be rejected because of minor inequities among the Lodges. A more conclusive answer, however, is
that it is a sad commentary upon California Masonry if we . have
reached the point where we measure our Masonic charity and brotherhood and our inter-Lodge relationship by cold financial standards and
with mathematical accuracy, or if a more advantageous and worthy
system of conducting our charity is to be rejected because forsooth
to date the charitable gifts of one group of our Masons have been
disproportionate to those of another group.; it is to be hoped that the
Masonic charitable spirit of California has not yet become so petty
or fallen so low.
Another subject which deserves consideration is the administration of outside relief through the trustees of the Homes. Insofar
as outside relief is a substitute for maintenance at the Homes of
persons who are entitled to admission, it is a proper subject for administration by the tru~tees and for payment from the funds of the
Homes. However, there is a gradually increasing tendency to make
appropriations from Homes Funds for the assistance of worthy
Masons or their dependents who are not eligible to admission, either
where the Lodge is unable to afford the full relief sought, or where
for other reasons the trustees deem it advisable to extend the relief.
The Homes are conducted for the maintenance, either at the institution or elsewhere, of adults and children who are eligible for admission. The endowment trust exists for that primary purpose, and
at least in theory the appropriations which are made for maintenance
have that end in view. The administration of relief for those who
are not eligible to admission is foreign to the functions of the H omes
Board; doubtless the custom has arisen because of lack of other
Grand Lodge machinery for administering direct charity from Grand
Lodge to those who are not entitled to admission to the Homes; no
criticism can be made of the manner in which the appropriations have
been made or of their merit; nevertheless, an anomalous situation
has developed, and it is practically impossible for Grand Lodge to
tell today the amount which it is spending as a proper charge for
maintenance of the Homes, including outside relief which is equivalent
to residence, and the amount which it is expending for the assistance
of Lodges in charity to those who are ineligible to the Homes. If
Grand Lodge creates the committee for the administration of Grand
Lodge relief which is mentioned in Recommendation · IV of this
report, I further recommend that by appropriate legislation the administration of charity for either adults or children who are ineligible for

funds controlled by the Homes Trustees be used exclusively for the

not objectionable, and that it had been approved by the national
authorities of the Shrine; eventually I was advised that its conduct

XX. Expenses of Grand Officers.
While a substantial portion of the appropriation for expenses of
the Grand Master during the current year remains unexpended, I
recommend that the same contingent appropriation be made for the
coming year. Only lack of time and opportunity for travel about the
jurisdiction prevented the exhaustion of the appropriation, and it is
to the interest of Grand Lodge that the Grand Master be provided
with adequate funds for such traveling as he deems advisable and
possible. It is superfluous to say that the incoming Grand Master
will expend only such amount as appears necessary. The maximum
allowance should be uniform from year to year, and latitude should
exist for the varying demands of successive Grand Masters necessitated by expenses of travel.
The situation regarding expenses of Grand officers other than
the Grand Master is somewhat changed by the present plan of
districting the State, and the assumption of executive duties in their
respective districts by the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior and
Junior Grand Wardens. Independently of the fact that the making
of visits to Lodges or districts by these officers will tend to materially
decrease the traveling expenses of the Grand Master, it is self evident
that these officers should not be expected to personally bear their
traveling expenses in addition to giving their time, and I do not
believe Grand Lodge desires it. Section 70 of the constitution provides for payment of expenses of e.l ective Grand officers in attending
Grand Lodge "at any of its communications," which includes both
the annuai communication and special communications for cornerstones or other formal ceremonies; however, only a small percentage
of visits comes within this category. It has also been the custom
for many years upon recommendation of the Finance Committee
to annually adopt a resolution providing for payment of expense~ of
Grand Lodge officers "who may be traveling by authority of the
Grand Master." This is not a standing resolution and because of its
form there has been more or less hesitancy and embarrassment on
the part of elective Grand officers to present statements for traveling
expenses which in all propriety should be paid by Grand Lodge. I
therefore recommend that the form of the customary annual resolution
for payment of the expenses of the Grand Master be revised to include
the necessary traveling expenses of the Deputy Gra~d Master and the
Senior and Junior Grand Wardens when visiting Lodges or attending
other Masonic meetings in their official capacity in their respective

The conference to which Potentate Bruner apparently refers
was held on April 8th, but he was not present.
As previously noted, the Temples at Oakland and San Diego
did not participate in the enterprise, and so far as California is concerned;· it was conducted by the Los Angeles and San Francisco
Temples above noted, and by Ben Ali Temple of Sacramento. It is a
well known fact that tickets with their accompanying certificates
were sold broadcast throughout the State and that at least a very
substantial proportion of the pun;hasers bought them because of the
chance of receiving the $50,000.00 fi'rst prize or the secondary prizes
constituting the aggregate of $115,000.00. Many of the poor scraped
pennies together for a "chance" and frequent references were made
by those whom the Grand Master met on the street to their prospective chance of winning $50,000.00 The campaign was conducted so
extensively that even inmates of our institutions for maintenance of
the poor, singly or in groups, purchased blocks of tickets in anticipation of winning a prize which would permit withdrawal from the
institution and comfort for the remaining days of life.
Following this correspondence there were consultations between
Dfrector General Wm. H. Woodfield, representing the Shrine, and
myself, which climaxed in a general conference of the Convention
committee with myself, at which eight or ten of the leading representatives of Islam Temple were present. I repeated my views, as expressed in the correspondence, to the effect that obviously it was the
intention of the Shrine to either conduct a lottery or to bunco ticket

purchasers into the belief that they were acquiring a chance in a

a communication be issued to the Shriners of California advising
them that in the disposition of the $115,000.00 fund the committee
was to be restricted in its award by two rules, namely, that the distribution was to be strictly on a basis of merit for services performed
throughout the entire campaign for the raising of funds, and shall be
conducted by a method which shall not involve any element of
chance. I retained in my files a carbon copy of my memorandum
upon this subject, which at the time was delivered to the committee
at its request. Upon returning to the office, and on the same date,
I confirmed the understanding in a letter to Director General Woodfielq. Grand Lodge may be interested in two instances which illustrate the extent to which gentlemen who represented the Shrine on
this occasion are in touch with general Masonic affairs. During the
discussion l was asked what Grand Lodge could do if they proceeded
with their plans in defiance of it. I mentioned several possible things
which might occur, whereupon the inquiring Noble said "I do not
believe Grand Lodge would do anything like that anyway; how
many are there in Grand Lodge-fifty?" He appeared somewhat
startled when I indicated the normal attendance at Grand Lodge.
Another well known Noble stated that I should proceed in this matter
with caution, stating that if I were not careful "the Shrine may withdraw from Masonry." Several Nobles apparently agreed with him
but some of them were not so optimistic.
No action being taken pursuant to this understanding, I personally pressed the Director Gene.r at for action or an explanation, and
was informed by him, among other things, that there was a difference
of opinion among .the Convention Committee whether, and if so in
what manner and to what extent, the understanding above mentioned
should be performed. He also advised me that by reason of these
differences of opinion Mr. McNab had been authorized, by and as the
representative of the committee, to meet me and determine a definite
procedure which would be observed by the committee. On April 14th,
the Director General and Mr. McNab called upon me, reciting the
authorization of Mr. McNab, and as a result of our discussion it was
agreed that the Convention Committee would so control the disposition of the $115,000.00 fund that in its distribution no resort should
_be had to methods of chance; that the California participating Temples
would immediately notify all of their members of this fact and that
the Convention Committee would itself immediately advise all outof-State participating Temples of the same fact. I confirmed this
understanding in a letter ,to Mr. McNab on April 14, 1932, in which it
was recited that the lett~rs to be issued to California Shrine members

and to the Potentates of the various participating Temples should,
among other things, contain a statement that "full discretion as to
the awards rests with the committee, subject only to the limitation
that the fund is to be distributed in accordance with law and on an
exclusive basis of merit for services performed throughout the campaign, and without resort to methods which involve. any element of
chance." Following the recital of this language, my letter to Mr.
McNab concluded as follows:

At the conference of Grand Masters at Washington, D. C., in

On April 26th, I wrote a letter to the Potentates of Ben Ali and

I feel that the circumstances were such that the delay occasions no
criticism. As to whether his Temple should have discontinued further
selling of tickets, I express no opinion; in fact, I am not in a position
to state that further sales were made, and I think I am correct in
saying that at no time was the sale of tickets intensively pressed at
Sacramento.

At no time has Potentate Skeggs attempted in any way to observe
either the letter or the spirit of the agreement for the issuance of a
notice to the members of Islam Temple. He not only failed to issue
the statement, but in the next Islam Temple bulletin there appeared
a circular letter addressed to the Nobles and signed personally "John
H. Skeggs, Potentate," in which he reminded the Nobles of the
distribution of $115,000.00 at the Convention to those aiding in carrying forward the Convention, and then stated:
"The real service men a·n d women will be those who are holders of
certificates of merit. Each Temple of Shrinedom will appoint one representative to the Convention Awards Committee. This committee will be
in full charge of the granting of the awards. I have appointed our Orator,
Noble Harry K, Wolff, to serve as the representative of Islam Temple on
the Convention Awards Committee." ( Italics mine.)
Upon receiving this bulletin on May 3rd, I called the attention
-0f Director General Woodfield to this breach of the· agreement, with
the result that he promised to promptly and personally place the

in the next issue of "Convention News" (a bulletin issued to the
membership of Islam Temple from time to time during the campaign),
the Director General over his personal signature published the agreed

the committee, but subject to the limitations specified in the correspondence which has been already quoted; thus to the extent of his
ability conforming to the agreement in this respect.
On May 3rd I wrote a letter to Potentate Bruner of Los Angeles,

On June 13th a circular was issued by the Campaign Committee

On June 1st I wrote Potentate Woodfield repeating intimations
which had been made at Los Angeles that the understanding was for
the purpose of saving mY "face and to give me a record, but that
through either evasion or ignoring the understanding, a system of
awards would be adopted by which ticket purchasers would have the

I reminded him that the agreement was · not made to give me a
record, nor with any expectation that it would be disregarded, and

In the same letter I again mentioned the public announcement which
I had made at the.conference of Grand Masters at Washington.
Early in June, general publicity was given throughout the country
to warnings issued by the Department of Justice condemning as
illegal the promotion of lottery schemes among fraternal organizations. On June 10th an official letter was sent by the Department of
Justice at Washington to our Grand Secretary, Brother Whicher.

The body of the letter was addressed "to all fraternal organizations"
and presumptively it went to the Secretaries of all Masonic organizations throughout the country. This letter condemned, as a criminal
violation of Federal lottery laws, the sale of tickets to entertainments
by Fraternal organizations in conjunction with which the purchaser
is entitled to a chance at cash prizes.
On July 29th the newspapers contained lists of the winners,
scattered over the .country, of the prizes in the $115,000.00 Shrine
Awards.
On August 9th I wrote Director General Woodfield asking that
he advise me what procedure was adopted by the committee "for the
distribution of the Shrine Award of Merits Fund." O n August 11th,
he replied to me as follows:

82

"In reply to your letter of August 9th, I wish to state that I
have no knowledge of the exact method of which the $115,000.00 was
awarded.
"You will recall that I sent a letter to each Potentate who participated requesting that he name one member of his Temple to act
on a committee to determine the awards. At that time I instructed
the Potentates that the only limitation was that the awards be disposed of without resorting to lot or chance.
"The day the matter was disposed of I was very busily en~aged
with the handling of the motion picture pageant and the affairs of
the convention and the matter was left entirely in the hands of this
representative committee. While I do not know this to be a fact, I
am informed that no Californian participated or was present during
the awards because of the fact that so many ball tickets were sold
in California, and it would be the consensus of opinion t hat many of
the awards would be made to Californians; therefore, it was considered a better policy to eliminate the California representatives.
"On behalf of the Shrine Convention Committee, permit me to
thank you for the splendid address you made during the opening
exercises of the Imperial Council. Your constructive talk was a fine
contribution to our national demonstration of optimism which the
press and leaders of the nation have proclaimed as the year's most
outstandingly patriotic offensive against the depression."
On August 15th I wrote John L. McNab, Esq., who advised with
me as-the official representative of the ·convention Committee, asking
him "whether the award was made in conformity with my letter to
him which was okayed by Director General Woodfield, and which
' itself was confirmatory of the conversation of these two gentlemen
with myself. On August 22nd he replied as follows :
"I must apologize for the delay in answering your letter of

"I only returned to the City this morning from a hunting trip

"Personally, I know nothing_ whatever concerning the method
of award adopted in the Shrine Convention. However, I have been
inform·ed that the Shrine Convention appointed a representative from

each Shrine to form a Committee on Awards. On this committee, I
understand, there was no representative from the Grand jurisdiction
of California. I am informed that the situation was explained to them
and they were told that it must be worked out in a legal manner and
that thereafter it went into session and reported the awards. Concerning the basis upon which they were worked out I have not the
remotest knowledge. The report was filed and I understand that
was the end of the transaction so far as any connection the Shrine
officials had with it.
·
I have been assured that it was carried out in the spirit of the
letter which you wrote."
I am informed on the authority of a Noble who was ·present at
the drawing that a normal procedure for a lottery drawing was
pursued, the certificates being dumped in a pile on the floor and a
disinterested person drawing the winning numbers in succession.
It is practically self evident that this or some similar procedure was
followed. There is no pretense that the prize winners were designated
upon any basis of superior merit for services rendered or that the
winner of the $50,000.00 prize performed any greater service than
thousands of other ticket purchasers who received nothing. It is
generally claimed (and correctly so far as I can ascertain) that no
representative or Noble from California was present at the drawing;
thus apparently endeavoring to shift responsibility to N obi es from
. other jurisdictions.
Personally I prefer a crook to a coward. ·
I am unable to see wherein the California Shriners in authority
can safely hide behind a skirt of protested ignorance of the procedure.
The men in charge of this Convention were California Shriners and
California Masons. They were in control of the fund. A definite
oral and written agreement was made by the Director General of the
Convention and by .Mi:. McNab, purporting to act by authority of the
Committee, that in the award there should be no resort to any method
of chance, and that the awards should be made strictly on the basis
of merit for services rendered. Publicity was given to the participating
Temples throughout the country and to the Nobles of California that
this agreement would serve as a limitation upon the authority of the
committee making the awards. If the procedure for awards did· not
conform to the agreement, it was within the power of California
Shriners and California Masons to withhold payment, for the custody
of the fund was with them and publicity was given to their agreement.
Having failed ro exercise the control which they possessed, they
cannot shift responsibility through claims of ignorance or a contention that the committee in their absence violated the agreement. Nor
can the Shrine itSelf evade responsibility. It was within ·its power
to control both Islam Temple and its Convention Committee.
The Chief Rii.bban of: Islam Temple, Noble George J. Hatfield,
participated in the conference which I held with the Shrine Commit-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

85

tee, and I came in contact with him on other occasions in this connection. It is with very sincere pleasure that I am able to state that in
every instance he co-operated with and supported me. At the com·
mittee meeting he was obliged to leave before the conference closed
and as he left he made a statement which was typical of his attitude
throughout: "Before I leave I want to state that I want to do whatever the Grand Master desires, and my vote is for whatever he requests." In fairness to him I wish to state that in this report I
purposely disclaim intention of either express or implied criticism
of him, as I do not feel that responsibility for subsequent developments rests upon him.
· It is unfortunate that the Shriners, as an organization, which possesses such tremendous possibilities for fellowship and effective civic
and moral service, and whose rolls are honored by the names of
some of our most respected citizens and most illustrious Masons,
should permit itself to be discredited and its legitimate influence
prostituted by the irresponsible acts of a comparatively small percentage of its members who are not Masons in fact, and who should
never have been made Masons in name. It is unfortunate that there
are repeated instances in which these same irresponsible Masons
and . Shriners by their public acts reflect disrepute upon their organization. It is equally unfortunate that to the man upon the street the
name "Shriner" is the equivalent of "High Mason" and that to those
not versed in our fraternity Shrinedom represents the pinnacle of
Masonry. It is even more unfortunate that legitimate Masonry must
suffer, both in reputation and in fact, from this condition, and because
the Shrine tolerates conduct which is, and men who are, a disgrace
to Masonry and to the Shrine itself. It is a condition which cannot
continue indefinitely and the day will come, if it is not at hand, when
Masonry must pay the price for its own complaisance and condonat.i on; mere words will not change facts, nor will they restore tarnished
prestige to our fraternity ; the influence of Masonry depends as much
upon the respect with which it is regarded as upon the principles
which it professes or practices.
Possibly I have exaggerated in my mind the importance of that
which has occurred; this I leave for you to determine. With the
near approach of an annual communication of Grand Lodge, I have
felt that it was neither my province nor my responsibility to direct
the action, if any, which shall be taken. I have placed the facts
before you and the issue is in your hands. Numerous courses of action
suggest themselves, all or any of which are possible if you deem them
advisable. I shall suggest only a few of them and these are submitted
without reco.mmendation, as I believe that this body is competent
to decide for itself, and that it should for itself assume the responsibility for action or non-action.

1. If, in the opinion of Grand Lodge, Masonic offenses have
been committed, it is within its power to direct the prosecution of
charges against at least those, whether leaders or otherwise responsible, who have conducted this enterprise. It requires neither a
prophet nor the son of a prophet to foretell the tremendous inftuence
which will be brought to bear on behalf of the accused if this course
is followed. In no event is it practical to prosecute charges against
all who have participated, for their name is legion.
2. Possibly it is within the jurisdiction of this body, without
trial, to impose such, if any, punishment as may be deemed proper
upon those whom Grand Lodge deems guilty. Such action should not
be attempted without an approving opinion from the Jurisprudence
Committee.
3. Members of constituent Lodges may be prohibited from acquiring or retaining membership in the Shrine so long as the Shrine
requires Masonic affiliation as a prerequisite to Shrine membership.
4. Affiliation by a member of a constituent Lodge may be prohibited in any organization (other than York and Scottish Rite
Bodies) which makes Masonic affiliation a condition precedent to
membershp, but which does not subject itself to control by Grand
Lodge. The advisability of such action involves consideration of
whether Grand Lodge is willing to assume the responsibility for such
control.
5. It may be made a Masonic offense for a member of ·a constituent Lodge to acqqire or retain membership in any organization
which requires Masonic affiliation as a prerequisite to membership,
and which permits or suffers to go unpunished, action on the part
of its membership which is contrary to the rules or practices of Blue
Lodge Masonry, or which would constitute a Masonic offense if the
particular action were related to Blue Lodge membership. The
objection to such a rule rests primarily in uncertainty of enforcement.
·
6. It may be made a Masonic offense for any member of a constituent Lodge to be guilty of an act which brings or tends. to bring
discredit upon .any organization which requires Masonic affiliation
as a prerequisite for membership, in the same manner and to the
same extent as if the discredit directly affected a Blue Lodge or
Blue Lodge Masonry. Frequently, acts are committed in connection
with other organizations or the meetings of other organizations, which
bring discredit, but under circumstances where serious question arises
whether Blue Lodge Masonry is directly affected. The justification
for such a definition (if deemed advisable) rests in the indirect reflection upon Masonry in general wherever an organization which requires Blue Lodge Masonry as a prerequisite is discredited.

7. Merely by inaction, this Grand Lodge may tacitly approve the
Shrine's procedure, and thereby go of record throughout the land
that no action is merited, and that the Shrine's attitude conforms to
the standards of Masonry.
The returning of Federal indictments against men who have b~eµ
involved in similar enterprises conducted by other Fraternal organizations under identical management, is current knowledge and not
history which requires recital. At the writing of this report a Senator
of the United States, who is a former cabinet officer, is on trial under
such an indictment. The present enterprise of the Shrine was under
investigation by the Grand Jury when these indictments were returned and it is stated in the press that the failure to return indictments' against Shrine officials was due to the inability of investigators to connect Shrine officials with the distribution of profits; why
such inability exists is not disclosed. The Western Union Telegraph
Company has been indicted for the distribution of the literature connected with the award of $115,000.00 in prizes at the Shrine Convention at San Francis.co, but Shrine officials themselves to date
have escaped.
Whether or not the Shrine has technically evaded the laws of
the United States, apparently at least it has successfully ~efied the.m.
It is for this Grand Lodge to determine whether the Shrine h~s w1~h
equal impunity defied Masonry and the Grand Lodge of Cahforma.

felt that the use of this plan was in any view of the matter regrettable
at this time, and I addressed a letter to the Sciots suggesting that
fact and indicating my opinion that it was inadvisable to continue the
enterprise. While the Department of Justice disapproved this plan,
also, no such decisive action was taken as occurred in connection with
enterprises of the type of that in which the Shrine engaged. The
Pharaoh of the Sciots immediately issued an edict prohibiting the
conduct of such an enterprise by the Sciots and the Pyramids which
already had launched a campaign recalled all books, whether completely sold or not. In its own enterprise the officials of the Shrine
neither prohibited the conduct of the enterprise, nor stopped the sale
of tickets, nor ordered the recall of books.
The obvious desire of the Sciots to conform to the wishes and
standards of Grand Lodge and to remove grounds for objection, to
the end that the relationship between the two bodies may be harmonious, is in contrast to the attitude of the Shrine. Which of the
two organizations is the more creditable is a matter upon which there
may be differences of opinion; I am a member of the Shrine and I am
not a member of the Sciots; nor do I hold a brief for the Sciots, but
to my mind the facts speak for themselves. An ancient teacher once
asked which of two sons did the will of his father, the one who said
" I go, Sir," but who went not, or the disobedient son who afterward
repented and went.
Appreciation
Preceding successive Grand Masters have so properly and adequately expressed appreciatiort for the activities of our Grand Secretary and our Grand Lecturer, that the subject although ever new is
almost threadbare. This year and the present Grand Master have
proven no exception. California Masonry owes to both of these
officers a debt which neither words of appreciation nor financial
remuneration can pay. Their assistance and their wisdom and experience have been invaluable, and they richly deserve the satisfaction we trust they derive from a realization of the love and respect
which exists for them throughout the jurisdiction, and the high esteem
in W'hich they are held by every Grand Master with whom they come
in contact. Nor can I miss this opportunity to express for both the
jurisdiction and myself personally the appreciation we owe the Deputy
Grand Master and the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens. They have
been always ready to answer every call, and to assume every responsibility; the assistance and co-operation which they have rendered in their respective districts has, I believe, far more than
compensated my own inability to come in personal contact with all
sections of the jurisdiction. Time forbids the merited tribute I would

Sciots
The message of the Grand Master at the last communication of
Grand Lodge severely criticized the Sciots because of public and
fraternal activities in an effort to promote the business interest of
individual members of the organization. Following the communication, representatives of the Sciots called upo~ me and assured me that
every effort would be made to correct any improper conditions. I am
glad ·to be able to report that apparently everything which is possible
was done to remove the grounds for criticism mentioned in the Grand
Master's message. At the meeting 'of the Supreme Pyramid at Stockton in November, the use of the abbreviation or initials "BOA" was
prohibited; deputies were charged with the duty of preventing vulgar
or offensive conduct at any ceremonial or function, with authority to
immediately suspend for violation ; the use of the word "Mason" was
eliminated from the ritual and a commi.ttee was appointed to make
the necessary changes to that end. I was requested to immediately
call to the attention of the Sciot authorities any report of objectionable conduct or action, and was assured that prompt action would be
taken if investigation substantiated the report, and that it was the
desire and intention of the officers of the Supreme Pyramid to maintain proper standards 'bf gentlemen and Masons. I have no reason to
doubt the good faith of both actions and statements, and feel that
credit should be given to the organization and its officers for the
position which has been taken.
Shortly following the action by the Department of Justice, occasioned by the distribution of $115,000.00 at the Shrine Convention,
and similar action by other Fraternal organizations, it came to my
attention that two of the Sciot Pyramids were endeavoring to raise
funds through the sale pf blankets under the well known punching
system. This is a plan which has been followed by various organizations from time to time, and at which, so far as I know, no particularly

REPORT OF GRAND SECRETARY

Conclusion
Such is the Grand Master's report of his year; his record rests
in the events themselves and 'Yords can neither add nor detract. With
all its pleasure and all its honor, the year has held for me much of
disillusion and disappointment-disillusion that my accomplishments
have been so slight, if any, and disappointment that I have been able
to give so little. It is my only hope that any impress which has been
left is for better and not for worse. I can only say that although
mistakes and deficiencies doubtless have been numerous, I have to
the limit of physical endurance and, mental equipment done the best
I can. My heart is in this Grand Lodge and my best wishes go to all
the Brethren. The friendships of the year have been many and those
friendships and the countless acts of kindness and courtesy which
have come to me, are among life's priceless memories. I wish for this
Grand Lodge every accomplishment, for succeeding officers every
success, and for the brdhren every measure of happiness and prosperity.
Fraternally yours,
ROBERT B. GA YLOR.D,

Grand Master.

Duplicate Charter
Fort Crook Lodge No. 575 lost its charter by fire on the 16th of
December, 1931, and by order of the Grand Master a duplicate of the
original charter granted October 11, 1923, duly certified, was issued.
Roster of Members
At the last annual communication of Grand Lodge, a recommendation
was adopted (Proc. 1931, p. 513) directing Secretaries of Lodges to

Salary of Grand Secretary
The finances of Grand Lodge are in a healthy condition. We· have the
goodly surplus (October 1, 1932) of $260,000 in cash and sound liquid
securities, besides $589,300 in non-liquid stocks. But notwithstanding this,
in deference to demand for retrenchment, I respectfully recommend that
the salary of the Grand Secretary be reduced ten per cent.
Income and Disbursement
An approved report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, adopted last year (1931, p. 707) provided that "the Grand Secretary
should add to the forms for annual returns an additional sheet for the
inclusion of a summary of the income and disbursements of each Lodge."
This was done, but the returns as to these items were disappointing. One
hundred fifty-nine Lodges did not so report, and I did not communicate
with the Lodges not reporting for the reason that had I done so it
would have been impossible to close the books in time for this an~ual
communication. The Lodges reporting showed gross receipts of $1,637,131.52, and gross disbursements of $1,630,650.19.
Emergency Relief Fund
Pursuant to the order of Grand Lodge at the last annual co~nmnica­
tion, I closed the account of the Emergency Relief Fund, and transferred
the entire amount, $14,224.46 in cash, and four first Liberty loan bonds
of $1,000 each, to the General Fund, delivering it all to the Grand Treasurer.
