Unfinished Business
Recommendation I of Grand Master Ross (Proc. 1931, p. 469) "that
Grand Lodge, in its .Pay of Members, should include all expenses and
not only those incurred for transportation." The Committee on Policy
and General Purposes recommended that a committee of three be appointed to make a study of the question and report at this communication
(p. 722-3) .. The Committee on Finance also reported (p. 750), recommending "that the subject · of the pay of members and per diem be postponed
until the next annual communication."

Report of Auditors
Finance Committee, Grand L odge, F. & A. M. of California:
In accordance with your authorization, we have audited the accounts
of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California for the fiscal year ended
July 31, 1932 and submit herewith certain financial statements as follows:
Exhibit A: Grand Secretary's Report of Cash Receipts and Dis·
bursements-General Fund. · •
Exhibit B: Grand Secretary's Report of Cash Received for Account
of Masonic Homes.
Exhibit C: Grand Secretary's Report of Cash Receipts and Disbursements-Emergency Relief Fund.
Exhibit D: Grand Treasurer's Re1J0rt of Cash Receipts and Disbursements.
Exhibit E : Grand Treasurer's Report of Assets on Hand July 31,
1932.
This audit covered the cash funds received during the year ended
July 31, 1932 from the annual returns for the fiscal year ended July 31,
- . 1931. Funds received and on hand at the date of our audit from annual
returns for the fiscal year 1932 were not included in our examination.
We certify that' the attached statements, with exception as to the
stated value of the securities on hand, set forth the condition of the· Grand
Lodge, F. & A. M. of California at July 31. 1932, and that a proper
accounti!1g has been made of all receipts and disbursements.
Respectfully submitted,
RucKSTELL & LAND, Certified P ublic Accountants,
By FLOYD T. WEBB.

discharge of his trust. It is apparent .that vital and important matters

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Regarding action on charitable matters, his letter and message contain
sound constructive advice, reminding us of our obligations but calling attention to limitations that must be observed in the use of Masonic funds.
We thoroughly concur in the Grand Master's condemnation of the
misuse of Masonic affiliation and Lodge rosters for political purposes. Our
fraternity can not hope to maintain its prestige if members persist in
violating its ideals and endeavor to embroil it in political controversies.
The thoughts of the Grand Master on the matter of non-payment of
dues should receive the careful study of all members of Grand Lodge,
and representatives should see that this matter is given due consideration
by the officers of their respective Lodges.
The committee desires to call attention to the admonition regarding
Masonic keys. Do not violate your oath or .encourage others to do likewise.
Masonic education is a matter that means a great deal to this jurisdiction. During the past year the George Washington Bicentennial Celebra- ,
tions have been of a real educational value and have produced beneficial
activity. The suggestion of the Grand Master on the educational program
question appeals to us as meriting a trial ; it will furnish a new stimulus
for Lodge activity and should increase attendance.
Startling to Grand Lodge was the report of the Grand Master regarding his experience with the Shrine Lottery. Apparently a direct violation
of State and Federal laws; engineered and manipulated by Masons; the
Grand Master's reliance upon assurances of Master Masons in his jurisdic.tion breached ; officials of other fraternal organizations under criminal
prosecution in Federal Courts for a like offense; the Shrine, known to the
public as a Masonic organization: we are indeed confronted with a problem
that calls for the calm and deliberate consideration and sound advice of the
experienced leaders of the Grand Lodge of California. This is a situation
that cannot be passed by; it is now for us to "assume the responsibility for
action or non-action."
In approaching the close of this administration, Masonry of California
desires to give fitting recognition to a leader, honest with his moral convictions, one who values the worth-while things of this life, one willing to
listen to the opinion of others, but firm when convinced he is sound in his
position. A direct and able speaker, possessing a personality congenial
and sympathetic-a man true to his friends, fair to his opponents and
with an abiding faith in his God. Brother Gaylord, the Brethren of this
jurisdiction express to you their sincere and lasting appreciation.
FOSTER G. DYER,

ANNUAL ORATION
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers and Brethren of Grand Lodge:
I am not unmindful of the fact that you have suffered me this day
to stand where many honorable men have stood. With pleasure we have
listened to their eloquence as they reached into the archives of memory
and unfolded before our minds the philosophy of Masonry. I, too, have
thought that I might take you on a journey from Babylon up the beautiful
Euphrates, thence westward by Tadmor in the wilderness, and from thence
down through the corridor of time to the present hour. Such a theme has
all the alluring beauties of a sorceress, and the story when told is much
like the vision of Mirza. Or I might have chosen to take up the story of
the trade schools established by Numa, second king of Rome, who reigned
from 716 to 672 B. C., followed the mystic story of Masonry along the
ever widening and deepening stream of the civil law as it flowed on
down through the ages, stepped aside a moment to see an intellectual
Hebrew Hercules baffle and confound the Roman governors and listen
to his eloquence as he stood upon Mars Hill delivering the most daring · .
and powerful oration recorded ·in the history of man. But I have selected
a less pleasing theme and more difficult task. Less pleasing, because I
shall endeavor to point out that, as Masons, we have a duty to perform
vital to the life of the Republic in which we live, and more difficult because I shall seek to show that Masonry is a Battle and not a Dream.
From the Babylonian captivity to the present hour the great eternal conflict between right and wrong has never ceased. Why were the chosen
people of God suffered to be thus carried away? Was it not because they
had forgotten the God of their fathers? Did not Zedekiah refuse tbe aid
and deny the existence of Jehovah; and was not his Kingdom and the
Temple destroyed, the holy vessels carried away and his people driven
into captivity? In the very beginning of our Masonic life the Bible is
given to us as the rule and guide of our faith and we are taught that it
is to be the great light in our profession; we are told that in it we will
learn the important duties which we owe to God, our neighbor, and ourselves. To God, by never mentioning His name but with that awe and
reverence which are due from the creature to His creator ; by imploring
His aid in all our lawful undertakings, and by looking up to Him in
every emergency for comfort and support. We are also taught that
Masonry is calculated to impress deeply upon our minds a firm .belief in
the existence and attributes of a Supreme Being, and that we should have
a due reverence for His great and sacred name. Such are the teachings
of Masonry, and every one who takes the obligation is bound by those
teachings. The eternal laws of God are written into the heart of the
universe, and the entire world is ruled and guided by those laws. For

113

our guidance He has laid down only such laws as were founded in those
relations of justice that existed in the nature of things antecedent to the
laws of Moses or any written law or precept. These are the immutable
laws of good and evil, and they are written by the finger of God upon
the heart of man and shalt remain eternal and unchangeable for the
guidance of humanity throughout all future time.
In those days of long ago there came the wave that caused the loss
of faith in God, and when faith went out, fear moved in. For centuries
thereafter, want and crime and cruelty and fear spread their blighting
curse over the race. In the beginning of the sixteenth century Martin
Luther kindled the fires of reason, burned away the burdens of ignorance
and superstition and planted the seeds of hope and faith in the hearts
and minds of the human family. The lightning of his intellect flashed
across the dark, threatening clouds of doubt and unbelief, and the rumbling
thunder of the Reformation was heard in the distance. From out the terrific storm that followed came the American Republic.
Our forefathers founded this Republic on the unlimited suffrage of
the millions of their fellowmen. They spread the mantle of responsibility
upon the shoulders of the people, and with a faith in both God and man
they wove into the Constitution of our country the web of perpetual
existence. One hundred and fifty-six years have passed aw~y since they
declared that God intended all men ·t o be free and equal; alt men, without
restriction, qualification or limitation. As we look back over the intervening decades our hearts must throb with pride when we consider the
a~hie~e~ent of having successfully grappled with, and disposed of, quest10ns mc1dent to human progress, some of which threatened the very life
of the Nation. Across the pages of history there has never been written
such a chapter of accomplishment. The constitutional safeguards thrown.
around the human family by the builders, who laid the foundati~n of
this Nation, have lifted up the people until they, as sovereign citizens, ~it
upon the throne of freedom trammeled only by constitutional rights.
We should make no mistake about the active energy of .the c~nstitu­
tion and laws of our cduntry. With all its roughness and faults the fa~t
remains obvious ·t hat it is the greatest foundation of civil .go~~rnment
known· to history. It gives energy to the wheels of progress, broadens the
avenues of education and places in the hands of the people the power to
determine and extend the limits of their liberties. ·
Our fathers realized; as we do, that this Republic could not 'survive
nor could a people enjoy the benefits of free institutions unless there was
a free, popular education, unimpaired by religious bigotry, ra~ial hatreds
or the selfishness of man. Macaulay said, "It is universally allowed that,
by some means, government must protect our persons and property. This
~eing admitted, can it be denied that the education of the common people
is a most effectual means of securing our persons and our property·?"

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Fully realizing this principle, our immediate ancestors established the free
public school system in order that not only our persons and property
might be secure, but that future generations might not go through life
bearing a burden of prejudices heaped upon them by ignorance. A thousand
foes have in the past and are today assailing our public school system.
Men and women clothed in the garb of American citizenship pose as
teachers in our schools in order · that they may pour the deadly virus of
their disloyalty into the minds of our children. In my official capacity I
have met and grappled with this hydra-headed monster in our schools
within the last six months.

come out from our higher institutions of learning preaching their deadly
atheism, agnosticism, communism, and those other isms which are all
bastard brothers of disloyalty.
There is a rising tide flowing from out our universities that is bearing
the youth of our country away to their spiritual doom and our nation to
oblivion. Grandeur of intellect without truth and morality is a delusion;
it is the union of those gifts and virtues which alone can elevate man to
that dignified station which God intended him to occupy.
These institutions of learning of ours, from the little red school
house to our great universities, should become shrines of patriotism filled
with the spirit of hope and faith, of freedom and justice.
"Long should pause the erring hand of man before it dares to clip
away with the chisel of human reason, one single word graven in the
enduring by the hand of the Infinite God."
It is well fo remember that this nation was founded to carry into
practical effect the beneficent principle that government is instituted for
the advancement and improvement of the people who determine the
government. This is peculiarly true of our nation, for the American
Republic was organized primarily to give to the people of this nation
a freedom denied to them in other lands, to inculcate a love of liberty, to
promote happiness and dispense justice, giving to the people the full
enjoyment of life. We are distinctively a liberty loving people. We believe in the right of freedom of speech, of an untrammeled conscience,
of civil and religious liberty and the dignity of labor. We should never
lose sight of these exalted principles in the turmoil and wild mad rush
of every day life.
The future welfare of our country depends upon our attitude toward
the enforcement of our laws and the tone and spirit in which we perform
our duties as citizens. Our faces should be set against the vain display
of wealth and earthly power, and set -towards rational enjoyment and a .
faithful performance of those services to our country which would
annihilate the influences that are seeking to undermine our system of
government.
As a correlative of our duty to uphold the law it is equally incumbent
upon us to suppress the evils that exist, everywhere tending to lawlessness
and anarchy. We should, too, on every occasion instill in the popular
mind an undivided and unswerving devotion to the American Republic.
We should teach without prejudice and with the kindest feelings that
every citizen should, regardless . of the place of birth, fraternal, political
or religious affiliations, hold this nation above any organization on the
face of the ~arth; that it should receive our undivided loyalty and the
efforts · of our lives should be put forth to preserve it in all its purity .
and strength.

11'

It is time that we, as loyal American citizens, awoke to the dangers
which beset our cherished institutions. This is not a time for silence.
We should not be lulled to sleep by sophistry nor allow the smoothness
of political flattery to blind our minds or obscure our visions concerning
the important question of Public Education. We here have a duty to
perform, vital to the existence of the Republic in which we live. T~e allimportant factor in public education is the school teacher, for he is the
one who does more to direct the mind and mould the character of the
American citizen than any other agency outside of the family, and the
requirements for an American teacher ought to be patriotism of the
highest and most unswerving character, to the end that he be a formative
influence that would enrich the hearts and minds of the youth of America
with patriotic thought. It is our duty to demand such qualifications in
all those who seek to teach the children in our schools.
Theodore Roosevelt said, "To educate a man in mind and not in
morals is to educate a ·menace to society." Some of the most powerful
lessons which wu learn are taught us in the every day lives of men in
their ·every day work, and no man should be allowed to teach in our
schools or universities who, has not reached into his own soul, searched
for and found the -spirit of America. There is a necessary relation between the love of God and the love of countfy. Throw the pilot overboard
and your ship will run upon the rocks and be lost. Leave God and the
moral law out of our schools and universities and the end of the Republic is in sight.
When we think of all the sacrifices and glories of the past, of the
struggles and hardships endured by our fathers and mothers, it appears
to me that our Masonry should be baptized .into a new hope for "humanity.
We cannot hang the shield of our faith in the armory of the past and
expect the deeds of our fathers to release us from the responsibility that
is ours.
America has nothing to fear from outside foes. The only danger to
our national life lurks within the borders of our own couritry: Many of
the enemies of our institutions, along with others who are imported,

115

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

If the principles upon which our country rests are similar to the
fundamental principles of Masonry, and they are in a marked degree, it
is because the spirit of freedom moved throughout the fraternity, giving
energy and power to the voice of liberty. Across the ocean the voices of
Samuel Adams and John Hancock shook the thrones of Europe.
"Freedom of speech is God's training school in which men are educated," and we should use it in ail its power and glory to blast criminals
from their strongholds, fetter and destroy the agencies of crime, and
place American ·citizenship and honor above the tongue of reproach, By
printed page and public utterance we should kindle the fires of righteous
indignation in the hearts and minds of our people against all those who
defy our laws, to such an extent that it will rise a living, vital force that
will descend in fury and destrciy every enemy of society.
Organized greed and crime have snatched the scepter of power from
the hand of decency and honor, and we have lost the sense of God and
the ability to .enforce the law, until a child is not safe in its crib in the
home of its father. The hour has struck when we must consider it a
patriotic duty to emphasize a devotion to the fundamental principles of
the Republic and the majesty of the law. Is the spirit of Washington
lost in the maw of Greed? Are the fires of seventy-six entirely quenched
and the ashes cast to the four winds of heaven? If not, what inftuence
is it that distorts the mind, contaminates the soul and dries up the stream
of American courage in our veins until we sit unconcerned while this
heritage of ours, that has come down to .us at the price of blood, is
trampled in the dust and yet we are not aroused from the slumber of
·
indifference?
Masonry is a Battle and not a Dream. A battle against the vicious
and consuming. elements which .tend to. destroy mankind is the chief busi~
ness ..of Masonry. If .lbere is to be progress we Ga.tlllot escape the conftict.
That :which is Masonry is in constant conftict with the forces of error..
Th.e momentous lesson written in the blood of patrlot.s on · ~ tho'Usan<,!
fields of battle teaches us that it is our duty to see that the free cur.rent
of our country's cOO:Stitutional rights runs on ~obst~~cted. If this 'cu~::
rent .is to continue to widen and de~pen and wash itself .clearer as it . ru~s.
on the agent of civilization, it must find its source in the he.a rts and minds
of men suc!t as are he.re assembled, springing from th.cir .souls and issuing·
fr911) their lips in the daily walks of Ii fe,
· · .·
. The foundation .upon which shall rest not only the progress ·and
.de.velopment of the race, but the future safety of our liberties, mu.st be
laid in the. heart.s and minds o~ our children · .in ·infancy, and upon their
souls m~st !>«; inscribed, ."Under God my first duty. is to.
co.utttry.''. .·
·We need the courage, the moral character, the firm determfnation
and the Masonry of Washington to enable us to stand as a solid. phalanx,.

on the side of truth and justice, in the great eternal conftict between
right and wrong; to lift this noble brotherhood above the common level
of fraternalism and place it upon a higher plane of endeavor worshiping
God, honoring the state and obeying the law.
On this auspicious occasion, rejoicing in the memories of long ago
when California contributed the spirit of her people, together with her ·
golden stores, to preserve this union, we ought as patriotic Americans to
pledge anew our loyalty to the nation of which we are a part. We ought
to. regard every agency of the government as a memorial to the memory
of those who eontributed so much that freedom might be the heritage
of humanity. We ought to look upon all of our institutions as reminders
'of those who fought and labored that we might enjoy the inestimable
benefits of a free nation. We ought to utilize every inftuence in our
'power to teach our citizens a reverence for our National Constitution,
a high regard for the institutions of the nation and a patriotic ardor for
the advancement and integrity of our citizens.
Let us hope and pray that as the years roll away the great eternal
Ruler of the Universe will shower His blessings upon the American
·people, lead and guide our nation in the paths of peace and prosperity,
so that our Republic may stand as a beacon light of · justice, admired
and respected by all the world as the brightest hope for humanity.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of Califomia:
It is with a keen sense of pleasure that I hereby present my twentyfifth annual report of my stewardship. In rendering this report of the
activities incident to my duties as Grand Lecturer, I am forcibly reminded
of the hearty co-operation given me by the vast majority of the brethren,
as well as the valued aid and assistance on the part of each Inspector
during the year just passed. This friendliness has always been evident,
and this year's contacts have differed only incidentally. The splendid tenets
of our Craft have often been brought home to me with recurrent force,
when, perhaps weary and worn out, I have been refreshed by hopeful,
pleasant words and smiles broadcast from friendly faces. These features
of my work have seemed to make my tasks easy and have indeed filled my
heart with gratitude.
I have been assisted materially by the prevailing spirit of a fraternalism, transcendent in its earnestness and charitable in its judgments.
I have received reports from all the Inspectors, all of whom report
the Lodges under their respective supervision to be getting along as well
as can be expected under the circumstances. Most of the Lodges however
are doing very little degree work, many of them supplying their meeting
nights with social and educational• programs; which have proven very
satisfactory.
I cannot say too much in praise of the Inspectors. They have always
been most loyal and always ready and willing to assist and co-operate in
·
every way possible.
A Brother has aptly expressed the definition of fellowship : "·Fellowship is the word which utters, s~ far as a word can, the deepest meaning,
the noblest feeling within the heart of Masonry. This is the truth which
the words of the ritual labor to express and which even symbols are dumb
to interpret. Fellowship! This was the vague something within Masonry
which our early brethren instinctively and half unconsciously groped
after and prized. Men of rank and men of wisdom, men of low degree
and simple men, felt that here was some new thing, something they only
half defined, but something which was wonderful beyond words. We
have not used that word Fellowshrp enough. We have not used enough
the sentiment, the truth, which this word tries to utter." "Fellowship,"
says some one, "is life's most savory delight." It is Fellowship which
makes this Institution a Fraternity. It is the very heart and soul of
Masonry.
I have accompanied the M:. W:. Grand Master at many installations,
dedications and corner-stone layings. The messages which he left on those
occasions were both interesting and inspiring and were greatly appreciated by the brethren.

119

I have visited every district in the state and some of them twice, and
have found the officers and brethren always willing and anxious to perfeet .
themselves in the ritual.
I am ind.ebted to t-he V:. W:. Grand Secretary and his assistant for
many courtesies extended to me in his office during the year.
In spite of the condition of the country, several new Temples have
been erected this year: at Red Bluff, Knights Landing, Lindsay, and
Willits. Several Lodges have taken over buildings and remodeled them.
These Lodges have - taken advantage of the opportunity in building at
·this time. This I am sure will stimulate a greater interest in the Lodges.
All these will be dedicated following Grand Lodge by the incoming Grand
Master.
A Third Degree will be conferred by officers of the Oakland Lodges
under the auspices of Oakland Lodge No. 188.
Thanking the Grand Lodge and the brethren for the confidence reposed in me as your Grand Lecturer.
Respectfully submitted,
THOMAS

J. BAKER,

Grand Lecturer.

During the year ending September 30, 1932, ten Lodges or Temple
Associations have conducted correspondence with your Committee. The
majority of these were only of minor matters, which asked the Committee's opinion as to spending money to remodel their hall or buy a lot, and
only a few involved any great amount of funds. Most of the Lodges felt
that in the present financial depression, they should keep their funds intact
and refrain from going into debt.

ten years, at a monthly rental of $120.00, the entire second floor of a

MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
TRUSTEES REPORT
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
As required by the Constitution, we herewith submit a report of
the property, condition and operation of the Masonic Homes for the
fiscal year just ended.
Immediately after the close of Grand Lodge on October 16, 1931,
the Board organized as follows:
President, C. M. Wollenb~rg (1934);
Vice-President, James B. Gist, Senior Grand Warden;
Chas. Albert Adams (1933);
Samuel E. Burke (1932);
John Stewart Ross (1935);
Frank W. Mixter, Deputy Grand Master;
William A. Sitton, Junior Grand Warden;
William P. Filmer, Treasurer ex-officio;
John Whicher, Secretary ex-officio.
The year has been a trying one, but it is not necessary to remind
you of the business situation nor of the difficulties incident to a proper
maintenance of the Homes, other than to report that the increase of
dependents of Lodges and the decrease of our revenues have added
burdens to the conduct of our business as your agents · charged with
relieving Lodges of the care of their indigent members, to an extent
never before experienced.
State Aid and Tax Relief
In all the history of our Homes it has been the steadfast policy
of Grand Lodge and of the Trustees to maintain the poor of the craft
without invoking the provisions of the State Constitution respecting
public relief for dependents in institutions. In view, however, of the
financial situation and reduced revenues, and having in mind that
institutions similar in character to ours are all receiving aid from
public funds, your Trustees, at a general meeting held February 27,
1932, concluded that they would take advantage of the provisions of
Article XIII, Section lY.a of the Constitution of the State of California, as it was adopted by the people at the general election of
November, 1920, reading in part as follows:
"All buildings, and so much of the real property connected therewith as may be required for the occupation of institutions sheltering
more than twenty orphan or half orphan children, receiving State aid
shall be free from taxation; •••"

126

The necessary steps were taken before the State Department of
Social Welfare and the Assessors of the counties of Los Angeles and
Orange, and the Masonic Homes of California are now relieved
taxation on all the lands and buildings belonging to the Homes at
Covina and Balboa, a yearly saving of approximately six thousand
dollars. The Homes will continue to be relieved of taxation at Covina
and Balboa as long as they shelter more than twenty orphan or half
orphan children subject to Sta.t e aid. The rules of the Department of
Social Welfare with regard to payments for relief to institutions are
very strict, · but this year there are twenty-nine of our children who
come within the provisions of the State law and the rules of the Department, and we will benefit to the extent of $1,129.00 for the first
half of the year, in addition to a large saving in taxes.

of

Outside Care
Following our policy, inaugurated several years ago, of maintaining children at private homes and with the mother whenever
possible, instead of placing them in the Covina Home, we have in the
past year placed 32 children outside the Home. The total number of
children now being assisted outside the Home is 68 from 36 Lodges,
at a monthly expense of $1,085.00, an average per month per child of
$16.00.
We also are contributing $1,850.00 per month to 63 Lodges, for
eighty aged people. The total monthly payments for the relief of
dependents outside of the Homes aggregates more than thirty-five
thousand dollars a year-a severe tax on the Homes revenues.
The above observations are suggested to us largely because of
the continually increasing demands upon the Homes, particularly the
Home for adults at Decoto. Ten years ago there were in the Decoto
Home one hundred and fifty adults dependent upon the Lodges; fiv~
years ago the number had increased to two hundred and twenty-five;
one year ago there were three hundred and twenty-six adults at the
Decoto Home; and now, notwithstanding the loss by death in the
year of sixty-two, you are caring for three hundred and forty-one,
almost the limit of the room capacity of the institution.
Field Worker
In November, 1929, we authorized the Superintendent of the
Covina Home to employ a field worker. A woman trained and experienced in that line has been employed continuously in such capacity
·
since that date. Her duties have included:
(a) The investigation of applications for admissions to both the
Covina and Decoto Homes when such applications originated in or
near Los Angeles.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

126

127

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

(b) The making and executing of plans by which outside relief
or home aid is substituted for admission to the Homes, in that class
of cases where such measures were applicable.
(c) Contact · with families or relatives of children in the Covina
Home, in order that the Home may deal with the children more intelligently, and in order that children may be returned to their relatives . whenever improvement in the financial or domestic conditions
warrants such return.
(d) After-care work for children discharged from the Home, to
assist them in getting a proper start in life.
The employment of a person in this capacity is in line with the
practice in the bes_t institutions in the country. The Trustees have
been able to act more intelligently in determining a large number of
applications for admissions in both Homes because of information
which was secured through this field worker. Lodge officers and
committees of investigation are often handicapped through lack of
experience and skill in collecting information requisite to a proper
determination of requests for admission to the Homes. We feel that
the results so far obtained through the services of our field worker
have been abundantly justified, not only from the standpoint of an
outright saving, but also from the standpoint of rendering the right
kind of aid to those whose care we undertake.
In one case a mother applied for the admission of her two children,
a boy and a girl, to the Masonic Home. After studying the case the
field worker recommended that a monthly allotment of money be
made to assist the mother to keep the children at home with her, and
the application was . so decided by the Trustees. At first the mother
was much disappointed and resented the refusal of the Trustees, to
admit the children to the Home. Within a few months however, when
the new arrangement had been placed on a successful working basis,
she expressed herself as profoundly grateful that she had not been
allowed to separate herself from her children in accordance with her
request when the application was made. We urge all officers of our
Lodges to fully co-operate with our field worker when she approaches
you in the discharge of her duties.
New Forms for Applications
In March, 1932, the Trustees adopted and placed in use new forms
of appfications to take the place of the old application forms of admission to the Covina and Decoto Homes. The new forms were designed somewhat after the manner of those in use in the Pennsylvania
jurisdiction. They are more complete than the old forms and call for
a much greater amount of information.
In conformity with what has come to be our practice they are
applications not specifica_lly for admission to the Homes but rather

for Masonic relief, leaving for determination by the Trustees whether
relief if granted shall be by means of admission to the Homes or by
other means.
·
They call for careful work by the committee of investigation of
the Lodge in which the application originates. After that committee
has made its report and the same has been acted upon by the Lodge,
the application is then reviewed by the Inspector of the district, who
forwards it to the Trustees of the Homes with any comment or
recommendation which he cares to make.
·
We feel that the new forms of application are a distinct improvement on those previously in use and wiH result in a more careful and
discriminating consideration both by Lodge officers and by the Trustees of the Homes before applicants are received into our care.
In taking measures to secure more exact information concerning
those for whom relief ,is requested, both through the field worker an~
through the new application forms, it has not been the intention of
the Trustees to make relief less accessible to those who really. need
it and merit it. However, in the stress of present economic conditions,
we . feel that we are justified in giving the most careful scrutiny to all
applications in order that the funds available shall not be denied to
the r!!lief of deserving cases because of having been allotted to other
cases which had a lesser claim or no claim upon us.
A Word for the Old People
The men and women residents at the Decoto Home are in general
contented, even happy, although very naturally it is difficult for some
of them to readily readjust themselves to a new environment. This is
particularly so with those who have lived for many years in one
private home of their own. The Superintendent and Matron do all
in their power to relieve any condition of home-sickness, and most
of the residents soon adjust themselve.s to their new mode of living
and 'in a few weeks make new contacts and new friendships that.
prove to be a panacea for the loss of the old.
Lodges and members could, and should, render a great service
to their residents at the Decoto Home by writing to them now and
then, to let them know they are not forgotten, and these letters
should take practical form by the inclosure monthly of a .little spending money-say a dollar or two--for knickknacks not provided by the
HCime-not necessarily for essentials.
Motion Picture of Covina Home
A new motion picture of life at the Covina Home is now available
for Lodges and Lodge entertainments. It was the gift of the brethren
of Mount Olive Lodge No. 506, and is a faithful representation of the
daily life of the children.

128

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CAJ.IFORNIA

A scenario was written by Brother Fred Kelsey in collaboration
with other members of the Lodge, and the picture was "shot" during
four days of strenuous work by a crew of twelve picture men, with
an equipment which included a light generator and a dozen Kleig
lights.
The story, as clearly told in the picture, is of an eccentric bachelor
who has amassed a fortune in the diamond fields of ·Africa returns
to New York and learns that the only daughter of his dead brother
is an inmate of an orphanage in California. He traces her to the
Masonic Home at Covina, and comes to the Home full of wrath that
his niece should be in a poor house, resolved to take her away and
lavish upon her everything that money could buy. He finds that she
is not keen about leaving, and proposes to show him something of her
home and its daily life. They go on a tour of the institution, taking
an afternoon and evening and part of the next day. As the uncle
sees the life there his conception of it undergoes a change and after
fully viewing the Home he leaves to his niece the choic~ of going
With him to a life of luxury or of remaining at the Home. She
promptly elects to remain until she finishes high school. Uncle
Charlie is satisfied, returns to New York and adds a codicil to his
will leaving a goodly share of his estate to the Masonic Homes.
Uncle Charlie was played by Brother Charles Crockett well
known as the impersonator of the Grand Master of Hamburg ~t the
get-together dinner in Los Angeles in 1929.
The reels of this interesting picture are now available for the
use of Lodges on request either to Trustee Gist at Los Angeles or to
Trustee Wollenberg or the Secretary of the Homes at San Francisco.
The onl! res.triction as to their use is that they must be displayed by
men tramed in the work of handling moving pictures.

Every possible economy has been practiced. The salaries of staff and
employes have been reduced. The cost of supplies is lower than ever
before, and we have brought down the per capita cost per day at the
Home for adults from 88.6 cents to 77 cents. And at the Home for

we appear before you with a deficit of $9,SS0.19 for the year, which we
are asking Grand Lodge to assume.

adequately providing for our Homes, either throllg'h an increase of per
capita tax or by other means and par ticularly for the rapidly increasing
cost of outside relief, due to demands caused largely by unemployment.

Scholarships
At the present time ten children, graduates of the Home and the
high · school, are participating in the Scholarship fund, at a total annual expense of $3,290.00. These boys and girls all evince interest in
their studies, and in due time will become self-supporting, useful men
and women. ·
Doubtless you will be interested to know that Grayson Merrill, a
graduate from the Covina Home, has finished his second year at the
Naval Academy, Annapolis, and that in a class of five hundred young
men his average standing in engineering, mathematics (in which he
itood 15), electrical engineering and physics, English and History,
and modern language, was forty-five.
Appreciation From a Beneficiary
The following letter of appreciation from an aged woman whose
husband is a chronic invalid, receiving outside relief, is published
because too often beneficiaries complain rather than thank the fraternity for assistance rendered:
"It is with much gratitude and appreciation that I am writing you
this letter for my dear husband and myself, and I trust you will
pardon the seeming liberty I am taking in doing so. But I do so
much want to and have wanted to for some time write and thank
you for what the Masonic Home of California is doing for us, and
we appreciate your great kindness and consideration, more perhaps,
than you have any idea.
"And I only hope and pray that I am worthy of the aid given
us. I know my husband is. He has always been so fine and good.
"It will be three years in September since this seeming misfortune has befallen us. While physically my dear husband is helpless,
thank God, the Giver of all good things, his mind is just as active as
it always was, and he is so patient at all times, and has such a wonderful disposition, and these are the things you know that help us to
carry on. That in caring for him, it is really a labor of love.
"There are times when a feeling of discouragement would try
to creep in and the clouds try to hide the sun, still behind it all I
know the sun still shines, and I realize I have much, oh so much to
be grateful for, and truly I am.
"Again let me thank you and the Trustees of the Homes from
the depths of my heart for my dear husband and me for the aid given
l!s by the good Masons of California. May God bless you and them.
"Gratefully,"

Report of Auditors
To the Board of Trustees, Masonic Homes of California:
In accordance with your instructions, we have made a general
·audit of the books of account of the Masonic Hoines of California,
giving particular attention to the verification of the Balance Sheet
as at July 31, 1932. We present herewith the following statements:
Statements of Accountability for Funds and Properties
Exhibit A: Statement of cash receipts and disbursements, (2
pages).
Exhibit B: Balance sheet, July 31, 1932 (2 pages).
Exhibit C: Statement of net worth.
Schedule B-1: Summarized statement of Entertainment Fund.
Schedule B-2: Summarized statement of Scholarship Fund.

Secretary's Report

Sundry Explanalory Comments ·
After a general review and analysis of the nature of the items
being capitalized to the Covina Improvement account, and following
a conference with the office of the Grand Secretary, an adjustment
was made by writing this account down to an estimated value of
$20,000.00. This adjustment is reflected in the Balance Sheet under
Exhibit B and in the Net Worth account under Exhibit C.
We have written off the note of August and Marie Kangris in
the amount of $1,680.96, due since 1927, on which no principal or
interest payments have been made since that date. This note is considered valueless. This note has been carried as a part of the securities
Special Rule No. 16.
By way of explanation, we wish to point out that, under Exhibit
A, the summarized closing statement setting out the composition of
cash funds as at July 31, 1932, contains certain amounts due to and
from the Endowment Fund bank accounts. These items consist of
transfers not made as at July 31, 1932.
Certificate
We certify th~t, in our opinion, the attached statements, with
exception as to the st;lted value of the securities on hand and the
actual values of the fixed properties at Decoto and Covina, set forth
the condition of the Masonic Homes of California at July 31, 1932,
and that a proper accounting has been made of all receipts and disbursements.
·
Respectfully submitted,
Rucx:STELL & LAND, Certified Public Accountants.
By FLOYD T. WEBB.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Report of Superintendent-Decoto

To the Board of Tr~tees:
I herewith present for your consideration my twenty-third annual
report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Decoto, California,
for the year ending August 31, 1932.
There has been the usual reutine in the management of the Home,
without any special changes, during the past year.
A year ago the Administration building, consisting of five floors
and basement, was· completed. Since then the rooms have been comfortably furnished, and are now occupied by the women residents.
The rooms they vacated in the East Wing building are now occupied
by men residents of the Home.
The men and women residents of the Home are now permanentl'Y
located, which has enabled the management to systematize the workings of the several departments and has led in no small measure to a
more practical carrying on of the daily life of the Home, and so
meeting the physical, mental and spiritual needs of our large family.
Members-There are now at the Home 341 residents-184 men
and 157 women. During the year 79 persons have been admitted48 men and 31 women ; 62 have passed away-40 men and 22 women.
There have been two departures.
Health-The general health of the Home has been normal, with
the exception of those who have become infirm and feeble owing to
advancing years.
Hospital-There are now 50 persons being cared for at the Coleman hospital. The facilities afforded by our hospital department
enable our physician and nurses to give every care and attention to
those who are ill. Day and night nurses are in constant attendance.
Industrial-Alt the members of the Home are encouraged to
render some service in keeping with their strength, and during their
leisure hours to interest themselves in healthful and wholesome diversions for their general well-being. During the past year a number
of the Brethren have contributed to the welfare of the Home by their
services in the engine room, carpenter, paint, and barber shops, care
of the garage, mail, passenger and freight service, kitchen, pantry,
vegetable room, laundry, store rooms, clerical work, telephone switchboard, care of elevators, flower beds, watering trees and shrubs, care
of walks, roads and lawns, vegetable garden and poultry yards, janitor
work and many other light duties in a general way.
The women of the Home attend to the making, marking and
mending of linen sheets, pitlow slips, table cloths, etc., also assist in
the preparing of fruit and vegetables, in the kitchen and dining rooms,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

153

diet kitchen, clerical work, attending telephone calls, music room,
showing visitors about the Home, care of their rooms, the halls and
general light household duties.
Farm-There has been no change in the management of the farm.
The greater part of the hill ranch has as in the past been leased either
on shares or cash rental. Our share of the hay crop has been more
than sufficient for the needs of the farm departments, the surplus
being sold in the local market. The orchards have supplied plenty of
fruit, figs and nuts for table use, the surplus being sent to the drier
and stored for winter use. The garden has furnished a variety of
vegetables, berries and greens. The chicken ranch has supplied a ll
eggs for table use; 12,000 have been put down in water glass. Alt
over and above our needs have been sold in the San Francisco market.
There has been a slight decrease in our water supply, owing to
the lowering of the water level in connection with our deep well
pump. So far we have been able to keep our reservoirs full at a ll
times, and they have peen equal to all demands made upon them for
household, lawns, fire and irrigating purposes.
Social Life-All holidays have been observed, with appropriate
exercises. The specials are those which were held on New Year's
Eve, New Year's Day, Lincoln's and Washington's Birthday, Easter,
Memorial Day, Fourth of July, Hallowe'en, Thanksgiving and Christmas.
Many splendid programs, stage plays, band and orchestra concerts, have been provided during the year by visiting Lodges, Eastern
Star Chapters, and friends, for the entertainment of the members of .
the Home, the evening often closing with dancing. From time to time
entertainments are prepared entirely by members of the Home, consisting of vocal and instrumental music, readings, recitations, community singing, stage sketches, cards, games, dancing, etc. Tuesday
evenings are devoted to cards, and Friday evenings to chorus practice.
The croquet grounds are well patronized during the day. Services are
held every Sunday afternoon in the Assembly hall. A reading class
for the blind meets daily in the reception room, during which the daily
papers are read to them by one of the ladies of the Home. A number
of the members of the Home have radio sets in their rooms. T his
privilege is particularly appreciated by those who are blind and by
those who are being cared for in the hospital. The club rooms and
the reception room also have radios, which may be enjoyed at any
time during the day and evening.
Library and Club Rooms--There are now 5,800 books on the
shelves of our main library and branches located in the several departments of the Home. The Masonic Hill branch of the Alameda
County Free Library enables our family to obtain many of the latest

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

books, and an opportunity for special ones. In addition, we are the
recipients, through friends and members of the fraternity, of daily
papers, magazines and periodicals, which are placed on the tables of
the library, club rooms, and social halls.
Arrangements have been made whereby members of the family,
a few at a time, may enjoy an outing to nearby places of interest, also
an occasional visit to nearby Lodges and Eastern Star chapters. During the year many trips were made to Oakland, San Francisco, San
Jose, and towns in the vicinity of the Home.
Grand Master Robert B. Gaylord, officers and members of the
Grand Lodge have made a number of visits to the Home during the
year, and a large number of Brethren from various Lodges have spent
many pleasant hours with us: The number of visits this year indicates
an increasing interest in the welfare of the Home family.
I desire to express my appreciation of the efficient and conscientious work on the part of the officers and employees whose earnest
efforts have been a factor in maintaining a high standard of service
throughout the several departments of the Home, and to thank the
Board of Trustees for their kindly assistance and for the many acts of
courtesy received.
·
FRANK B. HARTMAN, Superintendent.

Report of the Superintendent-Covina
To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes:
During the past summer, while on her vacation, the Home nurse,
"Nurse Jane," as the children familiarly call her, visited some of the
former girls of the Home, who now live in San Francisco. After
her return she wrote a letter about her visit, from which I quote. I
have substituted fictitious names for the real ones; the number in
connection. with each name indicates the dates of admission and discharge from the Covina Home:
"I took five days at the end of my vacation to pay a long prom-.
ised visit to Sally Smith (1922-1928), now Mrs. John M. Jones, who
lives in San Francisco. John met me at the Ferry and on the way
to their home was full of news of their little family. Sally has a
beautiful little girl two and a half years old and an equally beautiful
little boy five months. They are very well behaved children.
Sally is very stout, but otherwise the same Sally she was while in
the Home. They live in a rented house of five large rooms, nicely
furnished, with every convenience including an electric washer and
ironer. The next day, Charles Johnson (1917-1930) came to see
me at Sally's house. Charles has grown much taller and weighs
twenty pounds more than when he left us. He has finished his premedical course at Berkeley, where he has attained an honor-student
standing. I think seeing me made him homesick to visit the Home
again.

•

179

"Sally and I went to see Dora Hamilton (1916-1928) and Virginia
. Edwards (1913-1923) at Virginia's home. Virginia is t hin from
nursing her big husky boy, six months old. She is the same old
Virginia, happy with any present situation. I didn't see her husband
as he was on duty; he is a cook at a hospital. The other girls lik~
him,. and Virginia seems very much in love and that is all that
matters after all. Virginia's place is in one of those crowded apartment house districts-front room, small dark bedroom and kitchenette.
I just missed seeing Katherine Edwards (1913-1928). Dora Hamilton
was at Virginia's. She seems very much subdued and is not the
pert Dora of old. She is thin, smokes a lot, and says she is supervising night clinic at ...........•...... Hospital. After visiting there we
all crowded into John's car (John is a good sport and not afraid
of hen parties) and went over to Emma Nelson's (1922-1927). Emma
seems very happily married and has a very presentable husband. He
has steady work and seems to be doing well. Their baby is two
months old and does not seem to be doing well on the food she has
been getting. Emma phoned Sally on the morning of my departure
to get the address of the Clinic. The young mothers all decided that
they could get better service at much · Jess cost by patronizing the
Clinic. It was very amusing to hear the general talk of babies clinics
weights, ages, formulas, diapers, and such. The young h~sband~
were as much interested as the girls and expressed themselves as
freely.
"The following Tuesday Sally gave a luncheon for me, all
planned and engineered very nicely and successfully. E mma Nelson
came with her baby. Virginia couldn't get there as her husband
was starting on his vacation. Barbara Reynolds (1925-3()) and
Alice Reynolds (1925-1930) were there. They are both thin and
are working very hard at summer school. I was interested to notice
the congenial way the girls visited-how they were pleased at each
other's success and the absence of gossip about the Home and the
ex-Masonic Homers in general.
"As a whole I had a very interesting and enjoyable visit in
San Francisco."
I have thought it worth while to quote from this letter at length
because I think it contains in and between its lines the answer to .
a question which is often asked : Does life in the Masonic Home
produce normal human beings w.ho are capable of going out into
society and taking their place there in a natural and wholesome
manner ? It has sometimes been charged that an experience of
being brought up in an institution hinders boys and girls, particularly
girls, from a subsequent normal domestic life. Apparently their
experience in the Masonic Home has not had this effect upon the
lives of the girls referred to in this letter.

180

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Masons of California want the Covina Home to be a Home
and not an institution. They want it to be a place where children
who have been deprived of natural home advantages can live happy
lives while they are being instructed and trained toward useful and
successful careers. To attain these objects there must be a nice
balance between allowing on the one hand, the expression of their
spontaneous desires, and the r·equirement on the other hand, that they
take on the habits of civilized human beings. We are attempting
contantly to examine our own work and measure its achievements
in the light of these objectives.
The operation of the Home during the past year has been
substantially on the same lines as for the last several preceding
years. The present is not a time for innovations; we should be content if we can hold the gains made during previous years. During
the past year the objectives and problems of the Home have been
discussed in the weekly staff meetings, participated in by housemothers and others directly connected with the care of the children.
If you had attended these staff meetings from week to week throughout the year, you would have been impressed with the capable and
devoted effort that is being put forth by those immediately in charge
of our boys and girls.
We have our problems and they are not few. Child welfare writers
are prone to assert that all children are naturally "good" and that
only a little encouragement is needed for them to develop in the
most gratifying manner. If it were as easy as that our job would
have little significance. While most of our children learn with comparative ease those habits and attitudes which society requires, a
certain proportion in any group present problems, sometimes of the
most difficult character. In dealing with such children we must
have in mind the welfare of the problem child himself but must
not forget the welfare of the other children in the group. 'Sometimes
a child comes so completely into ·conflict with his environment at
Covina that it is necessary to remove him. This happens with boys
more often than with girls, not because they are worse but because
they are less docile, more adventurous and have · more initiative.
Nevertheless it may happen that in the interest of the peace and
harmony of the Home atmosphere they must be placed elsewhere.
To "expel" them for bad conduct under such circumstances would in
many cases be to place upon them · an unmerited stigma, and it would
not benefit them.
The fraternity is inclined to have a blind faith in their institution
at Covina, to believe that once a child is admitted within those portals
all will be well. If the Home is so arranged and conducted as to
rrieet the needs of the average child, by the same token the unaverage

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

181

child will need some other program. We have furnished this alternative
program for a limited number of children by placement outside the
Home with access to special school facilities or other special opportunities to meet the child's peculiar needs. For instance, one "bad"
boy was sent to the California Polytechnic School at San Luis
Obispo, where he successfully learned the welder's trade.
In June of this year five bo.ys and five girls of the Home graduated from the Covina High School and were returned to their
Lodges. In some of these cases the return to the Lodges was only a
nominal procedure, because during the years when the Home had
been caring for the child the Lodge had completely lost sight of its
ward. I believe there should be emphasis on the fact that when a
Lodge places a child under our care it agrees that it will "receive
said child when dismissed from the Home." What such "receiving"
means may be open to various interpretations. However, it should
be self-evident that it can not be regarded as the Home's duty to
carry its children to a point where they are fully capable of stepping
out into the world and proceeding without further guidance. Some
Lodges have regarded seriously their responsibility for their wards
upon discharge from the Home, making a sincere and effective effort
to help the boy or girl in getting launched in life. I think it desirable
that the Hom~ make a more systematic effort to keep Lodges
informed about and interested in their wards during their period of
residence in the Home. This could be done by a periodical report
dealin~ with their physical condition, educational progress, vocational
aptitude, general behavior, and character development.
Of the boys who graduated this year, one boy was fortunate
in obtaining immediate employment in a manufacturing company;
one boy has entered the Frank Wiggins Trade School in Los
Angeles to learn the trade of automobile mechanic. A third boy 1 who
finished his high school course with high grades, is ambitious for a
college education, but owing to demands previously made upon the
Scholarship Fund, it seems that it will not be possible for him to be
financed from that source. The two remaining boys of the graduating class have been returned to their mothers and both are looking
about to find such employment as they can.
One of the girls has entered a hospital to take a training course
for nursing; her expenses during her training will be taken care
of through her Lodge. A second girl has entered the University of
California at Los Angeles where she will take a course preparing
herself for teaching; her unusually high marks received during her
high school course as well as her general characteristics of resourcefulness and initiative seem to justify her ambition. She is fortunate
in the fact that her deceased father's life insurance was placed in a

182

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

trust fund to care for her education. Two other girls of this class
are taking courses in a business college, while another is planning to
enter a junior college.
There is a tendency for some of our young people to leave the
Home imbued with ambitions for academic education out of proportion to their ability. Sometimes, too, they announce vocational
choices, such as . dramatic director, radio announcer, costume designer, artist, aviator, airplane designer, which would only be justified in those having extraordinary ability. It is oftentimes our task
in these cases to translate their ideas into more practical terms.
A problem which must be constantly in our thoughts is that
of how much we should do for our children in the way of supplying·
them not only with necessities, but also with comforts and luxuries.
If we care for them on too restricted a scale, in other words, if we
make their lives in the Home too harsh and severe, if there is too
great a discrepancy between their scale of living and that of the
other children with whom they are associated in the Covina community, there is danger that they will become stamped with a sense of
inferiority that will destroy their courage and their sense of selfrespect. On the other hand, if they are given too much, if their
lives are too easy and effortless, they will become soft and flabby,
will have a false sense of their own worth, will feel. that the world
owes them a living, and will be ill-prepared to fight the hard battle
of life.
The test should be found in the reactions which they present
when they go up against the situations confronting them after they
leave .the Home. A study of the behavior and performance of the
Masonic Home children after they leave our care seems to me to
indicate that their life in the Hoine has not unfitted them to sustain
the trials of real life. While in some cases they leave us with
rather lofty ideas, and while some of their initial gestures would
· seem to indicate that they have been too much pampered, if we
follow them in their reactions in the face of stress and difficulty,
they exhibit a stamina and a courage which speaks well for their
training while in the Home. The world has a way of saying to
them in no uncertain terms, especially in these present difficult
times, that they are not so smart as they thought they were. The
thing that. is significant is the amount of "comeback" which they
show under these circumstances and the ability which they exhibit to
get up and keep on fighting when knocked down. While they do
not all make a good showing when confronted with difficulties and
discouragements, most of them do.
The rule which you adopted two years ago, requiring each boy
or girl having reached the age of sixteen to make an application for

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

183

reappointment annually, and to sustain that application by evidence
·that they merit to be carried in the Home another year, has undoubtedly had a most salutary effect. I~ has brought to these older
children a more just conception of their relationship to the Home,
and the value to them of its opportunities. There may be some
question as to whether we have not been too generous in granting
reappointments. In my judgment the applicant who is petitioning
to be maintained in the Home during his seventeenth or eighteenth
year should have some positive qualities and achievements to recommend him, qualities of co-operativeness and helpfulness in the Home.
He should be an active force in promoting good citizenship in the
Home community; he should be a leader, and a leader in the right
direction. His last year in the Home should be the year in which
he demands . the least and gives the most; he should be thinking
more about his duties than about his rights. If he cannot rise to
this conception of his relationship to the institution and to the
younger children in it, I question whether he should be reappointed.
JOHN M. DowNEN, Superintendent.

MORNING SESSION
Wednesday, October 12, 1932.
Grand Lodge was called on at 10 o'clock, the Grand
Master presiding.
The minutes of Tuesday's sessions were read and approved.
The Grand Secretary was directed to telegraph to Past
Grand Masters Thomas Flint and George M. Perine the
greetings of their brethren in Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON ACCOUNTS
To the M.' . w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Accounts has the honor to report that in conformity with the regulations of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge, we
have audited all bills which have been paid by Grand Lodge.
Your Committee has carefully observed the system of filing and
auditing all accounts of all current bills of the Grand Lodge and we feel
it opportune at this time to commend the Grand Secretary's office for the
efficient manner in which all accounts have been handled.
Respectfully submitted,
• -r
Lours SUTTER,
E. E. CONN,
PAUL NATHAN,

OTTO FREYERMUTH .

v. E. PERRY,

Committee.

Adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS
To the M.' . w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Returns herewith submits its annual report:
The business depression is still with us--only worse. So much so
that our fraternity has had to fall in line with the rest of the community

and report a falling off in membership. There is no need to raise a wail
of woe over the circumstance. We believe the loss is entirely due to the
distressful times, and not to anything wrong with Masonry.
The membership, as of July 31, 1932, is 140,636, which is a loss for
the year of 1,786. This is the first time a decrease of membership has
been shown.
Again there has been a falling off in the number of candidates raised.
This year 3,230 attained the third degree, compared with 4,465 in the
previous year.
Members holding dual membership increased 12 during the year, and
now number 22.
The number of deaths during the year is 1901, an increase of 134.
It is in trying times like these the test comes, and there is a survival
of the fittest. Three thousand one hundred and seventy-three have been
suspended for non-payment of dues, an increase of 571 over last year. And
4,941 members have had their dues remitted, compared with 2,959 for the
previous year. Some Lodges have suspended ten per cent of their membership for non-payment of dues, and remitted the dues of very few; and
some have suspended none, and remitted the dues of more ·t han ten per
cent of their membership. We believe each Lodge is the best judge of its
own affairs, but there must be a great difference in the membership of
Lodges.
Herewith follows the names of, the Lodges making annual returns and the
amount due by each :

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the M. •. w. ·. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report of its activities during the past year, together with its recommendations.
During the past year the Committee suffered an irreparable loss in
the death of its Chairman, Brother Arthur M. Ellis. He had pioneered
in this work and for four years had directed the activities of the Committee
and was looking forward with pleasurable anticipation to the completion
of our labors this year. His quiet, constant, painstaking research had given_
him a wider knowledge and insight into California's early Masonic history
than was possessed by any other member of the fraternity. Fortunately,
much of that knowledge has been reduced to written records and is preserved, but some very valuable information, the result of his personal
efforts during the previous year, has been lost to the craft through his untimely death. California Masonry. and the citizens of the State at large
will deeply miss his kindly presence and mourn his passing.
At the last communication of the Grand Lodge, your committee expressed the belief that it would be able to complete its research work in
the existing records of the subordina;te Lodges within the year. We are
pleased to report that we have practically finished our labors, with the exception of a few of the younger Lodges which have not yet finished the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

search of their records but have active committees earnestly endeavo~ing
·t o bring to conclusion their reports, and these will undoubtedly be · filed
.
' with the committee within a very short time.
In July of this year we were able to dispense with the services of our
field investigator who was employed to visit the different Lodges fQr the
purpose of locating old records and submitting reports o_n the interesting
and instructive facts contained therein.
We are also pleased to report that we were able to carry on this year's
activities at a cost much less than was estimated in our last Annual Report
and we have an unused ·balance of approximately $650 which is turned
back to Grand Lodge.
The activities and investigations of your committee covering the past
four years have cost Grand Lodge approximately $8,147.18. We consider
this an extremely conservative expenditure considering the time involved
in our investigations, the long historical period covered, the number of
Lodges visited and reported on, . the extent of territory necessarily
traversed, the vast amount of information collected and the numerous difficulties encountered.
. As a result of the labor of your committee during the past four years,
there is now a complete summary of the records and early activities of
subordinate Lodges on file in the offices of the Grand Secretary. These
files also contain the history and interviews of many of our very interesting
Fifty Year Masons, together with numerous humart interest stories involving the lives and activities of many of California's most colorful Masonic
characters; also historical facts connected with Masons in the State which
have never been converted to the printed page; facts which reflect and
interpret controversial questions having to do with events in which Masons
took a prominent part; a large group of pictures of the buildings in California dedicated to Masonic purposes; reconstructed and pieced together
stories and history of the activities of old Lodges whose records have long
been lost or destroyed ; copies of documents and papers of unusual historical interest connected with the official and personal acts of pioneer
Masons; and numerous references to valuable source material involving
California Masons and Masonry contained in the Bancroft and State
Libraries.
We have a separate file for each Lodge and all records are contained
in a steel cabinet under lock and key in possession of the Grand Secretary's
office so that the records will be protected from fire or mishandling. In
addition, there are two separate sets of records in the hands of the committee which are used for reference work without disturbing the master
file. These are kept in different locations and under fireproof conditions
as a further protection against loss.
Experience has shown that the work of preserving our historical data
should have commenced at the very beginning of our Masonic activities.

Many of our valuable records and treasures are known to have been lost
by fire. Others were lost through careless storage and the vicissitudes of
time. In several instances we have been able to locate lost records and
restore them to permanency. Each year results in new discoveries, and
with the interest that has been aroused throughout the state, we hope that
other dusty attics and remote places may ·bring forth additional records.
Every member of the craft can be of assistance in this matter and should
be ever alert in search of these early records and historical relics.
The committee again desires to urge upon the older Lodges-particularly those on the Mother Lode-the vital necessity of providing a safe
fireproof repository for their priceless records. T ime and fire are the
ruthless enemies of the written page and it is too late when these twin
destroyers have completed their devastating work.
We find that the Rosters and Tylers' registers of many of our older
Lodges contain the actual signatures of Masons who have stood high in
the hearts of the people of California and of the Nation and these valuable
records should be adequately protected and preserved.
Several California Lodges have adopted a unique policy which we
believe will be of interest and value to the Craft and should be followed
by all of the Lodges in the state. They are keeping scrapbooks in which
are posted newspaper clippings and other printed matter relating to the
activities of their members, the Lodge and the community. As time progresses, these scrapbooks will contain material not found in Lodge books
and records and will furnish much valuable data for future Masonic
Historians.
At the last Annual Conununication, Grand Lodge instructed this committee to prepare a Masonic play having for its purpose the portrayal of
the lives and activities of those interesting Masonic characters who in the
early days played a conspicuous part in the development of northern
California. ' We were instructed to present the same at the present session
of Grand Lodge. We accordingly collected the necessary historical facts
and a drama was written by Brother Jesse M. Whited. Brother John
McEwing was selected to direct and present the same. W hile Brother
McEwing was gathering the proper information for correct costuming
and staging of the play, he was stricken and never recovered. In the very
limited time that was left, it did not seem advisable to make any further
attempt to present the drama at this time. The manuscr ipt for the play
has been placed in the Grand Lodge files for use at a future date.
We have not seen fit to incorporate herein at length a resume of the
vast amount of material collected by the committee during the past year
but will content ourselves for the purposes of this report ·by presenting a
few items and stories which we think will be of interest to the craft:
· The committee continues to find evidence indicating that the Indians
in the early days were familiar with Masonic signs.

218

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In the early 60's Fred Peed, a Mason, was traveling.in the vicinity of
Fall River in northern California. He there met a Pit River Indian who
gave him a Masonic sign and informed him that the Hat Creek Indians
intended to kill him. The Indian traveled with him through that section
of the country. After leaving this friendly guide Peed came upon a band
of Indians with the chief riding in the lead, their bows and arrows ready
for action. His horse was crippled and tired and his ammunition exhausted; escape.was impossible. In desperation he gave the Masonic sign
of distress. The· leader of the group beckoned him to come forward. He
refused to do this. Presently the leader approached him, talked in a
friendly manner and directed two of his band to guide him on his way
north.
The following rather unusual incident occurred in San Francisco Bay
in 1849:
Brother Alexander Montgomery, after whom Montgomery Street
was named, was the commander of a vessel entering the bay. As the
vessel approached the inner harbor a passenger called his attention to a
vessel evidently in distress anchored some distance away. Montgomery
.directed his glasses toward the vessel and there beheld a man leaning over
its side waving a white rag on which was crudely drawn the square and
compass. He ordered a boat lowered and the crew boarded the vessel.
They there encountered an insane man who had taken possession, keeping
the passengers and crew at bay with a revolver and knife. They subd,ued
the mad man and rescued the crew and passengers, which included several
Masons. The one who had improvised and waved the signal was a Mason.
In the early 50's Dr. Ware was mining in the vicinity of Weaverville.
He built a dam and diverted the water of a nearby stream for use in his
mining operations. The miners placering on the stream below resented
this action and rather unceremoniously destroyed the dam and released
the waters. Dr. Ware preferred charges against the ringleaders and
procured their arrest..
Feeling ran high and as the evening approached a large group of
miners congregated in the vicinity of the principal saloon of the town and
were in the process of organizing a mob to hang Dr. Ware when a citizen
of the community apprised John Carr, a ·blacksmith, who had recently
joined the Masonic fraternity, of the fact that Dr. Ware was a Mason
and that the mob seemed intent on hanging him. Carr strapped on his
six-shooters and called to his side all those whom he knew tq be Mas 0 ns
and by quick, determined action frustrated the murderous intent of the
liquor-inflamed mob, thereby saving the life of a worthy bro.t her Mason.
Northern California has produced some of the finest citizens of the
state, among whom was Wi11iam Lowden, for many years an honored
resident of Trinity County and a member of the fraternity. He was the
father of good roads in northern California, having built ~he ~rst road in

th~t section ~rom Shasta to Weaverville. He completed that road of fifty
miles expe_ndmg thereon less than $30,000. Road engineers have estimated
that to build the same road today with its numerous cuts and fills would
probably entail an expenditure far in excess of that amount.
In his younger days Brother Lowden was a rider for the Adams Express Company. There was much rivalry between the Adams Company
and the Wells Fargo Company in their desire to procure the contract for
c~rrying t~e mail between Shasta and Weaverville. They agreed to decide the dispute on a horse race. Lowden was chosen to ride for the
Adams Compan~. But in ~he first ten miles of the fifty-mile race young
Lowden so outdistanced his competitor that the Wells Fargo Company
acknowledged defeat and its rider quit the race. But young Lowden rode
the full fifty miles in a time which has never been equalled between those
communities, :iding over dimly defined, uncertain trails, fording streams
and encountering at the end of the journey one of the most terriffic blizzards ever known in that section of the state.
In the town of Downieville in the early 50's a man shot a Mason
without provocation or excuse. A posse was formed and gave chase but
he made good his escape. Two years passed and word was received in
D?wnieville that the murderer had ·been apprehended in Oregon and was
bemg brought back for trial. The day the word was received a citizen of
the town, in a conversation with one of the merchants said that it had
been. his ?bservation in· the west that those who seriou~ty harm Masons
are. mvanably a_pprehended and brought to justice, and he expressed a
de~1re to know JUst how this desperado had been captured after so long
a time. He a~so expressed a desire to join a fraternity whose long strong
arm reaches mto every part of this half-civilized country. The merchant
he was then addressing was a Mason and on the night of the murder
had written a minute description of the assassin and sent that description
to all Masons he knew on the western coast, and one of tHese letters
reached a Mason in Oregon, who committed the description to memory
and thus, after almost two years, he recognized the killer of the Californfa
Mason and caused his arrest.
