Brother John Fischer, who resides in Placerville, is in many_respects
one of the most interesting Masonic characters in California and for 23
years he was Master of Hiram Lodge No. 43 at El D~rado: At the
Masonic celebration at Coloma in 1928, Grand Master Will Fischer, at

GRA:SD LODGE OF CALIFOR::-;'IA

221

the request of the members of Hiram Lodge, presented Brother John
Fischer with a large Past Master's Jewel, in appreciation of his long
years of service as an officer of their Lodge. Brother Fischer tells the
story of the trials and struggles of the brethren of Hiram Lodge as
follows:
"Old Hiram Lodge has upon its Roster the names of some of the
finest men in California and has held high the ·banner of Masonry on
the Mother Lode for over 75 years. Hiram Lodge waxed strong in the
old days and was an important factor in the moral and social life of the
community. Eventually the placers played out and the young Masons
scattered to the four winds and left but a few of the faithful to carry on.
"For several years the struggle was intense and then we suffered our
first major financial loss. Our Treasurer defaulted for $1,500, and left
us heavily in debt. The brethren met and counseled as to what action
they should take. Some were in favor of surrendering the charter but
finally each member went deep into his pocket and the treasury was
replenished and the Lodge continued its activities. Years later a second
Treasurer defaulted for $500 and again the faithful brethren resorted to
their almost depleted pocketbooks and old Hiram was able to meet its
obligations. One night in September, 1923, the alarm of fire was sounded
throughout the little town of El Dorado and, lo and behold-the Temple
of Hiram was in flames and in a short time nothing was left but a
pathetic heap of ruins. Everything belonging to the Lodge was lost.
The next morning I visited the site of our beloved Temple to view the
remains. It almost broke my heart as I looked upon that mass of fallen
bricks, twisted iron and smouldering debris that once had been the pride
of the Masons of old El Dorado, and as I turned to go away, the tears
streaming down my weatherbeaten cheeks, in abject despair I cried aloud,
'Goodbye Hiram, this is the last.' But today I regret my lack of faith.
I underestimated the spirit of California Masons, for when the news
spread throughout the state that the beloved Temple of old Hiram-that
old Lodge that never acknowledged defeat-was in ashes, the great heart
of California Masonry responded and, thanks to that ·wonderful spirit,
we were able to erect a new Temple on the spot hallowed by the memories
of more than half a century."
.
The following story was related to the committee by Brother C. F ..
McGlashan, who was the author of the History of the Donner Party:
"When a young man, Brother McGlashan lived in a little mining
town on the Mother Lode. It was his custom during the summer evenings
to frequent the principal salopn of the town and, as a mere observer,
enjoy the festivities there indulged in. One evening, while standing in
the corner of the saloon, his attention was attracted to a large crowd of
miners congregated in front of the bar.

"At one end s.tood a rather tall, muscular man imbibing quite freely
and showing the effects of his indulgence. A~ the other en? of th~ bar
stood a much smaller man in conversation with some of his associates.
Presently the large man made some uncomplimentary. ·remar~s directed
to the smalJer man. The lie was passed and approbnous epithets were
voiced back and forth. The miners in front of the bar moved. back .to
give the anger-inflamed combatants a fair field. The large. fellow, w1~
deliberate step, approached the other end of the bar, takmg ~rom his
belt a large, ugly-looking knife, and indicating in no uncertain terms
the serious damage he intended to ·inflict upon .his much smaller antagonist, whose face was as white as a sheet and who stood there apparently
helpless, trembling like an aspen leaf. When the lar~e man approached
within striking distance, the smaller man made a sign and .the larger
man stopped as though he had encountered a wall, looked the little fellow
squarely in the eye, sheathed his knife and turned and _walked sl~wly out
of the room, a sober Master Mason, for when that sign was gr~en, he
remembered its significance which he learned the night he was raised to
the sublime degree of Master Mason."

Samuel Duncan, a Mason and a member of a Lodge under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, resided in San Bruno,

We appreciate the fact that the great body of the craft earnestly
desires that the history of Masonry in California be immediately converted to the printed page and made available.
During the past year insistent requests from brethren all over the
state have been received by the committee, urging that the data already
collected be placed in book form, that the membership may be stimulated
and inspired by the lessons of those sturdy pioneer brethren who came to
California in the early days and who took a leading part in the affairs
of this state and its people. With this sentiment, the committee is in
unanimous accord. We believe that our history should be prepared and
published in suitable form as soon as is . practically possible; however,
the preparation and publication of a history as comprehensive as ours,
covering a period from 1826 up to date, involves problems of policy and
finance which we ·believe are not within the purview of this committee
to solve.
We originally were commissioned and instructed by Grand Lodge to
pursue research work and to gather and preserve facts pertaining to
the history of Masons and Masonry and we have obeyed that mandate
to the letter. It is true that in our reports last year we requested authority
to investigate this question of preparation and publication and were so
authorized, but after consulting with the best historians in California

224

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and later conferring with many of the most active members of Grand
Lodge, we have reached the conclusion that it is part of wisdom to refer
this matter to the incoming Grand Master for appropriate action. We
therefore respectfully recommend that the incoming Grand Master be
instructed and empowered to appoint a committee whose duty it shall
be to devise ways and means whereby the available Masonic historical
data may be prepared and publish~ in suitable form.
While this is in the nature of a final report by your committee, the
gathering of historical data is never fully completed. History is constantly in the making and our acts today are history tomorrow. For these
reasons there should be a continued effort to keep our historical record
up to date; however, we feel that this work can be done on a voluntary
basis without the aid of a field investigator, as was required in going
d~rough our former records. No further appropriations are needed for
this work at this time. It can be carried on by voluntary service, just as
much of the work has been done in the past by committeemen without
remuneration, ·by Inspectors, by subordinate Lodge officers, and by . the
local History Committees.
· We find that there is much follow-up work to be accomplished-all
of our Fifty-Year Masons should be interviewed and their stories obtained ; sources of information not yet investigated should be scrutinized;
some of the reports on important Masonic personages and events are
fragmentary and incomplete and should be supplemented and verified.
We believe that the Committee on Masonic History should be continued
during the ensuing Masonic year, and will so recommend.
We desire to express our appreciation for the generous, whole-hearted
co-operation afforded the committee by the present Grand Master, the
Past Grand Masters, and our Grand Secretary, Brother John Whicher,
and his patient, hard-working staff. We also desire to acknowledge the
deep debt of gratitude we owe the Inspectors and local Lodge committees
for the exceptionally fine work they have performed and the very great
assistance they have rendered the committee. Without exception they
have heartily responded to our many requests for help and have greatly
lightened our burdens and shortened our work. This is the true spirit
of Masonry-the spirit which has characterized the members of the fraternity as far back as our investigations have gone. It is this spirit which
has made our history of which we are so justly proud.
We hereby respectfully offer the following resolution and move its
adoption:
1. That the Committee on Masonic History be continued
during the ensuing Masonic year.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

225

2. That the incoming Grand Master be instructed and empowered to appoint a committee to work out the most feasible
and economic plan for the preparation and publication of the
History of Masonry in California.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The Committee appointed by the M. ·. W. ·. Grand Master to assist
the constituent Lodges in the celebration of the George Washington Bicentennial begs leave to submit the following report of its activities:
On January 25, 1932, the M.". w:. Grand Master, in a circular
letter to the Masters and brethren of the Lodges, called -attention to the
observance this year by the American people of the 200th anniversary of
the birth of George Washington and suggested that our participation
should be twofold, to-wit: as Lodges and as individuals. To assist the
Lodges in this observance, he appointed two committees, one for the
northern and the other for the southern portion of our State. A copy
of the Grand Master's said letter is hereto attached for more further
particulars.
Pursuant to said appointment said Committee addressed to the Masters of the Lodges a letter under date of February 11, 1932, urging a
participation by the members of the Lodges in all civic celebrations and
requesting that a committee be appointed in each Lodge to arrange and
supervise cclebra~ions within the Lodge. We' recommended that several
Lodge meetings be arranged to consider Washington in at least three
different phases, to-wit : As a man, as a Mason, and as a citizen. A copy
of said letter is attached hereto for further particulars.
On February 24th, 1932, we again addressed a communication to each
Master of the Lodges and enclosed a report blank for his use in reporting
to us the meetings held by his Lodge. A copy of said report blank is
hereto attached. In said letter we also enclosed a booklet of suggested
programs. In arranging these programs we sought to give a diversified
choice and in connection with each suggested program cited a large number of reference books which fully covered the desired subject and which
were obtainable at any public library.
Later, about March 5, 1932, each Inspector in the Jurisdiction was
furnished, without cost, with a copy of Tatsch's "The Facts About
.George Washington as a Freemason" for the use of the Lodges in his
District, and the Masters of the Lodges were informed of that fact.
A supply of said books was also made available through the office of
the Grand Secretary to individual members of the Craft at a nominal cost.
In addition to the foregoing, each Committee had voluminous correspondence with individual Masters, Lodge Committees and members
of the Craft in connection with George Washington Celebration. Although

GEORGE WASHINGTON BICENTENNIAL CELEBRATION
To the Masters and Brethren of the Constituent Lodges of this Jurisdiction:
The observance this year by the American people of the 200th anniversary of the birth of George Washington is most fitting because of his
outstanding contributions to the founding and the development of the
nation and .the perpetuation of the institutions and principles to which it
is dedicated. It is peculiarly appropriate that the Masonic fraternity
participate in this observance.

229

The extent to. which, and the manner in which individual Lodges
shall conduct Masonic observance of this outstanding event must be left
to the discretion of the respective Lodge and its officers. It is strongly
urged, however, that through Lodge meetings (either several or collecti~e) we tak~ advantage of ~he opportunity thus afforded, not only to pay
t~1bute t~ this .great Masonic character, but also to emphasize the principles of integrity, manhood and citizenship which he so fully exemplified.
!he day of his birth doubtless will be so generally celebrated through
pubhc observance that many of our Lodges may find it more desirable
to observe this year in their private meetings other anniversaries more
directly connected Masonically with the life of George Washington.
Appropriate dates will readily suggest themselves, but the following
are mentioned as illustrations:
George Washington was initiated on November 4th; he .was passed
on March 4th; he was raised to the sublime degree of Master Mason on
August 5th. The oath of office as president was administered to him on
April 30th by Robert R. Livingston, then Grand Master of the State of
New York; he was obligated on the Bible of St. John's Lodge of New
York, which is still preserved as a treasured relic.

!o

assist our Lodges in this observance, two committees have been
appointed, one for the northern and the other for the southern portion of
our state. The members of the committees are:
. Northern Committee: Wesley W. Kergan, Russ Building, San FranCJsco; Harry L. Todd, Postoffice, San ·Francisco; Albert F. Shulte,
c/o Standard Oil Co., 225 Bush Street, San Francisco.
Southern Committee: Dwight W. Stephenson Citizens' National
Bank Building, Los Angeles; Frederic J. Brudi, 622 West Magnolia
Street, Inglewood; Stuart M. McHaffie, 702 Pacific National Building,
Los Angeles.
In due course these commitees doubtless will address further communications to the Lodges. The National Commission has provided an
?bundance. of literatu~e covering every phase of the life of George Washm~ton, with suggestions appropriate for diversified types of meetings.

February 11, 1932.
To the Masters of the Constituent Lodges of this Jurisdiction:
The Grand Master in his letter of January 25th has already brought
to your attention the George Washington Bicentennial Celebration. We
hope you have already appointed a committee that your Lodge may take
its proper place in the celebration.
While we join with the Grand Master in urging a participation by
our members in the various civic celebrations, we feel that · our Lodges
should have meetings of peculiar interest to their members as Masons.
We would recommend that you arrange several meetings to consider
Washington in at least three different phases: As a man, as a Mason,
and as a citizen. Surely the example of Washingion is one worthy of all
emulation and his words should strike. a responsive chord in every
Mason's heart.
We will very shortly send you literature which will be of assistance
to you. In the meantime, we suggest that a reading of Washington's
Farew~ll Address will itself bring to your mind topics for meetings which
will be highly entertaining to your members. In the January issue of the
National Geographic Magazine will be found in short form an accurate
account of Washington's life. A study of these two, which can be obtained at any public library, will ena,ble a speaker to thoroughly prepare
himself. We can also recommend Tatsch's "The Facts About George
Washington as a Freemason," which will be available through the Grand
Secretary's office at fifty cents a copy after February' 18th.
The Masonic chronology of Washington may be briefly summarized
as follows:
March-Passed.
April-Took oath as President on Masonic Bible.
May-Dedication of the Washington Masonic Memorial at Alexandria, Va.
August-Raised.
September-Signed Constitution as President of the Convention.
November-Initiated.
Fraternally yours,

Tyre, Grand Lodge, Ancient, Free and Accepted Masons."

colored.

Federation of Human Rights" as the general Grand Body with headquarters at Larkspur, Colorado.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON FORMS
FOR VARIO US PURPOSES
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
At the last annual communication of Grand Lodge, Grand Master
Ross recommended that certain forms now a part of the Constitution that
are not mandatory in fact be eliminated therefrom, but that they be retained and published with other informative matter. The recommendation
.was referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, which
committee reported that "Grand Lodge approve as to policy .. ., but that
the proposed changes in the Constitution be referred to the incoming
Grand Master and Grand Secretary and reported upon at the next annual
communication." This was adopted.

240

GRAND LODGE. OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We have given careful consideration to the proposed changes, and
are of the opinion that many of the forms should be considered as standing
resolutions and be eliminated from the Constitution.
We therefore recommend that all forms now set out as part of the
Constitution as sections 233 to 250, inclusive, be eliminated from the Constitution but be included in the published volume under the general title
of "Forms for Various Purposes,'' and be numbered consecutively for
convenience of reference.
We recommend that all matter now contained in the Constitution as
sections 251 to 260, inclusive, relating to procedure for trials for unmasonic conduct, be eliminated from the Constitution and published therewith
under the general title of "Manner of Trial, and Forms of Charges and
Proceedings."
We further recommend that section 261, which authorizes the Finance
Committee to annually set aside three hundred dollars for the purchase
of a present to the retiring Grand Master, be repealed as a part of the
Constitution and retained as a standing resolution. .
.If the above recommendations meet with the approval of Grand Lodge,
the C~nstitution will end with section 232.
We further recommend that section 73 of the Constitution be amended
by striking out the words "in the form prescribed in sections 159 and 161"
and "in the form prescribed in section 235" ;
That section 75 be amended by striking out the words "in the form
prescribed in section 239" ;
That section 98 be amended by striking out the words "in the forms
prescribed in sections 246 and 247" and the words " in said section 246
hereof";
That section 159 be amended by striking out the words "in the form
prescribed in section 243."
And that the Grand Secretary shall, in making up the copy for the
Constitution, cause to be printed a footnote after each of sections 73, 75,
98 and 159 calling attention to the Form appropriate to each of said
sections.
ROBERT B. GAYLORD,
Gra1id Master.
JOHN WHICHER,

Grand· Secretary.

The report was adopted except as to the proposed
amendments to the Constitution, which were referred to the
Committee on Jurisprudence. That committee reported

241

recommending the proposed amendments, and all the sections so recommended for amendment and repeal were
accordingly amended by unanimous vote.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON LIBRARY
To the M.". w:. Gratid Lodge of California:
It has been my pleasure during the past year, as chairman of your Committee on Library, to abide with patience the outcome of our country's
enforced depression. I have enjoyed such distinction as came to me in the
absence of other emolument, in the prestige given one for service on a
Grand Lodge committee. For all this I am thankful. I trust the future has
a long season in store for us, wherein a greater interest in the acquirement
of craft knowledge will be manifested. I shall always be ready to further
the interests of this jurisdiction either as a lecturer on Freemasonry, or as
exemplifier of ritualistic rendition.
DENMAN S. WAGSTAFF,
JOHN E. HOUSTON,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
WEEK ON THIRTEENTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE
To the M .. W . Gratid Lo~ge F. & A. M . .of California:
Each year for several years past in commencing our report attention has been called to the continued growth of the observance in
public favor as evidenced by increased attendance at the public meetings and by the newspaper publicity given it. Never before however
has this. been so apparent as it was this year. And never before were
the programs throughout the state generally so well designed to
accomplish the purpose in view.
In our report last year we pointed out that the space devoted by
the newspapers to any occurrence is generally in proportion to the
public interest displayed. And we called attention in detail to the
increased publicity given the Twelfth Annual Observance. This year
this was even more marked, especially in editorial comment and in
the publication of special articles. Last year the proclamation of the·
Grand Master was published in 107 daily and weekly papers and this
year Grand Master Gaylord's proclamation was reproduced either in
its entirety or in part in 161 different publications.

243

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Our clipping service was discoptinued in the interest of economy
on April 1st. By that time however a total of 1337 articles, both
editorial and news matter, had been reported. The success of the
week from the publicity aspect was so apparent at that time that it
was believed unnecessary to entail further expense. The increase in
newspaper publicity was undoubtedly due to the activity of the local
publicity committees. · In a report from our Director of Publicity
reference is made to the increase in the number of chairmen of local
committees in touch with him from 42 in 1930 to 103 this year. The
value of these local publicity chairmen is in their visits to their local
press which not only insure a closer attention to publicity matter sent
out by our committee, but serve to increase the interest in local
happenings.
In many instances, indeed it seemed wherever possible, Masters
of Lodges named local newspaper men as publicity chairmen; and
the wisdom of such action was evidenced by the result. It may be
said that generally speaking the publicity received from either the
urban or rural press is in proportion to the activity of the local committees. And in this connection we feel it incumbent to again call
attention by way of appreciation to the fact that many of the smaller
papers which ordinarily could not well afford any considerable portion of their limited space devoted columns to the observance; and
in many instances were largely responsible for the public interest
displayed.
Extraordinary as was the amount of publicity received, even
more significant was the nature thereof. Not only were the news
reports unusually complete and detailed with photographs and cartoons, but there were more and longer editorials published than ever
before. Many of the photogra.phs were of the participants or scenes
in tableaus, plays and pageants commemorating the Washington
Bi-Centennial; and the cartoons in some instances appearing in connection with news reports and in others as special features of the
editorial pages. There was one which appears from the report to
which it was attached with other newspaper clippings, to have attracted unusual attention; and it seems to us well worth describing.
It depicted a school room with the teacher seated at her desk smiling
behind a paper which partially concealed her face. In front of her
were two snickering pupils with books upraised in front of them
and in the corner, and the evident object of the smiles and snickers,
was a figure of consternation sitting on a stool, crowned with the
traditional "dunce cap" and labeled "Uninformed Critic of Our
Schools." Over the teacher's desk on the wall. was a placard "Public
Schools Week April 25-30." It was a pungent stricture on that
criti£~siµ which is too often the result of ignorance, and a graphic

reminder of the opportunity afforded through Public Schools Week
to become advised and informed of the purposes and accomplishments of the modern school.
There were also this year an increased number of special articles
of a sort usually appearing in 'only educational publicatic;ms. Some of
these explained in detail the difference between modern ed~cational
methods and those in vogue when the parents of today were m school
and called attention to the tremendous changes and evidence of
progress during the last twenty-five years and to the n~cess~ty for a
changed curriculum in our schools. Others .gave detailed mf?r~a­
tion of their local schools and particularly with respect to activities
of which the general public have little knowledge; such as trade
and continuation schools, and opportunity and other special classes
for the handicapped children. No greater contribution could be made
to the movement in which we are engaged than was received from
the newspapers throughout· the state.
The radio was another form of publicity of which mention should
be also made. There were broadcasts from many stations of infor~
mation similar to that given by the newspapers. And there was at
least one station, and perhaps others which were not reported, from
which every day during the week was broadcast an address on an
educational topic or an announcement of some sort germane to Public Schools Week.
As was explained last year, it is virtually impossible to convey
in a report of this character anything like an adequate idea of the
success achieved. And each year it becomes more difficult to make
appropriate mention of specific observances which well deserve it.
This year we shall not even attempt to do so. Instea~ ":'e pur?ose
endeavoring to give a composite view of the observance m its entirety
throughout the state with only occasional reference to some particular report.
For those who continue to use attendance as the yardstick with
which to measure success, we may say that in one city on a single
night there were held twenty-one separate meetings with an estimated gross attendance of 25,000 people on that night alone; and
that there were from 6 to 10 meetings on each of the other nights of
the week with the attendance at many of them exceeding the capacity
of the auditorium. And in another city it was estimated that approximately 30,000 persons visited the schools during the ~eek. In
a report from a third community (and where, by the way, 1t was at
one time apparently believed that a fitting observance could. not be
held but which for several years past has reported outstanding success~) the following statement appears:· "This was the greatest
Public Schools Week observance that has ever been held in this
city and it is evidenced by the fact that 26,000 people visited the

242

244

245

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

schools and attended the evening programs." In that report, by the
way, mention is made of the fact that many programs were arranged
and given during the week without any solicitation on the part, and
in some instances even without the previous knowledge, of the general committee in charge of arrangements. This is extremely significant as indicating the extent of the growth of the observance in
public favor.
Over-flow meetings were reported from all portions of the state.
The comment of one Master with respect to his observance was that
"The only bad feature was the fact that the auditorium of the high
school was not large enough to accommodate all who desired admission." To consol~ him we may say that there were reports of
many observances which had similar "bad features."
There · was also a material increase in the number of visitors to
the schools, and particularly to the rural schools. In one county in
·addition to the visits by the parents of the children and others in the
district, every rural school was visited by representatives of twentyfour .different civic and fraternal organizations through arrangements
made by the County Superintendent.
In a previous report attention was called to the trend in the
direction of making the public meetings only incidental features of a
program extending over the entire week with visits to the schools
and practical demonstrations of actual work being done, exhibits of
school work of all sorts and kinds, and pageants presented by school
children exemplifying school objectives as its dominant features. At
that time this was noticeable only in the larger communities. This
year it extended to the small rural districts.
The promise made last year for even greater success in the rural
districts was this year certainly fulfilled. There were several reports
from communities in which every elementary school in a un.ion high
school district held an observance of its own on one day of the week
and then joined with all the other schools in the district in an evening
meeting held at the high school. And even in the very sparsely
settled districts an observance of some sort was held in the little one
room school. In more than one instance one or both parents of every._
child enrolled was a visitor to the school; and some of the programs
compared very favorably with those of the urban schools. As was
the case last year, there were some in which the program would
have been virtually impossible in a city school, and which was of
tremendous benefit to all who participated-teacher, pupils and parents. What was accomplished in these little rural schools was due
to the splendid co-operation received from the county superintendents and the rural supervisors under the .direction of the State De~
partment of Education..

Again this year a "Bulletin" designed especially for the use of
teachers in the one and two room schools was issued by the State
Department. Superintendent Kersey in his report to the Governor's
Council made extended reference to the observance which he stated
was characterized by a well planned program of activities throughout
the whole of the state of California. In commending the observance,
Superintendent Kersey said, "The wi~e. significance o~ Public Schools
Week will be reflected in the fine spmt of co-operation be~wee~ the
school officials and the general public brought about by an mtelhgent
understanding of the nature and purpose of the mo.dern program. of
educatien. This close co-operation is especially important during
these abnormal times if education is not to suffer."
The "intelligent understanding" to which Superintendent Kersey
referred was sought to be conveyed not only through the public
ad.dresses and the school programs with visits to the schools and
school exhibits but as well by means of printed and mimeographed
bulletins and ~irculars .distributed at the public meetings. Data of
all so.rts were given including the cost of the schools throughout the
state generally estimated on the average daily atten.dance and the
cost of the schools of the particular district, with details thereof, and
an explanation of the various funds.
As was perhaps to be expected; there was this year more than
the usual attention given to the cost of public education. At the
present time when curtailment of school expenditures is a subject of
the greatest consideration throughout the country: parents and othe~s
may reasonably .be expected to evince unusual interest not ?nly m
hat the schools are doing, but as well in the cost of education. In
;is connection we quote from an editorial in a publication which
always has been exceedingly generous in the amount of space devoted to the observance of Public Schools Week.
"Public Schools Week is not a new observance. It has
been held annually for a number of years. This time however there is a new attitude upon the part of the general
public and Public Schools Week, inte~tion~lly or no~, h~s
brought to the front the feeling of sat1sfact1on and pride m
the fact that the children of today have so many more educational advantages than the past generation or two. ·• · .
"This year Public Schools Week finds the people in a
different frame of mind. They have just been called upon to
pay their taxes; their taxes are high and there is much tal.k
of more taxes. On top of this the money to pay them is
harder to get. Then, too, there is the talk of shifting the
burden of the school taxes from the counties to the state.•. ·

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"Public Schools Week with its demonstrations of the
fine work done by the public schools should also bring before
the people the desire to have the public schools conducted
most efficiently. The fundamental and essential departments
of our educational system we want to be carried on in a most ·
thorough fashion and we are willing to pay the costs, but
there is no room for 'frills' in our present scheme of things.
This week brings us a new evaluation."

In many communities in addition to the meetings held in the
school auditoriums there were meetings held for the observance of
Public Schools Week by the service and other luncheon clubs and
by organizations of various sorts and kinds. In some instances the
program was presented by pupils from the schools and consisted of
vocal and instrumental music with perhaps a brief talk by a high
school student, while in others, particularly at luncheon meetings,
there was an address delivered by a school administrator. In one
city there were thirty-four of these meetings held during the week.
And as an evidence of the care and detail with which the arrangements had been made mention may be made of the fact that as a
part of the report of the observance there was a list of these organizations with the names of the president and secretary of each
and the date of the meeting. This was typed and had been evidently
prepared in advance; while in pencil was the name of the speaker
assigned t-0 each meeting. There was thus brought to the men and
women composing the membership of these organizations information with respect to the schools which otherwise they never might
have obtained. It also served as splendid publicity for the week's
program and without doubt encouraged visits to the schools ·by those
who desired further information.
School exhibits of all sorts and kinds were again this year an
outstanding feature of the observance in many communities; and
there was an increased number of instances where merchants contributed space in their show windows for the display of school work.
The most attractive of these window displays were of course the
so-called "live exhibits" where the pupils gave an actual demonstration of many of the cultural, vocational and homemaking activities
of the schools, including clay m-0deling, block printing, book binding,
art leather work and home economics. And hardly less so was the
exhibition in a store window of two reels of motion pictures illustrating the activities of adult classes in session. It was an exceedingly novel method of acquainting the public with the work being
done in adult education.
Included with other exhibits at one school there was a complete
display in the cafeteria -0f food sold to the pupils with tags showing
the price charged for each. In connection with the mention of food,
reference may be here made to what must have been not only a very
interesting, but an extremely significant, feature of the program of
a particularly well designed observance. It was a "Father and Son
Night" at a junior high school where the boys. and their fathers sat
down to a dinner which had been prepared in its entirety by 12 boys
enrolled in the cooking class. Its significance is in the indication of
the extent to which boys are availing themselves of the opportunity

It is particulariy gratifying to your committee to note an evident
willingness on the part of those in charge of an observa.n<:e to avail
themselves of the experience of others. Many features whi"ch were
unique at the time to which reference to them was made in our
reports were this year a part of the program in other communities.
For instance, there were several observances including as an outstanding feature what was generally termed a "Back to School Night"
wit~ the parents in attendance not as visitors but as pupils. This is
one of the most effective methods which could be devised of giving
the parents an insight into the work being done by the children and
of establishing a proper understanding between the parents and the
school. There were several variations of this reported. There was
however one feature common to all of them. The parents were in
attendance in the classes in which their children were registered and
there received the lessons which ordinarily would have been given
the children and in exactly the same way. And as they moved from
one class to another they were afforded an opportunity to meet all
the teachers. In some instances the periods were of the usual length
and in others they were cut to such time as would ·make possible a~
entire. day's program being given. When the parents were gathered
in the auditorium for the "assembly" period they there received the
program provided for the pupils of the school. The school nurse
gave such instructions to the parents as she ordinarily would have
given to the children respecting the care of the teeth, health, etc. ;
and the principal gave the usual instructions with respect to fire drill,
use of the grounds and lunch permits. In some instances this was
varied by holding a student body meeting in which the parents
represented their children:· Amusing features were introduced such
as requiring all parents late to classes to report to the prihcipal's
office for a tardy slip before being permitted to enter the class room.
And in one school the young teacher informed the clerk of the school
board who was late for one of the classes that it would be necessary
for her to be on time if she expected to be permitted to continue in
school. Wherever this feature was introduced it received extremely
favorable comment and will undoubtedly be continued as a permanent
feature of the observance.

to learn to cook. In the early stages of this activity it was only for
what was termed "camp cooking" that the boys enrolled. Many of
them are now taking exactly the same courses which were originally
provided only for girls. In passing it may be said that in even what
are termed "occupational courses" there is none, or at least very few,
exclusively pursued by either .sex. Confirmatory of this it will be
possibly recalled that in one of our previous reports in referring to a
certain observance mention was made of a .g irl who had given a
demonstration of electric welding. And it is no longer a rarity to find
girls enrolled in automotive courses, and more commonly in certain
courses in home economics in which is given instruction in electrical
wiring, care of electrical appliances and simple household plumbing.
The unusually large number this year of plays and pageants was
probably due in part at least to the fact that there was in this way
afforded a splendid opportunity for the observance of the Washington
Bi-Centennial during Public Schools Week. In one city which this
year well maintained the high standard previously set, all the exhibits
and programs (and many elsewhere throughout the state) were built
around the Washington Bi-Centennial theme with plays and pageants
introducing Mt. Vernon, Valley Forge, the First Inauguration, Washington's Farewell Address and other incidents of his life. Instead of
the usual exhibit of dancing there was the stately tread of the
minuet; and the music was of colonial days. In some instances there
were very elaborate productions presented by high school and junior
college students; and in others the program consisted only of tableaus by the smaller children. In some of the particularly small
communities where no attempt was made to present a play or pageant
or even a tableau the address of the evening was a patriotic one
with the First President as the subject. Whatever the form of the
program it of course accomplished the desired object of centering
the attention of the children and of their parents as well on George
Washington.
·
·
The foregoing will, we hope, give some idea of what we feel well
warranted in saying was without doubt from every point of view the
most successful observance of Public Schools Week ever held. Of
course what was accomplished would have been impossible without
the sympathetic aid and assistance received from the school people
and from civic and fraternal organizations of every sort, and character, as well as from churches, theatres, newspapers and radio
stations. As was of course to be expected, all the co-ordinate bodies
of · Masonry and allied organizations co-operated wholeheartedly
everywhere with the Lodges. _And we feel that special mention
should he made of the part played by the Order of De Molay in one
of the observances. There were twenty-eight boys selected, one of

-w hom at every public meeting .delivered a five minute "key note"
talk in which a brief history was given of the beginning and growth
of the system of public schools in that community. The talks given
by these boys might well have served as the theme of a more extended address by the "speaker of the evening."
W ~ also deem it simple justice to apprize Grand Lodge of the
action of a chapter of the Order of Eastern Star. With the heads of
the co-ordinate bodies of Masonry, and of the Sciots and Shrine, the
Grand Matron of the Or<ler of Eastern Star each year issues an
edict calling attention to Public Schools Week and decreeing that no
chapter shall hold any meeting or give any entertainment that may
possibly conflict with any meeting held for the observance of Public
Schools Week; and she, herself, arranges her itinerary so that she
makes no official visits during that week. It appears however that
a chapter in the southern part of the state had inadvertently arranged for a reception to the Deputy Grand Matron of which the
outstanding feature was to be a banquet. When this came to the
knowledge of the Master of a Masonic Lodge in the community he
immediately wrote a letter of protest to the Matron of the Chapter.
This was only four <lays before the date set for the reception; and
as he subsequently explained it was with the hope of preventing
anything of the sort in the future and with no expectation, or even
thought, that the affair would be cancelled on such short notice.
Nevertheless immediately upon the matter being brought to her
attention the Matron cancelled the arrangements which had been
made and postponed the reception; and this notwithstanding the
fact that reservations had been made for a banquet for 400 people.
It was certainly a fine gesture which we believe will be commended
by Grand Lodge. Our committee has made suitable acknowledgment to the Matron of the Chapter and also to the Grand Matron.
We close our report with a quotation, slightly changed, from an
address made by the chairman of a committee of arrangements at a
public meeting which brought to a close an exceedingly successful
observance. What he said of the observance in that community is
likewise applicable to the observance in its entirety throughout the
state:
"The real success of the observance just closed cannot be
measured by the attendance at the various events or by the publicity
received. If those who attended our meetings, visited our schools
and viewed the exhibits have become really informed of what is being
done and the reason for it; if the wide public interest manifested
continues unabated; if there results that spirit of co-operation between the school people and the general public which is dependent
upon an intelligent understanding of the modern program of educa-

RITUAL FOR PAST MASTER DEGREE
]. Lynn Goode, Inspector of the 81st Masonic District,
presented the following:
Whereas, section 224 of our Constitution sets out that "This Grand
Lodge recognizes no degree of Past Master conferred by any authority not
holden under a legitimate Grand Lodge, acknowledging only the order of
that name as it exists in the ceremonies attending the installation of the
Master-elect of a chartered Lodge; which order shall be conferred only
by a convocation of Masters or Past Masters, not less than three in number who have thus regularly received it."
And whereas, many associations of Past Masters have been formed
within our jurisdiction for the purpose of conferring what they term the

252

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

STATEMENT OF INCOME AND EXPENSE
Fiscal Year Ended September 30, 1932

Past Master's degree, which associations have no legal Masonic standing
and no uniformity of procedure or ritual. Therefore, be it
Resolved, that a form of ritual be prepared by the Committee on
Ritual, for use throughout the jurisdiction, for the proper preparation of
Masters-elect, the conferring of which shall be a prerequisite to installation of Masters of Lodges.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES U. C. MASONIC CLUB
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The Trustees of the Masonic Club of the University of California,
Inc., submit herewith the report of the audit of the finances of the Club,
together with the proposed budget for the ensuing year.
Nothing out of the ordinary has happened at the Club during the past
year, beyond the fact that the present condition of depression, which is
felt by students attending the University as well as by all others, has resulted in the Club House affording opportunity for recreation and social
intercourse among the several hundred Masonic students daily using the
place probably to a greater degree than at any other time during its history.
Were it not for the maintenance of the institution at the University, many
of our young people of Masonic affiliation would be utterly deprived of
the opportunities for that much needed fine association and close contacts
among students that the Masonic Club affords, and which they otherwise
could not enjoy.
The proposed budget for the ensuing year calls for an expenditure of
practically forty per cent less than that provided for the year just closing.
All salaries have been reduced twenty-five per cent for the ensuing year,
and consolidation of various activities results in a budget twenty-five per
cent less than the actual expenditures of the last year.

seen emergencies, to carry on as heretofore.
.

Kempton continue~, in her quiet and affectionate manner, in the capacity

IRA F. THOMPSON.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your special committee appointed by the Grand Master to study ways
and means of increasing the Endowment Fund, begs leave to report:
The Grand Master, through his many years s.ervice to the Craft, and
particularly his service as a member of the Homes· Board, has come very
definitely in contact with the ever increasing calls for relief from members
of the fraternity and their dependents. He sees the need of increasing the
Endowment Fund and has taken this means of bringing it to your attention.
Your committee has given the matter very careful study and agrees
with the Grand Master that something definite and concrete should be done
to increase the Endowment Fund. You have but to turn to the statistics
so widely published and advertised by our great American life insurance
companies for proof as to the financial mortality of the average man. Our
fraternity is made up of average men, and we must necessarily conclude
that .the members thereof will have the average financial mortality. With
these facts in mind, a look to the future is indeed convincing that it is
important that we begin at once to build a fund that will be sufficient to
enable future generations to maintain the standard of relief we have
enjoyed.
In passing, your committee wishes to pay its tribute to the present
members of our Homes· Board and those men who have served you in the
past. They have given unstintingly of their time and energy to the interest
of the Craft and for the well being of the resident members in each of
our Homes. We commend them to you and assure you that they are
handling a difficult 'job well, and certainly should not be burdened with
the problem of securing the necessary funds to carry on their work.
It is a well known fact that from the early history of this country,
educational, religious and charitable institutions have been founded and
owe their success to endowments, which is particularly called to our attention in the State of California by Stanford University, originally created
through an endowment and perpetuated by the same and additional endowments; the University of California at Berkeley and Los Angeles created
by the people of California is indebted to endowments for a great deal of
its wonderful work. Like mention could be made of many other institutions in this state, which have received endowments from those who wish
the perpetuation of like ideas, that is, from former students and those
whose financial ability allows them to assist their fellow men.
The Endowment Fund may be increased in several different ways: by
contribution of cash or other properties, by bequests and through life insurance. The problem is to familiarize members of the Craft with our
Homes, their present and future needs.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is the opinion of your com111ittee .that there should be a continuous
progra111 of edtication and that the "present Homes Board be requested to
have printed such information as would in their opinion be of interest to
the Craft in general and would likewise tend to create in them an interest
in their institutions; this material to be used by the co111mittee or com111ittees that 111ay hereafter be appointed to carry on the endowment work.
Your cotnmittee recommends that one month in each year be set aside
and designated by the Grand Master as Masonic Homes month, during
which every Lodge in this jurisdiction will be expected to hold a meeting
or meetings in which they will familiarize the members of their Lodge
with the Homes to the end that they may know of our present and future
endowment needs, and that each Lodge maintain a standing conunittee on
Masonic Homes.
We recommend that every Lodge, through its Secretary, be required
to furnish to the Grand Lodge the name and address of every attorney in
their Lodge and that these attorneys be circularized and informed of the
needs of our Masonic institutions, and whenever possible that they direct
attention to Masonic endowments and suggest to their clients that the
Endowment Fund may be mentioned in their will.
·
Likewise, we recommend that each Lodge, through its secretary, be
required to furnish to Grand Lodge the name of every life insurance man
that is a member of their Lodge and that they also be circularized and given
information regarding our Homes and their needs that they may in tum
direct the attention of their clients to Masonic endowments.
With these thoughts in mind and the emergency which exists, your
committee recom!llends for adoption the following:
That a committee of fifteen, to be known as "Masonic Homes Endowment Board of California," be created. The members of said committee
be appointed· by the Grand Master and shall serve for a period of three ·
years. The first committee of fifteen so appointed shall, at the first meeting of said committee, draw lots so that their terms shall be fixed and
that five members of said Board shall serve for one year, five for two
years, and five for three years, and thereaf.ter the Grand Master shall
fill all vacancies on said Board.
•
The Grand Master shall appoint the Chairman of said Board and
said Board is. hereby authorized to employ an executive Secretary and
such other clerical force as is deemed necessary.
Said Board shall have the power to collect and invest funds in conformity to the regulations of Grand Lodge.
The Grand Treasurer to be the custodian of said funds and shall pay
the net income of such funds to the trustees of the Masonic Homes at
least annually.
The members of said Board shall be entitled to actual necessary
expenses incurred in the performance of their duties, claims for which

shall be itemized and presented to the Grand Master foe his approval. And
when so approved shall be presented to the Grand Secretary who shall
draw his warrant in payment of same on the Grand Treasurer.
This Board shall make such rules and regulations as it shall deem
necessary to carry on the work that may now or hereafter be assigned
to their Board.
That the sum of $5,000.00 be and is hereby appropriated from the
general funds of Grand Lodge for the immediate use of said Board. .
ROLLIE W, MILLER,
WM. P. JEFFRIES,

God has seen fit in His infinite wisdom to call members of the Grand
Lodge to their final reward.
Among those who have departed are several who have rendered distinguished service to Masonry, and the committee regrets that time will
not permit them to go into great detail regarding the service, given so
unselfishly, by these brethren.
Chief among those who have rendered exceptional service is Frank
M. Angellotti, Past. Grand Master, and for many years a member and
chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee. Brother Dana R. Weller, Past
Grand Master, has been designated. to give us a more detailed account of
the virtues and accomplishments of Brother Angellotti.
Your committee can not refrain from mentioning four others who
have rendered exceptional service to Masonry; they are Michael D. Lininger, John M. Dunsmoor, Arthur M. Ellis and Theodore J. Milliken.
Michael D. Lininger received his degrees in White Marble Lodge No.
238, in the Jurisdiction of Iowa, and affiliated with Eureka Lodge No. 16 in
the year 1883. From 1883 until the time of his death Brother Lininger was
a laborer in the vineyard of Masonry, serving as Master of his Lodge for
six years, Grand Bible Bearer for seven years, and Inspector for twentynine years.
John M. Dunsmoor, a Past Master of Hollenbeck Lodge No. 319,
gave up the private practice of his profession to assume the important
duties of Secretary of the Masonic Board of Relief of Los Angeles more
than thirty years before his death. His pleasant smile and encouraging
counsel during all those years were the means of starting many a distressed brother on the road to winning back his place in the community
which he had formerly occupied.
Arthur M. Ellis, a Past Master of University Lodge No. 394, served
as Chairman of the History Committee of this Grand Lodge for many
years, and was never too. busy about his private business to go out of his
way to learn about early Masonry in California.
Theodore J. Milliken was Master of Tehama Lodge No. 3 in the year
1902. At the expiration of his year as Master, he was elec~d Secretary
of his Lodge and occupied that position for many years. At the annual
communication of Grand Lodge in 1915 he was appointed Grand Pursuivant
and served in that capacity until the communication of 1924. He occupied
a position of public trust in his community and was greatly beloved by
his brethren and by the community at large.

We who served under him on the Jurisprudence Committee feel most
poignantly the loss
his genial manner, his engaging presence, his sound
reasoning, his excellent leadership.
Notwithstanding all the honors which came to him, and which he so
richly deserved, he never lost the human touch. Always modest, unassuming, gentle and kindly, never for a moment did his demeanor suggest that
he was other than one of us, an humble seeker for the truth, laboring
shoulder .to shoulder with his brethren in the endeavor to brighten the
world and elevate mankind.
Such, in brief, is the life history of our friend and brother. None but·
those who knew him best and loved him most can realize the extent of
our loss. Words are but feeble and futile expressions of emotions at a
time like this.
As the lengthening shadows indicate the setting of the sun, and the
eventide of life approaches, we become more and more impressed with the
knowledge that ere long our sun )Vilt set, to rise on the morrow, bright and
glorious, on that other land where our friends have gone to enjoy the
eternal life, and who will greet and welcome us on our arrival.
May the Great Architect grant us so to live that we may be found
worthy to a place by the side of our dear friend and brother to whom
we bid an e~rthly "Farewell." ·

PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK
The following communication was received from the
California Association of Public School Superintendents,
in annual session at San Francisco:
The public schools serve as democracy's agency for the perpetuation
of American ideals in the young generation, and for training children for
intelligent and effective citizenship.
The public schools provide the means whereby all children of whatever race, creed or ability are provided with the opportunity to develop
their individual aptitudes, to improve their status, to acquire the ability
to adjust themselves to the complex social order of their day, and to learn
to work together harmoniously for worthy social purposes.
The effective functioning and the moral and financial support of this
democratic institution depend upon a clear and comprehensive understanding by all the people of the purposes, methods and financing of the public
schools.
Such understanding ·has been ably promoted by the observances of
California Public Schools Week.
The California Association of Public School Superintendents expresses to the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California

272

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

its ~reat .apprec~ation of the foresight of the Grand Lodge in estat>lishing
California Pubhc Schools Week and of sponsoring its observance annually.
Thi.s Association arid i~s members individually pledge their wholehearted cooperation in observing California Public Schools Week in the
various districts of the state.
'
A copy of this resolution is to ·be forwarded immediately by the Secretary to the Masonic Grand Lodge now in session in Oakland, California.

The Grand Secretary was directed to wire the .thanks
of the Grand Lodge to the Association for its appreciation
of our work for public education.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRAND LECTURER'S
REPORT
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to which has been referred for consideration the
report of the Very Worshipful Grand Lecturer begs leave to report as
follows:
For twenty-five consecutive years our Grand Lecturer has been able
to report progress in the fellowship and fraternal feeling existing among
the Masons of this jurisdiction--;i condition largely of his own making.
During this quarter of a century he has fanned the flame of Masonry in
~v~ry nook and corner of our state. In his endeavor to perfect the ritual1stic work he has never sacrificed substance to form. His guiding principle
has always been that the ritual is but a means to an end-not the end
itself; and that if Masonry is to serve its true purpose, we must have
proper ritualistic interpretation as well as proper ritualistic ·instruction.
It js this concept of his responsibility that has made of his work a real
livjng force fo Masonry.
During his many years as Grand Lecturer he has seen the Fraternity
double in size and influence and it should be a source of everlasting satisfaction to him that his work has contributed to this result in ·such large
measure.
Twenty-five years of devoted service to a worthy cause is something
to be admire~ and emulated by all men and as we look back over his Jong
years of service we cannot fail to be inspired thereby.
Our Fraternity has gained prestige through his service and our jurisdiction is a better place to live in by reason ·of the truths he has exemplified
through our ritual.
We congratulate him; we congratulate Grand Lodge.

273

GRAND J,ODGE OF CALIFORNIA

And lastly, we trust that for many years to come, his kindly countenance, his genial smile and .his devoted service to the Fraternity will continue to promote fellowship and spread the everlasting truths of Masonry
in our Lodges.
EARL WARREN,
FosTER G. DYEK,
ALBERT F. SHULTE,

Committee.

Adopted.

REPORT OF BOARD OF ~ONTROL
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lotlge of California.:
In presenting to Grand Lodge its report of its activities during the
year, the Board of Control believes that it is fitting and proper to recite
first of all the results of the efforts of the respective Boards of Relief to
secure reimbursements from Lodges of other jurisdictions and to reduce
the· amount of reimbursements requested from this Grand Lodge. Despite
the fa<:t'that more actual relief has been given this year than ever before;

274

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALlFORNIA

despite the fact that more money has been expended by the Boards of
Relief, individually and collectively, yet the reimbursements approved and
recommended to the Finance Committee are less than ever before. It is
true that the Board of Control has found it necessary to reject some of the
requests for reimbursement which have ·been presented, but your Board
has felt and now feels that these. requests are not justified, that the relief
was not granted in accordance with the procedure and regulations adopted
by Grand Lodge.

This small amount may seem unbelievable, and yet the fact remains
that that sum is all that has been requested and that sum is all that has
been granted. It is declared, however, and substantiated as well that not
one single case of relief has been slighted or neglected by the Board
of Relief.
At the risk of being criticized for repetition, we again call attention
to the record of reimbursements granted by Grand Lodge since and
including 1925.

In these matters of reimbursement, we desire to again call the attention of Boards of Relief and Lodges to the fact that each year the list
of jurisdictions which refuse to reimburse for relief extended without
pre-authorization is steadily growing. As a matter of fact, if the Boards
and Lodges are following the letter of information sent out by this Board
. last year under the sanction of the Grand Master and approved by Grand
. Lodge, no relief except temporary or emergency will be granted u,nless
said Boards or Lodges secure prior authorization. Many foreign jurisdictions refuse or neglect to reimburse even after authorization has been
given. The Board of Control has been of assistance many times quring
the year in securing these long delayed and often ignored promises to pay.
Reference has been made heretofore to the refusal of English and
Scottish Lodges to authorize the expense of funerals of deceased brethren
in this jurisdiction and warning has been given not to extend relief in any
considerable amount to brethren of these Lodges without evidence of their
good standing.
There .are many life members of Scottish Lodges in this jurisdiction
who are not entitled 'to relief. But this matter has been cleared somewhat
by the following excerpt from the 1931 Proceedings of the Grand Lodge
of New York:
"The Grand Lodge of Scotl;aild has called bpon the members of their
Lodges to abstain from proposing or admitting to Freemasonry any men
who are about to emigrate before they can possibly become grounded in
the principles of the Craft and have been instructed adequately as to the
duties devolving upon them as Master Masons.
"Brethren who have decided to emigrate are to be furnished by their
respective Lodge Secretaries with the addresses of the appropriate District

Your Board, with a great deal of satisfaction, reports that Boards
of Relief are working in greater harmony and accord with the Board of
Control than ever before; and that through this accord and cooperation
the procedure. and business methods of the various Boards of Relief have
become m?re and more systematized and coordinated.
Whereas, at the time of organization of the Board of Control there
was a misunderstanding and misconception on the part of B~rds of Relief
and Lodges as to its objects and purposes, and in many cases both Lodges
and Boards of Relief acted at cross purposes and in variance with directions and requests of the Board of Control, now these same Lodges and
Boards are working with the Board of Control in every respect.
During this session of Grand Lodge conferences have been held with
the Secretaries and other officers of the respective Employment SerVices
and Boards of Relief, which conferences have resulted in a general expression of unanimity of purpose and objective, and a proposed further
uniformity in much of the procedure of these organizations.
While your Board of Control realizes, and has many times declared,
that c?arity or relief cannot be standardized or made uniform, yet it is
becoming more and more apparent that the methods and procedure of
distributing or dispensing relief can be made uniform. Our Boards of
Relief and our Employment Service are demonstrating the truth of that
statement, and their reports to the Board of Control which are transmitted to Grand Lodge each year, show conclusively that they are using
uniform methods, reducing the overhead, using judgment instead of unwise sympathy, and making their funds and the funds of Grand Lodge do
greater service than ever before. Particularly is this so in the matter of
reimbursements requested from Grand Lodge to cover e~penditures made
by the respective Boards of Relief in behalf of brethren from foreign
jurisdictions where the foreign jurisdiction Lodge refuses to make reimbursement. Year after year since the organization·of the Board of Control,
these reimbursements have decreased until today the total is less than the
amount once requested by a single Board of Relief. As an outstanding
example of what can be done by a Board of Relief in securing .reimburseiµent from foreign jurisdictions, there is included in this presentation the
report of one Board of Relief which .has expended for relief during. the
past year the sum of $41,854.11 and which has requested from Grand Lodge
reimbursement of only $567.13.

Me~tings: The work of the Board of Control during the year cannot be recited her~. The Board is a continuing committee. Its work
extends from one Grand Lodge session to the succeeding session. It involves a volume of correspondence during the year. It requires conferences
with Lodges; with Boards of Relief ; with individual Masons. Five
meetings of the Board have been held since Grand Lodge of 1931: One at
Los Angeles in February, a second at Long Beach in April, the third at
Los Angeles in August, a fourth in San Francisco in September, and the
fifth · during this session of Grand Lodge in Oakland. At each of these
meetings, the officers of the Boards of Relief have been invited to attend
and to participate in tlte proceedings.
Your Board of Control appreciates the splendid cooperation and
assistance of our Most Worshipful Grand Master and his generous indorsement in his annual message. We appreciate, too, the kindly courtesy and
assistance of our Worshipful Grand Secretary.
We do not find any disposition generally on the part of well informed Masons, either singly or in groups, to avoid doing their share
toward the relief of the worthy distressed brother or his dependents, but
all too frequently we find an erroneous idea in the minds of some Masons
and more frequently among their dependents "with respect to just what
kind of aid and how much they may or may not be entitled to receive. It
should be very definitely stated and emphasized that Freemasonry is not
an insurance or benefit organization; that there are no weekly, monthly
or yearly allowances of any kind or character. We should say without
hesitation that Masonic relief is not a right, it is a privilege which Masons
gladly extend to a worthy brother in distress or to his worthy dependents.
In these days we have gotten away from the personal element in many
of these matters largely because · of the conditions under · which we live.
We don't have the close contact of former years. We are dependent upon
organizations to carry out the spirit of our Order.
We are therefore of the opinion that it is highly important that Grand
Lodge should through some agency bring to the attention of its Lodges
just what is the position of Masonry upon the question of Relief. The
Grand Lodge of indiana has enacted a provision requiring the establishment and maintenance by each Lodge of a Masonic Relief Fund. This
law clearly recognizes the duty of a Lodge in matters of relief, but in no
way assumes that there is any obligation or contract to pay to the applicant for Masonic relief any specified sum or any sum, for that matter.

We readily reach the conclusion that the whole purpose of Freemasonry is to create the will and the desire to do those things wbich will
make the world a better p1ace to 1ive in and those who 1ive in it wiser
and happier.
Statistics.
Statistics form a large _part of the background o-f business endeavor.
They play a very important part in the handling of Boards of Relief. The
statilrtical knowledge and the experience already gained form a basis f01'
the improvement of future service.

from the liecrdaries of the respective Boards of Relief and from information gleaned from the audits of certified accountants and it js believed that

to the Board of Control during its deliberations.
It is the opinion .of the Board .of Control that considerable progress
has been made during the last fiscal year, .in a further standardization of
the operations of the Boards of Relief and methods pursued in the extension of relief. The Board further feels that, largely due to this feature
ai the work, there has been a very considerab1e reduction in the amounts
of money requested from the Grand Lodge as reimbursements.

San Francisco: The San Francisco Board of Relief is composed of
members from each of the fifty-four lodges, and two meetings are held
each month. During the year a per capita assessment of twenty-five cents
per member was levied.

San Jose: The San Jose Board of Relief is composed of members
from each of the five Lodges, Chapter and Commandery. Meetings are
held quarterly. A per capita assessment of twenty-four cents per member
was levied during the year on Blue Lodge members, and twenty cents per
member on other Lodge members.
There is one paid employe, a secretary, who receives a salary of $50.00
per month. The secretary is bonded in the amount of $500.00. There is
one automobile used.
·

· The paid employes are the secretary, who receives $300.00 salary and
$50.00 automobile allowance monthly, and a typist or clerk who receives
$75.00 monthly.

Requests for Reimbursements
At no time during the existence of your Board of Control have the
demands for relief been greater than during the past year. Without exception, all Boards of Relief have extended relief far in excess of any
other period. It is with a great deal of satisfaction and gratitude, therefore, that we are pleased to report a very substantial reduction in the
amount being asked for reimbursement. Satisfaction in the knowledge
that our relief has been rendered without stint or niggardliness and with
every thought of our Masonic responsibility, and gratitude for the splendid cooperation, efficiency a.nd business-like methods of the Secretaries
of our various Boards of Relief.
During this communication of Grand Lodge your Board of Control
has had for consideration requests for reimbursement in 121 cases. After
completing our findings we have approved requests in 101 cases, totaling
$4,428.68. This is less than last year by 13 cases and $2,030.26. The
numbers and amounts of the requests approved are :
4 cases-California Jurisdiction ..........................................$1,230.00
79 cases-From 26 other U. S. Jurisdictions .................... 2,214.68
18 cases-From 5 Foreign Jurisdictions ............................ 846.70

Employment Service
The Board of Control has given painstaking consideration to the work
of the Masonic Employment Service as organized in the several communities of the jurisdiction, and desires to commend the brethren in charge
for the splendid results obtained. Getting jobs for unemployed brethren
reduces the call for relief, and funds carefully expended for this purpose
are frequently more of an investment than an expense. Reports show that
two thousand (2000) more positions were secured this past year than
during the previous twelve months.
It is gratifying to note the improvement in the methods and efficiency
of the several offices. Greater care is being given to the selection of persons sent out to fill positions so that they may reflect credit to the Service
and to the Craft. Several of the offices are carefully building up the Employers' List to facilitate ~his placing of the increased number of applicants and to encourage the filing of applications by those qualified for
the very best positions.

Appropriations for Service Bureaus
In the matter of- allocating Grand Lodge funds to the employment
service, the Board of Control is convinced that a definite plan must be
outlined as a basis for making equitable appropriations. A survey will
be made and data arranged for future guidance. In the meantime, bearing
in mind the importance of the work and the need for strict economy, your
Board of Control has recommended appropriations for the respective Employment Service Bureaus totaling $10,300, as follows:

$10,300.00

Financial Reports
Attached hereto is a comparative statement for 1931 and 1932, showing
sources of income and the expenditures of the respective employment
service bureaus; the total applications received and positions secured;
the cost per unit for each placement and the percentage of the expense
borne by Grand Lodge. This statement is made a part of this report.

Standard forms for registering applicants and keeping records have
been recommended by the Board of Control and unanimously approved by
the representatives of all the employment offices. This will tend to increase the efficiency and uniformity of this service and make possible
greater cooperation between officers by the interchange of information.
The Masonic Employment Service should become the most valuable agency
of its kind in a community.

Adopted:
Your Committee on Grievances, to: which was referred Trial Record
No. 758 from Rising Light Lodge No. 397, begs leave to report as follows:
The accused was charged with unmasonic conduct on two specifioations .aoousing· him on two occasions of violating the Wright Act and that
he was convieted in the Courts of such violations. He was found guilty on
both specifications and upon the charge of unmasonic conduct and sentenced to a reprimand. The record is fatally defective for two reasons:
First, it shows that the summons was issued on July S, 1932, and was
served on the accused on July 6, 1932, although the Commissioners were
not elected until July 12, 1932. The explanation given for this action by
the Secretary was that the Master was afraid the accused would leave
Orange County as soon as the accused got out of jail and the Master
wanted the accused served while he knew where to find him. Sei:tion 199
of the Constitution provides that "If the accused be within the jurisdiction
of the ·L6dge; the summons and copy of the charges shalt be Issued and
served upon the accused at least ten days prior to the day appointed for the
trial, etc."
Section 198 of the Constitution provides "The Master will then name
the time and place for the first meeting of the Commissioners, keeping in
view the convenience of the parties and the time allowed the accused
for appearance, and will direct the Secretary to notify each Commissioner
of his election and of such time and place of meeting, either in person or
in writing, and - will also direct the Secretary to notify the accuser of
such time and pljlce of meeting, and will have prepared for his signature
a summons which he will cause to be served, etc."
This the Master is required to do at the time the Commissioners are
elected. This is the Master's only authority to cause such summons to be

306

307

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

issued. We are compelled to find that the summons purporting to have
been issued on July 5, 1932, was not legally issued and therefore its service
did not confer jurisdiction to try the accused. It is true the Master did at
the time the Commissioners were elected direct the Secretary to cause
a summons to be prepared for the Master's signature. This, however, does
not appear to have been done. The files in the case show two certified
copies of the conviction of the accused in the Municipal Court at Los
Angeles, but the Secretary's minutes of the trial do not disclo!e that such
certified copies were offered in evidence or that any evidence was offered
at the trial. The case must therefore be reversed .. As the Commissioners
under section 204 of the Constitution, did not take on adjournment to another date, but purported to have finished their labors and adjourned sine
die; we are of opinion that the case can not be retried before such Commissioners, but that if it is desired to proceed further with the matter a
new commission will have to be elected, and a new summons issued and
served on the accused in compliance with our Constitution after such
Commissioners are elected.

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred the petition of
G. R. S., expelled by Berkeley Lodge No. 363 in 1929, report that petitioner
was found guilty by a trial commission and sentenced to reprimand; that
Grand Lodge in 1929 raised the penalty to expulsion; but that no showing
is made by the petitioner on his behalf why petition should be granted.
We therefore recommend that the petition for restoration of G. R. S. be
denied without prejµdice.

We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:

Resolved, that the decision of the Trial Commissioners herein be
and the same is hereby rever~ed and said cause be and the same is hereby
remanded for a new trial with directions that a new Trial Commission be
elected and a new summons be issued in the manner provided by the
Constitution after the election of such Commission and thereafter served
on the accused.

Adopted.
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 728, from Alturas Lodge No. 248, on appeal by the accused, are of
opinion that ample evidence was introduced to sustain the findings of the
Commissioners and we see no reason to disturb their verdict.
We therefore recommend that the verdict of guilty and sentence of
expulsion be approved.

Adopted.
