Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 757, from Live Oak Lodge No. 61, find that the accused was convicted by summary method provided by section 192 of our Constitution.
The record shows that the accused was convicted in the Superior Court of
Alameda County of a crime classified as a felony, but was given probation and not imprisoned. We therefore offer the following resolution and
move its adoption:
Resolved, that the action of Live Oak Lodge No. 61, in expelling accused from the rights and privileges of Masonry, be and the same is
hereby reversed, and the said Lodge is directed to take such action as may
be consistent with the facts and the Masonic law applicable thereto.

Ado.pted. (Earl Warren and A. W. Brouillet, members
of the Committee, did not participate in this report.)
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record No. 714, from Plumas Lodge No. 60, begs to report: The charges
were preferred by the Junior Warden by direction of the Master, and the
accusing Master presided at the trial. Accused was not present and no
witnesses testified. The minutes of the meeting of the Trial Commissioners show that copies of seventeen letters, copy of a bank check for $35.00,
copy of a protest, and copy of an affidavit of a Sheriff in Utah stating that
the accused could not be located, were presented. The Commissioners
found the accused guilty and fixed the penalty at expulsion. In cases where
the Junior Warden prefers the charges at the direction of the Master,
that Master can not preside. The Grand Master should have been requested to designate a Past Master to preside. But in addition to this
irregularity, no competent evidence was adduced. The seventeen . letters
were not identified, no proof was made to show by whom. they were
wr~ten, or whether the statements contained in them were true or false or
hearsay. Your Committee is of the opinion that the judgment must be
reversed, and offer the following resolution and move its ·adoption :

Resolved, that the judgment in the case covered by Trial Record No.
714 be and the same is hereby reversed and the case remanded for a
new trial.

Adopted.

Your Committee on Grievances, to. ·which was referred Trial .Record
No. 747 from· Oroville Lodge No. 103, covering the trial of one E. H. D.,
a member of L@yalton Lodge No: 359; begs leave to report as follows ::
The accused was charged with unmasonic conduct under specifications, thl!·gist·of which is that'the accused was engaged in bootlegging and
that although he· had been Mice convicted before the courts he was still
engaged as such and was thereby bringing the Masonic fraternity into
disrepute. The accused was not present at the trial, but wrote a letter
to the· Lodge. confe"Ssing his guilt 'on all charges. In addition to this admission there was other competent evidence of his guilt. In his letter, above
referred-to, the accused expressed the hope that the· future might offer him
something- "more· worthy of a living as· a Master Mason." While not so
stated", the· implication is plain that he· expects to' continue his present line
of endeilvor until something more promising presents itself. The trial
commission found accused guilty and· fixed his' penalty at suspension.
Id view
his steadfastness to his• present line' of endeavor and the
uncertainty as- to how long he may continue to follow it, we feel that all
uncertainty as to his status as a Mason should be removed.

Your Committee on Gt-ievance&, to which was referred Trial Re(!Ord
No. 713, begs leave to report as follows:
,one A. W., a member of Big Bear Lodge No.· 617, was accused of
unmasonic conduct under one specification charging the commission of an
assault upon a brother' ·Mason: By order of the Grand ·Master the trial
was transferred to Redlands Lodge No. 300. While the ·order of transfer
is· made over the signature of the Grand Secretary, this was pursuant to
dinotions of the Grand Master. The accused, thFollgh his counsel, :objected to this transfer and insisted upon being tried before Big Bear
Lodge-. No. 617, of which -accused was a member. Neverthelcss,1.the trial
was conducted before commissioners elected by and from the membership
of . Redlands Lodge.

.J

310

'

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Section 43, subdivision 9, of the Constitution, authorizes the Grand
Master to transfer upon the request of ·Master to whom charges of unmasonic conduct have been presented, the trial of the .a~cused to some -0ther
Lodge whenever, in the judgment of the Grand Master, the convenience of
witnesses, or other good cause, makes such transfer necessary or expedient. In this case the Master of Big Bear Lodge was the perS-On assaulted,
and while the record does not show a request by him that the case be
transferred, we are pf the opinion that the order of transfer, under the
circumstances, could be made by the Grand Master of his own volition
and that under these peculiar circumstances such order was entirely proper.
Over the objection of counsel for the accused, members of Big Bear
Lodge were excluded from attending the trial. Your Committee finds no
Constitutional provision or previous decision of Grand Lodge dealing with
this question.
Unquestio!l4bly, members of the public who are not Masons should
not be permitted to attend such trials. Li~ewise, it is equally clear that
the presiding officer should, and does, have the power, in his discretion,
to exclude witnesses. As to Masons attending such trials a variety of
views may and does exist. On the one hand is the argument that trials
should be open and free to attendance by members of the Craft in the
interests of fair dealing and in conformity with the practice in the courts
of the land. On the other, it is urged that Masonic trials should be as
secret as possible to avoid undue publicity and notoriety, even within the
fraternity itself. Also, in cases where factions exist with respect to an
accusation, and this not infrequently occurs, attempts might be made to
pack an audience because of the influence upon the trial commission thus
to be obtained. After careful consideration of these and various other
views, your committee is of the opinion that the matter of th~ attendance
of Masons, known or properly vouc·hed to the presiding ·officer as such,
should be entrusted to the discretion of the presiding officer, and that, in
the absence of a showing of an abuse of such discretion, his judgment
should he final: At all events, in this case we find no miscarriage of justice
because Masons were excluded.
·
The evidence sufficiently shows the commission of .the assault alleged
in the specification. As a matter of fact the accused admitted the assault
but attempted to establish self defense; his defense in this respect wa~
weak and evidently not accepted by the trial commission. In addition
however, the accused offered to prove circumstances leading up to and i~
extenuation.of the assault. He offered evidence that the person a~saulted
had circulated false and malii;ious statements concerning him and that
such statements had. beei:i made to the wife of the accused for the purpose
of brealdIJg up his hqme. This offered ev.i!ience was excluded. In this
we ie;e;j :m e;rror was committed. In view of the fact that a trial commission has the duty of fixing the penalty as well as determining guilt, anrl

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

311

in view of the provisions of our Constitution, particularly those of section
200, giving the accused the right of showing matters in extenuation, we
think this evidence should have been received. An unprovoked assault
with nothing shown in extenuation may well merit one penalty, while an
assault resulting from provocation and for which extertuat ing circumstances may be shown, may merit another. In reaching this conclusion we
have in mind the ruling of Grand Lodge made in 1878 which indicates a
somewhat contrary view. (Section 398, p. 371, Digest of Decisions--1932).
However, we feel that the views herein expressed are more in harmony
with our present theory of Masonic trials, and more consistent with the
provisions of our Constitution.
The trial record discloses that while the commissioners found the
accused guilty of the specification, no vote or determination was had upon
the charge of urunasonic conduct. In conformity with former rulings of
Grand Lodge we· find· it necessary to recommend a reversal because of
this fact.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:

Resolved, that the finding of guilt of' the trial commission on the
specification and the fixing of the penalty at suspension be and the same
hereby is set aside and vacated and that the matter be . remanded for
a new trial.

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record

The accused was proceeded against under section 192 of the Constitution.
It appears from the record that the accused was convicted by his plea of

therefor. Thereafter, and while accused was in jail, the Secretary of the
Lodge on October 14, 1931, sent to him by registered mail a notice under
section 192 of the Constitution and addressed it to his home, where the
return receipt was signed by an agent. No other proof of service was
made. On January 8, 1932, the accused, having failed to demand a trial,
was expelled.
It has been repeatedly held by Grand Lodge that the above does not
constitute proper notice to the accused under section 192 and that it can
not be made the basis for expulsion.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Resolved, that the action of Paul Revere Lodge No. 462 in expelling
the accused be and the same is hereby reversed and remanded for further
proceedings.

Adopted.

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Having had under consideration that-portion of the Grand Master's
message, under the caption "Shrine Lottery," your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes reports as follows:
Your Committee is in complete and unreserved sympathy with the
motives which actuated the Grand Master in the extended and various
proceedings set forth in his message. His conduct was courageous and
determined and directly in line with his duty, which is the duty of every
Mason, to preserve unsullied the reputation of the fraternity. While insistent and persistent in his course, he nevertheless conformed precisely
to the courtesies and amenities properly applying to inter-fraternal communications. There is evidence to support the conclusion that the consideration extended to those in control of Shrine affairs was in important
respects reciprocated less in substance than in form.
We believe we sense a disposition on the part of numerous members
of Grand Lodge, supporting as do they, and all of us, the unassailable
rectitude and propriety of the Grand Master's conduct, to take action of
a corrective nature if proper grounds for such action exist. In all candor
and fairness, however, it must be admitted that no definite evidence is
before Grand Lodge at this time, establishing as a fact that such grounds
do exist.
Masonic membership is a prerequisite to membership in the Shrine.
This is a Shrine regulation and not a Masonic law. Our Grand Lodge has
never recognized the Shrine as a Masonic body, and there is no justification
whatever for the opinion widely held by the profane as well as by many
Masons and Shriners that a member of the Shrine is a "high Mason."
Perhaps Grand Lodge has been negligent and unwise in that it has never
taken orderly steps to educate Masons to a clear understanding of these
facts. Since Grand Lodge recognizes no connection between itself and
the Shrine, it is obvious that Grand Lodge can not undertake or assert

Degree Teams
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered that
portion of the message of the Grand Master relating to degree teams. We
note that he has made no recommendation for legislation on this subject,
but as a ruling has given his views on the general practice in Lodges of
using degree teams on more or less frequent occasions. In the opinion of
your Committee his views seem to be clear and dictated by sound judgment. Under proper supervision degree teams can add to the impressiveness
of the work, and if the team is formed at least partially from members
of the Lodge it gives them an added interest in the work. However, the
degree teams should not control the work, but should be invited by the
Master to participate. And before extending an invitation the Master
should assure himself of the proficiency of the temporary officers. Your
Committee feels that there is no alternative but to place this responsibility
directly on the shoulders of the Master of the Lodge. We therefore concur
most heartily with the views of the Grand Master.

Adopted.

The Grand Master in his message referred to the proposal made at
the last communication of Grand Lodge to revise the pay of members,
and which was referred to this communication. At that time it was called
to the attention of Grand Lodge that many Lodges made very generous
provision for the attendance of their representative, and that by placing
the pay on a more equitable basis it would not be necessary for Lodges to
appropriate additional money for expenses of their representative. While
no figures are available, the plan proposed would undoubtedly increase the
expense to Grand Lodge and the expenditure by individual Lodges would
be limited only by the restraint that Grand Lodge would wish to put upon
them. It is the opinion of your Committee that Grand Lodge expenses
should not be increased at this time and that the expenditure of Lodges
for representatives be left to the discretion of its officers and members. We
therefore concur in the recommendation of the Grand Master that no
action upon this subject be taken at this communication.

Adopted.

Lodge Rosters
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered the

states that such rosters are used continually for commercial and nonMasonic purposes, and to prevent this recommends that appropriate legislation be adopted which will prevent Lodges from issuing rosters with any
information except the names of members, with the possible exception
of the names and addresses of officers. Undoubtedly there have been
many instances of the misuse of rosters and the practice can not be too
severely censured. Your Committee, however, is of the opinion that enactment of the proposed legislation will not prevent exploitation. A roster
with names only can be fairly completed as to addresses by the use of
city and telephone directories· and the only alternative would be to prohibit
the publication of all rosters. To do this might work a hardship on the
Lodges. The rosters are issued generally for legitimate reasons and many
members make use of them for Masonic purposes. Their importance
varies with the individual Lodge and can not always be known by Grand
Lodge. Your Committee is of the opinion that this matter is one which

To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was referred the communication from the Officers Association of the 66th
Masonic District, suggesting that the offices of Senior and JuniOl" Deacon
be made elective, has had the same under consideration and reports
as follows:
Among the reasons assigned in support of the proposal is that "many
times those who have been appointed to fill the minor offices, whether
capable or not, are permitted to continue through the chairs" ; also that
"the membership as a whole should have a voice in selecting those who
are to govern the affairs of their Lodge."
The governing officers of a Lodge are the Master and Wardens. No
other officers, except through the incompetence or neglect of the Master
and Wardens, can exercise governing power, and even the powers entrusted
to them are limited. These officers, together with the Secretary and Treasurer, who are important administrative officers, are elected. If members
of a Lodge permit the election of incapable brethren to executive offices
they have but themselves to criticize. A Lodge which will elect incapables
to its most important offices would probably elect incapables as Deacons.
Among the Junior officers of a Lodge Senior Deacons are of first
importance. Their duties should be performed capably and with dignity.
Your Committee is in agreement with the suggestion of the Officers Association of the 66th District that persons appointed to serve as Senior

due certification of the proficiency of brethren appointed to serve as Senior
Deacons, such certification to be based upon the Senior Deacon's lecture
in the second degree.

Refund of Unearned Dues
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered
the recommendation of the Grand Master that appropriate legislation
be enacted requiring the refund of unearned dues, whether for current
quarter or otherwise, and does not concur in the recommendation.
Under the Uniform Code of By-laws dues are payable quarterly in
advance. They are not payable daily, weekly or monthly, nor for any
greater or less period of time than one quarter of a year. At the beginning of the quarter the member becomes indebted to the Lodge for dues
for one quarter and on payment thereof the money so paid ceases to be in
any sense or to any extent the property of the member. The money becomes the absolute property of the Lodge. There are no strings to it and
the member retains no claim to it or interest in it or any equitable right to

325

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

any part thereof. The fact is that a debt was incurred and was discharged
by payment and the fact can not be altered by any subsequent" events.
The severance of membership by death, withdrawal, suspension or otherwise will not alter the fact nor will it create a right in a member to
money that he does not own and in which he has no interest. The case is
otherwise as to dues paid for a quarter or quarters beginning subsequent
to the date of such severance of. membership. In view of the foregoing
we are of the opinion that there is no such thing as unearned dues as
respects the payment. for a current quarter. We do not favor shortening
the dues paying period to one month or any lesser time which would be
necessary if refunds are properly to be made for parts of a quarter.

Grand Lodge Relief
The Grand Master recommends appropriate legislation for the appointment of a permanent committee to inve;tigate applications for and
to administer· Grand Lodge relief of every type. He met the situation by
appointing a special committee to deal with the subject.
Your Committee is of the opinion that the burden of direct investigation in matters of Grand Lodge relief should not be imposed upon the
Grand Master and that such work should be delegated by him either to
a special committee or to one of the several instrumentalities of Grand
Lodge already set up. It appears to us that through the offices of the
Trustees of the Masonic Homes, the Board of Control, the Boards of
Relief or the officers of the subordinate Lodges prompt and adequate
investigations can be made and the wishes of the Grand Master efficiently
executed. We do not look with approval upon the multiplication of standing committees unless an urgent and persuasive reason therefor exists
and we believe that a new committee for relief work would result in
overlapping of functions and duplication of effort. For these reasons
your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends that no such
new permanent committee be set up.

Your Committee recommends that the legislation be not adopted.

Masonic Temple Associations
The Grand Master recommends legislation prohibiting Lodges from
investing any of their funds in the securities of any T emple Association without approval of the Committee on Financing Building Projects.
This recommendation appears sound to your committee for the reason
that Lodges .are prohibited from investing their funds without the consent
of said committee in buildings proposed to be erected, but after the erection of a building there is no restriction on such investments. If the
approval of this committee is a desirable safeguard in the one case, it
should be equally desirable in the other.
Your Committee thinks that Grand Lodge should go a step farther
than the Grand Maste·r has indicated, for the reason that there is no

326

PROCE.EDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

general provision in our law governing investment of the funds of subordinate Lodges. We are of the opinion that the subordinate Lodges should
be permitted to invest their funds only in bank deposits and in securities
legal for savings banks in the State of California or of the Territory of
Hawaii, except that they be permitted to purchase stock, with the approval
of the Committee ·on Financing Building Projects, of the Temple Association owning the building in which .such Lodge meets. We therefore recommend that section 87 of the Constitution be amended by adding thereto a
clause to read substantially as follows:

It is the opinion of your Committee that a Lodge should have the right,
not only to take and hold title in itself, but it should have the right,
at its election, to appoint trustees with administrative powers to manage
and care for the property and investments of the Lodge, but always subject to the control of the Lodge.
It has been the practice for many years for Lodges to appoint trustees,
not only to take and hold title, but to administer the real property and
invested funds belonging to the Lodge, and with rare exceptions this has
proven to be an expedient and business-like manner of caring for these
important concerns. The trustees are elected by the members of the Lodge
and are usually brethren in whom the members have confidence and to
whom they desire to intrust the actual management of their property interests. Moreover, these trustees are usually brethren of sagacity and
business experience who are deeply attached to the Lodge and are zealous
and faithful in the performance of their duties as trustees. It seems to
your committee to be a distinct advantage to the Lodge to have the benefit
of the service of such men and the continuance in office of the same
trustees over long periods of time is a recognition of this fact. Masters
and other officers of most Lodges are changed annually, but the trustees
of its property are continued from year to year, thereby giving a stability
to its business policies that could not otherwise be secured. The judgment
of faithful trustees who are charged with a definite responsibility for
management of property is apt to be as good, if not better than that of
a large group who consider such affairs intermittently in Stated Meetings
of the Lodge. It is true that human nature can not be entirely eliminated
in any of the busy concerns of the Masonic or outer world, and that sometimes a feeling of paternalism develops on the part of trustees, just as
it sometimes develops on the part of other persons elected or appointed by
Lodges. This feeling grows out of an abiding concern for the welfare
of the Lodge and is sometimes unfortunate and at other times fortunate.
However, should the Lodge become dissatisfied with a trustee or trustees,
it has the power by orderly processes to correct the situation and at all
times it retains over the trustees the power of veto and direction. In every
case a Lodge must delegate to some one or more persons, whether they
. be trustees or otherwise, the actual management of its business in connection with its property and investment s, because a group of one hundr.ed,.
five hundred or a thousand men can not attend to the details of collectmg
rents, paying insurance and taxes, purchasing securities and doing those
many things that are necessary to be done if any form of property of
substantial value is properly administered.
It is the opinion of your committee that each Lodge should have the
right to determine for itself whether it will itself own and hold its assets
and manage the same, or whether it will delegate this duty to trustees
elected by and responsible to it. We _therefore recommend that section 87

"All investments of funds (except Life Membership Funds,
the investment of which is prescribed by section 129) by a Lodge
shall be in securities prescribed as legal by the laws of California
or the Territory of Hawaii for investments by savings banks; or,
with the approval of the Committee on Financing Building Projects, in the capital stock of a Temple Association owning or
proposing to erect a building in which the Lodge meets or intends
to meet; or, with the approval of said committee, in the land and
building of a Masonic Temple or hall owned by or proposed to be
erected by the Lodge; or, by depositing the same in a sound and
reputable bank or banks."

Adopted.
Lodge Trustees
The Grand Master directs attention to the fact that no action was
taken last year upon the recommendation of Grand Master Ross that the
Constitution be amended to permit Lodges to take title to real and personal
property in their own names. He also directs our attention to the California statute which permits Lodges to hold title to property without
incorporation and the questionable right of Masonic Lodges to take title
because section 87 of the Consti~tion provides for the holding of title
through Trustees, but does not in terms permit a Lodge to hold title in
its own name. The Grand Master recommends that our law be changed
by eliminating the right of Lodges to elect trustees and by providing that
title to Lodge property shall vest in the Lodge.
It is not the province of your Committee to construe the law of Grand
Lodge, but it understands that section 87 requires a Lodge to retain control of its own funds and property, which it can do by taking and holding
title in itself, or, at its election, it may, through trustees provided for in
a standing resolution, who shall always be under its control, hold and
manage its property and investments. If trustees are appointed they are
always subject to the direction of the Lodge. It appears, however, that
there is some doubt as to the right of a Lodge to take and hold property
directly and therefore section 87 of the Constitution should be amended
to remove such doubts.

be amended by striking out the third sentence thereof and adding a new

"A Lodge may hold title to all of its assets with the power

standing resolution, who shall . always be under its control, hold,

Life Membership Funds
The Grand Master recommended that legislation be enacted for the
creation of a committee for the investment of all Life Membership Funds ·
now held by Lodges and such Life Membership Funds as may hereafter be
received by them. The reasons for the recommendation are:
(a) That such a committee could make a wider distribution and diversity of investment than the local Lodges ;
(b) That there is greater assurance of wise investment by a general
committee of experienced men than when made directly by local Lodges;
(c) That it would prevent a possible diversion of the fund from the
purposes intended to be secured thereby.

While this proposal has much to commend it, yet your Committee
is of the opinion that no showing has been made to indicate that it is necessary or even desirable to deprive the Lodges of the handling of their
respective Life Membership Funds. Until it is shown that the Lodges a~e
incapable of properly investing and managing their Life Membership
Funds, or that the same are being diverted for improper uses, we think
that Grand Lodge should not assume the responsibility for the investment
and handling of these funds and that the Lodges should not ·be deprived.
of what would seem to be their logical and rightful authority and duty
in the premises.
The present investments of Life Membership Funds would probably
show a great diversity and it would be difficµlt, if not impossible, for
Grand Lodge to take over the handling an\! management of these funds
and to accord to each Lodge an equitable and proper proportionate interest
in the whole. In some cases the Lodges have invested wisely, and in other
cases the investments may have been injudicious, and sometimes have responded to the needs of the Temple Associations to sell to the Life Membership Fund stock in the building in which the Lodge meets. For example,

GRAND LODGE -OF CALIFORNIA

329

if the Life Membership Fund of one Lodge consisted largely of non-income
producing Temple stock and that of another Lodge consisted wholly of
cash in bank or gilt edge income producing securities, it would require a
financial and diplomatic genius to apportion the combined property between the Lodges in a manner just an? satisfactory to each.
For many years Life Members;hip Funds have been authorized by
·our law and prior to 1931 the Lodge, with the approval of the Master,
could invest the funds i~ any securities ap.proved by the Master. A cur'sory examination of the laws indicates that prior to 1923 the original
amounts paid in were to be forever kept and maintained as and for a
permanent Life Membership Fund; and that in 1923 the law was amended
to provide that upon the death of a Life Member such sum as he shall have
paid into the Fund could be withdrawn therefrom and become a part of
the General Fund of the Lodge. In 1926 the law was again amended to
provide that original payments should be kept forever as a part of a permanent Life Membership Fund. In 1931 Grand Lodge also amended the law
to require that Life Membership Funds should be invested only in bank
deposits or securities legal for savings banks under the laws of the State
of California and Hawaii, permitting the Lodge to use the income
only of the fund. Thus it will be seen that for a period of more than
fifty years there were no restrictions upon the investments of these funds
and that for only a single year has a proper safeguard in the matter of
investments been provided. Your Committee has not at hand the data to
show the interesting vicissitudes that have occurred through the years in
the history of the different Life Membership Funds operated under the
. varying provisions of our law, but is of the opinion that there is a sufficient
dissimilarity of investment and management to prevent the aggregate of
these funds being set up for the proportionate benefit of the Lodges.
A survey of the field under discussion, using the returns of 1931 for
the number of Lodges and membership, and the returns of 1932 for the
other facts, discloses that, out of 580 Lodges; 169 (or 29%) have set up
Life Membership Funds; and that out of a . membership of 142,062 there
are 3698 (or 2.6%) who are Life Members. While only 29% of the Lodges
have Life Membership Funds, about 50% of the ·Masons in California
belong to Lodges having such filnds. We find that 26 Lodges have only
one Life Member; 76 have 5 or less; 97 have 10 or less; 132 have 25 .or
less and 37 have more than 25. Of this 37, sixteen have more than SO
Lif~ Members; 7 have more than 100, and the largest number of Life
Members in any Lodge is 301. The Life Membership F unds of three
Lodges are in excess of $25,000; of 14 Lodges in excess of $10,000 and
less than $25,000; of 15 Lodges in excess of $5,000 and less than $10,000; of
10 Lodges in excess of $3,000 and less than $5,000; of 44 Lodges less than
$3,000 and more than $1,000, and of 83 less than $1,000. ·

Exemption From Dues
Your Committee on :J:>olicy and General Purposes has considered the
suggestion made by one of the brothers to the Grand Master that all
members qualified to receive fifty-year buttons be exempted from paying
dues and is of the opinion that no such exemption should be granted.
It is the opinion of your committee, and has been the policy of this
Grand Lodge during all the years of its existence, that every member
should contribute to the support of Masonry unless his dues, in proper.
cases, were remitted. This duty of contributing to the Lodge for its support and that of the charities and other activities of Masonry is not affected
by the matter of years or of service, but is inherent in the character of a
Mason. Money is required to carry on our works and without money our
institution as an organization would come to a standstill and the usefulness
of Masonry would be seriously impaired if not destroyed. The burden of
providing sufficient funds for Masonic purposes should ·be evenly distributed on the membership and no one should be allowed to shift his obligation onto his brethren, for lightening the load of one by exemption
increases that of the other members. Many of our brethren of mature
years are better able to contribute to Masonry than many of the younger
brethren, because age does not necessarily indicate the extent of a man's
resources or ability to pay. Whether a brother be old or young, his dues
should be, and will be, remitted by the Lodge when the circumstances of
each individual case requires such action.
The Grand Lodge instituted the custom of presenting fifty-year buttons in order to honor and distinguish those certain brethren who have
for. half a century been faithful Craftsmen. It was a graceful and fraternal
recognition of long years of Masonic service, but it was not intended as,
and is not, the setting up of a free list. Masonry is a "way of life" and
from the highest · to the lowest, and from the oldest to the youngest, it
expects spiritual, moral and financial contributions from each according to
his capacity and ability. We recommend that the suggestion be not adopted.

Report adopted.

Grand Lodge Cuscatlan of Salvador. Conversations have been pe,nding for several years between this Grand Lodge and the Grand Lodge
Cuscatlan of El Salvador, which is regularly recognized by many of the
Grand Lodges in the United States, by the Grand Lodge of England and
other Mas~nic powers of the world. This Grand Lodge has renewed its
request for recognition from year to year and has furnished us with
its constitutions and ·other literature as a basis of ·examination and as a
reason for recognition.
The Grand Lodge Cuscatlan was constituted in the same manner as
the Grand Lodges of Costa Rica and Guatemala. In the Republic of El
Salvador it exercises supreme and absolute authority over the Craft Degrees and does not admit or countenance the. authority of any. S.upreme
Council or other Masonic body. The Grand Lodge has four Lodges on its
roster, and we are informed that care is exercised in the selection of Masonic material and that the members are mindful of their duty of' introducing into the membership only ~uch men as will maintain its standards
of quality and enhance the advancement of Masonry in the Republic.
Although Salvador is the smallest of the Central American republics; the
brethren there believe that further Lodges will be established.. ·
Your committee is creditably informed that Grand Lodge Cuscatlan
observes the ancient landmarks and evidences the practice of a genuine
and regular Masonry and we therefore recommend· that fraternal recognition be granted to it.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE
Decisions of Grand Master

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom were referred the decisions of the Grand Master as· set forth in his message, have had the same
under consideration and beg leave to report:
In decision number 1, rendered by the G1-and Master, two matters
are presented:
1. Relying upon a decision of Grand Master Rucker in 1888 (Ross'
Digest No. 593) to the effect that the word "ballot" as used in the
Constitution of the Grand Lodge means a "secret vote by balls or cubes or
slips of paper," the Grand Master has ruled that in neither Grand nor
subordinate Lodge may any officer be elected by "acclamation," that is,
by the Secretary or other person being directed to cast the unanimous
"ballot" of the assemblage for some one candidate. The record of proceedings of 1888 does not disclose the particular sort of · "ballot" referred
to in the question propounded to and answered by Grand Master Rucker.
We are constrained to conclude, however, that it must have had reference
merely to some form of "ballot" required under our traditional practices
to be secret. In sections 101 and 110 of the Constitution provision is found
for election to membership and for advancement to a higher degree after
objection interposed by means of a "secret ballot." The use of this
language in these instances suggests by implication that there may be action
taken. by ballot other than by a "secret ·baHot." We think the matter of
election of officers, when all are of one mind, clearly should come within
such implied category. It may be said, too, that the practice of Grand

337

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA ·

Lodge and of many subordinate Lodges. in this jurisdiction for years is
opposed to the Grand Master's ruling. Elections by acclamation through
t_he use of an unanimous ballot cast by the Secretary or other person have
never ·been questioned. This contemporaneous construction of the Constitution, long unchallenged, but confirms the conclusion to which we have
arrived. ~ e recommend that this portion of Decision 1 be not concurred in.

In paragraph C the Grand Master holds that a Lodge in this jurisdiction should not confer the degrees by request for another jurisdiction
on a candidate who is entirely unable to conform to the physical requirements, being paralyzed from the waist down and obliged to use a wheel
chair. We recommend the approval of this decision.

336

Adopted.
2. In Decision 1, the GTand Master held that the report of the Secre-·
tary in delinquents required in June and December should be orally announced, unless waived by appropriate action of the Lodge. We recommend approval.

Approved.
Decision II. In the first paragraph the Grand Master holds that a
Master continues in office until his successor is elected and installed. This
is in accordance with the provisions of section 135 of the Constitution and
should be approved.
In paragraph 2 the Grand Master decided that as section 139 of the
Constitution fixes sixty days as a reasonable time for the Master-elect
to obtain a certificate of qualification the same period should be construed
as a reasonable time within which he should present himself for installation in any event, though for good cause shown, and if it appears that the
Master-elect desires to assume his duties within a reasonable time thereafter, the Lodge might defer action temporarily, but that the Lodge should
not continue indefinitely without electing a Master. We are in accord with
this decision. The time which should be granted to the Master-elect is
necessarily left to the good judgment of the Lodge, but should not be
unnecessarily extended. We recommend the approval of the decision.
In paragraph 4 it is held that the Wardens who have been regularly
elected and installed continue to serve in their respective offices. We reccmmeild the approval of this decision.
Decision III that any Mason in good standing is eligible for ~ffice
is correct and should be approved.
In decision IV-A the Grand Master held that it was the duty of
the Master carefully to satisfy himself that a candidate was physically
able to comply with the requirements of the ritual. The Master and the
Lodge are invested with the power and duty of determining the question,
and should be held to responsibility in the exercise thereof. We recommend the approval of the decision.
In paragraph B the Grand Master holds that a brother desiring to
affiliate with a Lodge, who is unable to write by reason of physical affliction, may sign his name by mark, properly attested. We recommend that
the decision be approved.

In decision VA the Grand Master decides that where objection was
made to advancement of an Entered Apprentice in 1924, if no action
pursuant to the provisions of sections 110 and 111 had been taken, it was
the· duty of the Master now to proceed, and in the absence of any proof
to the contrary it is to be presumed that such action was taken. The
ruling is correct, and we recommend its approval.
In paragraph B an objection was made to one Master but no action
pursuant to section 110 was taken by him. Following the installation of
another Master, to whom the candidate had applied for advancement, the
Grand Master ruled that the procedure prescribed by section 110 should
be followed. There can be no doubt as to the correctness of this ruling,
and we recommend its approval.
Decision VII we approve.
In decision VIII, A and B, the Grand Master rules that imprisonment
pursuant to a conviction of a felony which subjects a Mason to summary
expulsion is a necessary prerequisite to such action, and that imprisonment
in a county road camp for three years, as a condition to the granting of
probation, constitutes such imprisonment as is contemplated by our law.
We believe this to be a correct statement of the. law and recommend its
approval.
Decision IX holds that it is the duty of the Junior Warden under
sections 189 and 192 to prefer charges without direction of the Master.
This is correct .and should be approved.
Decision XI, to the effect that a Lodge from which a Mason is suspended for non-payment of dues, retains penal jurisdiction to try him for
unmasoriic conduct, notwithstanding his residence within the territorial
jurisdiction of another Lodge, is correct and should be approved.

The Grand Master reports in decision XVII that~ he advised· a Lodge
that the brethren might attend a church service in Masonic clothing with-

339

out a dispensation. He stated that the decision was based upo~ a decision
of the Grand Master in 1888 that the members of a Lodge might appear
in Masonic clothing for the purpose of decorating the graves of deceased
Masons. It is argued that tribute to the Supreme Architect is a Masonic
duty of equal importance with respect for the dead. Whil~ it is true that
the worship of God is a duty incumbent upon all Ma~ons, this Gran~ Lodge
has never undertaken to legislate the manner in which such worship sha~l
be conducted or any church or other place in which it shall be done. This
is left to the individual consciences of the members. But this Grand Lodge
has said in section 116 of the Constitution: "No Lodge, nor any Mason,
shall ap~r in Masonic clothing in any public procession or at any public
meeting or place, except for the burial of a brother or for the performance
of some other strictly Masonic duty or ceremony."
There is no provision, of our law imposing a duty upon M~sons as su~h
to attend church services, hence it can not be said to be a strictly Masonic
duty, and Masonic clothing should not be worn. We recommend that the
decision be not approved.

All the above reports were adopted.
Evidentiary Value of Court Records in Trials
Your Committee on Jurisprudence have had under consideration recommendation of the Grand Master with respect to the evidentiary value
of legally certified records of State and Federal courts in criminal cases
in Masonic trials, and respectfully reports as follows:
The Grand Master asks "whether certified record of final conviction
in criminal proceedings is prima fade evidence in a Masonic trial of
guilt of the offense covered in the criminal proceedi?gs."
Your committee is of the opinion that this question must be answered
in the affirmative. Properly authenticated reporters' transcripts of t~sti­
mony taken in State and Federal courts in criminal cases and duly certified
records of proceedings and judgments in such courts have long bee~ recognized and received as evidence in Masonic trials, and have received the
approbation of Grievance Committees, and have been rep?'"ted to Grand
Lodge. These reports have been invariably approved by t~1s G~and .Body.
Such authenticated records, when presented and received m. ev1den~e
in a Masonic trial in this jurisdiction, undoubtedly make out a pr1ma fac1e
case as to all matters finally determined on the face of such record, and
may be accepted as such by the Trial Commissions.

Adopted.

· The amendment of 1931 ·to section 129 of the Constitution expressly
·defines what the resolution establishing Life Membership should contain
and therefore it is our opinion th;it the Grand Master correctly decided
that if .any Lodge has adopted such resolutions prior to the amendment of
1931 such Lodge should at once take affirmative action amending their
standing resolution upon this subject to conform to the amendment of 1931.
Feeling, however, that section 129 of the Constitution is unfortunately ·
worded in many particulars it is our opinion that the entire section should
be revamped for the purpose of making the same self-executing and correcting the error in the wording thereof to which our attention has been
directed by recommendation No. VI of the Grand Master.

mertt of .a Masonic trial pending the result of the trial in the civil courts,"
but the accuser objected to such a postponement on the ground that "he
did not consider he would be able to obtain justice in a civil action prior
to a Masonic trial."
In the opinion of the Grand Master "the spirit of our law contemplates deferring of Masonic ·trials under such circumstances," and he
holds that "in view of the avowed purpose of the accuser to institute civil
proceedings the Master is justified in postponing the calling of a meeting
to elect commissioners under section 193 until the trial in the courts of
the land has been determined, or until it shall appear that such a civil
trial is not contemplated," and this opinion, he states, "conforms to the
purpose which underlies the provisions of the first sentence in section 192."
The ·sentence referred to reads as follows: "When the charge is for an
offense which is the subject <if proceedings in courts of the land, the
Masonic trial may, in the discretion of the Master, be deferred until such
proceedings are concluded."
If the Master finds the charges presented to him to be sufficient, he
must call a special meeting for the election of commissioners (section 193,
Constitution), and the trial should not be deferred .under section 192
unless a condition arises as is contemplated by that sect10n. In the present
case: no action, based upon the offense included in the charges presented to
the . Master 1 is shown to be pending in court, and the fact that such a
proceeding may be planned would not justify the ~ast~r in. defe~ring the
Masonic trial. The Master is authorized to exercise his discretion as to
deferment only when court proceedings based upon the same offense h~ve
been brought in a court of the land, and if that situation does not exist,
then the Master must act under section 193.
. . We therefore recommend that the decision be not approved.

Right of Members to Attend Trials
Your Committee on Jurisprudence has had under consideration the
request of the Committee on Grievances that we should pass upon the
question of the right of Masons to be present at Masonic trials. We
assume that this refers to the right of the membership generally who are
not parties to the hearing, to attend the hearing.
It is the unanimous opinion of this committee that it is contrary to
the spirit of our Institution to declare, as a matter of law, that trials in
a Masonic Lodge may be conducted in secret, and that property avouched
Masons should be admitted. But we are also of the opinion that for the
present the question should be left open, and that if any exceptions-and if
any, what exceptions-should be made to this policy, should receive a more
thorough consideration and investigation than we are able to give at this
communication. It is our thought that this question should go over until
next year for more mature consideration and report, and we so recommend.

Adopted.
Amendment to Section 79
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referred the proposed amendment to section 79 of the Constitution, recommend that said
section 79 be amended by striking out therefrom the last sentence and
adding it to section 88, and changing the word "shall" where it occurs
therein to "may."

Adopted, and sections 79 and 88 of the Constitution accordingly amended by unanimous vote.

Masonic Homes Endowment Board of California
Sec. 37f. There is hereby created the "Masonic Homes Endowment
Board of California," to consist of fifteen members. They shall be appointed by the Grand Master and shall serve for a period of three years;
provided, that those first appointed shall draw lots so that five thereof
shall serve for one year, five for two years and five for three years.
Thereafter each succeeding Grand Master shall appoint five to serve for
three years. Any vacancy accruing on the board shall be filled by the
Grand Master, the appointee to serve for the remainder of the unexpired term.
Sec. 37g. The Chairman of the Board shall be named by the Grand
Master and shall serve for one year. The board shall provide for the
election of a Secretary and such other officers and employes as it may determine. The board, subject to the approval of the Grand Master, may
adopt and from time to time change or amend such rules and regulations
gove:ning its deliberations, modes of procedure and the like as may be
required and as shall best enable it, faithfully, efficiently and successfully
to carry out the true spirit, intent and purpose of its creation.
Sec. 37h. The Masonic Homes E~dowment Board of California shall
study, devise and carry out plans for the securing of adequate endowment
for the Masonic Homes of California. To that end, subject to the approval
of the Grand Master, the board shall issue such appeals, and from time to
time establish such contacts with persons disposed to contribute to or aid
in the creation or maintenance of an Endowment Fund for the Masonic
Homes of California, as may be deemed appropriate. The end to be attained eventually in this behalf is that a sufficient endowment shall be
created to make it possible for the Masonic Homes of California to be
supported from the income from such endowment, and complete reliance
upon the income derivable from Grand and subordinate Lodges thereby
avoided.
Sec. 37i. The board provided for herein shall collect, and pursuant
to regulations adopted by it and subject to the approval of the Grand
Master and the Grand Treasurer, shall invest funds and moneys contributed or inuring to the Endowment Fund herein provided for, and
at least annually shall cause the income therefrom to be paid to the
Trustees of the Masonic Homes for use in the maintenance and opera-

tion of the same. No moneys or funds may be invested in securities or
other properties save those now specified for investment of Endowment
Funds or as shall hereafter by this Constitution be permitted. All moneys,

placed in the custody of the Grand Treasurer of the Grand Lodge to be
held by him as such and to be by him accounted for as other Grand Lodge

Sec. .37j. No part of the Endowment Fund herein provided for, either

bOard, adopted as herein provided, and in conformity with the due and
appropriate exercise of the authority herein conferred.

THANKS TO EAST BAY BRETHREN
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California.:
Whereas, the representatives in attendance at this, the eighty-third
communication of the Grand Lodge, have had a most enjoyable time as the
guests of our brethren of the East Bay Lodges, due in no small part to
the splendid program provided by them for our entertainment, and that of
our ladies, we desire to take this opportunity to express to them our
hearty appreciation of their untiring efforts to make this, our first communication to be holden in the city of Oakland, one long to be remembered.
To our brethren of the Scottish Rite, we would also give our sincere
thanks for their great kindness in providing us with this magnificent
auditorium, with its wonderful organ, in which to hold our daily sessions.
And to the press of Oakland and the other cities around the Bay, we
desire to give grateful acknowledgment for their generous support and
co-operation in giving to our brethren of the craft the very interesting
accounts of our activities.
To our brethren of Alameda county we would most gratefully say
that your slogan, "Let brotherly love continue," has been most generously
demonstrated.
Respectfully submitted,
Ron G. GUYETr,

in the amount of $51.02. Your committee feels that if the Lodges pay
their just dues they should not be penalized for an error of one of their
officers. We, therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of $51.02 be and is hereby appropriated from
the funds of this Grand Lodge to reimburse San Francisco Lodge No.
360 for its overpayment of Grand Lodge tax for the years 1925-1931,
inclusive.

Adopted.

should be declined, for the reason that · there are a large number of
Lodges in this jurisdiction whose financial conditions are as bad or worse
than.that of the petitioner: Your committee offers the following resolution
and recommends its ·adoption:
Resolved, that the petition of San Buenaventura Lodge No. 214, located at Ventura, for the return of the Grand Lodge dues which said
Lodge paid on August }. 1932, be denied.

Adopted.

the funds.

expenses of the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior and Juni<;>r Grand
Wardens, when visiting Lodges or attending other Masonic 'meetings in

Grand Lodge officers.

resolution and recommend its adoption:

Masonic Homes
The most important subject that will come before this Grand Lodge at
this session, and for many years to come, is the support and maintenance of
the Masonic Homes.
More than two-thirds of the total revenue of the Grand Lodge is now
raised for the support of these Homes. The net operating expenses of the
Trustees of the Masonic Homes have increased from $140,538.65 in 1924,
to $231,280.91 in 1932. The greatest single item of increase can be traced
to Outside Relief (i.e., care of old folks and children outside the Homes).
In 1925 this amounted ·to only $3,210.00, whereas in the year 1932 it
amounted to $31,186.39.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

355

On July 31, 1928, the Trustees of the Homes had a net bank balance in
their Operating Fund, after allowing for all overdrawn fund accounts, of
$107,616.95, whereas on July 31, 1932, their General Fund Account was
overdrawn $5,299.63, and their indebtedness amounted to $376,713.11, which
was made up a~ follows :

As of July 31, 1932, the Trustees of the Masonic Homes were indebted
in the amount of $376,713.11, whereas we estimate that their income
for the year 1932-1933 will be $10,000 less· than their present operating
expenses. There are only two courses to pursue:
1 : To reduce expenses.
2: To increase revenue.
The expenses of maintenance of our Masonic Homes, together with
outside relief, have increased in proportion to our growth, and in order to
guarantee for them a future of increasing usefulness, we recommend that
the per capita tax be raised from SOc to 75c.
We offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved, that the sum of 75c per capita be levied upon the membership, for the maintenance of our Homes at Decoto and Covina.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

403

John M. Ross of Hakalau, speaking for his brethren of
the Hawaiian Islands, presented to the retiring Grand Master a royal lei, with the Aloha of his brethren.
The newly installed Grand Master was fairly taken off
his feet when Harry Beattie, in the name of the Lodges and
brethren of South San Joaquin valley, presented a gold gavel,
the messenger who actually placed the gavel in the hands of
the recipient being the son-a Past Master of Exet~r Lodge
-of the Grand Master. Incidentally it may be noted that
four sons and one son-in-law of Brother Mixter, all Masons,
were present.
Grand Master Mixter announced the appointment of
Samuel E . Burke as a member of the Board of Trustees of
the Masonic Homes, vice self, term expired.
The Grand Master clothed the retiring Grand Master
with the apron of his present rank, and also presented him
with a diamond studded lapel button of a Past Grand
·Master.
The usual interchange of lapel jewels, with felicitations
usual to the occasion, followed, and at 2 o'clock p. m., all
· business being now completed, Grand Lodge was closed in
Ample Form.
FRANK W. MIXTER,
Grand Master.

Grand Lodge F. & A" M. of California
REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
CORRESPONDENCE
October, 1932
BY JESSE M. WHITED

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
Herewith is submitted my TweUth Report as Chairman of the
Correspondence Conunittee. As usual, the views expressed under
the various topics are the individual ideas of the Chairman.
The author of the saying that "there is nothing new under the
Sun" never had the opportunity of serving as Chairman of a Correspondence Committee. One would think in an Institution as old
as the Masonic Fraternity practically every question had been considered or legislated upon, but a review of the Proceedings of some
sixty-eight jurisdictions decisively negates this idea. Generally the
same fundamental questions occupy the attention of Grand Lodges.
These continue to produce interesting features that keep them alive
and shows the inquiring or inventive turn of mind of the individual.
In considering the Fraternity at the present time, and questions
involved in its present or future, it is perhaps well to ask whether
we are to think our organization is a Fraternity, a Philosophy or
an Institution. Unfortunately for some reasons the three are so
interwoven that discussion as to any one of them must take into
consideration one or both of .the others.
In 1717 when the first Grand Lodge was established Masonry
was a Fraternity pure and simple, and its development for some
was along that line. Then came the efforts to prove the organization
the direct descendant of the Ancient Mysteries and with it came
the development of the Ritual. Then came the expansion along the
institutional line. This resulted in quantity production brought about
by the World War and change in modern business ideas and conditions. Whether or not it will ever be possible to return to the original
idea of being a Fraternity is a question.
Masonry in England, Ireland, Scotland and the British Commonwealths has continued more or less along the Fraternal plan.
While they also have their problems they do not seem to be as acute
as the ones affecting the Grand Lodges of the United States. They

REPORT ON CORRESPONDJ!lNCE

2

3

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

have not been vexed with such problems as to co-ordinate Bodies,
Financial Problems threatening their Charitable Institution, Ritualism, multiplicity of Laws, and other conditions with which we are
confronted.
A solution for us we believe is contained in the words of our
Grand Master, Robert B. Gaylord, speaking before the Grand Masters Conference in Washington, when he said:
"I believe, Brethren, if we thought less of degrees, if we thought
less of direct charity, and if we would go back more to the day
when we came together in our Lodges for fellowship, when we came
there because we found men whom we could trust, men whom we
loved, when we came to Lodge, because we loved going to Lodge
and extended charity, because we loved the Brothers, when we come
back to that day, our problems as to attendance, and our problems
in the future for Masonry will be solved. You had it in the pioneer
days in your States. We had it in the pioneer days in California and
to my mind it is the ideal thing for Masonry to go back to the spirit
of pioneer Masonry."
Some of the topics or conditions that have arisen during . the
past year which are not embodied in the general body of this Report
may be briefly summarized as follows:
ATTENDANCE: Indifference and lack of interest, as evidenced
by attendance at Lodge meetings where there is business or otherwise, we do not believe can be chargeable to any one cause. Those
who join through curiosity, have had that satisfied and are now only
members or left. The same applies to those who petitioned for business or social reasons. Those who are actuated by an admiration for
the Fraternity, its teachings and its works as such, are in the minority. Added to these causes must be the counter attractions of the
present, such as the automobile, the radio, the talkies and other
entertaining attractions. These possess a greater drawing power than
the average Lodge meeting.
One Grand Master advocates the idea that the test of a member's eligibility to remain in good standing in a . co-ordinate Masonic
Body would be his record of attendance in his Blue Lodge. In the
past some Jurisdictions made it obligatory upon members to visit
their Blue Lodges a certain number of times during each year. Even
this did not prove effective. The size of a Lodge is also a determining
factor. There is no doubt but what the small Lodge, where the mem- ·
bers know each other has a greater incentive for attendance than in
large Lodges.
BUSINESS MANAGER: The Grand Lodge of Wisconsin now
has before it for action at their next annual communication the ques-

~ion .o f appointing a Business Manager. He is to be all that the name
1mpbes as far as financial and business matters of the Grand Lodge
are concerned. When one peruses the financial statements of the
larg~r Jurisdictions it would appear that such a system possesses
considerable merit, particularly if we expand along financial and
institutional lines.

C~NDID~TES: ·we believe that now is the time wP.en perhaps
regulat1?ns designed t~ secure a higher class of petitioners should
be. considered. There .1s lack of Candidates at the present time. It
mig~t ~e well to consider whether, unless the standard is· raised and
adm1ss1on requirements made stricter, there will not be a tendenc
to recoup. our losses in membership and finances by again
for quantity rather than quality.
Some of the safeguards that might be adopted would be the
appea~ance of .the candidate and his proposers before an ex-officio
committee of the Lodge, composed of elective officers and Past
M~sters for examination. In other words if this investigation was
satisfactory the petition could then be presented to the Lodge and
the regulation investigation committee. Some Jurisdictions have mad
a standing committee of the Lodg:
itself, and .requ1~e .the petitioner and his sponsors to appear before
~~~· . A time bm1t between the election ol the candidate and his
m1t1ation, and also a limit between each degree would undoubtedly
have a beneficial effect. "That which is easily gained is lightly held"
and. a .~aiting list for candidates would be desirable if based ~n
des1rab1bty rather than numbers.

~he Investigati~g Commi~t~e

ETHIC~: Whether or not Masons generally have departed
from the Ethics of Masonry as embodied in the Ancient Landmarks
and the ritual is a question asked by some Grand Masters as well
as the student of present conditions. One Grand Master went so far
as to say that in his opinion one of the causes as to why fewer men
were seekin~ admission was due to the fact that the general public
had .lost their res~ect for the Masonic Fraternity by reason of "the
horrible. example~ of some members. Masons, both in high and low
places, m ~om.e instances ~av~ forgotten the duty that they owe to
the Orgamz~hon along this hne. The world is prone to judge by
such exceptions. These regrettable instances undoubtedly tend to
lower the esteem with which the profane regard the Fraternity.

EDUCATION-MASONIC: It does not appear that this problem has been satisfactorily solved by any one Grand Lodge that has
undertaken it. As Chairman Allen of North Carolina says: "In fact
the term Masonic Education is one just now to produce yawns. Ou;
Brethren as a rule do not want it; it does not either appeal to their

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

imagination or inspire them. But after all is said and done the fact
remains that something is badly needed."
As stated in previous reports, we believe that if a Candidate at
his initiation was presented, as they do in some Jurisdictions, with
a work dealing with the evolution of the Fraternity, its history and
ideals, and before being raised, required to state that he has at
least read the volume, it would produce practical results. There is no
doubt but the newcomer is curious and anxious to learn everything
possible regarding the Organization. That is the proper time to
furnish him the details regarding it. There will, of course, always
continue to be students of Masonic History, symbolism, etc., but
they are in the minority and their own initiative will solve the problem for them.

RECORDS: The experience of Committees or individuals
engaged in writing Masonic History shows that through lack of care
the early records of a number of Lodges have been lost or destroyed.
One of the Jurisdictions provides that Lodges must keep these in a
a fireproof vault. Another provides that they should be sent to the
Grand Secretary for safe keeping. Another Jurisdiction goes so far
as to send only the Lodge a photostat copy of its charter, retaining
the original
Official books, records, documents and original papers not in
current use we believe could be protected in no better way than
placing them in th~ custody of the Grand Secretary and stored in
a place where there would be no possibility of destruction. To the
present · membership they perhaps have little interest, but as time
goes on they become more and more valuable to the Fraternity
generally.

EDUCATION-PUBLIC: "Public Schools Week" of our Jurisdiction is an example of how Masonry can assist in the work of
preparing the future citizens of our country. While the~e is some
question as to whether this is a function of the Fraterruty or not,
still we believe perhaps "the end justifies the means." It does not
infringe upon the Ancient Charge that we should not concern ourselves with politics or religion. The Grand Lodges of Tennessee and
some of the other Southern States have interested themselves in the
education of the youth, and from the reports it \woul~ appear that
they are doing a worthwhile work and do not retret it.
0

FUNERALS : A number of the Jurisdictions have revised the
funeral ritual to eliminate the doleful and melancholy form in which
it was once written. There is a tendency to make the Masonic Funeral more of a private affair than a public function, which we believe
is commendable.
Two interesting cases arose recently. In one Jurisdiction, the
Grand Master prohibited a Lodge from holding a Masonic Funeral
over the body of a member who had confessed his guilt and committed suicide after being indicted for the murder of his wife. In
another Jurisdiction, a member maintained a "love nest" and his wife
learning of this went to the apart.ment, laid in wait for him and on
his arrival promptly shot and killed him. The newspapers gave great
publicity to the case. The family insisted on a Masonic funeral, an.d
under the laws of that Jurisdiction the Grand Master ruled that it
must be held. As he stated in his message, "What an advertisement
for Freemasonry." From the record there is no statement as to why
such a member whose character was generally known, was permitted to contin~e his membership. The outcome of the affair was a
change in the law which made a reoccurrence of such an affair
impossible.

6

TRIALS-MASONIC: There are three common methods of
handling Masonic trials. First by the entire Lodge, acting as the
Jury; second, by Committee selected by the Lodge, and third, by
special committee appointed by the Grand Master for each individual
case. The last method is growing in favor; it possesses the advantage of having experts who are familiar with many of the technical
details involved in Masonic trials, and furthermore would be uninfluenced by local conditions or prejudice. It also has the added merit
of greatly reducing the number of appeals and reversals, thereby
lessening the labors of the Committee on Grievances and Appeals,
and saving the time of the Grand Lodge by shortening the reports
of that Committee.
VISITATIONS: There seems to be a difference of opinion as
to the legality or propriety of a Lodge of one Jurisdiction visiting
the Lodge of another and exemplifying their ritual, either on one
of their own candidates or one of the home town. Some Grand
Masters permit and encourage it, while others take the 'position that
no ritual can be used except that one adopted by the Grand Lodge
where the work is done.
Lodges of California and Nevada have interchanged visitations,
and we believe with good results. It does make for fraternalism.
As the Chairman of the Vermont Correspondence Committee stated,
"We feel it to be a good thing for some of our Masons to realize
· that Vermont work is not the same as was used 'at the building of
King Solomon's Temple', and that wherever it came from it differs
in various localities."

LATE ARRIVALS: We regret that the 1932 Proceedings fr~m
West Australia, Rhode Island, Mexico, Saskatchewan, ~ew Mexico,
Virginia, Canada and Prince Edward Island were received too late
to be included in this Report.
As heretofore we desire to acknowledge our obligation to. the
writers of reports, Editors of Masonic publications a~d · other writers 1
from whose lectures we have borrowed the material or thoughts
which are directly or indirectly contained in this R~~ort. Whether
or not anything herein stated is educational, enterta~nmg or of any
value whatsoever depends upon the reader. The function of the Committee perhaps may be best expressed in the follpwing:
Drop a pebble in the water
Just a splash and it is gone,
But there half a hundred ripples
Circling on and on and on;
Spreading, spreading on out from the center
Going on out to the sea,

ADVERTISING
Advertising of all kinds, whether for financial or other reasons,
still continues to be a matter of legislation and opinion. Insurance
companies advertising as operating "for Masons only" have borne the
brunt of criticism. We hold no brief for such a practice, but of all
classes of business wherein this question may arise it seems to be
the only one that is under any supervision whatever. Such companies are regulated by National and State laws and subject to National
and State supervision.
An exception is made in. various Jurisdictions by allowing magazines, hospitals, supply houses, ce~terie6, etc., to use the word
Masonic. These are operated for private gain, and to be fair it
would appear that they should be subject to the same regulations as
insurance companies.
The placing of Masonic emblems on automobiles and business
literature and the display of emblems by an individual are open to
criticism and have been the subject of legislation. If the custom
prevalent in the Jurisdictions of the British Empire of individual
members wearing no emblems at all would ever become fashionable
it would have a good effect.
Publicity given to Masonic affairs has gone to such an extent
that there is practically little secrecy left regarding our Institution
~nd its activities. That at one time was a source of our strength.
Colorado (1931):
(Masonic Officers Association}: The Worshipful Masters and
Wardens of the Denver Lodges, associated together in the Denver
Masonic Officers Association, desire to call your attention to a most
discreditable practice which has grown up among the membership
and to curb which there appears to be no law in the Book of Constitutions under which we proceed for the protection of our membership.
This is the solicitation of our membership and our candidates for
all manner of commercial propositions such as insurance (supposedly
based on Masonic membership), magazine subscriptions for so-called
Masonic magazines, sales of Masonic encyclopaedias and many other
items.
This practice has grown to such proportions as to endanger the
peace and harmony of our Lodges and has threatened the sanctity of
the ballot.
Our candidates have been solicited for Masonic magazines and
talked to in such a way that they were afraid that, did they not pay
for the subscriptions, they faced the possibility of being blackballed

8

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

in the Lodge, and have appealed to the Lodge for prote<;tion from
such solicitors. And in some cases this discreditable solicitation has
been made before the committee of investigation of the Lodge has
been able to call on the candidate and make any kind of an investigation, the result being that the first word a candidate receives that has
any bearing on Masonry after his application is a solicitation for a
subscription.
Our Brethren, and in some cases candidates, have been solicited
for insurance, having as a requisite membership in the Masonic Fraternity, with such tenacity as to be terribly embarrassing, and when
the solicitation takes place while the Brother is standing on the
Entered Apprentice or Fellowcraft degree, places the Brother in a
most awkward position as he is afraid to refuse for fear of the .blackball. All of the Lodges have frequent complaints about this matter
and can find no laws under which it is possible to stop the practice.
Connecticut (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Grand Master of Illinois
rightly ruled the wearing of a Masonic emblem by the son of a
Mason as "very improper." 0. K. But we knew of a case where a
Mason naively gave his identification card to his daughter when she
set out on a trip. With equal naivette, she affected surprise when told
it was illegal.
Iowa (1931):
(Grand Master):. I think that the attention of the Craft should
be called to a situation, amounting to a real evil, which is found in
greater or less degree in all the jurisdictions. I refer to. the abuses
that have developed in connection with the activities of organizations
of a commercial or quasi-commercial character which limit their
membership and activities to Masons. These organizations vary
greatly in their nature-cemetery associations, insurance companies,
book and periodical publishing concerns. Agents not infrequently
take advantage of uninformed new-made Masons, persuading them,
for example, to buy insurance in the belief that it is a part of their
Masonic obligation to do so. The unfairness and the un-Masonic
character of this is clear. It seems to me that our members and the
interest of the fraternity should be protected against such abuses. At
least the new brother who knows nothing about Masonic law, traditions and usages should be protected. I urge upon the Brethren, and
particularly upon the officers of Lodges, that they inform new members that they are under no Masonic obligation whatever to buy
anything from anyone. Let us use our influence to prevent the commercialization of Masonry, and to protect its good name from injury
at the hands of selfish, profit-seeking men.

Missouri (1931):
(Grand Master): Other Grand Masters have had experiences
similar to mine with so~called Masonic papers. In the light of all
that has transpired, my own opinion is that the publishing of so-called
Masonic papers by individuals or private enterprises ought to be
prohibited and that if any such paper is published, it should be published by the Grand Lodge. Such papers as are now published are
a constant source of trouble and annoyance, resulting year after year
in controversies and arguments between the editors and the executive officers of the Grand Lodge, and do far more harm than good.
The constant temptation to publish a lot of stuff that has no
place in a Masonic paper in order to increase the revenue of the
publisher is irresistible.

Pennsylvania (1931):
(Grand Master): Recently, Secretaries of subordinate Lodges
have been enclosing with the Lodge notices separate slips or cards
announcing all kinds of social, musical, etc., functions. Some of these
notices have announced dances to which both sexes have been
invited. The present rulings that a Lodge notice shall contain nothing
of an outside nature have been grossly violated. I, therefore, decide
that hereafter notices of Lodge meetings shall be confined to strictly
Lodge matters, and no card or slip shall be inserted which shall contain any announcement which is not strictly a Lodge matter. No
information concerning card parties, dances, musicales, and entertainments of var.i ous natures, particularly where mixed audiences are to
be present, is permitted.

• • • • •

The Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania does not recognize such a
thing as Masonic life insurance. The Secretary of a Lodge, in his
official capacity as Secretary, has nothing to do with making proof
of death for the purpose of collecting life insurance. The Seal of the
Lodge is not to be used in attesting the death of' a member holding
a life insurance policy in a so-called Masonic life insurance company.
Virginia (1931):
(Grand Master): I have been deeply concerned during the year
to find that the Craft have been persistently circularized for business
and commercial purposes and I am satisfied that the wishes and action
of the Grand Lodge in this respect are being disregarded. During the
past few years, there have grown up in our Jurisdiction certain busi-

ness enterprises which, in the main, have been maintained and operated by members of the Craft who seek to do business with Masons
only, and appeals, both expressed and implied, are made to the
Masonic relationship. As I am advised, for the most part these activities have been confined to so-called insurance schemes, which are,
as a rule, conceived and born in an atmosphere of selfishness and
have for their ultimate object financial return to some individual or
group. In the first place, there is grave doubt of the soundness of
these schemes from an economic or actuarial standpoint and these
efforts are fraught with embarrassment and detriment to the parties
who may become interested in them and to the fraternity and to the
Grand Lodge whose duty, as I conceive it, is to protect the Craft and
to preserve the spirit and purposes of the institution. In the second
place, I am advised that there is grave doubt of the legality of these
activities from the standpoint of the laws of the Commonwealth
governing and controlling such enterprises, and we cannot afford as
Masons to become involved in doubtful practices.
