BUDGETS
The financial affairs of Grand Lodges and constituent Lodges
are governed by the same inflexible rules as in any other walk of
life. Some of the Jurisdictions have started at the ground fioor and
endeavored to place the affairs of the constituent Lodges on a business basis by insisting expenditures be put on an annual budget.
They in turn have followed the same example. Others are living
in the hopes that necessity will produce the same effect, rather than
direct legislation. Some have been wise enough to reduce the expenses of non-essentials, thus setting a good example. There is one
thing certain that any Fraternal ocganization to succeed must conduct its financial affairs on business lines. We marvel at the fact
that the constituent Lodges in some Jurisdictions are able to survive
on annual dues ranging from $2.00 to $5.00, with low initiation fees.
Illinois (1931):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Committee on Legislation, among other things, reported and had approved an amendment
to the by-laws extending the powers of a Committee on Lodge
Finances, so that every chartered Lodge would be examined and
reported upon annually and a budget prepared to be followed by
the Lodges. The committee was also empowered to consult with the
Lodges on the erection of temples, financing plans and other incidental measures.
Michigan (1931):
(Grand Master): No Lodge has a right to ask the other Lodges
of Michigan to carry its financial burden, in addition to their own.
We know that Brethren cannot all pay their dues, in a period of
depression, and we are willing to make allowances, but it is an interesting fact that a number of our Lodges went to their town banks
and borrowed money to meet their obligations to Grand Lodgeand if a Masonic Lodge lacks sufficient standing in the community
to secure credit at its bank, there is at least room for doubt that it
should continue to struggle along.
Mississippi (1932):
(Finance Committee): During our deliberations and in our troubles when we have tried to reach these conclusions, it was a consolation to us though no surprise that our Worthy Grand Secretary
appeared before us and out of the heart of love for Masonry said to
us: "Reduce my salary 25% and every employee of my office the same
amount and if you Brethren expect to save the serious situation, make
somewhat of a similar reduction in every department."

Nebraska (1932):
(Grand Master): In many instances I believe our Lodges are not
collecting sufficient dues from the membership to properly meet
future financial demands and obligations. We have fifty-eight Lodges,
the dues of which range from $2.75 to $4.50 per year. Many of them
have no surplus funds or relief funds, but are apparently collecting
only sufficient to cover limited current expenses. Brethren, this
matter should be given very serious consideration. With the passing
of time, our Lodges will more and more be called upon for financial
relief to their distressed Brethren; and while we are not an alms-giving
institution, we do have a duty toward the welfare of our Brethren
and their dependents and when the need is manifest our Lodges
should be in a financial position to respond to such need, and not be
compelled to say we have no money for welfare use. · I firmly believe
that no Lodge should collect less than $5.00 annual dues, which ,
after paying Grand Lodge dues leaves only $3.00 for local use. I
recommend that the minimum dues collect,ed by Nebraska Lodges
shall be five dollars per member per year.

North Dakota (1931):

(Gr<!nd Master): Masonry is not a cheap organization. It is going
to be more and more expensive, as it increases in usefulness. Talk
of economy is in order, but of retrenchment never. I am firmly of
the opinion that Lodges and Grand Lodges must be better financed
than they are at present and that Grand Lodges are going to take a
deeper interest in seeing that Lodges are sufficiently well financed
so that they are not handicapped in doing the things which Masonry
should do. In a very small measure increased dues will result in
suspension, but those who drop out of Masonry because they are not '
willing to pay for its proper support are of no value to the organization. Masonry will be stronger without them.

Western Australia (1931):
(Chairman CMrespondence Committee): The need for annually
budgeting their revenue and expenditure, and for the adoption· of
ordinary business methods in Lodges is appealing to a considerable
number of the American Jurisdictions, Canadian and the United

18

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

States. At one time-even within the reviewer's Masonic recollections, there was a fairly general belief that it was impossible to run
a Lodge, Grand or subordinate, on business lines, except in the ideas
of impracticable doctrimiaires, those whose theories only looked well
on paper. Today, the business idea is not only treated with respect,
but has been adopted in some quarters, and, what is more promising
for the realities of Masonic service, is becoming increasingly popular.
To the same recognition of the value of business principles in Masonic administration must be attributed the largely shared opinionin many cases translated into action-that the creditably enthusiastic
desire of Lodges for temple-building must be regulated by their respective Grand Lodges in the interests of the Lodges themselves, in
order that the usefulness of the latter may not suffer from financial
embarrassments. In introducing these . reforms, the Grand Bodies
are performing a wonderful service to the Craft, one that in the course
of a decade or so should prove greater than the sanguine anticipations
of their advocates, provided sufficient tact is exercised to prevent
friction, and "grandmotherliness" is avoided.
Wisconsin (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Conmiittee): A Grand Lodge can no
more continue to function without funds than can a bank, or any
commercial institution. There is great danger that Grand Lodges
may become too charitable and thereby create in their ~embers the
feeling that it is not at all necessary that they should be frugal and
saving in order to provide for their old age, but that the Masons will
care for them. The burden may become so great that a Grand Lodge
cannot m eet it.
DEPRESSION
Some one has said that "the optimist. is a person who does not
care what happens as long as it does not happen to him, and that
a pessimist is one who lives with an optimist." This seems to be
the present condition of a large number of us. Everyone has an
opinion as to the Cause, Effect and the Remedy. The excerpts under
this heading perhaps may not be considered seriously, but they will
help perhaps to cheer us up.
If we would adopt the practice of comparing our own lot with
those worse off, rather than those supposed to be better fixed, it
might tend to make us more contented.

Iowa (1932):
(Deputy Grand Master): I like the depression. No more prosperity for me. I have had more fun since the depression than I ever
had in my life; I had forgotten how to live, what it meant to have
real friends, what it was like to eat common every-day food. Fact is,
I was getting just a little high hat.
I like the depression. I have time to visit my friends, to make
new ones. T wo years ago when I went to a neighboring town, I·
always stayed at the hotel. Now I go home with my friends, stay
all night and enjoy home cooking. I have even spent the week-end
with some of the boys who have been kind enough to invite me.
It's great to drop into a store and feel that you can spend an
hour or two or three, or a half day, just visiting, and not feel that
you are wasting .valuable time. I like the depression.
I am getting acquainted with my neighbors. I n the last six
months I have become acquainted with folks who have been living
next door to me for three years. I am following the Biblical admonition, "Love your neighbors." One of my neighbors has one of the
best looking wives. I have ever seen. She is a dandy. I am getting
acquainted with my neighbors and learning to love them.
Three years ago, I ordered my clothes from a merchant tailortwo and three suits at a time.· All my clothes were good ones. I was
always dressed up. But now I haven't bought a suit in two years. I
am mighty proud of my Sunday-go-to-meeting clothes. When I dress
up, I am dressed up and I don't mean maybe. I like the depression.
Three years ago I was so busy and my w ife was so busy that
we didn't see much of each other, consequently we sort of lost in-

terest in each other. I never went home for lunch. About twice a
week I went home for dinner-at 6:30 o'clock. I never had time to
go anywhere with her. If I did go on a party, I could never locate
her. Since there was always a "blond" or a "red-head" available, I
didn't worry about it. My wife belonged to all the clubs in town.
She even joined the young mothers' club. We don't have any children,
but she was studying-and between bridge and going to clubs, she
was never at home.
We got stuck up and hifalutin. We even took down the old
family bed and bought a set of twin beds-on the installment plan.
When I would come home at night, if my wife was at home, she
would already be in her bed and I would crawl in mine. If I came
in first it was vice versa.
We like the depression. We have come down off our pedestal
and are really living at my house now. The twin beds are stored in
the garage and the old family affair is being used. We are enjoying
life. Instead of taking a hot water bottle to bed these cold nights,
she sticks her heels in my back just like she did before Hoover was
elected.
I am feeling better since the depression. I take more exercise.
I walk to town and a lot of folks, who used to drive Cadillacs, are
walking with me. I like the depression.
My digestion is better. I haven't been to see a doctor in a year;
I can eat anything I want to.
I am getting real, honest-to-goodness food. Three years ago,
we had filet mignon once a week, now we have round steak and flour
gravy. Then we had roast breast of guinea hen, now we are glad to
get sow-bacon with the buttons on it.
I like the depression. My salary has been cut to where I can't
afford to buy lettuce, spinach and parsley, and we can't afford to
have sandwiches and frozen desserts and all that damfoolishness,
which has killed more good men than the World War.
I like the depression. Three years ago, I never had time. to go
to church. I played golf all day Sunday and, besides, I was so darned
smart that there wasn't a preacher in West Texas who could tell me
anything. Now I am going to church ·regularly, never miss a Sunday.
And if this depression keeps on, I will be going to prayer meetings
before long.
I like the depression.
DEPUTY GRAND MASTERS
The functions of a District Peputy Grand Master, Inspectors,
Custodian of Work, Grand Lecturers, etc., are amply covered in the

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

21

Report from Wisconsin. While it is necessary that the organization
be handled along certain lines and through certain Officers, one of

the results of the present system is the standardization of every form
of activity of a Masonic Lodge, and following the letter rather than
the spirit of the law. The attempt to initiate new ideas is often practically nullified by such a system. It should be possible to strike a
happy medium.
Wisconsin (1932):
(Committee on Deputy Grand Masters): Your Committee appointed
by Grand Master William R. Graves to study and report on the
question of District Deputy Grand Masters submits the following
findings:
Questionnaires were mailed to fifty-seven Grand Jurisdictions
with which this Grand Lodge has fraternal rela!ions. Of these, all
but six responded.
Eighteen of those that responded do not use the District Deputy
Grand Master system.
Thirty-three use the system in some form.
In but one Jurisdiction (Kansas) is the appointment made by
other than the Grand Master. In this case the selections are made
by the Council of Administration or the Deputy Grand Master.
In all other cases the Grand Master appoints, although in Alberta
the nominations are made by the Lodges in each district and the
Grand Master confirms the appointments. The same holds true in
Quebec.
In thirty Jurisdictions the term of office is for one year, or at
the pleasure of the Grand Master. In two cases, Connecticut and
South Dakota, the term of office is for two years.
As to compensation, in Vermont the District Deputies receive
two dollars plus actual expenses from the Lodges visited. This is
the only Jurisdiction reporting compensation.
In twenty-one Jurisdictions expense money is paid, usually by
the Lodges visited: In eight Jurisdictions no expense money is paid.
The number of Lodges in each district varies greatly. The
smallest number in a district is reported by Texas where one district
has but one Lodge. In a number of states that are districts having
but three Lodges. In some cases it was found that districts have as
high as twenty-nine Lodges. The average seems to be from ten to
twelve Lodges in each district .
. In twelve Jurisdictions the District Deputies act as Grand Lecturers.

23

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

In all but three Jurisdictions employing the system, the office
of District Deputy, or its equivalent, carries with it no preference
or precedence as to the Grand Lodge line. Connecticut reports that
the office does carry preference, but c!oes not amplify the answer.
North Dakota answers "yes" and explains that the system affords
an excellent means of determin.ing a man's ability and that from that
standpoint it does carry preference. In Rhode Island, advancement
is made from "first deputy" to Grand Junior Warden.
It is illuminating to discover that in many instances District
Deputies have become Grand Masters.
In Alberta all but four Grand Masters have served as District
Deputies.
In British Columbia twenty-three Grand Masters were District
.Deputies.
In California nine District Deputies have become Grand Masters in the past thirty years.
In Canada "nearly all" of the Grand Masters have been District
Deputies.
In Connecticut all but three Grand Masters were Deputies.
Summarizing, we may report Florida, "several"; Idaho, seven;
Illinois, "most of them" have been Deputy; Louisiana, "very few, if
any"; Maine, "perhaps half"; Manitoba, "several"; Maryland, none;
Massachusetts, "most"; Minnesota, none; Missouri, eight or ten in
the last twenty-five years; New Hampshire, "several"; New Jersey,
fourteen; New Mexico, "quite a number"; New York, "most"; North
Dakota, five; Nova Scotia, three; Oklahoma, four; Oregon, two;
Pennsylvania, eight since 1894; Rhode Island, "nearly all"; South
Carolina, "only a few"; South Dakota, none; Texas, none; Vermont,
twenty-two.
In all cases District Deputies must be Past Masters. Other
qualifications are: Leadership, proficiency in law and ritual, executive ability, ability to inspect, devotion to the Fraternity.
Designations in some cases differ from that of District Deputy
Grand Master. In Minnesota they are called "District Supervisors";
in Iowa, "Special Representatives of the Grand Master"; in Maryland, "District Grand Inspectors"; in a majority of cases they are
termed District Deputy Grand Masters.
Michigan once had District Deputies but the· system was discontinued more than fifty years ago.
In a large majority of cases the report was highly laudatory of
the system. The good points expressed were principally that it affords a contact betweeh the Grand Lodge and the constituent Lodges,
which is much needed. The Grand Master is relieved of much

detail. Whete Lodge books are inspected the system results in
better reporting to the Grand Lodge. One report was " We could
not keep house without it."
Adverse comment was sought by your Committee, as well as
praise. It appears that some fear the possibility of the District
Deputies forming a "political machine." Others said the principal
difficulty was in finding men who would function. " It is necessary,"
says one, "that the Grand Master should have courage to appoint
the right men."

ELECTIONS
As stated under the excerpts from Kansas, and from decisions in
our own Jursidiction, it would appear to be impossible to make a
regulation that can absolutely prevent electioneering. The question
as to whether nominations are proper or desirable is becoming an
issue in some Jurisdictions.
It seems strange that the Mother Grand Lodge and Jurisdictions
in the British Empire, where the form of government is along the
lines of a monarchy or autocracy, permit the practice, while in the
United States, where a representative or democratic form of government is the standard, the practice is generally prohibited. Nominations for office at least would have the merit of presenting the qualifications of an aspirant. Mackey states the practice is permissible.
In one of the Australian Grand Lodges when the Grand Secretary died they advertised for his successor. The new official was
chosen from among nine who had presented their qualifications
through this method.
Connecticut (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): As Sir H ore-Ruthven
was the only nominee, he was declared re-elected Grand Master of
South Australia. Connecticut has an old-adopted decision declaring
with owl-like solemnity that "nominations are un-Masonicl'' In view
of the fact that British, Colonial, and even several United States
Grand Lodges allow nominations, there must be a large section of
the Fraternity indulging in " un-Masonic" practice. This scribe
frankly confesses that in our own Grand Lodge he has violated
this law. Bah !

(lurispnuience Committee): The following question was asked
the Grand Master and answered as follows:
1. H~s any Brother the right, in annual meeting, to address the
Lodge .with remarks for or against any other Brother who is in line
for office or who may be considered by the Brethren for election?
If not, has the Master authority to stop such remarks when attempted?
. Decision. It is of immemorial custom in our Order that no nominating remarks be indulged in during election of officers, and this I
construe to carry on to speeches relative to fitness of those Brothers
who may be considered for office. I therefore rule that it is improper
~o present candidates for office by nominating remarks or to discuss,
1~ open Lodge, by remarks addressed to the Lodge, any of the candidates who are considered for office.
The Worshipful Master has authority to cause any such attempted speeches or discussions to stop, and his decision cannot be
appealed from.
Which Decision your Committee approves.

GRAND LODGE
The custom of some Jurisdictions in having a Grand Lodge discuss and ratify measures previously passed upon by a Board of G~n­
eral Purposes has the merit at least of saving time. In those Junsdictions there is a shortening of the Session, an absence of detail and
a greater opportunity for sociability.
In the United States in a large number of cases the Proceedings
of Grand Lodge resemble very much the minutes of an annual meeting of a corporation. The members meet as stockholders, and _perform no other function than to ratify the action of a board of directors.

Among other matters to which the Grand Master (Texas) directed attention was the small amount of annual dues Lodges were
charging, with resultant financial embarrassment which is not surprisi~g when in some cases they were as low ~s 12s. 6d. a year;
~he inadequate arrangements of Lodges for financing temple building, and the need for a properly defined policy as to who should be
the owners of such buildings, iristead of the system of dual ownership obtaining in some places; and the advisability of constituting
a permanent committee on "Purposes and Policies of the Grand
Lodge." To British Empire Masons, unfamiliar with American
Maso~ic administration, the need for such a committee may appear
questionable, although the object aimed at is commendable. In
most Grand Jurisdictions in the Empire, all matters other than
benevolence are generally considered and reported upon to Grand
Lodge by the one body-the Board of General Purposes which in
the fi~s.t instance, takes care of Grand Lodge policies, Gr~nd Lodge
exercising the right of accepting, amending, or rejecting the Board's
recommendations. The system is so marvelously simple and works
so effectively, that the Mother Grand Lodge and th~ Daughter
Grand Lodge achieve results unsurpassed by any other system of
Masonic administration in the world. Besides, great reliance is
placed on the Masonic lex non scripta, that large body of established
usages and customs which constitute the Masonic common law. In
the United States of America the system is entirely different. The
work done by British Boards of General Purposes is parceled out
among numerous committees, each wearing a more or less highsounding title, and each reporting and recommending to Grand
Lodge. All these committees are constitutionally provided for, and
there seems to be a tendency in most Jurisdictions to form other
committees to do something else that has more or Jess suddenly
~ropped up. Moreover, their Books of >Constitutions are in many
instances crowded with original clauses, amended clauses, substituted clauses, et hoc genus ornne, all conceived with the best intentions, and supplemented by decisions, rulings, edicts, etc., until one
is given to wonder how many Worshipful Masters seriously attempt
to u~derstand this mass of law, to say nothing of the complicated
machinery of Mason.i c administration already referred to. The Empire sys.tern may not be so scientific as that of the Republic but to
this writer it has always appeared better adapted to achieve ~uccess
which is, or should be, the main object.

Philippine Islands (1931):
(Jurisprudence Co·mmittee): The resolution proposing ~he amendment of the Constitution by substituting the word "constituent" for

the word "subordinate," in. describing the Lodges, has been referred
to this Committee for consideration and report. ·
The word "subordinate," as used in our Constitution, means
1
•
"placed in a lower order, cIass or rank " and th e word " cons t'tuent"
means "serving to form, compose or make up; component or constitutive~" (Webster's New International Dictionary.)
We are of the opinion that the word "subordinate" is the proper
word and expresses the· relation of the Lodge to the Grand Lodge,
which is the Supreme Masonic power in the Philippine Islands.
The Grand Lodge is not composed of Lodges, but is made up
of Masters, Wardens and Past Masters of Lodges under the juris·
diction of the Grand Lodge.
We are of the opinion that the word "subordinate" is the proper
word to be used in connection with a Lodge in its relation to the
Grand Lodge, and that the word "constituent" would not be the
proper word to be used in that connection. ('Adopted.)

GRAND MASTERS
The results of the administration of a Grand Master are largely
reflected in the character or ability of the Officer himself. Results
are based upon his individuality and popularity. There is a tendency at present to deny dispensations to make exceptions to existing
laws or regulations . . The practice of asking the Grand Master for
rulings on matters covered by existing laws still continues a common practice.

Alabama. (1932):
(Grand Master}: There is an old saying that "advice is mighty
easy to give but mighty hard to take." There is much that needs to
be improved in our Grand Lodge and among our Lodges, and many
conditions which could be changed for the better, but as I am not to
take any of this advice, I shall refrain from administering.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Approval was given to
the recommendation to form a Past Grand Masters' Association
(Florida), "first within our own jurisdiction, and then with similar
organizations in our sister jurisdictions, and these in turn united as
a federal body of consultative capacity." This would be somewhat
analogous to our Annual Conference of Grand Masters, which also
has no legislative or judicial powers, being merely deliberative.

necessitated ·the passing of several letters in which it became necessary for me to call the Brother's attention to "the law in the case."

"I think our present Grand Master is too small for his job as

Vermont (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): In reporting his fraternal
visitations to other Grand Lodges, the Grand Master of New Jersey
used the term "Brother Jurisdictions,'' saying he did so out of deference to the Grand Master of New York, who, he says, has expressed

would merely call attention to the fact that what a man thinks most
of he has always feminized: his gun, his boat, his machines. The
usage is based on long practice and has excellent sponsors; and it
seems to us is in good taste. we disapprove the application of the
term "Brother" to a collection of the Brethren, not alone for its rarity
but for its lack of grace.

Washington (1931):
(Grand Master): The work required of a Grand Master cannot
be fully delineated. At every meeting some Brother or committee
has some problem to be solved. Advice is sought for temple plans,
or building material for a hall. Help by way of opinion has been
asked for Lodges which built temples beyond their financial ability.
The usual run of insurance agents have pestered, hoping for the
bars to be let down. Profanes sought to cheapen the Order and
enrich their pocket books by seeking a message from the Grand
Master to help sell what was termed a Masonic Log. Profanes endeavored to foster what they termed to be the "Masonic Review"
and their agents represented ads would be read twice a month in
local Lodges.

At this' distance it is well-nigh impossible to say to what extent
the officers of an American Grand Lodge come in contact with the
subordinate Lodges, or what is the precise nature of the supervision
which most of those Grand Lodges exercise through their executives.
Most of the American States are large in area, but only a small
number as large as Western Australia. The supervision is satisfactory, and no necessity is seen to constitute our Grand · Master a
sort of intinerant supervisor. Wherever he pleases to visit, he is
welcomed as the Chief Ruler in our Craft, but the Lodges 'have no
idea of regarding him in any other light. Realizing that he cannot
be expected to visit every Lodge, we have a system whereby present
and Past Grand Officers visit the subordinate Lodges as his representatives, and we have no such experience as Brother Phoenix indicates-unwillingness to accept a substitute for the Grand Master.
"The collar carries you everywhere" is a saying of which all of us
who have attained Gr·a nd Lodge rank experience the truth in the
pleasantest way possible-a warm and hearty welcome.

34

• • • • •

We see that Canada is discussing methods for relieving the
Grand Master from some of the burden which he now bears. Just
what form it will assume does not now appear, but it is evident that
some means will have to be devised, or those men upon whom the
duties of that high office devolve will have to be selected not from
the most able, but from those who are willing to accept it. Th.e
work is enormous and demands more than most men are able to
give it. We sincerely hope that they will solve the question so as
to retain the guiding hands of the able men who have until now
accepted the office.
Western Australia (1931):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Florida volume of
Proceedings is not a large one, according to the United States
standard (Masonic). Less than four hundred pages, as a matter of
fact, of which 176 are devoted to Proceedings and exactly the same
number to Fraternal Correspondence, and there are about two score
other pages. But the Grand Master-that is, the Most Worshipful
Brother who presided over the 1930 Annual-signalized his year of
office by singing his little swan song (annual address) of eighty-three
pages, of which just under thirty-two contain his rulings and decisions, these, in nearly every instance, being set out with all the
fullness of a Supreme Court judgment. Of course, everyone does
not believe in the counsel of Mr. Justice Hawkins-to "give your
decision and not your reasons"-but when one reads, in another part
of the Grand Master's address, that it is "the duty of the Worshipful
Master to absorb the contents of the Annual Proceedings as best
he can, and impart the same to his Brethren as best he can," one
can only hope that his powers of absorption are equal to digesting
thirty-odd pages of rulings and decisions.

Connecticut (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : As did Connecticut many
years ago, many Grand Lodges adhere to the custom of having an
"oration" at each annual. Occasional ones are worth close attention
and evoke thought on the part of the listener, but many were empty
verbiage or deal with trite and well settled matters, and are not
worth the time wasted in their delivery.
The advocates of this custom frequently put forward the pettifogging bluff: "This has been so long the custom that it has the
force of a landmark." To the thinking man, such plea is the rankest
nonsense.
Under present-day conditions of widespread enlightenment, the
busy man will waste no time listening to the prolix verbiage of long
speeches, sermons, etc. The present age is more a reading than a
listening one.

HUMOR
That the printed proclledings of the various Grand Lodges are
not always as dry and uninteresting reading as might be expected,
is evidenced by the following flashes of wit and humor which appear
in some of them. They at leaa relieve the monotony for the Reviewer, even if some of them have been heard many times before.
As a prelude, the Grand Master arranged that the Grand Matron
of the Eastern Star, with her associates, should make a call upon
them previous to opening. As the l_adies came in the men sang "Praise
God from Whom All Blessings Flow.'' What could have been more
appropriate? This over, the Governor of the State and others made
speeches, after which the Grand Matron made reply. She must have
been quite overcome, but recovered sufficiently to state tha t the Star,
instead of presenting a bunch of flowers to the Grand Lodge, as has
been the annual custom, proposed to present a cow to the Masonic
Home. Whether or not the aforesaid bovine was literally present,
in the Lodge room; to pass through the change in ownership from
the Star to the Home, is not revealed in the record. We may only
surmise. This is an intensely choice story-but it would be difficult
for anything more practical, helpful, to have been done, within the
cost limitation.

I am reminded of. a lady member of the congregation who complained to her parson that he always addressed his brethren but not
his sisters. He replied, "My dear young lady, I thought it was uqiversally understood that the brethren embraced the sisters." This
matter of the proper mode of address is really quite an intricate one.
I remember attending a meeting of clergy in Prince Albert 35, 37, 38
years ago, at which a newly ordained young padre said that he never
was sure of the proper way to address the dignitaries of the church.

the Right Reverend-the Bishop; the Very Reverend-the Dean, and
the Rather Reverend-the Rural Dean." As I happen to be a "Rather
Reverend Rural Dean" myself, I can tell the story and enjoy the joke.

While Grand Master Cooke (Maine) stated in his address that

ballots. In like manner, the experience of Maine in things Masonic
may serve to disclose to the fraternal world the advent of better
times, for Maine reports evidence of growth and a renewed interest.

There comes to memory an occasion when I saw the salutation
sign of Master Mason given in public inadvertently, but naturally.
The scene was the District Court room. The presiding judge was
the late Nathan Kingsley, an eminent Mason, a Past General Grand
High Priest · of the General Gra~d Chapter of the United States.
The grand jury had · come in to make their report. "Gentlemen, have
you anything to report?" came from the bench. The foreman, a
seasoned Mason, arose, saluted with the Master Mason's sign, delivered his indictments and sat down. The giving of that salutation
sign, done wholly unconsciously, suggested to me the impression,
deep in that foreman's mind, that in fulfilling his part in the administration of justice he was performing his duty as taught by M:lsonry.

Back in 1828 the school board of Lancaster, Ohio, refused a
permit for the use of the school house for the discussion of the
question as to whether or not railroads were practical. They stated:
"You are welcome to use the school house to debate all proper
questions in, but such things as railroads and telegraphs are impossibilities and rank infidelity. There is nothing in the word of God
about them. If God has designed His intelligent creatures should
travel at the frightful speed of fifteen miles per hour, by steam, He
would have clearly foretold through His holy prophets. It is a device
of Satan to lead immortal souls down to hell."

You know we are laboring under the difficulty that so many of
our members know very little of what Freemasonry actually is; its
background, its present possibilities and its future possibilities. I
heard of a man who came to the minister one morning after the
sermon and he said to him, "Say, Dominie, did you say that Dan
and Beersheba ·were two cities?" "Yes," said the Dominie, "of
course they are." The man said, "That's funny, I always thought
they were brother and sister, like Sodom and Gomorrah."
The amount of knowledge that some of our Masonic members
have with regard to Masonry is, of course, very deplorable. I heard
of a young woman who was asked on a certain examination to tell
about Magna Carta. Well, she had heard the name, but it did not
mean very much to her, so in ~riting the reply to the question she
said that Magna Carta was the name of a soldier in the Revolutionary' Army; that he was shot at the battle of Lexington and his
wife, seeing him fall, rushed forward, seized his musket and said,
"Shoot, if you will, this old gray head; but I am going to fight it
out along this line if it takes all summer." I am afraid there are a
great many of our members, if they were to be asked what Masonry
is, or to define Masonry, or to give any sort of intelligent statement
of what it is all about, they probably would have about the same
mix up of history that that young 'w oman had in her mind.

"I'd rather be a Baptist

There's lot of room in hell below
We can't have heaven jammed."

In Grand Lodges, as in our civil life, the practice still prevails
that "THERE SHOULD BE A LAW AGAINST IT." Former
Vice President Thomas Marshall once said that he thought the
Country would benefit if all the laws were repealed and the Ten

Commandments and the Declaration of Independence be enacted

The Grand Master of Michigan spent an evening of the Grand
Lodge session in an open discussion of finances. He was convinced
that the Grand Lodge should curtail its activities, confining them to
strictly Masonic functions, such as the laying of cornerstones and
the dedication of temples. And he urged that local self-government
on the part of the Lodges be encouraged. This is a sound doctrine
and preached all too infrequently. After all, the fundamental unit
of Freemasonry is the local self-governing Lodge. The present trend
is all toward the weakening of the individual Lodge and the centralization of power and activity in Grand Lodges. The loss of interest
on the part of the members of local Lodges, as a result of this tendency, should be given more serious consideration.
Saskatchewan (1931):
(Grand Master): I find that a number of Lodges are ignoring
certain approved rulings. The only conclusion I can draw is that
these rulings do not meet with favor, and that they were approved
without sufficient consideration on the part of the members of Grand
Lodge. I suggest that on matters directly affecting the internal government of constituent Lodges the vote for appr6val or non-approval
be not taken until the following annual communication of Grand
Lodge. This will allow the members sufficient time to become familiar with each ruling.

OBLIGATIONS
The penalties of our Obligation were taken from those of Common Law actually inflicted on pirates in olden days. In the early
part of the 18th Century they were abandoned, but Desaguliers wrote
them into the ritual and they have been there ever since. P. G. M.
Melvin M. Johnson of Massachusetts was the first to present the
matter of elimination or changing them to his Grand Lodge. New
York is the first Jurisdiction to take steps to teach a candidate that
the penalties are symbolic only.
Under the Grand Lodge of England Ritual, when a man receives
the Entered Apprentice Obligation, he is told in the Obligation itself
that the penalty is a symbolic penalty only.
Illinois (1931) :
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): During the past ,Year, in
at least two Grand Lodges, the subject of our obligations was given
attention. Of course for a long time there have been those who. have
contended that the obligations of Masonry were too long, that they
should be shortened, and that they were full of tautology, and a lot
more things that self-constituted reformers in the Fraternity project
simply because they thought they were smarter than anybody else
and wanted to stir things up. Then one Grand Master came out this
year and took. a fling at the penalties of the obligations. He told his
Grand Lodge that the penalties were of no use, for when the instructors taught the obligations to candidates they told them that
these penalties were not to be taken seriously and that they were
merely relics of the dark ages. The result was, according to this
Grand Master, that candidates being thus instructed construed the
interpretation to apply to the entire obligation, and for that reason
they disregarded their obligations after they had taken them, for the
reason that they understood that they were not to be considered

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

47

seriously. The Grand Master bri~ging these criticisms suggested
that the penalties be omitted from our obligations. In another Grand
Lodge there was a plea set up for the shortening of the obligations
and it was even suggested that one obligation might very well suffice
for all three of the degrees. The writer is frank to say that he believes that this revision of obligations might well apply to some of
our so-called higher degrees, but so far as the. obligations of Ancient
Craft Masonry are concerned, they should remain unmolested and
be handed down to future generations in their present form. The
present Masonic age seems to be characterized by a disposition to
want to change things-to remodel Freemasonry so as to make it
fit into this jazzy, joy-riding, luxurious, high-geared, speed-loving
generation. But, my dear Brethren, just the moment you do that
there will be no more Freemasonry. What we will have in its place
will be simply a social organization like our country clubs, our golf
clubs and our city clubs. If we are going to set aside our ritualism,
then we will have to put something in its place, and the only thing
that we can substitute will be poker games, because men won't play
any kind · of a game of cards that they can't play for money, and
other forms of amusement which Masonry now frowns upon. Now
it is true that the penalties of the obligations are barbarous in the
extreme. They are simply borrowed from an age that long ago
passed out of existence. There is no inclination whatsoever to inflict
them upon individuals. The person taking an obligation simply says
that rather than violate his obligation he would suffer certain things
to be done. The writer believes in the preservation of the old form
and language of the fraternity. Somebody said the other day that
the ritual of Masonry should be rewritten; that a lot of obsolete expressions should be deleted and the whole thing put into twentieth
century language. Whenever this is done the peculiar charm of
Freemasonry which has caused it to continue for two hundred years
will be lost, and the Fraternity will sink to the level of those organizations which pander to popularity and exist to no purpose.

OFFENSES
Unfortunately, like every other human institution, the Fraternity
has "its black sheep," and too often the general public judge the
entire organization by those "undesirable citizens" whose Masonic
connections are broadcast in connection with his offenses.

District of Columbia (1931) :
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): In the matter of discipline, the Grand Master of Nebraska was inclined to be somewhat
severe, vide a case where a Brother had been convicted in the civil
courts of possession of seven-eighths of a gallon of liiquor, and had
been suspended by his Lodge for a year as a result of the conviction,
he remanded the case for reconsideration, whereupon the Lodge
voted for indefinite suspension, although no sale of liquor had been
alleged. Seems rather a severe penalty for keeping a little wine on
·hand for the stomach's sake, and we sadly fear if every Brother who
might be found in like case so far as the possession of a modicum of
liquor is concerned, were to be subjected to a like penalty, reason
for losses in membership would be found without extended search.
Manitoba (1932):
(Chairman Corresp0'4dence Committee): A Brother in British Columbia having falsely represented himself as a Master Mason in good
standing for the purpose of gaining admission into Royal Arch Masonry, a commission appointed by the Grand Master withheld judgment because they were not sure that the offense was Masonic. The
committee, however, held that it was and recommended expulsion.
This judgment seems bizarre. The only offense against Blue
Masonry was an extra-mural deception no worse than that by which
an office boy gains leave to go to a baseball match, or many a man
gets an evening out. The real offense was against the Royal Arch,
probably induced by importunate solicitation on the part of its members, and one which they should have prevented by reasonable investigation. Unless Grand Lodge has legally constituted itself the
protector of the Royal Arch, the committee's ruling seems unwarranted.
Michigan (1931):
(Grand Master) : Despite all that has been said, and very plainly
said, too, about the misuse of the square and compasses in advertising, in promotion and in uncalled-for display, the Grand Master has
been obliged to rule this year, on more than one occasion, against

movements designed to connect Masonry with events from which
the promoters, either for personal gain or personal satisfaction, apparently intended to derive benefits which might not come to them
under normal circumstances. The Grand Master has ruled that
there can be no such thing as a Masonic prize fight, an all-state

·
The way must not be left open for men, of Masonic affiliation
or otherwise, to save their pet schemes, good or bad, by pinning a
Masonic emblem upon them.
Nor does the Grand Master favor a Lodge resorting to ballyhoo
methods to replenish its own exchequer or to unduly influence young
men in the community to take out petitions. The greatest appeal of
Masonry lies in its simple dignity and its rather awesome mystery.
There still exists the thick-skulled Brother who thinks it 'smart to
fill the candidate's mind with fears of "the goat"-to encourage him
to expect horse-play which he soon will find out has no part in
Masonry. To a lesser degree, perhaps, but almost as deadly, is that
type of humor which causes some Masons to look for things to
laugh at in connection with the Master Mason degree. The Master
Mason degree is not comedy; it is tragedy, One guffaw can in an
instant ruin for the Worshipful Master and his Lodge all the fineness
that has been built into the candidate's conception of Masonry. And
because the candidate, hoodwinked and doubly susceptible to what
he hears, registers the whisper or the giggle or the "haw-haw" of
some misguided Brother, he comes back to the next third degree
prepared to whisper, to giggle or to "haw-haw" at something, he
knows not what.
The Grand Master would greatly like to inject a paragraph in
regard to the popular habit Brethren in most, if not all, Lodges
have in rushing the door the moment a Brother is "raised," lest
they be caught and held, against their will, to hear the lecturt{sthe lectures which the Worshipful Master and his officers have
worked so hard to perfect and which means so much to the candidate who is seeking "further light" in Masonry. But this would be
sheer folly, for one cannot preach or legislate . men, even Master
Masons, into doing the right thing. There is a rather complete and
inspiring education in the various degrees of Masonry and it would
not hurt the average Mason if he were forced to hear this lesson of
the third degree once a month for the whole tenure of his life. Yet
the average Master Mason, having once heard the lectures, seems
much like the chorus girl who, when asked if she didn't want a
book for Christmas, answered, "Oh, no! I have one."

Missouri (1931):
(Grand Master) : I regret to note a growing tendency in some
Masonic Lodges to give boisterous picnics with baseball games,
races and other sports on Sunday. I recognize fully the right of
every Mason to choose his own religious views. But while individual
Masons whose religious views permit them to do so, may attend and
participate individually in such affairs, and I have no right to say,
and would not presume to say, that they shall not do so, I do strongly
feel that it is very bad policy for any Masonic Lodge to sponsor such
affairs or allow its name to be used in any way in connection ther_ewith. The church is the ally of Freemasonry. It is well worth while
for us to have the good will of ministers of the Gospel and church
officers and Sunday School teachers and superintendents. No good
can possibly come from incurring their ill will. They can be help~ul
to us in many ways. Many churches seriously object to Sunday picnics. When a Lodge gives a picnic on Sunday, it takes away from
the church and Sunday School many men, women and children who
are accustomed· to attend such services, and the inevitable result is
criticism of the Lodge and a feeling on the part of those who should
be our strong allies that we are opposing them, and that will surely
result in prejudicing them against Freemasonry. The slight degree
of pleasure gained by such Sunday picnics is more than offset by the
danger of arousing ill feeling where good will would be most helpful
to us. Many Lodge members are church members who disapprove
of such affairs on Sunday and are shocked by them. This tends to
cause division in a Lodge that gives such a picnic. I believe it
cheapens Freemasonry to give such affairs on Sunday.
Thus it will be seen that the traditions of our Order are strongly
against the doing of anything by any . Lodge on Sun?~Y except performing funeral services. Expediency and our traditions ahke are
against Sunday picnics in the name of a Masoni~ Lodge. Let us
refrain from the practice. There are other days m the week open
to us when we can give picnics to our hearts' content without offending anybody. Let us choose one of them for our Lodge frolics.

South Carolina (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Grand Master Fraser
(Nova Scotia) issued a circular letter to the Lodges throughout the
jurisdiction warning against the conducting of lotteries as being a
violation of the Constitution. It is a sad commentary upon Free•

for the gift without the giver is bare."
Tennessee (1932):
(Grand Master): Masonry does not conflict with good citizenship. The judge, juror, witness in court, citizen, ruler, official, or
voter can find no warrant in our law or ritual for the slightest disregard of the rights of neighbor or townsmen, or disloyalty to society,
state or nation, because he is a Mason; quite the contrary, and because he is a Mason, one is under special obligation to adhere to
those fundamental principles of justice, equal rights and integrity
which are the glory and safety of the state and nation, as well as of
honor, and for the protection to the individual. The common law,
and Masonic law as well, are in full accord upon the all"impor.tant,
far-reaching proposition, namely, that the rights and privileges of
every man are bounded on all sides by the rights and privileges of
his neighbors, and by a line clear and straight, and to that line he
must hew.

Vermont (1932):
(Grand Master): I regret that I am forced to allude to an incident of the past year which, to express it mildly, was most unfortunate.
A Masonic club in our jurisdiction which was probably over 90
per cent identical in membership with the Lodge in its home town,
conceived the idea that a substantial payment could be made on the
Lodge's newly acquired temple if the practices of a body claiming
. Masonic membership in the Islands to the southeast of our country,
and another body, the members of which are Masons, were put into
operation. This club proceeded to act and sent to every Lodge Secretary in the United States a book of tickets with promises of fabulous
prizes to the holder of the lucky number.
Up to this point I knew nothing of the scheme. My first knowledge of it came in letters from various Grand Masters and Grand
Secretaries, some of whom courteously inquired as to our regulations
and others flew off the handle with sharp and unmerited criticism
before they knew whether or not the recipient of their letters was
really the sort of Mason they intimated him to be. The Lodge in
which this club existed was immediately notified and directed to
cause the club to call in all tickets sent out, refund any money received, and call the whole scheme off, and I notified every Lodge in
Vermont and every Grand Lodge in the United States of the situation. The club in question at once convened and voted to do all
they had been instructed to do, and the matter lapsed, dead of its
own wrong conception.
I was surprised and rather upset that any body of Masons in
our State should even contemplate resort to such unmasonic, unethical, and actually illegal method of raising money as a lottery,
and the scheme started could be called by no softer name. We have
no specific legislation on the subject of lotteries and it seems to me

54

REPORT ON CORRESPOND.ENCE
REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

we ought not to need such legislation nor the stating in black and
white of so clear a matter of Masonic usage. Our oath requires us
to uphold and abide by the laws of our land and this ought to be all
the legislation needed to control and prevent any repetition of the
unfortunate incident.
I am not suggesting any discipline because; I feel that the fault
on the part of our Brothers in the club in question was more thoughtless than intentional, but Masons in Vermont should ever remember
that lotteries are frowned upon and should never be resorted to for
any purpose in which Masonry participates.
Western Australia (1931):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Bootlegging amongst

the opinion that if effect were given to the recommendation, it "would

the accused Brother to a fair and impartial trial, and deprives the
triers of the right to inflict such punishment as in their judgment is
justified under all the facts." Well, in Western Australia, the Board
of General Purposes reports to Grand Lodge the court conviction
and sentence, and recommends the Masonic punishment. Grand
Lodge either accepts the recommendation or fixes the punishment
itself. In either case there seems to be less possibility of miscarriage
of justice at the hands of an experienced legal tribunal, than where
the case is heard in a Lodge, where legal experience is about as inconspicuous as something which isn't where it ought to be. Moreover, the "fairness" and "impartiality" of a Masonic trial, such as
the Grand Master points to, does not seem to set up a right whose
destroyal should be followed by weeping, copious or limited, on
behalf of "fundamental" principles.
Iowa (1932):

(Grand Lodge B11lletin)
"Department of Justice Warns Against Lottery Tickets"
Under date of June 10 the Grand Secretary of Iowa received a
communication from the Department of Justice at Washington,

55

D. C., calling attention to the criminal statutes of the United States
pertaining to lotteries. It appears that the attention of the Department of Justice has been called to lottery schemes being promoted
among fraternal organizations. It has become a common practice
to distribute books of numbered tickets purporting to entitle the
purchaser to attend some type of entertainment and to receive, if
such purchaser happens to obtain a winning number, a cash prize.
Inasmuch as only recently two so-called Masonic institutions, or
institutions claiming Masonic affiliation, have circularized Iowa
Lodges seeking assistance in distribution of lottery tickets, this is a
timely warning. Such schemes are covered by the circular above
referred to. It might be well to cite Section 213 of the Criminal Code":
"No letter, package, postal card, or circular concerning any
lottery, gift enterprise, or similar scheme offering prizes dependent
in whole or in part upon lot or chance; and no lottery ticket or part
there.of, or paper, certilicate, or instrument purporting to be or to
represent a ticket, chance, share, or interest in or dependent upon the.
event of a lottery, gift enterprise, or similar scheme offering prizes
dependent in whole or in part upon lot or chance ; and no check,
draft, bill, money, postal note, or money order, for the purchase of
any ticket or part thereof, or of any share or chance in any such
lottery, gift enterprise, or scheme; and no newspaper, circular,
pamphlet, or publication of any kind containing any advertisement of
any lottery, gift enterprise, or scheme of any kind offering prizes
<lependent in whol.e or in part upon lot or chance, or containing any
list of the prizes drawn or awarded by means of any such lottery, gift
enterprise, or scheme, whether said list contains any part or all of
such prizes, shall be deposited in or carried by the mails of the
United States or be delivered by any· postmaster or letter carrier."
POLITICS
Of course, the Ancient Landmarks prohibit the participation of
the Craft as such in Religion or Politics. We do not believe that
indulging in politics from the partisan standpoint will ever be
attempted. If it should happen it would have disastrous results, as
evidenced by the fate of other fraternal organizations that have gravitated into that practice. As Masonry becomes more and more of an
Institution rather than a Fraternity or Philosophy, the consideration
of PUBLIC QUESTIONS that are actively before us at the present
time will furnish a field for good work. The work of Tennessee,
California and some other Jurisdictions in connection with the Public
Schools is an example of what we would class as politics not prohibited by the Ancient Charges.

(~rand Master): It has come to my attention that in some Lodges

Canada (1931):

(Board on Condition of Masonry): Your Committee has found a
little evidence in some localities of practices which must not continue
if Masonry is to be useful and respected as in the past. It has been
the pride of Canadian, as of English, Masonry that partisan politics,
whether national or municipal, have never been allowed to enter our
portals; and that sectional propaganda has found no place there. To
permit candidates or others to use our Lodges or their association
with Masonry for political or sectional purposes, by any method
direct ~r indirect, is contrary to the whole spirit of Masonry and is
most d1sloyal to our Order. There has been very little of this sort
of thing; it should be stamped out ruthlessly. Worshipful Masters
who permit it should be brought to realize the seriousness of the
offense; and the actual offenders should be made to feel the full
force of Masonic discipline. ·
Equally foreign to the spirit of helpful and self-respecting Masonry is the desire for publicity which has led in some cases to the
reporting in the press of the proceedings of private Lodges, even to
the names of candidates for the various degrees. Our Lodges should
be as safe from publicity as our homes. It cannot be too often repeat~~ that Masonry, at its best, ·is reticent and retiring; parade and
pubhc1ty are harmful to it; like charity, it vaunteth not itself.

Kansas (1931):
(Grand Master): There appears to be a feeling on the part of
some of the officers of our Lodges that the Lodge must justify its
existence by engaging in an organized way toward solving local
social problems, and I have found it necessary to remind them that
the floor of the Lodge is not a proper forum for the discussion of
problems which do not and should not concern Masonry. There is
no place in Masonry for organized action in connection with these
matters. The primary business of the Lodge is that of making
Masons, and if our membership rightly understand the principles
upon which Masonry is founded, they will be inspired to exercise
the highest ideals of citizenship. From the nature of our institution,
Masons are aligned on both sides of all public prO'blems and therefore
it is highly improper and a prolific source of discord to introduce
such questions for discussion upon the floor of a Lodge. It is true
that society will doubtless be benefited to the greatest extent where
the ideals of Masonry are translated into deeds through organized
effort, but the Lodge as such, or Masonry as an organization, is not
the proper medium through which these ideals are to be translated
into action. Masons will readily find in their several communities
other organizations through which they may fulfill their desire to
be of greater service to their fellow-men. I am persuaded that the
church is the logical medium through which every Mason should
seek to translate the ideals of Masonry into deeds, and thereby fulfill
his duty to God and to society.

warning them against having anything to do with resolutions in
favor of or against measures pending in Congress.
That such a letter was needed is conclusive evidence of the need
for real Masonic education. The more firmly we hold to the wise
custom of holding entirely aloof from political or religious controversy, the better it will be for Masonry. We can understand how
enthusiastic individuals, who are entirely sincere in their political
desires to further certain proposed legislation, so easily lose sight of
the wise limitations of the Masonic institution concerning such matters, but a little thinking on their part ought to convince them that
it is upon this very rock that French, Spanish and Italian Masonry
has split and lost much of its moral influence. If the Masonic institution is to stand secure it must forever put the taboo upon the
introduction of such matters into the Lodges of Freemasons.
Western Australia (1931):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): This Masonic evergreen
(politics) continues to flourish in some American Jurisdictions to
the vexation of Grand Masters' souls. Not only is it noticeabl; in
commercial enterprises, insurance undertakings, and the like, but the
Cr~ft is openly associated, as a Craft, with politics, despite what
reviewers may assert to the contrary. Publications professing to be
Masonic, and bearing the name of the Craft, are found inserting
advertisements for the election of candidates to the Legislature or
public office, and in these advertisements the Masonic standing of
the candidates is set forth in the most bare-faced and, therefore, improper style. Yet the conductors of those journals see nothing
objectionable in the practice, and if Grand Lodge authorities in those
places do, one does not find them taking the very strong measures
well within their competence to discipline not only the Masonic
conductors of the journals, but also the Brethren who either authorize
or permit the insertion of these objectionable notices. Mere fulmination is not enough.

• • • • •

During his year of office, Brother Freet (Missouri) was constrained to officially notify the Lodges that electioneering cards and
other campaign publicity of candidates for public office must not
be used in Masonic buildings nor in connection with Masonic gatherings. "It is entirely proper for a Freemason as an individual to
take an active part in politics," he says, "but a Masonic Lodge should
not be used to further the personal fortunes of any candidate for
office." Perfectly correct, but one cannot wonder that such things
happen so frequently in United States Masonry, when many Masonic
journals do the same thing, and that such ~odies as the Shrine and

the Sciots, which base their membership on the Masonic qualification, permit their members to use their membership in commercial
advertising.
PROHIBITION
The good and bad results of the 18th Amendment are reflected
in a small degree at least in the Fraternity, and particularly in the
Reports of the Committee on Grievances and Appeals. What occurs
on November 8th may perhaps be a start to settle this question.
British Columbia (1931):
(Chairman Correspondence Comm4ttee) : In the address ?£ the
Grand Master of Idaho is a copy of a long letter on the subJec.t ~f
prohibition, which the Grand Master sent to his Lodges. In it 1s
the rather remarkable statement that " the bootlegger transgresses
the laws of the land as well as the laws of Masonry." As to the laws
of the land, yes; but we demur to the stat~men.t tha.t t~e la~s of
Masonry prohibit anyone from selling or usmg mtox1catmg liquor.
The Masonic law of Idaho may prohibit it, but the laws of Masonry
do not.

• • • • •

In all my travels I have been very forcibly struck with the lasting
impression created among the Craft by many of my predecessors.
Not many years ago no banquet in honor of a Grand ~as.ter was
considered complete without spirit uous liquor. In one D1str.1ct apo~­
ogies were tendered to me for not giving expression to their hospitality in that time-honored custom. I was informed that it had been
discontinued since Most Worshipful Brother
had so
strongly shown his displeasure. In a London gallery hangs the
famous picture "Night" by that great artist and moralist, Hogarth.
He there depicts a characteristic night scene in the Lo~don stre.ets
of his time. Among the typical specimens of depraVlty hauntmg
these ill-lit ways, Hogarth has held up to the derision of all time
the figure of a Free Mason, staggering home drunk, still wearing
his apron and assisted by the Tyler of his Lodge.
No true Mason can regard this picture without a burning sense
of shame and without registering a resolution to redeem the Craft
from this stigma. I am sure that it is the prayer of every Mason
that we never relapse into that chaotic condition from which we
have emerged. It is my personal opinion that this gradual chan~ge
which is taking place among our people is not the result of prohibitive legislation, but of education.

Missouri (1931):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Wise men differ in· their
opinions of the ~olstead Act. But so far as we have been able to

62

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

discover, none of its opposers has proposed anything in its place that
commands respect. The Eighteenth Amendment is here to stay. Its
enemies can secure its repeal about the time a place with a much
warmer climate freezes over. The writer travels thousands of miles
every year and has met in his travels two drunken men in ten years.
There is drinking going on but the amount is small in Missouri as
compared with former years. We have many corrupt officials, but
we are landing some of them in Federal penitentiaries. Springfield's
former Chief of Police is serving a year at Leavenworth. Our Mayor
is under a two years' sentence. He was convicted on the testimony
of bad men and his appeal which is pending may release him. There
are good men who believe he is riot corrupt, but, like Old Dog Tray,
he got in bad company.
Two or three years ago nearly a quarter of a million of automobiles were stolen in one year in this country. Shall we repeal
our laws against theft? Wait till the Volstead Act has a fair chance
in an honest effort to enforce it by competent and honest officials.
To repeal the Volstead Act now, without substituting a more
efficient law for the enforcement of the Eighteenth Amendment,
would be a surrender to the criminal classes.

North Dakota (1931):
(Grand Master): One of the unpleasant duties of the Grand
Master is the issuing of orders of suspension of members who have
been convicted of a crime.
No good purpose would be served by reviewing the cases.
• There is cause for comment, however, in the fact that most of
them are for violation of our liquor laws.
By tradition and by our ancient regulations, Masonry stands
four square for law and its enforcement. "A Mason is a peaceable
subject to the civil powers-and is never to be concerned in plots
and conspiracies against the peace and welfare of the Nation." "If
a Brother should rebel against the State, he is not to be countenanced
in his rebellion."
The situation in regard to the Eighteenth Amendment throughout the Nation has come to the point where it would appear that
there is a conspiracy among many of our people to disobey the law
themselves, and to advocate and encourage its disobedience by others.
This is rebellion. Whenever a body · refuse to obey the law of the
land, it is as truly rebellion as though they took up arms against it.
This attitude upon the part of many of our people leads to disrespect
of all law, and tends toward anarchy.
Brethren, Masonry stands squarely for the upholding of the
duly constituted powers in the enforcement of all laws, including
the Eighteenth Amendment.
Your Grand Master calls upon you as Free Masons, and as
citizens of this State and this Republic, in your private life to observe
the law in spirit as also in letter, and by your word and deed to
uphold the officers of the law in their efforts to enforce the law.
This does not limit the right of any man to advocate the repeal
of any law which he considers unwise or to use every legitimate

64

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE
REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

method to obtain its repeal. Masons will differ, as other men will
differ, on the wisdom or the effectiveness of the law. But Masons
cannot differ upon the proposition that so long as the Eighteenth
Amendment is the law of the land, then they must personally obey
the law and support the government in its enforcement.
South Carolina (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The question of qualification of candidates for the degrees of Freemasonry, affected by the
connection of the individual with the government Liquor Commission, is being raised in Nova· Scotia; and Grand Master Fraser was
called upon twice to decide whether or not a man who was employed
by the Liquor Commission could be accepted as a candidate. He.
very properly decided that he was eligible. However, we may differ
as to the disposition of the question of the legislation concerning,
and the use of, alcoholic beverages, we cannot condemn the character
of a man who is in the employ of the government of the country in
which we live. Moreover, if the government, by majority vote of
its citizenship, is endeavoring sincerely to cope with a great problem•
through government control, how can such government hope to
realize its objective if honorable men refuse to accept positions of
trust in such a cause? And if such men are willing to lend their
efforts, why should they be condemned and disbarred from the fellowship of honorable men? We are offering no defense of alcohol,
but we recognize the democratic principle of government and the
righteousness of honest endeavor.
Vermont (1931):
(Clwirman Correspondence Committee): His review of Vermont
was short but inclusive. No, Brother Briggs (Missouri) , we are not
hoping for the return of the saloon. We would not have it back for
anything. We are not, nor ever have been, a drinking man. But we
still think the Volstead Act, as a reasonable interpretation of the
Eighteenth Amendment, is a piece of monumental assininity, which
will some day be superseded by more reasonable legislation. Under
it, the evils of drunkenness have been multiplied. Without it, we
could not be worse off.

RITUAL
The result of too much attention to Ritual, now that the Fraternity generally has had a breathibg spell through lack of candidates,
is a question that is receiving serious consideration. Ritualism in a
number of Jurisdictions has become a fetish. As it reached its present
importance through evolution, undoubtedly any change, either in the
work itself or the basic ideas regarding its value, can only be had
through changing conditions and education.
Connecticut (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): This, under California,
would show that, like us, he has no use for "degree teams":
"In other cases the degree teams were composed of men belonging to organizations which require that petitioners for membership therein shall be Master Masons. In one instance, at least, after
the Third Degree had been conferred, the newly-raised Brother was
presented with an application form, post-dated six months, for membership in the organization to which the degree team belonged."
Indiana (1932):
(Grand Master): At my request our Grand Lecturer has during
the last few weeks been making a report to me as to how often the
Ancient Charges have been read by the Lodges visited by him in
his official capacity. The reports develop an astounding set of facts.
He reports that one Worshipful Master said that' as long as he had
been a member of the Lodge he had never heard the Ancient Charges
read in the Lodge. His report on another Lodge stated the officers
reported they had never heard the Ancient Charges read in their
Lodge. He reported on another Lodge that the offic.e rs reported that
the Ancient Charges were seldom read in their Lodge. In another
report Brother Tolle reports that none present at the meeting had
ever heard t'he Ancient Charges read in their Lodge. These are just
samples of reports turned in in response to this inquiry made by our
Grand Lecturer.
What the situation is over the State with reference to this matter, I do not know, but I am of the opinion that the Ancient Charges

have not been read in a great many Lodges for a long i;>eriod of
years, and yet no doubt the Lodges wherein the Ancient Charges
have not been read are among those who are complaining of a lack
of interest in Masonry.
Masonry seems to have digressed from fundamentals and become
imbued with the commercial and social spirit of the age, and many
Worshipful Masters and Brethren have forgotten the true functions
of Freemasonry. The fundamentals of Freemasonry have not been
changed and the work of the Lodge is to confer the degrees in an
intelligent manner so that the candidate will be inspired to live a
well rounded Masonic life, and when this is done in the L odge the
officers of the Lodge will find that the Brethren will at once take
more interest in Masonry.
It is high time that we cease these excursions into outside affairs
and . that Masonry as set out in "The Charges of a Freemason extracted from the Ancient Records of Lodges Beyond Sea" be regularly .brought to the attention of the Brethren throughout the State
of Indiana for their Masonic instruction.
Kansas (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Having had the pleasure
of several very pleasant talks with Brother Gentry (Missouri) during
his visit to our Grand Lodge last February, we fee l free to offer a
little criticism to some of his views as expressed in his splendid address, and we note that he recommended that the usual Charge which
is delivered at the conclusion of the Lecture be withheld until the
candidate had passed the required examination in the Lecture of
the preceding degree, believing it would be more impressive and
valuable to the candidate.
We submit that there is some merit in his argument in favor of
such a 'change; however, if all Grand Masters were permitted to
recommend changes of this kind, would it not totally disorganize
our whole system of work? The Committee to whom t his subject
was referred by t he Committee on Grand Master's Address, reported ·
that nothing had been referred to them and therefore they had no
report to make. Just what became of this portion of the Grand
Master's ad'1ress we are unable to state.

Nevada (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Under "Visitations," the
Grand Master of Arizona states in part in regard to the rendition of
degree work: "We do not expect that our officers will be 'letter
perfect' in this respect." We agree with him and even venture to
say that we don't believe there is "any such animal." A great many
officers do their work in what we would term a faultless manner,
but if any man can give fifty-odd thousand words of Masonry without
changing a word once in a while, he deserves a monument far
greater than the one they are erecting in Virginia now.
New Hampshire (1932) :
(Grand Meister) : So far as I can discover the Grand Constitution
is silent upon the question of our ritual. There is in the archives of
Grand Lodge an official ritual and the Grand Lecturer for the State
has a ritual which is generally known as the official ritual of the work
of the three degrees in this jurisdiction. The Grand Lecturers for
the several districts are also furnished rituals which are supposed to
be official. No rituals are furnished to the subordinate Lodges. The
officers of a subordinate Lodge are thus supposed, at least theoretically, to have the work handed down to them by wor~ of ~outh
from past officers. It is well known, however, that written rituals
are in every Lodge, and in constant use. None of them has any official sanction. I regret also to say that printed rituals published
and sold by a commercial publishing house outside the State frequently find their way into the hands of officers of Lodges, although
containing many inaccuracies. Many warnings have been issued by
the District Deputy Grand Masters and by the Grand Lecturer, but
the evil persists. It is a difficult matter to handle.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): It is unfortunate that
Masonry at times has to suffer from the ill-advised entl1usiasm of
some of its members who try to incorporate a slapstick sort of
farce common to some other organizations, into the serious business
of Masonry. There is no place in the Masonic ritual for clowning

Nova Scotia (1931):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): ~rother Kies (Connecticut) does not appear to be satisfied with our reply to his query as
to why the conferring of the degrees should be limited to W. M.'s
and P. M.'s. Well, we have always been taught that when work of
this kind was to be done, such as conferring degrees-in other words,
making Masons-it required a Master in the Arts and Sciences to
do the work-in other words, a Ruler of the Craft. Mastecs and
Past Masters are, or are supposed to be, Rulers of the Craft and
better able to do this work, and for this and possibly other reasons
is why in our Jurisdiction we limit the conferring of the degrees to ·
these Brethren. To us it would appear incongruous to make a Mason
one evening, and the next meeting see him confer, say, the Master
Mason's degree. Is that your opinion, Brother Kies ?
Virginia (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): M. W. J osiah H . Drummond told the writer in 1899, and he later on made the same statement
in a brief address to Grand Lodge of Virginia in Alexandria, "that
Virginia had retained the Webb ritual, as agreed upon at the Baltimore Convention of Grand Lecture/s in 1843, in all its purity; that
his and other Grand Jurisdictions had made a few departures in
efforts to 'shorten the work'." He also stated that, "with these exceptions, Massachusetts was probably nearer than any of the older
Jurisdictions in keeping to the Preston-Webb forms."·
Like any development or departure from custom and practice,
some Lodges in Virginia were occasionally conferring the E. A.
Degree with the use of a feature that the Baltimore Conference
agreed to om:t, nearly fifty years after 1843. Florida and a few Jurisdictions still retain this feature.
Wyoming (1931):

(Grand Master): Reports have come to me that some Lodges
go back to their old method of doing work and inject novelties or
changes when I am not present. Naturally, these would not be done
when I was present. Such practices, if they are being done, should
be discontinued, not only because they are a violation of Section 255
of our Masonic Code, ·but for the simple reason that it tempts the
younger members to add further innovations to our work and mar

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

its impressiveness. I was told by an officer of one Lodge, where a
visiting Lodge had put on the Third Degree, that the work in the
second section was nothing but a farce owing to the way the candidate was handled. These things make it hard work to maintain
uniformity, and destroy the lessons we teach. I have visited a f~w
Lodges unexpectedly, when the officers were conferring a Third
Degree. I wish I had the time to describe to you the twentieth century paraphernalia that was used to put on a scene that took place
some thousand year·s before Christ was born. I sometimes · wonder
why they do not have a "police ambulance," a "mortician" and use
an up-to-date "auto hearse" in that part of the degree work.
The practice of some members scaring candj.dates for the degrees and making them believe they have to go through some awful
ordeal, should be severely condemned. It ru '. ns the impressions that
the candidate should get out of the work, as his mind is more on
what is to happen than on paying attention to what is being said,
and the Senior Deacon has to drag him from one station to another.
There is no place in our organization for foolishness or the joking
of candidates, and any attempt in so doing should be dealt with
by very decisive measures.

began, have gone home, or have gone out to the social room to visit,
smoke and swap yarns with each other, and only the officers and a
bare handful of members remain in the hall while the candidate
stands and listens to a long charge.
Throughout these charges the average candidate's tired mind is
unable to grasp what is said in the charge, often delivered near midnight, and he is wondering when it will end.
I think it would be far better to omit the charges at the close
of the degrees, and deliver them just after the candidate has passed
his proficiency lectures. When he is examined on the proficiency
lecture in the First Degree, leaves the hall, is voted proficient, and
ls brought back and stands at the altar while the' Worshipful Master
tells him that he has been found proficient, would be a fine opportunity for the Worshipful Master to deliver the charge in the First
Degree. The same course could be followed as to each of the other
lectures. The candidate would certainly get much more out of the
charges under such an arrangement than he could get as the charges
are now given. It is early in the evening when the examinations
occur; everybody, including the candidate, is wide awake, and a good
audience furnishes an incentive to the Master to do his best and a
candidate would thus receive a far better impression than he does
now.
I think some of the charges could be greatly improved by
shortening them. In some, a sentence here and there could well be
eliminated and in the charge in the Second Degree a whole paragraph might well be stricken out.
