RITUAL-REVISION OF
The recommendations of various Grand Masters, including that
of our own, that the Ritual of the present day should be shortened,
will as time progresses, we believe, gather momentum and result in
positive action. Our present Work has been changed and added to
until it bears slight resemblance to the source from whence it came.
Originally the Ritual played a small part in Masonry, but at present
it has assumed an importance out of all proportion to what it was
intended to accomplish through its rendition.
If it could be materially abridged, a time limit placed between
Degrees, and the candidate instructed regarding the Fraternity itself
as he progresses through the Degrees, benefits would result. That
plan would have a tendency to bring us back to the idea that we are
a Fraternity with Philosophy and Institutional activities playing
minor parts.

North Dakota (1931):
(Grand Master): I have talked rev1s10n of the ritual in many
meetings in the State. I have suggested that it is time that the penalties should be changed, that some of our claims to a very ancient
history should be eliminated, and that for the middle chamber lecture
be substituted a lecture on citizenship from "the ancient charges"
concerning "the civil magistrate supreme and subordinate."
I am not prepared to make any recommendation in regard to
such revision at this time, except that the Brethren give the matter
serious thought. I feel strongly that Masonry will benefit much by
such changes. There is nothing sacred about our ritual. It has been
revised many times. The things which are sacred are the eternal
truths upon which Masonry is builded. They are as true today as
when first given, a nd in all the revisions which have taken place
they have remained unchanged.

(Custodians of the Work): While we probably would not agree
with the Grand Master in his suggestions with reference to changes
and revisions in the Ritual, we do heartily approve of his efforts to
bring to the attention of the Craft a more complete understanding
of the fact that our Ritual comes from a time, centuries back, when
possibly historical accuracy was not emphasized so freely as now.
The discussion has brought clearly to the minds of the Brethren
that the thing which appeals to most men in our Ritual is its antiquity.
There is an aroma of the past in its language and diction. You can't
rewrite Shakespeare, neither can you rewrite our Ritual.
The purpose of Preston's Middle Chamber lecture was not so
much to present scientific, mathematical accuracy but to direct the
attention of the Craftsman to his need of knowledge and education
and give him a bird's-eye view of the then known field of knowledge.
It would be destructive to remove this lecture from our work.

Illinois (1931 ):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : There is nothing whatsoever wrong with Freen{asonry. The institution is just as stable
and just as vital as it has ever been. Its principles are founded upon
eternal truths which are as firmly established today as they were in
the beginning, and they are just as needful in the world as they
have ever been. It is now generally conceded by all that we are
passing through a period of readjustment. Individuals and institutions are slowly ·but surely coming back to normal. The trouble has
been, particularly in the United States, that we have suffered from
inflation. Corporation and business interest s, lured by the "will o'
the wisp" prosperity, were inflated beyond all reason. Because wages
and salaries were good !Oday, the individual took no thought of the
morrow and inflated his credit without any thought of the coming
day of reckoning. A going business had dreams of expansion and
erected new buildings to double its capacity. The individual bought
many things on the installment plan, all of which he is now striving
to pay for. It will take a little while for things to come back to
their former status, but the present indications are that the trend
is in that direction.
The whole trouble with Freemasonry was that along with other
things it suffered from over-inflation. During prosperous years Lodges
had but one idea, and that was to inflate the Lodge-to get all the
petitions possible without taking due consideration of the ability of
the applicants to understand and assimilate Freemasonry. Many new
Lodges were formed without any thought concerning the reorganization and elimination of many Lodges which were merely eking
out an existence, and which were no credit either t o their Grand
Lodge or themselves. Throughout all this there has been an element

of selfishness and self-indulgence. Grand Lodges have been reporting a large number of suspensions and dimissions. In a majority of

that the need for this is really a blessing in disguise in the United

• • • • •

Suspensions for non-payment of ·dues continue to exercise the
best minds in the different Grand Lodges. Among some leaders of
Masonic thought there seems to be an impression that even this,
which most of us regard as regrettable, may be a blessing in disguise,
and that it can well be left to itself, if it be an evil, to work its own
cure. Those who entertain this view appear to regard exclusions as
a kind of purifying fire that will eliminate "dead timber," and by
the law of the survival of the fittest, provide the best material. Such
a view loses sight of the duty of caring for the uncaring, and answers
the question, "Am I my brother's keeper?" in the negative. It is
comforting to realize that a kindlier view is taken by the larger
number, and they are seriously seeking for both cause and remedy.
So far, the indications point to a larger realization of the need to
interest the Brethren-especially the younger men on whom we
must depend for the future of our Lodges-in something more than
mere ceremonial. That a sitting Master and his officers find nothing
wearisome in ritual repetition is regarded as natural. But, as was
wisely contended by one of the American Masonic Education Committees last year, Masonry must realize that twentieth century forms
of recreation are in competition, and that the facilities for obtaining
it are always ready to hand. And it is urged that Masters may yet
recognize that if the Craft is to hold its members, especially the
younger, rulers of Lodges must reduce the number of their ceremonies
and provide for the Masonic education pf their members, instead of
calling upon them at every meeting to endure a ceremony which, by
its frequency, has begun to pall.

GEORGE WASHINGTON MEMORIAL
This project was started with the idea of erecting a fireproof _
building costing $100,000 to house the George Washington relics
belonging to Washington Alexandria Lodge. It was figured that
voluntary contribution of $1.00 per member would accomplish the
end. To May 12, 1932, the various Grand Lodges advanced $3,545,367.00, with additional contributions from other sources, making
a net total of $3,881,251.48. California has paid $158,290.70, or 111.1 % ,
based on a $1.00 per capita tax.
A year ago the plan was changed so that if the Memorial was
to be completed and an endowment fund established, the quota
would ha.v e to be raised to $1.70 per capita. Some Jurisdictions
pledged themselves to make such payment, prnvided all the other
Jurisdictions would follow suit. On the basis of $1.70, our Jurisdiction with its contribution of $158,290.70 is 34.6% under such an
allotment.
The Memorial has been dedicated, but whether or not it will
be possible to secure the additional funds to carry out the existing
plans is to our mind a very grave question. We have always held to
the belief that if this money had been used to endow a National
University it would have served a greater purpose and been a more
satisfactory memorial to the Father of Our Country.

Illinois (1931):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Once in a while as we go .
through life, we come across a man who has the courage of conviction. We are most of us disposed to follow the crowd and to
agree with the majority. It is a human trait to want to ride in the
band wagon, even if we can't toot a horn. But sometimes there
comes along a fellow who doesn't want to ride, and says that he
believes that he will go along by himself. Now such a man is Daniel
]. Muri, Grand Master of Montana. In his annual address to h is
Grand Lodge he had something to say about the George Washington Memorial. In substance it was this: He said that in the building
of this monu.ment to George Washington the Masons had lost their
heads and had allowed the heart to govern common sense. He
granted that it was to be a most beautiful Masonic monument to
an illustrious Mason, but he thought that a more useful memorial
could have been planned. Instead of putting $5,000,000 'into stone
and marble for people just to go and look at, there could have been
worked out a memorial that would have been of practical benefit
· to coming .g enerations. Brother Muri points out that the structure,
which is being completed, will involve continual expense with inadequate returns (except sentimental journeys for the appreciation
of beautiful architecture and relics). He thinks that a program might
have been devised which would have carried the respect for George
Washington, and which at the same time might have resulted in
some' human benefit. Brotlier Muri emphasizes the fact he is just
as full of sentiment as anybody else, but he thinks that more could
have been accomplished if a little common sense had been used as
an ingredient along with the monument. Well, there are a lot of
us who have thought the same thing, but we just didn't have backbone enough to stand up and say it. The writer was present at the
first meeting at Alexandria, Virginia, when it was proposed that a
building be erected ' to house certain relics of George Washington,
which would cost in the neighborhood of $100,000. I t was expected
that this building, in addition to the museum, would have a Lodge
hall which might be a replica of the old hall in Alexandria, and
which would furnish a home for Alexandria Lodge, which, of
course, would be custodian of the building and the Washington
relics contained therein. It was a simple idea and practically everyone present at that ~eeting was in accord w ith it. Then others
came along with more exaggerated ideas and the proposition was
to erect a building costing $500,000, and then others came along
and a-dded to the amount until now it has reached the grand total
of almost $5,000,000; $5,000,000 invested at five per cent would yield
$250,000 per year. The average school course costs around $1,000.

out with the avowed intention of expending only one hundred thousand dollars and has expended in excess of three millions of dollars,
and is still planning the expenditure of some two millions more.

YOUNGER GENERATION
Regardless of what we may think of boys and girls they ar e
stubborn facts. They have been with us from time immemorial and
will continue to be. Whether Masonry should interest itself with
them in the formative period of their lives is a question. Regardless
of the viewpoint, Secretary of Agriculture, Arthur M. Hyde, summarizes the difficult:es as follows:
"Boys and agriculture are equal and parallel sufferers from a
plethora of advisers, whose numbers, good intentions, and volubility,
as well as output, cannot be excelled by any other industry. Advice
on both these themes has increased in geometric ratio to the population, multiplied by the increase in means of communication. In
the case of both boys and agriculture, that advice makes Jeremiah
look like a dumb neophyte-or, as we modernly put :t-a piker.
The lamentations poured out upon the heads of both boys and
farmers are firmly rooted in sorrow and look to a future of complete
darkness through which no star of hope dares stab a single ray.
"Another point of similarity lies in the antiquity of our respective industries. It is said that King Tut, when his sleep of centuries
was rudely disturbed by archeologists, held in his hand a clay tile
upon which was written a farewell address, which began with the
lamentation that the boys of that day were ruining the country, and
wound up with copious advice upon the farm problem. * * *
"No matter how ornery or low-down our boys may be at times,
we nevertheless shall continue to rear, berate, cherish, castigate, forgive, and eternally to love 'em. Our devotion is instinctive and
universal. We cannot help it. Consciously or unconsciously we see
in the boy the man who will carry on what was passed down to us,
and finish what we have started. We advise them copiously and
inconsistently against the very errors we personify. We lecture
them sternly against our own shortcomings. This is because we want
them to be better men than we are. We expect them to straighten
out into 'homers' all the foul balls that have glanced off our bat."
Any organization that has for its object educating the boy of
today, who is to be leader in the years to come, is not merely serviceable but a necessity.
South Australia and Victoria appear to have adopted the "Progressive" idea. The statistics of the Order of DeMolay show only

Nevada (1931):

Address of De Molay Joseph Jackson, Jr., Before the
Members of the Grand Lodge
.
It is a steadfast spirit such as DeMolay's which calls to a boy
m the adolescent stage of his life, when he may make of his career
anything he chooses, regardless· of what his past life has been, no
matter what his immediate surroundings may be. Mainly he has
two courses. He may cast his character, on the one hand, in the
scraggly mold of unworthiness, shiftlessness, and selfishness. He
may so fashion his purpose that it will never permit him to lift a
. finger to help his fellowman. He may meet people with a shifty'
eye and a limpid handclasp. On the otlter hand, he may cast his
character in the dye of genuine worthiness, making his main forces
the pursuance of public service, truth, and loyalty, making himself
a man who can look the whole world straight in the eye, one of
whom any father should be proud to say "Son."
We do not claim that we can accomplish all of this character
moulding process. We do not presume to say that any boy cannot
develop such a desired character if he fails to enter our ranks. But
we do say this: "Give us a boy who shows even a remote· leaning
towards following out the principles for which the name DeMolay
stands, and we will so direct him throughout the adolescent stages
of his life, so aid him in his gropings for truth, that it will be infinitely . much more easy for him to be a better man than had he
stayed out of our order altogether, and it is fairly certain that his
feet will never stray far from the path along which our teachings
have sent him.
It has never been our purpose to seek out tarnished stones so
set i.n the rut of indifference that they cannot be pried apart.' so
unmmdful of the better purposes of life that we should be tarnished
in our associations with them. Neither do we set up to be reformers
nor is it our desire to be looked upon as simon-pure, snobbish and
aloof. Snobbery is probably the last thing to which a DeMolay could
stoop. It is the task of a DeMolay to dig deep down into the soil
seeking out diamonds in the rough, so that they may be subjected
to a thorough grinding process, and turned out beautiful polished
gems of manhood.
.
The third lesson teaches cleanliness of the mind and body. Here
the growing boy is aided in crossing the pitfalls of immorality and
degradation. He learns to let alone the star-dust which so often
traps unguided youth. Next comes the lesson of devotion to God
and to the service of the universal brotherhood. This is followed
by the great lesson of love for country, aiding youth to hear the

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

91

clear call for intelligent citizenship, and the following out of dem~
cratic ideals. In this lesson is taught the true value . of the public
school with the deep-seated learning that knowledge 1s power only
when lntelligently, actively and loyally applied.
I said before that there were two reasons for the growth ?f t~e
Order of DeMolay. You have heard the first. The seco~d hes m
the wonderful stalwart backing given us by. the Masonic Order.
Masonic inter;st is all that we could hope for it to be, and much
more. That you have labored with us, toiled with us, often at great
sacrifice of personal time and comfort, asking for no return, makes
us indebted to you in a way we shall probably never be able to repay.
Still youthful, perhaps, yet you have passed beyond the period
of preparation for manhood. You have ta~en you~ feet fro~ the
threshold, and have passed on into your precious heritage of w1sd?m
and experience. You have learned to apply the lessons ?f devotion
and sacrifice of service and loyalty. You have established yourselves as citi~ens. Yet, having done all this, you are n~t conten.t to
rest idly, having instead chosen to turn back a?d build a bridge
across which those who come after you may pass m safety.
!And now in closing, I am going to paint for you a picture, a
picture of a i'nan standing on a lofty pedestal, his right. hand extended slightly f~rward and downward. His fingers stretch out
towards a small plodding figure, which climbs slowly. upwards. T~e
eyes of the figure are glued to the platform on which ~he man. is
standing, and he is drawn irresistibly onward by the light which
reflects from that face. The man represents the Order of Masonry,
the small figure represents the Order of DeM olay.
Thus we have it, age and wisdom on the one hand, youth ~nd
inexperience on the other, both with lofty ideals, one already ~av~ng
reached its station, the other mounting ever higher towards a s1m1lar
pedestal, that both may labor together for a ~ommon good, an~ now
separated only by those last few steps, which mark the period of
preparation which all youth must surmount before it enters the ranks
of manhood.
South Australia (1930):
(Grand Master}: It is not our custom to advocate any particular
activity of this kind, but for once I am going to ?e bo_ld enough to
5 uggest a possible outlet for our efforts. There 1s a little ?rotherhood in existence which has the same ideals, the same aims and
objects as we ourselves-I refer to the Boy Scout movement. We
have only to read the solemn vow wh~ch a S~ou.t tak.~s when. he is
·nvested to see how our ideals and ob1ects comc1de- I promise on
~Y honor to do my duty to God and the ,,King, to help other people
at all times, and to obey the Scout Law.

92

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

If _any of you have time to read the Scout Laws you will see
how ahke they are to the ideals and principles of Freemasonry. The
Boy Scout movement, like ours, is world-wide, it is open to every
class: color, an~ creed; both are founded on the strongest principles
of piety and virtue, both stand solidly for morality and strength
and character.

Therefore, the good Boy Scout of today cannot fail to become
a good Freemason of tomorrow, and what better service could we
do for our country or our Craft, than to take an active interest in
the character training of our youth, the boys who soon, as men,
will bear the responsibility of the well being of our country.
, There . are many ways in which anyone who wishes can help.
We can give moral and material support to our local organizations
and show the value we place on the movement. Some can take a
more active part.
We have thousands of boys waiting to be led and anxious to
b_e led, but unfortunately the supply of boys has outgrown the
supply of suitable leaders. There can be no better leaders of youth
than those who believe in an<l practice the principles of Freemasonry.
The Boy Scout movement is one which I have very much at
heart and in which I can see enormous possibilities for the future
of mankind. ·
I feel that it is so closely allied to Freemasonry in its objects
and its ideals that I am justified in commending it to the Brethren
for their personal consideration, although it may not be possible for
the Craft to give any official or organized recognition to the movement.
Victoria (1931):
(Grand Master) : But what I shall miss most is being able to
thank Brethren generally for their splendid support to the Boy
Scout movement. A letter I have received says: "At Korumburra
three new Troops have been staffed by Masonic Brethren." . Isn't
that glorious? Bring up the boys. " In as much as ye have done it,"
etc. From every point of view it is worth while. So thank them
from me; their reward will be great.

Grand Lodge of California. They carry on such a wonderfully well
organized work and report it in such an interesting way that I cannot
do it justice with a review limited to the space allotted me.
The Grand Master's recommendation in regard to the Grand
· Secretary was approved. I am glad to see a ·g ood Grand Secretary

The Grand Orator, William C. Hassler, delivered a very scholarly

but is too long to include in my brief review.
The~e is an interesting report on Masonic History.
The Report on Correspondence is written by Jesse M. Whited
and is his tenth review and, as usual, is written in topical form. It is

Grand Lodge some years ago established an annual "Public Schools
Week," having for its purpose the fostering of a greater interest and
knowledge by the public in their schools. Every Lodge is supposed
to arrange public meetings for this purpose and apparently the movement is an unqualified success.
To us in North Dakota this looks like real Masonic work, although
we opine that it will rub against the grain with Van Patten of Washington and Fly down in Texas.
The Committee on Masonic History presented a highly interesting report of Masonry in the early days of the state. While in no
way detracting from the noble work of the pioneers of the fraternity,
there are interesting items included which would indicate that being
a Mason in those days did not make every man a saint.
The Correspondence Report, which is Brother Jesse M. Whited's
tenth, is in topical form and in it he thoroughly covers the leading
questions which are being considered by Grand Lodges today.
Ohio:
The Foreign Correspondent, Bro. Jesse M. Whited, submitted
his tenth Report on Correspondence. He says that consideration of
the same general questions and conditions that have been before the
Craft for a number of years are practically along the same unchanged
line. • • • The report of Bro. Whited is a valuable production.

Brother Jesse M. Whited presents his usual review on the topical
plan, plus statistics. He reproduces a number of items from this
scribe's "hot air." Of just what interest these can be to California is
not apparent. Probably most, if not all, will find dissent. However,

they educe conclusions directly opposed to our own.
Florida:
So voluminous was the business ·of the Grand Lodge of California
that four days were required to transact the same, and over a thousand pages to report the proceedings, and no list of membership
either,
The address of Grand Master Ross was an exceptionally comprehensive record of devotion to the Craft, evidencing him to be a "just
and upright man and Mason." Only a few of the high spots of his
constructive administration can be mentioned.
It is a long way from the Golden Gate to Sunny Florida, and it
is not surprising . that Grand Master Ross did not know that the
corner stone of a church in Tampa was laid March 2, 1928, at night,
and by the Masonic Fraternity; and also that the corner stone of the
new Temple of Hillsborough Lodge, also in Tampa, was laid June
18, 1928, at night, by Grand Lodge as well, and under more colorful
conditions, including radio broadcasting, and so far as ye scribe
knows, was the first time in the history of Masonry that the corner
stone of a Masonic Temple had been laid at night.
R.' .E.". Jesse M. Whited presented the Report of the Committee
on Correspondence, which is in topical form. It is an excellent compilation of comments and selections, largely from the addresses of
Grand Masters and reports of committees. It is as interesting and
readable as it is informative. Five of the extracts are from the
Florida Proceedings. An Appendix names twenty-three Chairmen
of Committees on Correspondence in California, of which Bro. Whited,
the last, has already served eleven years. The California committee
has ten members, but apparently Bro. Whited does the work.
During the past four years the Grand Lodge has been gathering
data for the History of Freemasonry in California and which, when
completed, will, no doubt, be the largest and most extensive history
undertaken by any single Grand Lodge.
Indiana:
Brother Jesse M. Whited submits his usual excellent Report on
Correspondence in topical form.

Kansas:

Maine:

was observed with practically all Lodges taking part in their respective localities. Your Maine correspondent receives under separate
cover each year a full and detailed account of this observance by t he

Among the Grand Master's decisions is one allowing liberal construction of physical defects on the part of otherwise worthy applicants.

New Jersey:

very isolation of California in the old days when the wagon train or
the long sea trip were the only methods of communication, for this
was the formative period of California Masonry. In any event Cali~ornia. is refreshingly different. They have met the common problems

facile pen of such a. well informed Masonic student as Brother Whited.

"NEWS FLASHES"
One of the objecti~ns to the topical" form of review used by this
Committee on Correspondence is that it does not furnish a statement as to what is taking place in other Jurisdictions. Every Chairman writes for home consumption and we are no exception to the
rule. We believe that the Masons of California are more interested
in the general trend of Masonic thought than in the purely detail
work or statistics of any other Jurisdiction.
Under this heading we have gathered some of the outstanding
things occurring in other places. We believe they will be entertaining
as well as instructive and supply the want of details lacking in our
form of report.

Alberta:
· With reference to our relationship to other jurisdictions, there
is every evidence of a growing desire to draw more closely the
bonds of Masonic friendship . . . . I would like to see the day when
some association of Past Grand Masters might be formed, first
within each jurisdiction and these in turn united in a federal body
of consultative capacity.. .. As I see the things of life today we
are a lamen tably disunited organization without any collective inftuence whatsoever... . What an effect -we might have on the physical

from war!

Costa Rica:
A new Lodge has been constituted in the City of Alajuela, under
the name and number " Prospero Fernandez No. 12," so named in

other similar Orders from the country many years ago.
Czecho-Slovakia:
Eleven Lodges, 547 members; net gain, 65.
The comparatively small number of Brethren is due to extreme
care exercised in the admission of candidates. Each application must
be acted upon by the Lodge and then approved by the Grand Council
of Grand Lodge. In Czecho-Slovakia popular prejudice against Masonry has been kept alive for two centuries and is deep-seated in
some quarters, hence the Brethren feel they must constantly be on
their gu~rd and admit o·n.l y men under the tongue of good report,
preferably men known to and respected by the general publicgovernment officials, professors of universities, artists, leaders in
finance and industry, etc. Moreover, each member is required to b.e
present at every communication of his Lodge. Those who are absent
without reasonable excuse are suspended.

to form the Grand Lodge of England in 1717. I am told th4t English
Lodges limit their membership to 100, and when they e.tceed that
number a new Lodge must be· formed. Brother Robert I. Clegg, in
the Masonic Digest of California, says:
"An American visitor was invited to participate in a picnic
outing of an English Lodge, held on. the upper floor of a quaint
wayside tavern. He was impressed by the jovial spirit and general
enthusiasm with which everyone entered into the impromptu entertainment.
"How many members have you in this Lodge?" he inquired of
the Secretary, who sat at his elbow.
"Thirty-six," the Secretary replied, "and they are all here."
The American gasped. His name was on a Lod.g e roster that
bore several thousand others.
''With a congenial, happy lot of Brethren like this, I should
think you would initiate more members,'' he ventured.
"Well,'' replied the Secretary, "we usually have half a dozen
candidates in prospect. We initiate at least one a year, because the
officers naturally want to show they know how.. But, as to making
many more members--well, what for?"

•• • • •

Arising out · of an enquiry received by the Grand Secretary, the
Grand Lodge Solicitor was asked to express his opinion upon the
liability in law attaching to a Lodge in case of an accident happening to its Tyler, either during his actual attendance at the Lodge
meetings, or whilst journeying to .and fro between his residence and
the place at which the Lodge is held. The Grand Lodge Solicitor
is of opinion that there is no doubt that the Lodge would be liable,
as an employer, in the event of an accident to its Tyler in the circumstances.

The Pro Grand Master moved that £300 a year be paid to Lady
Robbins, widow of R.".W.". Brother Sir Alfred, who for eighteen
years was President of the Board of General Purposes. Lord Ampthill said:
"Just as the Public Service recognizes that it is right that pensions should be provided for widows, so we may well do likewise for
the widow of one who voluntarily gave us services which were invaluable to Grand Lodge and the Craft at large, and enabled us to steer
a safe course at !Dore than one highly critical period." The motion
was carried unanimously.

English Freemasonry has, during 1932, voluntarily subscribed
to the three Royal Masonic Institutions the gigantic sum of £280,-

798, whi\:h is just about sufficient to carry on the current work of
these institutions. This sum was collected by 12,270 Stewards operating in over 46 Provinces. The City of London contributed over
£65 per Lodge to the funds, or a total of more than £73,624.
Considering the fact that Great Britain has severely suffered
from the economic depression, the amount raised for English Masonic charity is surprisingly high and means that no doubt a great
deal of personal sacrifice was made on the part of the English
Brethren, in the name of humanity.

Massachusetts:

In 1804 Massachusetts abandoned the system of numbering its
Lodges. This was done on account of the confusion of numbers
that came about by the union in 1792 of a "St. John's Grand Lodge
of Massachusetts," which was founded in 1733 by Brother Henry
Price, and the "Massachusetts Grand Lodge" which was founded in
1769 under Scottish authority.

The Grand Master points out that many Lodges have dues
altogether too low. In fifty-eight of them the dues range from $2.75
to $4.50 a year. As a re~ult many have no surplus funds nor anything to supply immediate relief. He holds that no Lodge should
collect less than $5.00 per year. Such sum, after paying Grand Lodge
dues, would leave $3.00 for home use. By a thoughtful proportioning
of the $3.00 the Lodge would have opportunity to establish a neces- .
sary relief fund.

Miscellaneous:
Many Masonic Lodges are named after saints, those most commonly used being St. John and St. Andrew. In the United States,
fourteen Lodges have names derived from St. John, fifty-six from
St. Andrew, and eighty-nine from other saints .

• • • • •

The custom of Masons computing their time by adding 4,000 to
the current calendar year goes back to the first Book of Constitutions,
prepared by Dr. James Anderson, and published in London in 1723.
The title page of the volume carried the date: "In the year of Masonry, 5723: Anno Domini, 1723." Anderson himself explained this
in the second edition of the book in 1738 by saying that the world
was 4,000 years old at the birth of Christ, and as Freemasonry really
begun when God said, "Let there be Light," the year of Masonry
should be computed by adding 4,000 to the current date, therefore a
Masonic date when so written stands for "the year of Light," which
in Latin is "Anno Lucia"-hence we have the initials "A. L." preceding the figures.

• ••••

Many times we are asked why Masons ban Catholics from becoming members of their organizations. Catholics are not prohibited
from becoming Masons by any tenets of our Order, and some Catholics do become Masons, but since 1738 Catholics have been strictly
forbidden by their church, under penalty . of ex-communication, to

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENC'E

ANNUAL COMMUNICATIONS-MONTH OF MEETING

AMERICAN FREEMASONRY

January-Minnesota, Tennessee, Utah, Philippine Islands.

The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are
· generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly
speaking, they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish
Rite, for the one commonly called York is peculiar in its organized
proceedings only to the United States.

February-Connecticut, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Virginia, Quebec, Scotland.

The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar degrees.

April-Florida, New Jersey, North Carolina, South Australia,
Mexico (York), Porto Rico.

The symbolic degrees are conferred in a lodge and are the
Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is
by symbols.
·

May-Indiana, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, New York,
Rhode Island, New Zealand, Wes tern Australia.

The Capitular degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are the
Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent Master and the
Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degree of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of ·High Priests upon those who have
been regularly elected to preside over a Chapter of Royal Arch
Masons. They are called Capitular because they are conferred in a
Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning "done in a Chapter."
The ·C ryptic degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called "Cryptic" because the word "crypt" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take the
temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the
33rd, inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States
(which includes all territory south of the Ohio River and west of
the Mississippi River) the organization of the different bodies, and
the degrees conferred by them, are: Lodge of Perfection, 4• to 14°,

Frank Wilber Mixter
Grand Muter 1932-1933

Our Sixty•six~ Grand Master, pharmacist, soldier, banker, State
Senator, was ushered into this world on the 30th of December, 1873, at
Pekin, Illinois. His father was Horace L. Mixter, and his mother's
maiden name was Mary Katherine Sumner.
He received his Masonic craft degrees in Visalia Lodge No. 128 in
February and March, 1902, and withdrew in 1911 to join in the formation
of Exeter Lodge No. 424, being the first Senior Warden under dispensa·
tion and Master in 1912. The degrees of the Royal Arch were conferred
upon him in Visalia Chapter N'O. 44 in June and July, 1902, he subsequently affiliating with Exeter Chapter. No. 122, in which body he served
in every office, including that of High Priest. The Council degree~. were
received in 1917 in Fresno. He was dubbed a Knight Templar in November, 1'902, in Visalia Commandery, and the Scottish Rite,' 32°, conferred
in 1918-19 at Fresno. He is also a member of the Eastern Star, Shrine
and Sciots.
Brother Mixter has been active in craft Masonry from the date of his
raising. He served as Inspector of the Masonic district in which he resided
from February, 1917, until his elec.tion as Junior Grand Warden. In 1915
he was appointed Junior Grand Steward. At the annual election, October,
1929, the brethren of Grand Lodge, in recognition of his zeal and ability,
elected him to the office of Junior Grand Warden; in 1930, Senior Grand
Warden; in 1931, Deputy Grand Master; and in October, 1932, Grand
Master.

Our Sixty-sixth Grand Master, pharmacist, soldier, banker, State

upon him in Visalia Chapter No. 44 in June and July, 1902, he subsequently affiliating with Exeter Chapter No. 122, in which body he served
in every office, including that of High Priest. The Council· degrees were

in 1918-19 at Fresno. He is al§o a member of the Eastern Star, Shrine
and Sciots.

inspiring devotional service, preceded by the good old song,
'' Open . the Gates of the Temple," by the· choir .
. Dr. S.riape spoke as follows:
Most Worshipful Grand Master and brethren: Man's noblest aspiration is the quest of God; his deepest, purest affection, the love of God; his
sublimest ·c;ipacity, the worship of God. Goethe says that before a reader
may criticize an author he must be clear within. In the twilight a very
plain writing is illegible.
· The fool hath said in his heart, "There is no God," and he was right:
There is ·none-for a fool. He is not cleat' within, and there never will be
a God for him so long as he persists in remaining a fool.
No God? Then the Bible is the product of disordered brains. No
God·? · Then· the prophets were monomaniacs and their messages idle
utterances. No God? Then the Apostles were impostors and the Gospels
fairy: tales. No God? Then prayer is merely soul soliloquy and bdngs no
answer save the wild whisperings of. the wind. No .God? Then suffering

is insanity and suicide a virtue. No God? Then the fight against temptation is a fool's fight and might just as well end in sinful and selfish -indulgence. No God? Then. the belief of our craft is a false belief. No
God? Then David, sleeping in the wilderness, with stones for a pillow
and stars for a quilt, pursued by the usurper, and crying out in exultation,
" Oh God, Thou art my God," was a sentimentaHst carried away by false
hope. But just because there is a God, we that are here today would not
be here if t here were no God.
The trouble with Russia is that Russia is attempting to build a civilization with God left out; and it may be that that is the trouble with
America. We have lost the sense of God, and we should stand forth and
should make this our creed. As members of our !>¢loved craft we must
stand together and hold to Him. Our fraternity might well lead the nation
back to a sense of God, until men ever.ywhere shall recognize what was
meant by the poet :
"Every bird that sings
· And every flower that. stars the elastic sod, .
Every breath the radiant summer brings .
To the spirit is a word of God."

MESSAGE OF GRAND MASTER
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
We have assembled here today for the eighty-fourth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California. During the days of this
week we shall experience the joys and satisfactions of the renewal of
fraternal friendships and form new acquaintances to become the basis of
enduring friendships in the years to come. We shall hear and give consideration to the reports of those to whom was delegated the duty of
carrying on the activities of our fraternity in this Grand Jurisdiction
during the recess of the Grand Lodge, to review the work of-the past year,
to summarize its effect, and to plan for the future.
Responsive to the mandate of our Constitution, it is my duty to present
at this time a written message; setting forth my official acts during the
year, exhibiting the general condition of Masonry within the jurisdiction,
and recommending such legislation as may be deemed necessary or expedient for the welfare of the craft.
Entering one year ago upon the duties of this office, the highest within
the gift of the brethren of California to beitow, I did so with a recognition
of its importance and a genuine desire to be of service to the craft. It has
been my constant endeavor to administer the affairs of the office fairly
and impartially, with due regard to adherence to our fundamentals. I
appear before you today in all humility, cognizant of the fact that I have
not measured up to my own anticipations or the standards I had set for
myself ; but all my thought, energy and physical strength have been directed
toward the fulfillment of the purposes for which it was your pleasure to
select me to seek to accomplish.
It has been a strenuous year. Beset with adverse economic conditions
the world over, our Lodges have not escaped the evil results which have
obtained in connection with the problems of unemployment and depletion
of income from business, industrial and professional activities.
For the second time in our history the report of the Grand Secretary
will show that we have suffered a net loss in membership and how this loss
was incurred. While regrettable, this is not of itself so much a matter for
concern, and it is my hope that with a return of more favorable conditions,
which I believe we may confidently expect, these losses should cease. It is
a matter of concern, however, that so many of our Lodges are unable
to pay their Grand Lodge dues. This situation is at once reflected upon our
ability to make adequate provision for financing our Homes as well as
other normal activities of the Grand Lodge. During the present com-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

476

munication we shall find many difficult problems to be sctlved. I solicit
your earnest attention thereto for the reason that they will be of such
nature as to challenge your best thought and fraternal co-opera.tion.

Unemployment
-, Many of ·our brethren have, during the past three or four years, been
faced with the problems growing out of unemployment and its attendant
embarrassments. Curtailing of public and private enterprises in construction, ·retrenchments in commercial, · industrial and other activities have
conspired to increase' the number of those for whom there has been
opportunity for gainful occupation, and many members of our fraternity
have · felt the effects of this condition.
In the belief that the situation could with propriety be called to the
alteritioii of our Lodges, I addressed the following letter to the craft:
San Francisco, June 10, 1933.
To the Masters and Brethren of the Lodges of this Jurisdiction:
~ne of the vital problems confronting our Lodges today is that
resultmg from unemployment of large numbers of their members. The
effect of this condition has been a reduction in the ability of many brethren
to pay their dues and a very· considerable increase of appeals for relief.
Last year M.'. w:. Robert B. Gaylord, then Grand Master addressed a
communication to you in which he set forth his views upo~ the problem
of unemployment and strongly urged the appointment of competent and
energetic committees by all Lodges. I do not know the extent to which
the Lodges responded generally, but from information at hand, I feel that
much ·constructive good was accomplished. Believing that much can still
be done to relieve our unemployed brethren, I take this means of bringing
this impor~ant matt~r to Y?Ur a~tention and to urge that it be given your
·
prompt and energetic consideration.
. The following plan, in use by some of the Lodges and which has
proven successful, is recommended:
Two active committees are appointed in each Lodge : one on registration, the other on contact.
The duty of the registration committee is to list all unemployed
members · on a special card, noting such particulars as age, occupation,
f.lSjleri~nce, etc.
·
.. ,.·.The duty of the contact committee is to contact every employer pos~ibte, endeavor to enlist his co-operation and take note of his needs, if any,
a_nd· the · cham::es for preseht or future employment. It is, of course, partl-cttla'l'ly desirable that care should be used in the selection of the personnel
Qf. :these ,committees, because the contact committee particularly will be
y~.sted .. '¥~th the responsibility for selling the employer upon the idea of
co~operat10n.
·
,,' !,h~/iJ)ove is suggested because it is a plan now in use, and which is
prov1ltg ~trccessful. Other plans doubtless have been or will be worked
out. · The plan' or system devised is not so important as is the matter of
securing practical results, and I shall be very happy to be advised by any

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

481

Master as to what his Lodge is doing and what is being accomplished.
The important thing is that the need of our unemployed brethren is imperative and that we should feel it to be our duty as Masons to make it
possible for him to help himself by doing everything to aid him in obtaining employment.
Sincerely and fraternally,
FRANK W. MrxTER, Grand Master.
I am very happy to advise you that a great number of responses were
received and there is reason to feel that a large number of our Lodges
have by various means been instrumental in aiding unemployed members
in securing work. I commend to you, my brethren, the thought that we
should put forth every effort in the direction of helping a brother to find
a job. and thus put him in a position to help himself. Our Employment
Bureaus have done and are doing a splendid piece of work in this connection. The value of this service can be materially augmented by the
willing co-operation of the officers of Lodges and, in smaller communities,
through the appointment of a committee to carry out the purpose of a
program designed to be helpful in this respect.
Transfer of Trials
It is my duty herein to report transfers of trials to Lodges other
than those wherein the charges originated :
A case originating in George Washington Lodge No. 525 was transferred to Live Oak Lodge No. 61.
A case developing out of a retrial of a member of Live Oak Lodge
No. 61 was, upon the request of the Master of said Lodge, transferred
to McKinley Lodge No. 347.
A case originating in Big Bear Lodge No. 617 was, by order of Grand
Lodge at its communication last year, remanded for retrial. The first
trial having been held in Redland Lodge No. 300, I ordered the retrial to
be held therein, same to be presided over by Brother Oakley K. Morton,
Past Master of Evergreen Lodge No. 259, he having presided at the
former trial.
The case originating in George Washington Lodge No. 525 was made
the subject of extensive inquiry by me before ordering the transfer .
Finally, because of certain local elements in connection therewith being
of political character, I reached the conclusion that it would not only be
impossible to secure a fair and impartial trial in the Lodge of which the
accused was a member, but that the trial should be removed from the
immediate environment of the Lodge itself. With the feeling that the
interests of justice would be best served through such removal, I ordered
the trial transferred to Live Oak Lodge No. 61. I believe my action to
have been justified by the facts presented to me, as well as the authority
conveyed by Section 511, Digest of Decisions.

Early in the evening of March 10th, I was startled to receive the
news that an earthquake of consi'derable intensity had occurred in the
soutru;rn part of our state, the shock being felt m-0st heavily in Long
Beach and other nearby_ communities. Being at the time in Sacramento
in attendance upon the Legislature, I conferred with Brother William A.
Sitton, Senior Grand Warden, and as soon as possible thereafter established communication with Brother James B. Gist, our Deputy Grand
Master, in Los Angeles. As I was unable personally to visit the scene of
the earthquake, I requested Brother Gist to represent me in taking charge
of any matters affecting the welfare of our brethren which might be
brought to his attention. He immediately took steps to ascertain what
relief, if any, was needed and in other ways gave constructive assistance
to the working out of the problems involved. While there was reported
a most regrettable number of casualties resulting from the temblor among
residents of the stricken area, I am happy to be able to advise that none
of these were reported from among our membership.
Fotlowing my contacts with the Deputy Grand Mastei", I secured communication with the Grand Secretary by long distance telephone and
requested that he set up plans for taking care of emergency relief, should
soch become necessary. This was confirmed by telegram, and Brother
Whicher took the steps suggested; but no direct requests appearing, the
only contribution found to be desirable was that made to the Red Cross
in the amount of five hundred dollars.
With rare courage and enterprise, the citizens of the localities affected
entered almost at once upon a program of rehabilitation, and I am informed that this activity is making satisfactory progress.
It having come to my attention that a number of our Lodges had sustained damage to buildings or equipment, I appointed the f.oUowingnamed committee to make a survey of the situation and to advise me as t-0
the extent of the damage to Lodges :
Herbert C. G<>ldman, Los Angeles, chairman; Fred R. Pardee, Inglewood; Clark H. Shaw, Long Beach; Truman Van Dyke, Los Angeles;
Albert S. Crossfield, Wilmington.
This committee has filed its report, the result of some weeks of work
in assembling the desired information, and I desire at this time to express
my deep appreciation for the fine co-operation shown by Brother Goldman
and his committee for the energetic and intelligent manner in which they
approached and carried on tlte difficult task assigned to them.

I shall not here enter into details as to the extent of the damage and
financial losses incurred, this being left for the consideration of the
Finance Committee. Herewith, however, is a list of the Lodges, showing
their several locations, which were included in the report of the above
committee:

As one of the results of the disaster, many of our Lodges were
rendered homeless and a number of requests for permission to meet in
temporary quarters were received, a portion of these being accompanied
by requests for permission to change the dates of meetings for the time
being. Fully cogninnt of the provisions of the Constitution with respect
thereto, but recogniiing the fact that a situation amounting to a genuine
emergency existed, and acting under what I believed to be the general
powers of the Grand Master, the requested permissions were granted,
with the proviso, however, that when such other quarters were to be
occupied the same should first be approved by the District Inspector.

aid coming from other grand jurisdictions. This manifestation of truly
Masonic spirit is appreciated in a way beyond my power to express. Among

Grand Master's Conference
With a keen sense of personal disappointment I realized early in January that it would, because of my duties as a member of the Senate of the
State Legislature, be impossible for me to attend the Conference of (;rand
Masters at Washington. I therefore invited Brother James B. Gist, the
Right Worshipful Deputy Grand Master, to go in my stead; and he, at
considerable personal sacrifice, consented and attended the conference.
Brother Gist informs me that the meeting was replete with interesting
discussions and experiences and that much of benefit w<!-s gained through
contacts made with the Grand Masters of other jurisdictions and the opportunity thus created for an exchange of viewpoints and discussions of
many matters of interjurisdictional interest. The experience of Brother
Gist and those of our Grand Masters who have in the past attended these
conferences has been such as to lead me to express the hope that Grand
Masters in the future will attend in order that they may participate in the
deliberations to be had for the general benefit of all concerned.
For the information of the brethren I submit herewith the agenda of
the topics discussed at the conference. These cover a wide range of subject

Conforming to established custom and precedent, I caused to be issued
on January 16th of this year a proclamation for the fourteenth annual
observance of Public Schools Week in California. This constructive
activity,· originated by Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams during
his year as Grand Master, has shown constant, consistent progress as to
its observance and the very desirable results attained in bringing to the
attention of the citizens of ·our commonwealth the importance of that
greatest of all our institutions, our public schools. T)'ie proclamation
referred to above will be found in the appendix to this message. Because
o.f the character of the comment therein contained, certain parts thereof
might justify its rereading.
The report of our able and efficient Committee on Public Schools
Week will be presented to you during this communication,. and I would
strongly urge that you give it your eamest attention. You will learn from
this report, as I have learned from personal observation and inquiry, that
the observance this year was probably the most successful in point of
general interest and. attendance at the various meetings of. any heretofore
promoted. One of the reasons for this was the efficient and intelligent
manner in which details were worked out by the committee headed by its
splend:d chairman, Past Grand Master Adams. Another was that because

Officers' Associations
My observation during the past year has convinced me of the usefulness of this type of organization. These associations are functioning in
most of the districts of the jurisdiction and in my opinion have amply
demonstrated their worth. I have found that in many of our sparsely
settled districts, where the Lodges are at considerable distances apart,
many of the officers travel many miles in order to attend the meetings
there to discuss matters of interest, to exchange experiences and in many
ways to receive the benefits of the contacts with their brethren which are
thus afforded. I desire to express the hope that this movement shall continue, and that in districts where these associations have not yet been
formed, steps be taken to effect an organization, because I feel sure that
the carrying out of such program will return splendid dividends in the
satisfactions and fraternal benefits to accrue from this activity.
Our Masonic Homes and the Trustees
This afternoon you will have the opportunity to listen to the report
of the Trustees of your Homes. The report of the Board will be the
story of how the affairs of the Homes have been administered during
the past year. It will be a story containing much of human interest, as
well as one bringing to you the manifold problems connected with the
functioning of this important activity of our fraternity. I commend to
your earnest attention the reading of this report, not only for the interesting material it contains, but also for the reason that during this communication you are to be faced with the discharging of a difficult and perplexing
responsibility, that of making provision for adequately financing the support of our Homes for the coming Grand Lodge year. You need not be
~minded of the period of economic distress which has prevailed during
the past four years. The· effects of those conditions are, alas, too well
known. Individuals, firms, corporations, and, naturally, our Lodges, have
participated in the general situation to such extent as to make impossible
escape from a definite knowledge of their attendant effect. But through it
all our Trustees have shouldered the tremendous burden of carrying on
through adverse conditions in such way as to inspire us all with admiration for their constructive achievement in the face of great difficulties and
for their unselfish and untiring efforts to bring happiness and contentment

Board of Control and Boards of Relief
I feel that I should call to the attention of Grand Lodge the splendid
and constructive work being done by our Board of Control and the several
Boards of Relief. Under the capable and efficient functioning of the Board
of Control and Boards of Relief our program of administering relief
has gone forward throughout the year in most satisfactory fashion.
Numerous reimbursements for funds expended in behalf of distressed
brethren from other jurisdictions have been secured through the activities
of the Board of C-Ontrol which in all probability would not have been
received otherwise. The powers and duties of this Board under our Constitution are extensive, and properly so, because of their very nature. T he
report of this Board will be presented for your consideration next Thursday morning, and I invite your close attention thereto, because of the
interesting and important nature of this document.
The annual meeting of the Masonic Relief Association of the United
States met in Cincinnati October 5th and 6th this year. Feeling that the
presence of a representative of our Grand Lodge at the meeting of this
association could be productive of much benefit to the craft in California,
I requested Past Grand Master Reese, chairman of the Board of Control,
to represent us thereat. I recommend that his necessary traveling expenses
incurred in attending said meeting be paid by this Grand Lodge.
Our Boards of Relief are doing a fine work, and like the Board of
Control, are entitled to the sincere commendation of Grand Lodge for
the able and consistent manner in which their duties are being performed.
These Boards are well officered, and I am happy to be able to say, following considerable opportunity for personal observation, that they are performing a distinct service to our fraternity.
During the past year two <>f our Lodges attempted to withdraw from
the Boards of Relief in the cities wherein they were situated, but the
Board of Control disapproved the proposed action and submitted the cases
to me for attention. After carefully reviewing the entire matter, I approved the action of the Board of Control because I felt that to countenance such withdrawal would be a violation of the established policy of
this Grand Lodge, and for the further reason that the Board of Relief is
the only agency whereby the type of relief contemplated can be carried on
in orderly way in cities or communities having several Lodges within their
confines.

Masonic Education
In his message to the eighty-third annual .corrununication of Grand
Lodge in 1932, Grand Master Gaylord recommended that .a committee of
not less than three nor more than five be appointed by the incoming Grand
Master to study this question, and to report its conclusions at the next
communication of Grand Lodge. This ·recommendation was approved by
the Committee on Po-licy and General Purposes and adopted by Grand
Lodge. In conformity therewith I appointed the following committee:
Irving Magnes, Oakland; Jesse M. Whited, San Francisco; Lee T.
Mullen, Los Angeles; Ira F. Thampson, Los Angeles; A. Heber Winder,
Riverside.
The report of this committee, made after many months of intensive
study, will be rendered during the present communication. It is my sincere
hope that in the report of this committee there shall be found that which
can be made the basis for a constr11<;tive and intelligent program for the
use and benefit of the Lodges of this jurisdiction. I feel that there is
great need for something of this kind. In my addresses to the brethren
during the past year I have repeatedly stressed the importance of having
an activity of this type, authorized and carried on by Grand Lodge through
a proper agency, whereby our Lodges may be enabled to have as a part of
their regular operation, something of a nature to instruct, interest, entertain and educate (Masonically) the brethren. There are many reasons,
in my opinion, why this should be done. If we are to survive as a great
fraternity, striving always to attain those objectives pertaining to the
uplift and upbuilding of mankind for the betterment of humanity, and to
continue to foster and promote those precepts and ideals so intimately
interwoven in the fabric of our great Institution, we must do that which
will give promise of guaranteeing its permanency, instead of permitting its
possible lapse into lethargy and inactivity,
In connection with our consideration of this subject it should be
remembered that we are living in an era vastly different from that of only
a short generation ago. Development in facilities for transportation, communication, entertainment and in many other important matters has been
of such nature as to produce an environment and conditions vastly different
from those in which our fathers lived. It should be borne in mind that
the competition for the time of men is much greater than was the case
only a relatively few years ago, and that if we are to hold the interest of
the members of our fraternity we must do that which will keep alive in
them the allegiance they owe to their Lodges, to keep alive in their hearts
the desire to attend their Masonic meetings and-to lend their aid in carrying
on the functioning of our Institutian. For a long period of years following
the close of the World War our Lodges were busily employed in conferring the degrees of Masonry upon those who knocked at our doors and
were accepted. We did this almost to the exclusion of all else, and now

492

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

that there has come through the effects of the most serious economic
debacle in our history, a respite as it were, there is presented in the situation prevailing today an opportunity which we must not overlook to do
that which will keep our ·great fraternity in the forefront, where I am
su~e we all £:el i.t rightfully belongs. So it is my earnest hope that during
th.is co~mumcat1on there shall be ad?pted a policy and program dealing
with this matter, to the end that we may prevent the evil effects of inaction.
Reduction of Fees for the Degrees
In his message to Grand Lodge last year Grand Master Gaylord commented upon the fact that while no change in fees had been made by the
great _majority of our Lodges, there had nevertheless been a substantial
tendency toward such reduction, evidenced by the number of Lodges which
had submitted amendments to by-laws to that effect. During the first few
months of my incumbency as Grand Master, amendments to by-laws of
Lodges providing for reductions in the fees for degrees were submitted
for approval in such number as to appear to me to be a cause for real
concern. After giving this matter much consideration I addressed a communication to the several Lodges, calling attention to ~hat I felt to be the
evil ~ffect of this policy. This communication will be found in the appendix
to this report. All the amendments to which reference is made were 1 when
properly.certified, approved by me because I realize that it is solely within
the provmce of the Lodge to decide these questions. I felt however and
still feel that possibly in many cases due consideration as' to the effects
?£ red~ctions of this kind were not had, and for that reason felt justified
m callmg to the attention of the Lodges my views upon this subject. This
letter sets forth my viewpoint in such a way as to make it unnecessary here
t? repeat what was said therein. I would, however, again draw your attention t_o my comment upon this question in the hope that there may be found
therem enough .of merit to justify its rereading and consideration.
Consolidations
Throughout this report will be found many indications that a number
of our Lodges are not in the best of condition, and there is much reason
for the belief that little hope for improvement can be held out as to some
of them. I refer particularly to certain Lodges in metropolitan areas
small in membership, whose income has been found to be insufficient t~
me~t current expenses, and in many of which a condition approaching stagnat10n seems to prevail. I have always looked with favor upon the small
Lodge as being in many respects the most desirable type because of the
greater opportunity for better acquaintance among the members with the
result that generally a greater d~gree of fraternal spirit obtai;s and the
individual member secures more of pi;;r~on~l satisfaction thereby. But
Lodges, as all other forms of organizatiqn, can~ot overlook the practic~l
?r business side of affairs, and the Lodge that cannot° function within its
mcome might fail to justify its continued existence. It is my belief that

493

such Lodges should give careful consideration to the thought of effecting
a consolidation with another Lodge similarly situated, to the end that
through such consolidation a better Lodge, able to carry on as a useful
Masonic unit, could take the place of two weak and inefficient organizations.

Special Relief Cases
During the past year several cases were brought to my attention
wherein ~he desirability for prompt action seemed imperative. In regard
to each of them advice was sought from other officers of Grand Lodge,
Past Grand ,Masters and other brethren, and where the requested relief
was granted it was tendered only after careful inquiry and investigation,
and the conclusion had been reached that the expenditure of our funds was
fully justified. In this connection I have submitted to the Finance Committee the details, showing the names, amounts and the purposes for which
special relief expenditures were authorized.
For some of these matters we appear to have no well defined provision
for prompt and expeditious attention. It is my belief that the Grand
Master should be authorized to appoint a special committee when in his
judgment the same might to him be deemed necessary or desirable to assist
in the study of such cases of special nature as might be brought to his
attention. I refer to those cases of special character which do not at
present a~pear to fall within the purview of the Trustees of the Homes,
the Boards of Relief or the Board of Control to administer. I recommend
this for the consideration of this Grand Lodge. I further recommend that
so far as may be possible and advisable with respect to relief cases of
special nature, in so far as their requirements may be ascertained in advance, definite provision be made for same by this Grand Lodge for the
information and guidance of the incoming Grand Master.
Decisions
Many requests for rulings or decisions upon questions covering a wide
range of Masonic jurisprudence have been received during the past year.
A careful review of my files reveals the fact that in only one of these cases
was the question not already covered either in our Constitution or Ross'
Digest of Decisions, second edition. M,any were asked for the purpose of
clarification as to interpretation, in cases where the writer was genuinely
in doubt. Others, unfortunately, indicated either lack of search and study,
or inability to understand. In some cases questions were asked by a Past

Arrest of the Charter of Fairmount Lodge No. 435
Within a few days following my installation as Grand Master, a group
of Past Masters of Fairmount Lodge No. 435 called on me and, during
a detailed discussion, revealed the presence of a situation existing in said
Lodge as to be a cause for real concern. The statements made indicated
that for a considerable period of time rejections of petitions for the degrees
had reached a high percentage of those .received, that there was evidence
to support the belief that something in the nature of a conspiracy was
afoot as a result of which to unseat certain officers of the Lodge, and
further, a condition of inharmony which was threatening the peace and
fraternal well being of the Lodge as a useful Masonic unit. I thereafter
took steps to cause investigation to be made and learned that for some
years there had been prevalent rumors to the effect that this Lodge was
having internal strife and that its affairs had been made the subject of
study upon the part of some of my predecessors. Later, at my request, a
group of some twelve of the Past Masters of the Lodge, together with the
District Inspector, Brother R. G. Guyett, met with me to confer upon the
situation. As a net result of this conference I reached the conclusion that
the affairs of this Lodge were in such condition as to virtually preclude

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

495

possibility of adjustment without somewhat drastic action. Other stu~ies
carried on in various ways assisted me in arriving at the abo~e conclus.1on.
As a result of these investigations and studies l became convmced that·
There are two groups or factions among the members of the Lodge,
each faction desirous of directing the affair5 thereof.
That members of the Lodge have expressed the fear t~~t should they
present the petitions of friends for the degrees, such pett.t10ns would be
rejected in the ballot by a member or members of the opposmg group. .
That there had been a planned campaign for the purpose of unseatmg
certain officers of the Lodge at the annual election in December, 1932.
·
That there is some evidence to support the belief that a similar activity
was being initiated for the purpose of unseati?g certain other officers at the
forthcoming annual election in December this year.
Further, that a relatively small number of members are responsible
for the conditions prevailing in the Lodge; also,
That for the period of five and one-half years prior to July 1, 1?33,
more than forty-nine per cent of all the ~titians for the degrees received
by the Lodge had been rejected, notwithstanding the fact that the committees of investigation thereon had made full or full and favorable
reports.
Finally, being satisfied that there was little, if any, possibi~ity of the

In audition, the Grand Secretary forwarded a letter to be in turn
transmitted to the members of the Lodge, informing them of their status
and with suggestions in connection therewith.
Shortly thereafter I asked three of our Past Grand Masters to act as
a special committee for the purpose of further investigating th~ affairs of
the Lodge and after doing so to recommend to Grand Lodge with respect
to final action to be taken. This special committee will report its findings,
recommendations and c~nclusions at the first opportunity during the' present
communication.
Recommendations
Information reached me during the past winter which indicated that a
number of our Lodges were in unsatisfactory condition with respect to
finances, that unsound and unbusinesslike methods of handling the financial
affairs prevailed to some extent, and that the general situation was one to
justify some inquiry in regard thereto. Following some careful consideration, I invited three of our Inspectors, one of whom is a certified public
accountant, to serve as a special committee to analyze the financial statements of a considerable number of Lodges. This committee worked several
months and has filed its report, indicating that the statements of more
than one hundred Lodges had been analyzed and that this examination disclosed the presence of conditions of such nature as to warrant their consideration by this Grand Lodge. Among the conditions referred to may
be mentioned those growing out of the following causes :
( 1) Inadequate budgetary provision and in many cases no such provision.
(2) Amounts paid for rent wholly out of proportion to the normal
income of the Lodge. This includes leases in some cases made
apparently without proper regard to probable ability to comply
·
with the terms thereof.
(3) Some Lodges pay the Secretary a salary not warranted by income
and others spend too much money for a testimonial for the retiring Master.
(4) Life membership funds have in some cases been invested in the
stock of Temple Associations which are now in a condition' of
insolvency and from the assets of which there appears to be little

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

497

hope of salvage. This fund has in some cases been thus wiped out,
and the affected Lodges are .in no position to restore the same.
(5) Quite a number of Lodges include in their setting up of revenues
for the current operating expenses thereof, the funds received for
the degrees, a practice which I feel is open to question as to its
soundness.
I therefore submit for your consideration the following recommendations:
{l) That a new section be added to Article X of the Uniform Code
of By-Laws, requiring that the incoming Master in each year
appoint a Budget Committee whose duty it shall be to prepare a
budget on forms approved by the Grand Master and present the
same to the Lodge and the District Insp~tor.
:(2) That a new section be added to Section 150 of the Constitution,
requiring the Secretary to prepare a financial statement of the
Lodge each year as of December 31, and also an operating statement for the preceding year on forms approved by the Grand
Master.
(3) That all Temple Associations be required annually to prepare, on
approved forms, and to present to the Finance Committee of
Grand Lodge a budget for the succeeding year and a financial
and operating statement for the preceding year.
( 4) That no Lodge shall be permitted to enter into a lease of property,
real or personal, without the approval of the Finance Committee
of Grand Lodge, or that of the Special Committee on Building
Projects.
(5) That Section 88 of the Constitution be so amended as to limit the
expenditure of -Lodge funds for the purchase of a testimonial for
the retiring Master to $150.00.
(6) That Section 2 of Article VI of the Uniform Code of By-Laws
be amended to limit the salary of the Secretary to ten cents per
member per month.
Under our Constitution the Lodges are required to pay their dues. to
the Grand Lodge within fifteen days after the first day of · August each
year at the time the annual report of their transactions is submitted. Lodges
operate under a provision of the Uniform Code of By-Laws by which the
dues of members are payab1e quarterly in advance. While it is probably
true that many members pay their dues annually in advance, generally at
the first of the year, yet it is ~qually true that a majority of members pay
in quarterly installments. The requirement that the Grand Lodge dues be

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

paid in August works some hardship upon many of our Lodges, for the
reason that the Lodge must pay its dues at a time when its receipts are at
lowest ebb.
I therefore recommend that the Constitution be amended in such way
as to provide that the annual dues of Lodges to the Grand Lodge may be
made in two installments, one with the filing of the annual report, the
other on or before some definite date in February of each year.
