The Grand Secretary
For something over a quarter of a century the manifold and complex
duties of the Grand Secretary's office have been ably administered by our
genial friend and brother, John Whicher. Twenty-five Grand Masters
have come and gone during that period. They have, each in their turn,
received from our Grand Secretary, as I have received, that full measure
of co-operation, support and consideration it has been his delight, because
of his nature, to render. His genial and courteous disposition, his comprehensive knowl~ge of Masonry and its jurisprudence, and his unfailing
willingness to aid and assist "his less informed brother" have made smooth
many rough spots in the road during the past year. These qualities have
endeared him to all my predecessors, and it is with sincere and genuine
gratitude that I here express my lasting appreciation for the privilege of
having for the past year been so closely associated with that wonderful
man and Mason, John Whicher.
Long and consistent service should properly entitle the on~ performing
it to a respite. In my opinion our Grand Secretary is entitled to a rest,
both for his own well being and in order that at its conclusion he may
return to us with renewed vigor, health and energy, ready to resume his
duties.
I therefore recommend that Brother John Whicher be granted a three
months' leave of absence by this Grand Lodge in order that he may enjoy
a real vacation, and that such leave be made available to him at his pleasure
during the coming winter or early spring.
The Grand Lecturer
Our capable and efficient Grand Lecturer, Brother Thomas J. Baker,
·has completed the twenty-sixth year of his tenure as the custodian of the
esoteric work of this grand jurisdiction. So ably and conscientiously has
his work been done that we may well take full measure of satisfaction
in the knowledge that for purity of rendition and faithful adherence to
our forms and ceremonies our Lodges are uniformly most excellent.
I desire to express my deep appreciation for the splendid assistance
and the fine co-operation consistently accorded me during the term of my
office just closing by our Grand Lecturer. He has at all times been ready
and willing to give me the benefit of his knowledge and experience, has

499

has in every way given evidence of the possession of those sterling qualities
we all so much admire. I congratulate our Grand Lecturer upon his long
term of constructive service to Masonry, and felici tate this Grand Lodge
upon having received a service so ably performed.
Inspectors
Fortunate, indeed, is the Grand Master who serves through his year
with the co-operation of that fine body of men whom we know as our
District Inspectors, when that co-operation is manifested in the degree that
has obtained during the past Grand Lodge year. I know that the same
degree of fine co-operation has been the privilege of all my predecessors
to enjoy. Knowing most of these splendid Masons personally, I realize it
could not have been otherwise. Our Inspectors give unstintingly of their
time, their energy and even of their personal funds in carrying on the
important duties of their positions, and they do this without hope of fee
or reward, because of their love of and devotion to the principles of our
great fraternity. During the past year the assistance of this group has
been of inestimable value to me in the administration of the affairs of my
office, and I desire here to express my grateful thanks and sincere appreciation for their loyalty and the whole-hearted and unselfish support they
have so generously accorded me. My high regard and fraternal love to
you, my brethren of the corps of Inspectors of California.
Appreciation
It is with real pleasure that I give expression to my feeling of genuine
gratitude to the officers of Grand Lodge who have given me such unwavering, loyal and helpful aid and support during my term as Grand
Master. Many of them have, at considerable personal sacrifice, accompanied me on various journeys and in other ways have given abundant
evidence of their co-operation and interest. To enumerate them would be
but to submit the roster of the officers of Grand Lodge, because on every
hand there has been indicated on their part a sincere desire to render a
service in the giving of which they have contributed unstintedly of their
time and energy. To my fellow officers of Grand Lodge I offer my sincere
thanks for the truly wonderful assistance they have accorded me. This
manifestation of the true spirit of Masonry stands out most prominently
among the delightful experiences of the past year.
Conclusion
The stewardship with which you invested me one year ago is almost
ended, and in a few short days I shall transfer the mantle of authority and
hand the gavel to my worthy successor. May I bespeak for him the same
full measure of courtesy, consideration and fraternal regard it has been
my privilege to receiye at your hands. We are now about to engage upon

500

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the transaction of the business for which we have assembled, and we have
behind us the record of eighty-three years of com1tructive acbieveinent by
this Grand Lodge. May the record of this communication add another
bright page to that history. May we in the days to come use our best
endeavors to work together in a spirit of fratern:il concord and harmony,
so that when our labors are completed we may return to our respective
places of abode with .the satisfied consciousness that in all that was done,
the spirit of our great fratc:rnity was uppermost in our minds and hearts,
and that in all our actions we had been inspired by the principles of the
Golden Rule.
Yesterday is behind us; let us prepare for tomorrow. Let us look to
that Great Divinity Whom We Adore for inspiration and guidance in
attending to the important mattel"S before us. May we have faith in God,
faith in our institutions, and faith in our fellow men. And thus inspired
by faith, may we have the courage to look with confidence toward the
morrow and the fulfillment of its brighter promise.

Fourteenth Annual Observ<M1ce Public Schools Week

To the Masters, Wardens and Brethren of the Several Lodges of This
I urisdiction :
The genesis of the Annual Observance o.f Public Schools Week was in
the crisis with which public education in the United States was then
confronted.
And now again schools are being closed or maintained with shortened
terms ; children, particularly in rural districts,. are being denied the education to which they are entitled; educational service heretofore considered
absolutely essential to a modern American school system-such as the
maintenance of kindergartens, night schools, and special classes for mentally and physically handicapped children.---is being discontinued or materially curtailed; vocational courses and manual training for the "hand
minded" boy are being abandoned, and the opportunities suited to the
varying needs and capabilities of individual boys and girls are being materially restricted. In some respects the situation is not dissimilar to that
which immediately followed the World War, but with an entirely different
cause.
The Nation is in the throes of an acute social and economic disturbance. Every governmental activity is being rigidly scrutinized; and the
universal demand for a reduction in public expenditures has naturally
affected school budgets.
No real friend of our public schools wilt countenance waste and extravagance in their operation; nor will he view with complacency, in this

The old rule bv which petitioners were measured is good today, that
no man should seek the privileges of Masonry unless he has not only a
sufficiency for himself and family, but likewise has something to spare for
works of charity and mercy.
We have had in the past many periods of severe business depr~ssi?n,
and we have invariably had full recovery. At the annual commumcation
of 1871, Grand Master Leonidas ·E. Pratt, in his annual message, used
these words: "It would be a false and hollow pretense to congratulate
you today on another season of abundance and prosperity. The year has
not been one of general prosperity to this coi;nmonwealth, as idle h~ds,
diminished incomes and unusual calls for charity, have too often testified;
and I do not prop~se to mock your intelligence, nor .my own sense _of
truth and propriety by the assertion of ample rewards for honest mdustry." And at th~ next annual communication, 1872, this same Grand
Master opened his address to Grand Lodge by saying that "For twelve
months past we have been. the recipients of bounties uncle.served, :ind ~he
surroundings of today are m marked and happy contrast with the situation
a year ago. I could not then, without mockery of truth, congratulate you
on a season of material prosperity; but today the land is burdened with
the weights of surpassing harvests, and rich beyond precedent with its
wealth of fatness. Then we could rejoice at nothing save the doubtful
blessing that our lives had been prolonged to behold another annual festival· but today no wealth of gratitude can be in excess of what we owe the
ben~ficent Father, Whose paternal hand has given us all."
Our Lodges, it is true, are not increasing in members~ip, but a n:iere
increase of names on the rosters is no cause of congratulation at any time.
I fear we are overburdened with members with no lofty ambition to keep
faith with that first declaration required of every novitiate before he ever
enters a Lodge room, that he seeks the privileges of Masonry because of
a sincere wish of being serviceable to his fellow creatures. Better far that
our Lodges should secure a few men who may become workers in the
Masonic vineyard, who will be given intelligent attention by the officers and
the older brethren, who are able. to support themselves and their families
and yet have something for works of charity and mercy, than that fees
should be reduced merely for the accommodation of petitioners and the
doubtful propriety of an immediate accumulation of money which later
will almost of a surety be required for the relief of those who may be
induced to join because of reduced fees.
FRANK W. MrxTER, Grand Master.

San Francisco, May 25, 1933.
Dear Sir and Brother:
A Special Election will be held in California on Tuesday, June 27,
1933 at which the voters will express their sentiments with respect to
elev~n propositions submitted to the people by the direction of the State
Legislature.
All are important measures, but reference is herein made to only four
of them.
No. 1 is a constitutional amendment calling for the repeal of the
present taxing system and proposing what is generally known as the Riley-

GRAND LODGE 0~' CALIFORNIA

'

503

Stewart Tax Plan. If adopted it will provide a different basis of support
for public education in our state and will ameliorate the burden now
imposed on real estate.
No. 3 is a measure to legalize betting on horse races under the parimutuel plan.
No. 4 is a constitutional amendment which would increase the amount
of property not now subject to taxation by exempting private and parochial
schools. It would apply to all private educational institutions of less than
collegiate grade not conducted for profit and would exempt not only buildings and equipment with grounds not exceeding ten acres in area but
also all securities and income used exclusively for the purposes of' education.
The proposition with respect to the repeal or retentim1 of the Eighteenth Amendment will appear on a separate election ballot.
As a good citizen it is your duty to vote at this election; and if you
are not to be at home on election day you should avail yourself of the
absent voter's p.rivilege by making your application to the County Clerk
(or Registrar of Voters) not more than twenty, nor less than five days
·
'
before the election.
The Masonic Fraternity makes no effort to influence the judgment
or control the action, of any of its members; and how you vote must b~
determined by the dictates of your own conscience. It is, however, hoped
that every brother will carefully study the various measures in order
that he may be fully informed and advised with respect to the consequences of the adoption or rejection of any proposition.
Sincerely and fraternally yours,
FRANK W . MrxTER, Grand Master.

Unpaid Grand Lodge Dues
Last year fifteen Lodges failed to pay their full dues to Grand Lodge,
and by resolution presented by the Finance Committee and adopted, the

605

delinquent Lodges were requested to execute notes for the amounts due,
payable six months after October 14, 1932. These notes have been paid
with- the exception of six amounting to $1,587.20.
For the year ended July 31, 1933, fifteen Lodges have made partial
payments, the balance due being $5,973.80. Twenty Lodges have made no
payments, the delinquency amounting to $7,869.75. The .t otal of unpaid
dues by Lodges is $13,843.55. This delinquency is largely because ef frozen
funds in closed banks and building and loan associations, and not by
reason of depleted treasuries.

Conference of Grand Secretaries
At the last annual communication Grand Lodge recommended that
th~ Grand Secretary should attend the annual conference of Grand Secretaries at Washington, D, C., and appropriated five hundred dollars to
cover the expenses of the trip. This action by Grand Lodge was much
appreciated by me, but inasmuch as it appeared that our revenues should
be conserved, I took the liberty of declining to make the journey and left
the full amount of the appropriation in the treasury.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Budget
The budget compiled last year by the Finance Committee estimated
the receipts for the current fiscal year would be $127,849.00, and the disbursements, including appropriations, would be $122,628.60. The actual
receipts were $127,242.16, and the actual disbursements were $123,599.88.
The assets of Grand Lodge as of July 31, 1933, amounted to $12,392.11 in
cash and $165,089.80 in sound securities, besides 58,955 shares of Masonic
Temple stock, now paying a small dividend. The net increase in Grand
Lodge assets over last year was $3,350.82.
Tokens for Veteran Masons
The demand for fifty-year buttons fqr those of our brethren who have
reached the half-century mark in Masonry continues. In the year last
past 110 of these tokens have been issued, making a grand total of 891
since the inauguration of the custom in our jurisdiction. The dean of the
veterans _this ~ear is James Harrison Henry, San Jose Lodge No. 10,
wh~ received his Master's degree April 27, 1869, in Lincoln Lodge No. 199,
Blairstown, Iowa, and affiliated with San Jose Lodge August 5, 1889. This
vetera~ bro~her ~as for many years one of the outstanding business men
of Cahforma. His home now is at Portland, Oregon.

To the M. ·.
Grand Lodge of CoUfornia:
Another year has just closed. I he1-ewith 'submit my twenty-sixtti annual
report, giving an account ·of my activities. It has been quite similar ·in
many respect~ to the last few years. While most of the Lodges have done
!mt Utt1e degree wcirlr, they ·have all ·been doing their Masonic duty in
taking care of -the wants of their needy brethren as they should. Many
of the brethren have had a hard time in the payment of their dues, but
most (J}f the LOOges have met this situation by allowing the members to
pay on the installment plan, which !<ias .proven very satisfact©ry and has
been the means of getting dues that they possibly would not have gotten
otherwise. Many brethren have been suspellded. I am sure that some -0f
these could have been saved had the proper investigatkm been made of
each case.
I have visited almost every district in the State, ·arid have found the
Lodges 1n fairly good position, most of them ta.king advantage of the
opportunity in providing· social and .educational programs for their ·members. T!Ms -is highly commendable, and has also a tendency to ina-ease
attendance.
'
I have reports from all ·t he Inspectors, and they report the Lodges
under their supervision, most of them at least, in fine style in spite of the
hard times. This speaks well for the stabiiity of the Lodges, although
some of them have had to resort to their reserve funds. I am quite sure
that a bright future awaits us shortly, which wiU be most gr~tifying, and
we will soon forget the lean years.
I have made quite a number ·of visits with the M. ·. w. ·. Grand Master
this year to the LOO~s and have attended many Grand Lodge ceremonies.
All have been much appreciated by the brethren. These contacts with the
brethren and Lodges have produced. good res1dts.
Much has been said in the past about .the cond.i.tcting-of funerals. This
is, however, a very important subject, and one that each Master should

522

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

consider very carefully, for it is one of the Masonic ceremonies that is
done before the public, and should always be well done. There are more
favorable comments on this ceremony when well conducted, not only from
the brethren, but from the public. Masters should ask some Past Master
or a member of his Lodge, who has a good voice and a good appearance,
to act for him in case he does not.feel competent or capable of doing the
ceremony nicely. The performance of this not only reflects on his Lodge
but on the fraternity as well. The public is not always as charitable as
they might be in their comments. This is not a criticism, but merely
calling the attention of the Master to a very important subject. I trust
that each Master will give due consideration and act accordingly.
Two of my earnest and enthusiastic Inspectors have been called to
their reward: Dr. Samuel Tilden Gillispie, Inspector of the lllth district,
died June 23, 1933, and Cralis Dexter died July 3rd. Dr. Gillispie had been
Inspector for about four years. He was a very conscientious man and
Mason and beloved by his brethren. Brother Dexter had been in ill health
for a year or two. He was a good man and Mason, a devoted husband and
loving father. He had been Inspector for more than ten years, a competent
and efficient one. Both these brethren will be greatly missed by the Grand
Lodge and by their Lodges. May their souls rest in peace.
I desire to express my thanks and appreciation to Brother Whicher,
Grand Secretary, and his assistant, Brother Hobbs, for the many courtesies
extended .to me in ·his office during the year.
There is quite a problem confronting some of the newer and small
Lodges, that vitally affects their existence. With comparatively no candidates for some time and many of the members unable to pay dues, and the
funds of the Lodge getting low, they are in real distress. This could
largely be avoided by consolidation. Of course, I realize that most of these
Lodges, for sentimental reasons, do not desire to lose their existence, but
you cannot maintain a Lodge on sentiment alone. I believe that some of
the Lodges would be willing to consolidate, at least for awhile, thereby
saving the upkeep and overhead expenses; then when times improve they
could form another Lodge, if desired. I believe this is the only solution
for some of the Lodges; at least it is worthy of consideration.
Many thanks are due the Grand Lodge and the brethren for the leave
of absence accorded me last Grand Lodge. I had a most enjoyable vacation on my trip East. May I again express my appreciation to the Grand
Lodge for their continued confidence in me as your Grand Lecturer.
Respectfully submitted,
THOMAS

J. BAKER.

Referred to the following committee: William B. Ogden,
·
Lloyd E. Wilson and Alfred F. Breslauer.

ignored. In the merciless competition of the present active American
life we must therefore apply our code.
I am convinced that in the reconstruction work of our country
the first admonition of Freemasonry must be applied if we are to
endure as a powerful nation. It appeals to me as reasonable to expect
the members of that organization to exercise that doctrine and endeavor to influence others to
likewise. "No man should ever enter
upon any great or important U'1dertaking without first invoking the
blessing of God," is an admonition just as important to a nation's
life as to a Masonic life. Remember, it is the combination of a competency of Divine Wisdom and the pure principles of Freemasonry
that make him the ideal man and Mason. A republic can be no better
than its citizens. History is replete with examples of nations who
experienced a rapid dedine when they abandoned their spirituat faith.
"Where there is- no vision the people perish" is a maxim never successfully contradicted. True, our part in the drama of life is· brief. If
you feel otherwise, wander around through the big trees· of California,
which average 3000 years of age, or study the water hi-story of this
State as interpreted by the geologists. You will be surprised >iow you
diminish in size. Keep in mind, however, that we are building for the
fuhtre, and our children will carry on the lofty ideals we instiII in them.
A beloved American leader told us: "The things of the bol!ly are good;
the things of the intellect better; but best of all are the things of the
soul; for, in the nation as in the individual, in the long run it is character that counts.-" "Chihlren do as their parents do. not as they say."
Juvenile p.roblems will decrease in this generation and those to come
when all adults keep in mind that we should be building a spiritual
temple and fitting our minds as living stones to be used in that eternal
home.. Then will come success and prosperity, because spiritual faith
brings confidence, which Cicero defines:

do

"Confidence is that feeling_ by which the mind embarks in
great and honorable courses with a sure hope and trust in itself.'"

world is getting smaller. Inte:r-conummication is now a matter of
minutes, and we listen to.world events and addresses on international
issues almost daily. How is this enlarged picture affecting us? The
numerous frictions and "isms" of the OM World are infecting our
public life more and more. It is human nature to learn rapidly the
words of songs one hears sung freq11ently. The need for a 100. per cent
Americanism is therefore a vital one. Our brother, that outstanding
Am.erican of all time, Theodore Roosevelt, aptly phrased it when he
proclaimed "There is no place in this country foe hyphenated Americans." The Declaration of Independence and the Constitution of the

In the vast orchestra playing the symphony of life each can express himself through his chosen instrument. The tones he produces
however, n:iust blend into the harmony of the music. If played alon~
or out of time the effect is discordant. Many who placed their all in
mater!al wealth and lost have committed suicide. The collapse of
mat_enal va.lues has left many people unbalanced in numerous ways.
Social readJustment must follow as our citizenship regains its natural
balance. As this balance is regained it will develop a new social life.
~asonry i~ ~urely a social relationship, teaching men the right principles of hvmg. The opportunity is here for it to do a wonderful
work. In Masonry there is no question but what I am my brother's
keeper. Why not endeavor to stamp this new social life with those
fundamental principles of our Institution which have proven so worthwhile to us?
Today's challenge, then, to our fraternity is to apply more completely its principles within our ranks; that duty we owe to God,· that
loyalty we owe to our country, that fellowship we owe to our neighbor
and brother. That doctrine, in real action, will influence scores of
others beyond the boundaries of our organization, not only of the
present generation but also the coming generation. We are charged
to assume that leadership in the present recovery program.
"We are all blind until we see
That in the human plan
Nothing is worth the making if
It does not make the man.
"Why build these cities glorious
If man unbuilded goes?
In vain we build the world unless
The builder also grows."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SEGREGATION
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The committee to which was referred the segregation of the various
matters contained in the address of the Most Worshipful Grand Master
reports as follows :
The message which the Most Worshipful Grand Master has submitted for your approval is a complete and comprehensive report of his
stewardship during the year just past. It is full of the kindly spirit of true
brotherhood which characterizes the sterling qualities of our Grand Master.
A study of his address makes us realize immediately that the deliberations
of this communication of Grand Lodge have been launched with a message
·which instills in us renewed hope and a determination to carry on the high
principles for which Masonry stands.
The various matters contained in the address will receive the attention
of Grand Lodge through its regular committees, and we therefore recommend that they be"segregated and referred as follows:
To the Committee on policy and General Purposes, we refer those
portions of the address under the headings :
3.2 per cent beer.
Masonic education.
Special relief cases.
Recommendation No. !-referring to amendment to Article 10 of
the Uniform Code, concerning the budgets for subordinate Lodges.
Recommendation No. 2-referring to addition to Section 150 of the
Constitution, concerning annual financial statement of subordinate
Lodges.
Recommendation No. 3-referring to annual budget and financial
statement of temple associations.
Recommendation No. 4-referring to lease of property, real or personal, by subordinate Lodges.
Recommendation No. 5-referring to amendment to Section 88 of
the Constitution, limiting expenditure of Lodge funds for purchase of testimonial.
Recommendation No. 6--referring to Section 2 of Article 6 of the
Uniform Code of By-Laws, concerning an amendment to limit
the salary of the Secretaries of subordinate Lodges.
To the Committee on Jurisprudence, we refer those portions of the
address under the headings :
3.2 per cent beer.
Recommendation concerning the changes in Sections 54 and 137 relative to qualifying Senior Deacons.
Arrest of charter oJ Fairmount Lodge No. 435.

under the heading :
Board of Control and Boards of Relief, referring to the financing of
the trip to the meeting of the Masonic Relief Association of the
United States, held at Cincinnati, Ohio.
That portion of the Grand Master's address, under the heading, "The
Grand Secretary," wherein ·he recommends that the Grand Secretary be

opinion of the committee is worthy of the earnest consideration of Grand
Lodge, and we refer this matter to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes for their recommendation.
In closing this report, we desire to compl4ment the Grand Master on
the brevity of his decisions, and the graciousness of his manner in .the
conduct of the affairs of Grand Lodge.
Most Worshipful Grand Master, the brethren of this Jurisdiction
express to you their sincere and lasting appreciation.

Homes.

MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA
TRUSTEES REPORT
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Trustees herewith submit the forty-second annual report of
the property, condition and operation of the Masonic Homes for the
fiscal year ended July 31, 1933, as required by the Constitution.
Immediately after ·t he close of Grand Lodge in October 14, 1932,
the Board organiz~d as follows:
President, Charles M. Wollenberg, term expires 1934;
Vice-President, James B. Gist, Deputy Grand Master;
Chas. Albert Adams (1933);
.
John Stewart Ross (1935);
·s .a muel E. Burke (1936);
William A. Sitton, Senior Grand Warden;
Randolph V. Whiting, Junior Grand Warden;
William P. Filmer, Treasurer ex officio;
John Whicher, Secretary ex officio.
We reporte4 to you last year that "it was not necessary to remind
you of the business situation nor of the difficulties incident to a proper
maintenance of the Homes, other than to report that the increase of
dependents of Lodges and the decrease of our revenues have added
burdens to the conduct of our business as your agents charged with
relieving Lodges of the care of their indigent members, to an extent
never before experienced." In the year just closed, 118 adults and 84
children have received outside aid at a cost of $45,000; 29 children
and 90 adults have been admitted to the Homes. On the 31st of
August, 1933, the Home at Decoto had 359 wards of the Lodges, a
net increase for the year of 18. Death took its usual toll of the old
folks at the Home, 66 of whom passed away. There were six departures from Decoto, and 17 children were honorably dismissed from
the Coviria Home.
Responsibility of Lodges to Children
Last June 17 children were honorably dismissed by reason of
graduation from 'high school, or because of having attained the age
of 18 years. In every instance the Lodge was notified and requested
to, provide employment for such children, and in no instance was
employment secured. It is the age-old truism, "Out· of sight, out of
mind." But the members of our Lodges ought to assume some of the
responsibility for the future of those of its wards who, until graduation

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

533

from the Masonic Home, are cared for through your Trustees· by the
entire fraternity; and it does not reflect credit on the individual members of Lodges to shirk the duty of taking a fatherly interest in the
boys and girls of deceased brethren. These children are dismissed at
an age when they seriously need a warm and welcome friendship on
the part of the brethren; they need employment; they need the fostering assistance of friends who can be trusted to direct them in paths
of good conduct; they need to be directed in their new environment
to keep good company. They stand in truth "where the brook and
. river meet,'' and will become good and usefu) men and women, real
ornaments to society, if given the _personal attention of the brethren
of their respective Lodges. The converse is, that without this personal
attention they are too apt to become discouraged and fall into evil
ways. Every Lodge should take special pride in securing employment
for its dependent children.
Responsibility of Lodges to the Aged
In numerous annual reports we have referred to the evident
efforts of Lodges to shirk responsibility to their aged members and
to their endeavors to attempt to throw the care of such members
on to the entire fraternity-that is, on to the Homes. In our annual
report for the year 1925 we stated that "Your Trustees are embarrassed at times by being compelled to deny applications for admission,
although the widest latitude is accorded to all Lodges, consistent with
w)lat we conceive to be our duty to the whole membership of the
jurisdiction," then citing an instance of a brother and his wife who had
been denied admission to the Home on the ground that the applicant
had received his· Masonic degree only two years prior to application,
at the age of 72, and had been suffering from a severe heart ailment
for seven years before he became a Mason We took the view that
the responsibility for the care of this distressed member and his wife
belonged not to the entire fraternity, but solely to the Lodge, and
denied the application.
It is with some hesitancy that this lack of Lodge responsibility
should be again referred to, because the brethren who compose our
Lodges are rightfully to be assumed as being far-seeing men of sound
judgment. But cases such as are noted above continue to be brought
before us. Only three months ago four applicants were denied admission, all of them doubtless being worthy men. One was the case
of a brother who was made a Mason at the age of 68, who owned no
property at the time of his admission and carried no life insurance.
The second case was that of a member who carried $5,500.00 life
insurance and was in receipt of State aid in the sum of $30.00 a month.
He lived with a daughter, but as the report of his condition disclosed,
"he had a tendency to complain regardless of what is done for him."

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The third case was that of a man 55 years of age, married to a
capable woman, nothing seriously the matter with him physically,
but who had been out of employment for a considerable time. The
Board is in full sympathy with this man, as well as with the thousands
of ·other men and women who are unable to secure employment
through no fault of their own; but it is obvious that the Masonic
Homes cannot admit those whose only distress is that of temporarjr'
lack of gainful empl<Jyment. The care of this brother is properly the
problem of the Lodge and the community in which he lives.
The fourth case was that of a member who was received by dimit
from another jurisdiction in July, 1929, at the age of 69. At the time
of his election to membership he was holding a political job at a
salary of one hundred dollars a month, with no other resources.
Now, it was not a pleasant task for your Trustees to deny the
applications of the Lodges for these brethren. They doubtless needed
help, yet we adhere to the proposition that Lodges must take note of
the probable liability that attaches to every member, and not try to
shift the burden of relief to the fraternity at large.
These problems and embarrassments are presented that you may
be informed of the manifold and pressing demands made by the
Lodges. We are endeavoring to faithfully administer the wonderful
trust assumed by us as the agents of this truly sympathetic and
generous jurisdiction-the fifth largest in the United States and the
sixth largest in the world-and as stated in our report for the year
1926, "in the hope that Lodges. may realize that the Homes are maintained by you for the purpose of caring for those of our brethren who
are actually dependent, their wives, wid<Jws, mothers and children,
and not for mere convenience." And, too, the individual Mason should
not forget that he has obligations to relieve the distresses of his lessfavored brethren, and that all relief work should not be. left to the
Lodges or the Homes.

Finances
Applications for admission to the Homes and for outside relief
continue to increase, and revenues-particularly from fees of initiates
-have decreased. In the year just dosed, Lodges remitted the dues
of nearly eight thousand members, with a consequent unavoidable
loss of Homes revenue. Ten years ago, with a membership of one
hundred thousand, and a twenty-dollar fee from each initiate the
cash receipts from that source alone amounted to $173,320, wlth a
~u.r~lus of funds for building purposes. This last year, ~ith a tax on
1mhates of twenty-five dollars, the receipts from the same source
amounted to only a little over $56,000.
.Many ~odges have not paid Home dues. Six Lodges are still
partially delinquent for dues that should have been received at the
close of the fiscal year July 31, 1932. For the fiscal year just closed,
twenty-four Lodges have made only partial payments, and thirty-two
_Lodges made no payments at all! This failure to pay was due in most
1~st~nces to frozen assets in closed banks and building and loan assoc1at10ns, not because of depleted treasuries and in the course of
revived business will be received. Yet with ~II this we are in much
better condition than many other jurisdictions. For instance, in one
Gran? Lodge with a membership last year of 140,000, three hundred
and e1ghtee~ ~od~e~ defaulted in their dues to the amount of $160,000.
One large JUnsd1ct10n showed a deficit this year of $215,000 in its
Home fund.
We are fully aware of the difficulties and financial embarrassment of some of our Lodges, and of their loss of revenue occasioned
by the non-payment of dues by unemployed members; of their frozen
assets by reason of closed banks, and the reduced numbers of applic~nts for memb.er.ship: We are in full sympathy and understanding
with all these d1fficulhes, and of the desire on the part of numerous
Lodges to have Grand Lodge reduce the per capita tax. But the cold
fact remains that we all have serious obligations to the poor of our
fraternity .which cannot be evaded and which should be squarely
faced. It is not necessary to remind our brethren that it requires
money to conduct the Homes; but what Mason is there who will not

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

freely and cheerfully give something-even at some sacrifice of pleasures or luxuries-to enable our great fraternity to suitably maintain
the aged men and women, wards of the craft, whose evening days
would be in gloom and despair without the helping hand and the
willing purse of their brethren? What Mason is there who can view
the dependent children under .our care without a pull at the heartstrings and a moistening of the eyes, and a feeling of thankfulness
that he is permitted to be one who has assisted in part in bringing
happiness to the many boys and girls who, except for the fostering
care of the Masonic fraternity, would be wards of public institutions
or roaming our streets as vagabonds. Our giving to these Homes is
truly a benediction.
Your Trustees, with the hearty co-operation of the employes of
the Homes, have instituted many economies during the past year,
and have brought the budget down to a point where the income from
the per capita tax, fees of initiates, and sundry other revenues, will
undoubtedly balance the necessary expenditures.
Notwithstanding mounting costs, we feel that the present per
capita tax should not now be increased, and that it will meet all the
requirements for the conduct of the Homes. We therefore ask that
the same be fixed at seventy-five cents for the ensuing year.

To the Board of Trustees, Mas01iic Homes of California:

We certify that, in our opinion, the attached statements, with
exception as to the stated value of the securities on hand, and the
actual values of the fixed properties at Decoto and Covina, set forth
the condition of the Masonic Homes of California at July 31, 1933.
From a general review and examination of the records~ we are of the
opinion that all receipts and disbursements are properly stated.
All of the general securities listed under Schedule B-3 have been
donated, with the exception of ten shares of stock of the Glendora
Water Company stated on the books at cost. The stated, ~r book
value, in the case of donated securities represents the value placed
upon the securities at the time of donation. Where such value has
been difficult to determine, because of its being an unlisted or closely
held security, or of uncertain value, then the par, face, or a nominal
value is entered on the books solely as a matter of record. Notes
receivable values represent the unpaid portion of notes receivable on
hand. Insurance policies are listed on the books at the face or value
recoverable upon death of the insured, as a matter of record.
The securities contained within the Students' Loan Fund, Schedule B-2, are stated on the books at cost, with the exception of the
100 shares of Masonic Temple Association received by donation and
valued on the books at par.

PROCEEDINGS OF TH:BI

Report of Superintendent-Decoto Home

To the Board of Trustees:
I hereby present for. your consideration my twenty-fourth annual
report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home at Deco.t o, California,
for the year ending August 31, 1.933.
In making a report of the activities of the Decoto Home for the
past year, I find that there have been but few changes, · and the
management of the Home has been substantially the same as in
former years.
We have endeavored to maintain a social atmosphere in keeping
with the ideals of our fraternity and to bring to all the members of
our family Gs large a measure of contentment as possible into the
daily lives of alt who are enjoying the many comforts of our Home.
This has been a busy year, and the admission of new members
and the personal care given each one has created a splendid spirit
throughout the several departments of the Home.
Members-There are at the present time 359 residents-195 men
and 164 women. During the year 90 persons have been admitted, 48
men and 42 women. Sixty-six have passed away-33 men and 33
women. There have been 6 departures.
Health-The general health of the Home has been good, with
the exception of those who are infirm and feeble owing to advancing
years.
Hospital-There are now 50 of our members being cared for in
the hospital department. The facilities afforded there enable our
physician and nurses to give every care and attention to those who
are ill. Day and night nurses are in constant attendance. Additional
room, when needed, can be provided by the completion of the interior
of the second floor of the two wings of the hospital building.
Industrial-There has been a greater individual effort on the
part of the members of our large· family to interest themselves in the
general routine work and to contribute their part, according to their
strength, to the general well-being of the Home. During the past
year a large number of men and women residents have contributed
to the welfare of the Home by their services in the engine room,
carpenter, paint and barber shops, care of the garage, mail, passenger
and freight service, kitchen, pantry, vegetable room, laundry, storerooms, office work, library and reception room$, telephone switchboard, floral decorations, care of elevators, flower beds, watering trees
and shrubs, care of walks, roads and lawns, vegetable garden and
poultry yards, janitor work and many other light duties in a general

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

559

way. Dur.ing the year, all minor repairs have been attended to by
brethren of the Home. The women of the Home attend to the
making, marking and mending of linen, sheets, pillow slips, table
cloths and napkins, etc., also assist in the preparing of fruit and
vegetables in the kitchen and dining rooms, diet kitchen, clerical
work, attending telephone calls, showing visitors about the Home,
music room, care of their rooms, etc., and general light household
duties.
Farm-As heretofore, the greater part of the hill ranch has been
leased or on cash rental. The farm has supplied plenty of fruit, figs,
berries and nuts for table use, the surplus being dried and stored for
future use. The returns from the hay crop have been fair. The garden
has supplied a variety of vegetables, etc. The chicken ranch has
furnished all the eggs for table use, the surplus being sold or preserved for winter use. Our deep well pump continues to furnish a
plentiful supply of water for household, garden, irrigating purposes,
also for fire protection.
Library and Club Rooms-There are now 6000 books on the
shelves of our main library and branches located in the several departments of the Home. The Masonic Hill branch of the Alameda
County Free Library enables our family to obtain many of the latest
books and an ·opportunity for special ones. In addition, we are the
recipients, through friends and members of the fraternity, of daily
papers, magazines and periodicals, which are placed on the tables
of the library, club rooms, and the ladies' social halls.
Social Life-The social life has been greatly enriched during the
year by literary and musical entertainments given by generous volunteers from Oakland, San Francisco; and nearby towns. Our Assembly
Hall, with our modern stage and moving picture equipment, has
made possible ·the presentation of dramatic plays given by visiting
Lodges and friends, all of which has contributed to the pleasure of
the members of our-family. The evening programs often close with
dancing. Card parties are held in t he library and reception rooms
every Tuesday evening. Chorus practice on Friday evenings. Every
Sunday afternoon finds the residents of the Home with their visiting
friends congregated in the Assembly Hall for Sunday service, after
which a selected program is given by the Home orchestra.
All holidays have been observed with appropriate exercises. The
specials are those held on New Year's Eve, New Year's Day, Lincoln's Birthday, Washington's Birthday, Easter, Memorial Day,
Fourth of July, Halloween, Thanksgiving Day and Christmas. All
these programs are prepared and presented by the mem bers of the
Home.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GKANU L.ODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The croquet grounds are well patronized during the day.
A reading class for the blind and those with failing eyesight meets
daily in the reception room, at which time the daily papers, etc., are
read to them by one of the ladies of the Home.
A number of the members have radio sets in their rooms. This
privilege is particularly appreciated by those who are blind, and by
those being cared for in the hospital department. The club rooms
and the reception room also have radios, and can be enjoyed _at any
time during the day or evening.
Arrangements are made whereby members of the family, a few
at a time, may enjoy an outing to nearby places of interest, also an
occasional visit to nearby Lodges and Eastern Star Chapters. During
the year many trips were made to Oakland, San Francisco, and
towns in the vicinity of the Home.
Grand Master Frank W. Mixter, officers and members of the
Grand Lodge have made a number of visits to the Home during the
year, and a large number of brethren from various Lodges have
spent many pleasant hours with us. The number of visits this year
shows increasing interest in the welfare of the Home family.
I desire again to thank the members of the Board of Trustees
for the kindly consideration always given in meeting the varied problems of the Home, which has in no small degree shaped and moulded .
the moral and spiritual strength of our family life.

To the Trustees of the Masonic Homes:
During another year the Covina Home has carried on its appointed
work of protecting and caring for dependent children of Masons in
this jurisdiction. A little boy in the Home had heard about the
depression, and that it would probably have some effect on what he got
for Christmas. Christmas came, and with it many toys and playthings. Surveying his gifts he said, "I hope there'll be another depression next year." In spite of the depression the w°"k of the Home has
gone on. It has been a year of retrenchment of expense, of doing
without many things which we would like to have had, but the essential mission of the Hom.e has continued to be accomplished.
The buildings an<l furnishings have been maintained in the best
repair possible with a reduced budget, though they are beginning to
show the result Of several years during which practica1ly no replacements of furniture or floor coverings have been made, painting reduced to the minimum, and many other repairs postponed.
D~ring the past summer, in order to reduce· expense, the use of
the summer camp, Camp Tucker at Balboa, was greatly curtailed.
Instead of moving the whole membership of the Home to the Camp
for two months, small parties were sent there for stays of from one
to three weeks. Fortunately there was little oppressively hot weather
at Covina this summer, and the children got along very happily. In
this connection the splendid swimming pool at the Home, donated
three years ago by Mrs. Almina Runyon, was a life-saver. No part of
our equipment is so much used or enjoyed as this pool.
No material change has occurred during the year in the mode of
operation of the Home or its plan of handling the children. The
accommodations for boys are taxed to the limit; there are a few
vacancies for girls. For some reason there is a tendency for our aid
to be demanded more frequently for b-Oys than for girls. Of the last
100 admissions, 58 were b-Oys and 42 were girls.
Our chief aim continues to be to give the boys and girls who
come to us a real home, a place of abode where they can have those
privileges of happiness, security, and training which are accorded to
the child in a good private family. It can be truly said that we have
little institutional repression and discipline. We think it better to
have too little discipline than too much. Yet abundant evidence comes
to us that our children are well behaved. They are welt thought of
by the townspeople of Covina, and they have exce11ent rating in the
public schools where they attend with other chifdren. They do well
after they leave us. In some instances, perhaps, th~y temporarily
show the effect of "too much good treatment" in the Home, but, on

588

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

the other hand, they exhibit unusual adaptability and capacity to
adjust themselves to the hard necessities of life.
One of the best measures of what we are doing for the children
is found in their own comments after they have left us and seen
something of the outside world. Last year a 15-year-old girl was
withdrawn from the Home by a wealthy aunt, and placed in an
excellent and high-class boarding ·school in the East. After being
there for a time she wrote to one of her friends in the Covina Home:
"I have told everyone here that I come from the Home and
have shown them pictures I have of it, and they all look at me and
ask why I ever left such a place and came here. I am beginning to
wonder that, too, because you can't imagine the difference between
the Home and this. It is lovely here, and not strict at all, but there
is something missing that we had in the Home-so appreciate it
while you can."
The relationship of the children in the Home to the fraternity
which is maintaining them is both interesting and important. We do
not refer to the children as either "guests" or as "inmates," but
rather as "members" of the Home. They know .that they are here
as the wards of California's 140,000 Masons. They are entitled to a
feeling of securi.ty a~d of being the objects of solicitude. Yet they
must not be spoiled. Tqey must not get the idea, "The Masons are
going to take care of us till we're 18;'' or as has happened in some
instances, "The Masons have got to take care of us." As they reach
the later years of their membership in the Home it is important that
their thinking on their relationship to the Masons shall be reasonable
and just. The help given them is a charity, and not the result of an
insurance contract. They must know this and yet their self-respect
must not be destroyed.
Our instruction to them is that the Masons have voluntarily undertaken their care, have assumed a parental relationship to them
with its attendant expense, for .the satisfaction of seeing them become
worthy men and women and good citizens. The relationship between
themselves and the Masons, we tell them, is not one-sided but reciprocal. They as well as the Masons have a part to do; their part is to
make the best possible use of their opportunities and not to make
unnecessary demands upon those who are maintaining them. If they
do this, when their time comes to depart they can leave us with no
sense of diminished self-respect by reason of the fact that their rearing
was in a Masonic rather than in a natural home.
Thousands of Masons visit the Home each year. This contact is
a not unimportant factor in shaping the children's thinking as to their
relationship with the Home and the fraternity. Sometimes, unfortunately, visitors show a patronizing or pitying attitude toward "the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

589

poor little inmates of the orphanage." In some cases they want to
distribute largess in the form of gifts or coins; in other cases, to
tip the girl who has been asked to act as hostess and show them about
the Home. On the other hand, visitors who are wiser or more
thoughtful will assume the attitude of kindly and interested elder
friends, and will leave those children with whom they have talked
feeling encouraged, inspired, and built up in their self-respect. I am
glad to say that in general the visitations of Lodges to the Home have
been so conducted as to have a beneficial effect upon the children.
We need a better system of follow-up of the children who have
left the Home. These young folks going out into life need more
guidance and aid than is given them in many instances. Lodges differ
greatly in the amount of interest and help they give their wards who
leave the Home. Some make a serious and effective effort to get the
youngster started in life; others express interest but do nothing
effective; still others take 1;10 interest.
The boy or girl who leaves us has at most a high school education, but no specific vocational training. Between the time they leave
us and the time they become self-supporting there is a transition
period when they need guidance and help which in some instances
they are not receiving. There should be a more systematic and
effective scheme of after-care.
A recent study of the home conditions of the children in our
care shows the following:
. Ten per cent of our children are full orphans, 81 per cent half
orphans, while 9 per cent have both parents living. The 81 per cent
who are half orphans are made up of 48 per cent whose fathers are
dead and 33 per cent whose mothers are dead. The children whose
parents are both living represent ten families. In seven out of the
ten cases, there has been a moral failure on the part of one or both
of the parents; in the other three, physical invalidism is the cause of
the child's dependency. Compared with other institutions for dependent children, a very small proportion of our cases origina~e from
what are known as "broken homes."
We find it necessary and desirable to keep in touch with the relatives or families of the children in our care. If we are to do intelligent
work we must know them not only before the child comes in, to
determine whether he should come, but after he comes in, to determine how to handle him and how long the need for our care continues.
In this connection the work of our field worker, Miss Noel, has been
invaluable during the past year.
The number of children in outside care under our supervision is
now 56. Nine of these are in foster homes; 47, representing 20 families, are with their o~n mothers.

590

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We have problem cases. In any large group of children there are
bound to be some who do not progress in the environll'N!nt which is
suitable for the average. If they are very far out oi line they may
interfere with the progress of .the others. For some of our problem
cases we have during the past year been utilizing the aid of the California Child Guidance Clinic. Their aid in study, diagnosis, and recommendation as to procedure has been valuable. During the coming
year we shall have in residence at the Home two graduate students
of the Claremont Colleges, who will help by making psychologi.cal
examinations and in bringing the difficult cases to and through the
Child Guidance Clinic. They will also help in furnishing skilled recreation leadership, ·a thing of which we have long been in need.
During the past year the Boy Scout Troop in the Home has been
in flourishing condition. It has attained the greatest degree of efficiency in its history. It continues to have the faithful and devoted
leadership of Brother William Hoogendy~ as Scoutmaster.
This report would be incomplete if it failed to mention the work
of our staff of employes, especially those who live and work in direct
contact ·with the children. On these latter we must depend for success
in bringing up our children. They must be on duty Sundays and holidays, and often from six in the morning until nine at night. Theirs is
taxing work, calling for patience and understanding and all the finest
qualities of character.
Staff meetings of this group of employes are held each Monday
forenoon, at which time through conference and discussion we s·e ek
to clarify our vision and to gain new inspiration for our great work.
JoHN M. DOWNEN, Superintendent.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
WEEK ON FOURTEENTH ANNUAL OBSERVANCE
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Fourteenth Annual Observance of Public Schools Week was
not only the most successful, but with the possible exception of the
first, the most important ever held. And the recognition of its importance, by both the general public and those in charge of the
arrangements in the various communities, was undoubtedly responsible for the unprecedented success achieved.
In the arrangement of the pr<J¥rams, apparently more thought
than ever before was this year given to the fact that their primary
purpose is the dissemination of information, and not mere entertainment. And from the reports it would likewise appear that never
before were the people so eager to avail themselves of the opportunity
afforded for obtaining first hand information of what the schools are
actually doing.
The widespread interest was undoubtedly due to the critical situation of public education throughout the nation generally, as well as
in this state. There was general knowledge of the bills which had
been introduced in the Legislature for the curtailment of expenditures
for public education, and of the charges and counter-charges bandied
back and forth in the discussion of the proposed legislation. On the
one hand, it was being said that the schools were inefficient and were
wastefully and extravagantly administered; and in reply there came
from the school people the direct charge that on the score of economy,
and taking advantage of the financial depression, there was an organized drive of national scope to seriously cripple the public schools,
and to discredit and imperil public education. The parents of the
children and the patrons of the schools were dazed and bewildered.
They wanted to know the truth; and, fortunately, in the observance
of Public Schools Week there was provided an opportunity for
obtaining the facts.
It has come to be very generally understood that the best way of
· learning what is being actually done in and by the schools is by personal visits; and there were few programs this year which did not
·. include this as a feature of the observance. One school reported
being visited during the week by 3500 parents. In many instances
there were the usual special programs prepared for the visitors; but
in others they saw only the daily routine of the school. In connection
with the visits to the schools, there were distributed printed or mimeographed sheets containing interesting and informative facts and
figures, such as the nuri1ber of children in average daily attendance

613

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

in that particular community, the increase over a period of years, the
cost of maintaining the schools, salaries paid the teachers, comparison
with costs in other communities, and much information of like nature.
There were also short articles concerning the so-called "fads and
frills"-explaining the reason for their being included in the school
curriculum.
It will be perhaps remembered that in our report last year in
describing the types of exhibits of school work, reference was made
to "livi; exhibits" in show windows of children actually at work under
the direction of a teacher. One report this year included an account
of a demonstration school installed in a downtown building with the
classes and teachers being changed twice daily. The school was carried on not only during the usual school hours, but as well during the
evenings from seven o'clock until ten, and on Saturday from eight
in the morning until four in the afternoon; and as a 11art of the exhibit
there were several reels of motion pictures of actual work being done
in the schools. Needless to say, it attracted an extraordinary amount
of 4ttention and served a two-fold purpose. It was not only fine
publicity for the week's observance, but what is far more important,
made it possible for a large number of people who did not have time
to visit a regular school to acquire that information which could not
otherwise be obtained.
The instances in which "open house" was held in the schools were
even more numerous this year than heretofore. In one large city
where in the past the evening meetings were the main feature of the
week's observance, every school in the city sent out special invitations
to the parents to make a personal visit; and arrangements were made
so that parents might confer with their child's teacher. The success
of this feature of the observance was due primarily to the splendid
efforts of the principals and teachers; but fine co-operation was received by each school from the Parent-Teacher Association connected
with it.
'
·
'

It is our desire to make this report very much shorter than is
usually presented; and we shall therefore not make extended mention
of even the most notable of the observances reported. We cannot,
however, forbear a very brief reference to three; and the reason in
each case will be obvious.
The first is that of a little mountain Lodge of about fifty members, heid in the face of what might have seemed to be unsurmountable
obstacles. Fire had destroyed the hall in which the meeting was to
be held, and there was no other hall in the community. The nearest
possible meeting place was five miles distant, with the intervening
road blockaded by snow from three to six feet deep. Volunteer snow
shovelers labored for three days to open the road, and an extraordinarily successful meeting was held.
From time to time in these reports have appeared references to
what at the time were· unique features of an observance, some of
which were' thereafter, and very properly, incorporated in other programs. This year in one community Public Schools Week was inaugurated with an unusual service which had been arranged by the
pastor of one of the churches. He had on the platform with him two
boys---one from the grammar school and the other from the high
school, whom he introduced as representing the youth of the community, with their lives before them but not knowing what was to be
done with them. He then called for bids for the services of the youth.
Four men responded by each giving a five-minute talk on his particular occupation or profession as a good investment ior the lives
of these boys and explaining what, in· his judgment, were the necessary qualifications for success. It was a splendid illustration of the
necessity for that guidance and counsel which have become a part of
the work of the modern school system.
Much of the criticism of the present day school on the part of
parents is due to their failure to take into account the extraordinary
progress in the soda!, economic and industrial life of the nation,
which has necessitated a change in the currkulum as well as in the
methods of instruction. In one community this year progress in
public education was graphically portrayed by means of a pageant
presenting a series of scenes giving glimpses of types of educational
opportunity from the period when education was left to philanthropic
effort, religious motive or private initiative, down to the present time.
There were three characters who carried on a dialogue furnishing
the connection between the scenes, and explaining the aim of each
period from the time the pupil learned to read in order to be able to
read the Bible, until today when the modern progressive school is
characterized by participation in, rather than by preparation for, life;
and by ideals of energy, originality and initiative.

612

As has been already indicated, the people ever;where enthusiastically and in extraordinarily large numbers availed themselves of
the opportunity to obtain first hand information of just what the
. schools were or were not doing. In a report from one city the number
was estimated at "not less than 60,000"; and in another it was said
that "somewhere near one-half of the entire population went to school
during Public Schools Week." In addition to those who visited the
schools and were in attendance at the public meetings, thousands had
information with respect to the schools brought to them in their
luncheon and service clubs through speakers detailed for the purpose.
In one of the reports are listed forty-eight different organizations to
which speakers were sent.

615

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In connection with our reference to the change in the type of
programs, mention should be made of the improvement in the character of the addresses given at the public meetings. There were but
comparatively few instances this year in which the speakers indulged
only in glittering generalities about that "little red schoolhouse" and
the advantages of education, instead of detailing the facts so eagerly
sought by the people. As was to be expected, and as was proper and
desirable, considerable attention was devoted. to school expenditures,
and the reasons for the increased cost.
There were several reports this year of public meetings at which
the principal addresses were delivered by high school students who
were able to speak with personal knowledge of the worth of the
modern school. And in this connection we think mention may properly here be made of the fine work done by one of our Island Lodges
in fostering an essay contest among the pupils of the public schools,
in which the writers, mostly of foreign parentage, told what the
schools are doing for them. The following quotation from one of
the prize winning essays would seem to be an answer to the complaint
not infrequently heard that "fundamentals" are being neglected for
"frills and fads":
"A high school is not merely a school where only textbooks are
used. It is also a sort of government and community. Here I am
given various chances to develop my executive abilities, if I have any.
I learn to plan, lead and also use my own judgment in many affairs.
As a citizen of the community I am thrown into a melting pot where
I know ,how to work and associate with people of different races."
It is difficult for anyone who has not had an opportunity to read
the reports received by our committee and the mass of newspaper
clippings constituting a part thereof to realize the amount of information with respect to the schools that must have been acquired by the
people during Public Schools Week. The extent of newspaper publicity, by the way, is almost unbelievable. In one community there
was received from a single newspaper a total of 275 column inches-an
equivalent of over one and a half full eight-column newspaper pages.
And this was typical of the situation throughout the ~tate generally.
Again this year there were published a large number of special articles
of the sort ordinarily appearing in only educational publications; and
during the week there was much information published concerning
the local schools which perhaps would not have appeared at any other
time. There were several newspapers which ran a series of contributed
articles; and it is interesting and significant, too, that some of the
articles were written by pupils in the schools. There were also, of
course, a large number of editorials both in the metropolitan and rural
press. Many of the news stories were illustrated with photographs
and cartoons.

The broadcasting stations were likewise exceedingly generous in
the amount of time devoted to the observance; and this, as will be
readily apprehended, was not the least valuable method of disseminating the desired information concerning the schools.

614

The complete success of the observance in the accomplishment of
its purpose is perhaps best indicated by two widely differing comments to which we here call attention. One commends and praises
while the other criticizes and condemns; the difference being accountable to their origin. The first is a quotation (with the permission of
the writer) from a personal letter from the Superintendent of Public
Instruction to a member of pur committee; and the other is an
excerpt from "The Monitor," the official organ of the Archdiocese
of San Francisco. Superintendent Kersey writes:
"The schools were being tried before the tribunal of the
people. Upon every hand we had individuals asserting themselves
as authorities concerning education. These powerful stabilizing
forces that joined with us who are in the profession and supported
our contentions for the children of the state, represent the great
strength in this state that is, after all, the driving force for the
welfare of civilization as it is accomplished through education.
"Public Schools Week in 1933 came at a most opportune time
for the advantage of our schools and in the spirit of that week,
which for 1933 was the same spirit that has always prevailedfathers, mothers, citizens and taxpayers accepted the invitation to
enjoy an opportunity of real looking-in on education. California
parents have never been wrong long about anything that affected
their children, and once we were able to get the parents in the
spirit of a great public urge to come to the sanctuary where their
children daily met with the teachers, then it seemed that the
whole tide of bitter opposition to education began to turn.
"We in education attribute to Public Schools Week great
credit for its contribution to the public schools of California during days of crisis, for schools can run without everything but
pupils, teachers and the approval of parents.
"There are major issues confronting education which we
must continue to consider together. No longer can educators
solve their problems without collaboration of citizens. We need
to plan amply in advance the program of Public Schools Week for
1934 so that in keeping with the difficulties ahead all forces interested in public education may speak the same language and unite
strength for the same common purpose."

Now, accepting the ·definition of propaganda as a plan for the
propagatio~ ·of a doctrine or system of principles, we are, of course,

propagandists for our system of public education. As Masons we
u.n~ualifi~dl! subscribe to the belief that an educated and enlightened
c1t1zensh~p is the first great care of a progressive state, and that upon
our public schools depends the hope for the perpetuity of a free and

The school is the door of the future. From it will flow in an everwidening stream the ideals, the institutions, the civilization of the
ftiture-of our future. That this spontaneous and widespread interest
may ·be enlightened, strengthened and preserved, that the energies
and aspirations to which it has given rise may be usefully directed is
the purpose of Public Schools Week.
'
. Such necess'.ty for channelizing common interest and energies by
~ctlve and organized movement has been finding expression, especially

1? the last two decades, in a growing tendency toward the organization of those interested in the various phases of our social ci~ic and

have thus been enabled to contribute their efforts in research and

617

In .r ecent years the public schools have been called upon to take
over many functions formerly exercised by the home and other institutions. The growth of our great centers of population has resulted in
the disappearance, in a large part, of the type of home which, even
as late as thirty years · ago, could accord to its children a valuable
education of its own-in handicraft, in homemaking, in social arts and
mutual responsibility. Technical advancements, niechartical invention,
political and economic evolution, call for an intensive and specialized
instruction and training which throw a heavier burden on the school.
This burden cannot be lightened by merely striking from the list of
subjects taught these later additions to the curriculum. The community is inexorably bound, in self-protection if not in honor, to make
provision for its children's future and its own.
Adequate provision demands first of all a firm basis of knowledge
of existing facilities, their aims and purposes, their cost, the probable
result of their curtailment pr the substitution of possible alternatives.
Such knowledge can never be gained by desultory and occasional
visits at graduation time or to clear up some difficulty encountered by
a child. The closest co-operation between the school, the home and
the community as a whole is most essential. The great parent-teacher
organization affords a splendid point of contact between the school
and the home, the value of which it would be difficult to over-estimate.
But the community as a whole has a tremendous investment in the
schools. These last few years have taught us the painful lesson that
the safety of many of our investments depended upon factors as to
which we had neglected to inform ourselves. In many cases these
factors were not accessible to our knowledge, and with the bes.t will
in the world, we were perforce kept in ignorance. Not so as to our
school investment. Every phase of school activity, from business
manager's report to kindergarten maypole dance, is available to our
inspection; and in any fairly complete Public Schools Week program
there is afforded an opportunity for the citizens of that community
to obtain the knowledge which should determine their attitude toward
their schools.
Yes, we are propagandists for our public schools. And so, too,
are those thousands in the Parent-Teacher Associations, the service
clubs and the" other social and civic organizations who, with the school
people, so eagerly and cordially join each year in the undertaking in
·which we are engaged. And no less so are those owners, publishers
and editors of newspapers, and the directors and managers of broadcasting systems and radio stations, without whose sympathetic aid
and wholehearted co-operation that undertaking would not have attained its present proportions.
·
This does not mean, of course, that we believe (and much less
that we endeavor to persuade others to believe) that our schools are
the best that could be devised, or even as good as perhaps they can

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

618

619

be made. We do believe, however, that much of the criticism to
which they are being, and always have been, subjected is more than
likely due to a lack of information which is readily accessible. Of
course, criticism of our schools is inevitable. And it is perhaps
desirable-certainly at least in so far as it is constructive and made
with a knowledge of conditions. And even destructive criticism, if
honest and sincere, as it frequently is, may result in bringing about
commendable changes.
The nature of the propaganda in which we are engaged would
probably be best indicated by the following quotation from the proclamation issued by Grand Master Mixter, requesting that the Fourteenth Annual Public Schools Week be observed by all our Lodges
according to custom:
"The genesis of the Annual Observance of Public Schools
Week was in the crisis with which public education in the United
States was then confronted.
"And now again schools are being closed or maintained with
shortened terms; children, particularly in rural districts, are being
denied the education to which they are entitled; educational service heretofore considered absolutely essential to a modern American school system-such as the maintenance of kindergartens,
night schools and special classes for mentally and physically
handicapped children-is being discontinued or materially curtailed ; vocational courses and manual training for the 'hand
minded' boy are being abandoned, and the opportunities suited
to the varying needs and capabilities of individual boys and girls
are being materially restricted. In some respects the situation is
not dissimilar to that which immediately followed the World
War, but with an entirely different cause.
"The Nation is in the throes of an acute social and economic
disturbance. Every governmental activity is being rigidly scrutinized ; and the universal demand for a reduction in public expenditures has naturally affected school budgets.
" No real friend of our public schools will countenance waste
and extravagance in their operation; nor will he view with complacency, in this time of financial distress, any expc!nditure, however desirable, which may be safely and reasonably deferred until
a more favorable economic condition prevails. But he will not
make this an excuse for withholding such support as is necessary
to preserve our public school system intact and to insure its
functioning satisfactorily.
"It is in such a time as this that it is especially important that
the people everywhere should have definite and authoritative
information with respect to their schools. Here in California the
Fourteenth Annual Observance of Public Schools Week furnishes
an opportunity for acqui.ring that information."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCING '
MASONIC BUILDING PROJECTS
To the M.' · W.' . Grand Lodge of California:'
During the year ending September 30, 1933, thirteen Lodges or temple
associations have conducted correspondence with your committee but the
'
majority of these were of minor importance. ·
The_commi.ttee reviewed the following projects:
Oakdale Lodge No. 275, F. & A . M., situated at Oakdale:
On January 16, 1933, this Lodge was given permission to loan to
Riverbank Lodge No. 459, situated at Riverbank, the sum of $700 to assist
them in paying the remaining obligations contracted in remodeling their
building, with the understanding that at least seven of the members of
Riverbank Lodge, financially responsible, endorse the note, and that repayment be made monthly or semi-annually.
Oakdale Lodge reported that they had sufficient · funds on hand to
make such loan without impairing their ability to meet their obligations.
Hollenbeck Lodge No. 319, F. & 4. M., situated at Los Angeles:
On February 17, 1933, this Lodge was given permission to purcha~e
from its members, for retirement, $6,000 notes, at par, said notes being
the obligation of Hollenbeck Masonic Temple Association.
The financial statement furnished your committee showed that Hot-.
lenbeck Lodge had sufficient funds on hand, and that they were the owner
of all capital stock of the Hollenbeck Masonic Temple Association · that
the only indebtedness of said temple association as of December 31, '1932,
was $42,022, represented by the outstanding notes of said association and
that these notes, during the past seven years, had been reduced from
$64,760; and that Hollenbeck Lodge had, from time to time, purchased
these notes so that the same might be retired.
Holtville Lodge No. 425, F. & A. M., situated at Holtville:
On May 22, 1933, this Lodge applied for permission to purchase a
building in Holtville for the sum of $10,000, but as the Lodge did not
have on hand, nor available, sufficient funds to finance 'the purchase the
application was denied.
'
Anaheim Lodge No. 207, F. & A. M., situated at Anaheim:
On May 1, 1933, this Lodge was given permission to purchase five
shares of stock of the Anaheim Masonic Temple Association, at $50 per
share (par value $100), or a total of $250.
It wa.s r_eported that the stock had paid 6 per cent dividend during
the past eight years, that the total number of shares issued was 470, and
that the Lodge was the owner of 279 shares.
