Signal Hill, being the same location as their former hall, which had been
destroyed by earthquake in March, 1933.
Kaweah Lodge No. 665, F. & A. M., situated at Woodlake:
On August 31, 1933, this Lodge was given permission to enter into a
lease for a term of ten years at a rental of $20 per month, for the second
story of a modern brick building at Woodlake, and to expend $200 of their
funds for remodeling the premises.
Their financial condition indicated that they would be able to make
this investment without any financial difficulty.
Correspondence was also had with
Mt. Shasta Lodge No. 281, F. & A. M., situated at Anderson;
Garden Grove Lodge No. 586, F. & A. M., situated at Garden Grove;
Riverdale Lodge No. 496, F. & A. M., situated at Riverdale;
Searchlight Lodge No. 567, F. & A. M., situated at Long Beach,
but no permission was granted for the expenditure of any funds.
Your committee again congratulates the Lodges and temple associations on the excellent manner in which they have handled those financial
problems which have been submitted to us.
We have received full co-operation from all of the brethren in their
effort to comply with both the spirit and letter of the Constitutfon governing the investment of funds and assuming obligations on leases.

R U LES AND REGULATIONS OF THE MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

EDWARD E. REINKE.

OF CALIFORNIA, ADOPTED FEBRUARY 11, 1933

I. Origin and Purposes
The Grand Lodge of California at its annual communication in 1932
created the Masonic Homes Endowment Board of California, to consist
of fifteen members appointed by the Grand Master. The purpose of said
board shall be to study, devise and carry out plans for securing an adequate
endowment fund for the Masonic Homes of California; to issue appeals

624

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

for contributions to the fund ; to establish contacts with such persons as
may be disposed to aid in the creation and maintenance of such a fund;
and to carry on a systematic and continuous effort in this behalf until an
endowment has been created which will provide an income sufficient to
support the Masonic Homes of California and thereby lessen or entirely
relieve the burden now imposed upon Grand Lodge and the subordinate
Lodges of this jurisdiction, and . to perform such other duties as are
prescribed by the Constitution.

II. Members
The Masonic Homes Endowment Board shall consist of fifteen members appointed by the Grand Master and shall serve for three years ;
provided, that those first appointed shall draw lots so that five thereof
shall serve for one year, five for two years and five for three years.
Thereafter each succeeding Grand Master shall appoint five members of
the board to serve for three years. Any vacancy on the board shall be
filled by the Grand Master, the appointee to serve for .the remainder of
the unexpired term.
III. Powers of the Board
The endowment board shall have power:
Subject to the approval of the Grand Master, to adopt and from time
to time change or amend, such rules and regulations governing its deliberations, modes of procedure and its activities, as may be required and shall
best ·enable it faithfully, efficiently and successfully to carry out the true
spirit and purpose of its creation.
2. To collect funds, subscriptions and pledges to said endowment fund
and to initiate and stimulate every proper effort in that behalf ; to secure
such bequests and devises as may be obtained from charitably disposed
Masons and others; and to encourage gifts by way of life insurance,
annuities and otherwise.
3. To invest, in conjunction with the Grand Master and ·Grand Treasurer, the funds and moneys contributed to or inuring to said endowment
fund and at least annually to cause the income therefrom to be paid .to the
Trustees of the Masonic Homes for use in the maintenance and operation
of the Masonic Homes. To manage, care for, conserve, liquidate, exchange, sell and otherwise handle in conjunction with the Grand Master
and Grand Treasurer, for the use and benefit of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, any real or personal property belonging to said endowment fund or to which said fund is entitled by reason of any legacy,
devise, gift or transfer.
4. To delegate duties to, or apportion responsibilities between, subordinate sections of the board, committees or members.
5. To appoint, and remove at pleasure, all officers, agents and employees of the board and to prescribe their duties and fix their compensation.

625

JV. Officers
1. The officers shall be a Chairman, appointed by the Grand Master,
two Vice-Chairmen, a Secretary and such Assistant Secretaries as may
from time to time be designated. The Treasurer of the Grand Lodge of
California shall be ex-officio the Treasurer of the board.
2. The Chairman shall preside at all meetings of the board. He shall
have general supervision and direction, subject to the authority ~nd control
of the board, of all the activities and business of the board. He shall sign
all contracts and other instruments for and on its behalf when authorized
by the board, and shall perform such other duties as are incident to his
office or may be properly required of him by the board or the Grand
·
Master.

3. One of the Vice-Chairmen shall be a resident of the north half of
the State of California and the other of the south half thereof. In the
absence or disability of the Chairman a Vice-Chairman shall take his
place and perform his duties. Each Vice-Chairman shall, in the part of the
State designated by the Chairman, take a leading and active part in assisting tl)e Chairman to further the efficiency and progress of the work of
the board.
4. The Secretary shall issµe notices for all meetings, keep accurate
minutes thereof, sign with the Chairman such instruments as require attestation, conduct the correspondence of the board, file and safely keep
all papers belonging to .the board, and perform such other duties as are
incidental to his office or may be properly required of him by the board.
He shall receive and receipt for all moneys and property payable to the
board,. keeping an account thereof, and shall forthwith turn the same· over
to the Grand Secretary for .the Grand Treasurer.
The Secretary, and any officer having control of property, shall furnish to Grand Lodge a good and sufficient bond to be approved by the
Grand Master and in such sum as shall be approved by this board.
5. The Treasurer shall have the custody of all moneys and securities
belonging to the endowment fund and he shall hold them in the same
manner as are the funds of Grand Lodge held by him as Grand Treasurer·
provided, that the endowment money and securities shall be kept separat~
and distinct from all other funds and that correct books of account of
said endowment fund be kept by him. He shall perform such other duties
as are incidental to his office or which may properly be required of him
by the board.
·
6. The Assistant Secretary shall perform such duties as may be from
time to time prescribed by the board.

V. Meetings
1. Regular meetings of the board shall be held quarterly at such time
.and place as the board may determine and the Chairman in the call therefor may designate.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
PROCEEDINGS OF THE

626

2. Special meetings of the board may be held at any time upon the
call of the Chairman or of five members of the board, the place of the
meeting to be fixed by the Chairman, or in his inability to act, by the
Grand Master.
3. The annual meeting of the board shall be held on the last day of
the annual communication of Grand Lodge at a time and place fixed by
the Chairman.
4. Five members of the board shall constitute a quorum for the
transaction of business.
5. Notice of all meetings shall be given in writing and mailed by the
Secretary to each member of the board not less than ten days prior to
the date thereof; provided, that a meeting can be had at any time without
notice if all the members are present thereat, or if the absent members
sign in writing a waiver of notice of such meeting, which waiver is made
a part of the record of such meeting.

VI. Funds
1. No part of the endowment fund heretofore accumulated or hereafter acquired shall ever be used for any purpose other than the maintenance and operation of the Masonic Homes of California, and all the net
income from the endowment fund shall be paid to the Masonic Homes of
California for its use in maintaining and ~perating said Homes.
2. The members of the board shall be entitled to their actual expenses
necessarily incurred in the performance of .the duties devolving upon
thent as herein provided, claims for which expenses shall not be paid out
of the endowment fund but shall be presented to the Grand Master, after
approval by the Chairman, for approval and payment from the general
fund of Grand Lodge.

VII. Finance Committee
The Chairman shall appoint three members of the board as a Finance
Committee, to act conjointly with the Grand Master and Grand Treasurer
in making investments of endowment funds, in making exchanges of securities and in making sales of securities belonging to the endowment fund.
The Finance Committee shall also keep a record of all transactions in connection with the handling and investment of said funds and shall report
thereon at each meeting of the board.

VIII. Committees
1. The Chairman shall appoint from time to time such committees as
are necessary or proper for the transaction of the business of the board
and for the solicitation and collection of moneys and property for the
endowment fund.
2. The Chairman shall appoint such committees as may in his opinion
be necessary to co-operate with the Inspectors, with the Masters of the

627

Lodges, and the brethren of this jurisdiction, with the primary objective
that in every Lodge a special Endowment Committee, consisting of not
less than three nor more than five members, shall be appointed which shall
foster the interest of the endowment fund and see that its merits are
brought to the attention of every member of this jurisdiction and any other
persons interested.

IX. Endowment Fund Month
One month in each year shall be designated by the Grand Master as
"Masonic Homes Endowment Month" and, unless the Grand Master otherwis_e designate~, the month of May in each year shall be set aside, duri~g
which. the vano~s subordinate Lodges of the jurisdiction shall bring to
the minds of their members and other persons interested, the claims of the
endowment fund for their sympathetic attention to the purposes for which
the same is to be used.
The Chairman shall appoint suitable committees to direct the work
of Endowment Month so that the fullest benefits may be derived therefrom.
X. Amendments
These rules and regulations may be amended, altered or repealed in
whole or in part by a majority vote of the entire board at any meeting
thereof, provided, that no amendment thereof shall be effective until the
same is approved by the Grand Master.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History begs leave to submit the following report of its activities during the past year.
Your Committee, since the last annual communication, has been engaged in the continuation of its work carried on during the past five years.
We have actively assisted the History Committees of local Lodges in
searching records and in the final preparation of their reports. Many personally written narratives dealing with the activities of our "Fifty Year
Masons" have been prepared and filed. Numerous human interest stories,
heretofore obtained, have been carefully checked and verified. Some very
interesting records and manuscripts having to do with the lives of early
day Masons have been received. Some new material has been discovered
and preserved, dealing with the following pioneer Masons: Sam Brannan,
who played a leading role in the early life of San Francisco; James F.
Reed, the only Mason of the ill-fated Donner party to reach Sutter's Fort;
Mark Twain, whose Masonic activities in the West have been considered,
until recently, to have been confined entirely to the Lodge at Angels Camp.
Some interesting sidelights on Peter Lassen, whose personal life has been
somewhat shrouded in mystery, have come to our attention.
We have collected some stories of the early activities of our first
Grand Master, which will materially contribute to a better understanding
of his eventful career.
We have had occasion to investigate and study the proceedings of the
San Francisco Vigilante Committee of 1856 and preserve the constructive
records of the members of that organization who were affiliated with
Masonry.
The committee at present is engaged in an effort to obtain a full and
complete history of Isaac Roop, who during the early days took an active
part in northern California Masonry.
During the past year some interesting facts, connected with the lives
of the Masons who took a leading part in the formation of California's
first Constitution, have been obtained.
We have also, during the past year, earnestly endeavored to gain
access to the personal papers of Abel Stearns, the first Mason to come
to California. In this matter we are attempting to follow up the work of
Brother Arthur M. Ellis, who spent considerable time in an effort to obtain
for Grand Lodge the records of that colorful Masonic chara~ter.
We have also, through careful investigation, been able to correct many
inaccuracies of fact which inadvertently were incorporated in the reports
filed by some of the local Lodge committees.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

635

The members of your committee have also undertaken the task of
laboriously going through the forty-one volumes of Grand Lodge proceedings and properly indexing interesting material and facts contained therein
which may be used in the ultimate preparation of our history.
In the reports of our Past Grand Masters, we find some very interesting and instructive Masonic data. The grand orations are a veritable storehouse of eloquent delineation and interpretation of Masonic principles and
ideals. Carefully chosen excerpts from the Grand Master's reports and
from grand orations should be incorporated in the final volumes of our
history. We venture the asser.tion that not one Mason in five hundred has
had the opportunity or occasion to peruse their cop.tents and enjoy the
pleasure or benefit which more fortunate brethren have received who have
dug out the nuggets of eloquence and wisdom contained in the reports and
orations. If these gems are made a part of our written history, the entire
body of the craft may greatly profit thereby. With this in mind, your
. committee at present is pursuing the work of carefully picking out and
indexing this material for future use.
Many local Lodge History Committees have not as yet filed their
reports, and we respectfully urge that they endeavor with all reasonable
despatch to complete their labors and forward same to the committee or
the Grand Secretary.
For the sake of brevity, we have not seen fit to follow our custom
in past years and give in detail in this re!)Ort the many human interest
stories which have been received during the year. Most of them were
received too late to enable tlie committee to fully verify them ; therefore,
we deemed it advisable to omit their recital herein.
In view of the fact that there is still additional work to be perfected
before the final draft of our hist~ry is completed, we recommend that the
Committee on Masonic History be continued.
LEON 0. WHITSELL,
MARK A. SA WRIE,
DAVID TULLOCH,
RoscoE L. CLARK,
CHAS.

E. HAAS,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLICATION OF
MASONIC HIST ORY
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California·:
Your committee, appointed with instructions to investigate the most
feasible ·and economic plan for the preparation and publication of a history
of Masonry in this State, begs leave to submit the following report:
The preparation of the history and its publication are distinctly different phases, and will be discussed separately in this report.
In our investigation of the proper plan to be adopted for the preparation of the historical manuscript that would be in desirable form and ready
for the printer, we have had the benefit of the advice and co-operation of
many of the best informed members of this Grand Lodge. We have consulted numerous active members of the California Historical Society and
members of other organizations majoring in California history. We have
also discussed the matter with other members of the craft and distinguished
citiz.ens of this State who are recognized authorities in this line of literary
endeavor. As a result of such investigation and study, we feel that we
have selected a plan which will vouchsafe a reliable and interesting history
at a minimum of cost.
We are of the opinion that a work of this magnitude should be under
the general direction of one competent writer. He should be a member of
the craft, and his reputation for accuracy should be beyond all question.
He should be given full authority and responsibility and should be in a
position to personally write the major portion of our history.
We feel that in thus placing respons'ibility in one directing head of the
writing staff we will assure correlation and continuity which are vitally
essential to the successful perfection of a history covering so wide a range
of time and territory. We believe also that certain phases or period~ of
our history can be best prepared by certain outstanding members of the
craft who are peculiarly conversant with the local history of certain parts
of the State.
We are further impressed with the fact that it would be highly desirable that there be· incorporated in the text of the work certain historical
data and information having to do with the pioneer members of the craft
aside from their purely Masonic activities. Many of our early-day Mason~
played a most conspicuous part in the settlement of our State, the formation of its government and the development' of its institutions. Historical
events with which our membership has been closely identified should be
treated in some detail, that a proper background may obtain and that the
lives and activities of these brethren may be better understood and inter:.
preted. This requirement calls for authorship with a comprehensive know!-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

637

edge of Californi history as well as Masonic history. The person chosen
to undertake this r ponsibility should be authorized to edit and finally
pass upon the materia used.
We have here ·brie outlined the procedure which we deem advisable
in the proper preparation of our history. We have not definitely determined upon the personnel of a staff such as is suggested by the foregoing
conclusions. · However, we have carefully canvassed among the members
of the fraternity for the best available talent to undertake this work.
A number of competent members of Grand Lodge have expressed a willingness to prepare certain phases of our history with which they are familiar.
Their services will be without compensation and as a contribution to the
craft.
The matter of finding a competent individual who could devote the
necessary time to writing the major portion of this history and in supervising the preparation of all material, is somewhat difficult. Such men as
we have found are not in a position to give the necessary time without some
compensation. One brother, who has had years of experience as· a Masonic
writer and who at one time prepared a very creditable history for one
grand jurisdiction, would gladly undertake the work, but would be unable
to perform the service without sufficient remuneration.
As heretofore stated in this report, one of the most important phases
of the preparation is what is technically known as "editing" and finally
passing upon the manuscript before publication. This is work of ·prim;iry
importance, and we feel that we are exceedingly fortunate in having found
a Masonic brother who is most competent to assume this responsibility and
who is willing to perform this service without remuneration and, as he
modestly terms it, this will be his "slight contribution to Masonry:"
The brother to whom we refer is Francis Farquhar. He is a writer of
historical works of wide-spread circulat ion. He sustains a reputation for
historical accuracy which places him almost in a class by himself. He has
had years of experience in editing historical material. H is final approval
of a work of this character will be a guarantee to the critical student of
California history that scrupulous exactitude has characterized its preparation.
We find that at least one year will be required for the proper preparation of a history along the lines that are suggested by our findings and
recommendations. We therefore . suggest that Grand Lodge approve the
selection of Brother Francis Farquhar as the one to edit and pass upon
the final manuscripts before publication. We also suggest that certain
brothers of the craft be authorized to proceed with the preparation of
individual .phases of our history, as recommended by the committee, upon
the approval of the Grand Master.
Your committee fully appreciates the financial stress and strain under
which Grand Lodge is Row laboring, and in view of the lack of funds at

OF U. C. BERKELEY CLUB HOUSE

T o the M.". w:. ~na Lodge of Califo-rnia:
During the past "X_ear, although the Trustees of the Masonic Club of
the University of Cali~rnia, Inc., and the management of the club house
have been compelled to'.cut all operating costs to the bone, and have
greatly reduced the cost of activities in connection with its social service
work, the institution has, during this period, more than justified the faith
of the fraternity in maintaining it.
Several hundred students of Masonic affiliation and connection at the
university, like the great majority of the student body, have been_existing
on curtailed allowances for their support. Consequently, the activities of
the Masonic Club have been a tremendous factor, not only in sustaining
the morale of our own students, but , as testified to by the officers and
faculty of the university and student leaders, in contributing· in equal measure. toward preserving the morale of the student body as a whole. The
influence of several hundred students constantly in contact with the beneficent surroundings of the club has proved a stabilizing force to the
entire student body.
Nothing has happened during the year to disturb the peace and goodfellowship which have prevailed at the club, and the quiet, dignified and
efficient leadership of Mrs. J. }I. Quinn, the hostess, has continued with
renewed affection and confidence on the part of our student body. The
activities of the club have been. carried on·as best they could be with the
decreased budget allowance made one year ago. No happening of special
interest has occurred at. the club that is worthy of note at tbis ~ime.
The Trustees of the club have submitted to the Finance Committee the
result of the annual report of the club for the year ending September 30,
1933, prepared by Messrs. MacEachern & Macintyre, certified public
accountants of San Francisco, and present herewith the proposed budget
for the next ensuing Masonic year. The auditors' statement has been
personally verified by the Chairman of the Executive Committee of the
Board of Trustees, including a check of the bank balance and bills payable,
as reported.
As is shown by the audit, the social ser~ice expense at the club has
been reduced to such an extent as to make the Trustees and the management feel they have been almost niggardly in that respect. In . view of
the times, however, the Trustees and the management cheerfully met the
situation, with the result indicated.
The proposed budget fo r the .ensuing year is within a few dollars of
the proposed budget presented last yea r. The Trustees feel that the club
house, managed in the same careful manner as during t)1e past year, can
be maintained even with the greatly reduced contribution t oward social

REPOR-}\)F U. C. ~OS ANGELES CLUB HOUSE
To the M:. w:. ~nd Lodge of California;
Your Board of hjrectors of the Masonic Club of the University of
California at Los Anglijes, fraternally submit their report for the year
ending September 30, 1933.
The financial statement is reflected by the report of Brother Reynold
E;. Blight, certified public accountant, which is made a part hereof and
which has been filed with the Finance Committee. We, however, direct
attention to the following items:
First: Referring to the deposit in the United States National Bank
in the sum of $8,473.49, which represents the balance there deposited at the
time that institution was closed, and which has heretofore been mentioned.
It will be remembered that last year we reported a dividend of 25 per cent.
Since then we have received a dividend of 10 per cent, and we are informed
that a third dividend of 25 per cent will shortly be paid, making at the time
of its payment a 60 per cent recovery. The reports concerning the possibility of being repaid all of the remainder are somewhat conflicting, and
the prospects may best be described as problematical.
Second: There ~ill be noted an item for improvements in the sum of
$1,589.74. This not only represents a minor alteration for the improvement
of the supervision and control of the club house, and certain furniture for
the better equipment of three rest rooms, but also the replacement of the
roof. For some time we have had trouble with storm waters leaking
through. At one time, it will be recalled, we found it necessary to waterproof the exterior walls. Then it was discovered that, due either to a
rather severe earthquake which shook this section two or three years ago
or to some defective construction, the concrete slab underneath the tile
was permitting the rain to filter through. If we were to save the interior
plaster from ruin it was deemed necessary to remove all the tile, repair
the concrete and insert water-proofing between it and the tile and refasten
the tile by a system invented since the original roof was laid. This was
done, and a twenty-year guarantee protects against a recurrence of the
trouble.
Third: It will be observed that as a ·result of the last item our disbursements for the year were the sum of $8,258.92, the sum received from
the Grand Lodge $6,581.30, and other receipts $710.20, making an excess
of disbursements over receipts of $967.42. We think attention should also
be directed to this item for the.purpose of illustrating the wisdom, when
Grand Lodge is again able to do so, of setting aside a reasonable sum to
represent depreciation of building and furniture in order to care for just
such unexpected emergencie!I'. Also, it should be observed in this connection that we decreased the salary of the resident hostess from $1,800

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
FAIRMOUNT LODGE
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
After receiving from the Most Worshipful Grand Master letters
designating us a committee to investigate the condition existing in Fairmount Lodge No. 435, we proceeded to meet and consider the situation as
it existed in that Lodge at the time of the order of arrest of its charter.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

645

Very slight investigation quickly disclosed a condition of affairs that
was most lamentable and unfortunate. For a period of over six years, two
small groups, together totaling not more than twenty to twenty-five members, have been in active opposition to _each other.
We have not deemed it necessary to determine ·the merits or demerits
of the various contentions advanced by the two factions, for we felt that
the situation now is such that it is no longer a question of who was right
or who was wrong, and that nothing could be gained by an investigation
which would perhaps only intensify the antagonisms already existing between the two groups. We further believed that one solution of the whole
matter, other than dissolution of the Lodge, would be the withdrawal, if
possible to procure, of the leaders of the factions, thus permitting the
remaining large majority on the Lodge's roster to retain their memberships in the Lodge, and to further retain the assets of the Lodge, which
are of no small amount.
The members of one of the factions, with but little hesitancy, announced their willingness to comply with the proposal, but the members
of the other group set up conditions which preclude a satisfactory solution
of the matter at this time, if at all, and it would seem that the "radical
operation" of dissolution of the Lodge should follow if the trouble is to be
definitely ended. We are not yet ready, however, to see the rights of over
five hundred Masons so seriously affected by the actions of a very small
number, for it must be kept in mind that among the majority of the
members of this Lodge are many Master Masons who are well along in
years and who, with others who may be, in some other way, unfortunately
situated, could probably not gain membership in other Lodges. The loss
of a charter brings in its train many unfortunate results, and we therefore
felt that the brethren should be willing to play the role of "martyrs" and
seize the opportunity to save the charter and the assets of the Lodge for
the many brethren who otherwise are made the victims of the factional
strife on the part of a limited few; but our efforts along the lines of the
plan .suggested have not met with the success hoped for.
We are not impressed with the suggestion of a division into two
Lodges. The sentiment against the formation of any additional Lodges
in San Francisco is too strong to be overcome at this time, and, further,
two Lodges created under the conditions existing would each lack the true
spirit of Masonry which should characterize a Masonic Lodge.
We would therefore report and recommend as follows:
We believe that the order of the Grand Master in arresting this
charter should be appr~ved without hesitancy. Drastic action became
necessary, and the Grand Master was justified in taking this step to terminate a condition which could not longer be tolerated.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

646

647

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We recommend :
1st. That the charter of Fairmount Lodge No. 435 be continued under
arrest until the next ahnual communication of Grand Lodge, unless
sooner restored by the Grand Master in the manner herein suggested.
2nd. That the incoming Grand Master be authorized to appoint a
committee of three members to continue the investigation of the conditions
in the Lodge and to make such recommendations fot the restoration of
the charter as It shall deem likely to restore harmony in said Lodge.
3d. That the Grand Master be and he is hereby authorized to restore
the charter of the Lodge_ under such terms and conditlohs as he may deem
necessary to itrtpose.
4th. That if the Grand Master shall determine that it is not for the
interest of Masonry to restore the charter, then he shall direct that charges
be preferred against the Lodge, looking to a revocation of said charter. '
GEORGE L. ]ONES,
CHAS. ALBERT ADAMS,

Be It Resolved: That the twenty-three brethren of Fairmount Lodge
No. 435, F. & A. M., named in a set of resolutions dated October 6, 1933,
and signed by one hundred and forty-three ( 143) members of said Lodge,
be, and they are hereby ordered by this Most Worshipful Grand Lodge to
absent themselves from any and all meetings, or other activities of Fairmount Lodge, from and after this date, and until such time as this order
is rescinded or otherwise amended. And they are further directed to refrain
froln taking any part, directly or indirectly, in the election or appointment
of any officer of the Lodge; or of attempting, directly or indirectly, by
letter or otherwise, to influence or induce any member of the Lodge to do
any certain thing that might tend to disturb the peace and harmony of the
Lodge, on pain of being deemed guilty of unmasonic conduct.
That the said twenty-three brethren are directed to keep themselves
in Masonic stahdihg by paying their dues to the Secretary of Fair~ount
Lodge on receiving proper notice.
·
Further, that they be permitted to apply for Masonic relief 1 whenever
necessary, through the San Francisco Board of ~elief, of which Fairmount
Lodge is a member, and that any relief so granted shall be considered
a charge against Fairmount Lodge.
That in the case of any of the above mentioned brethren who is a
life member of Fairmount Lodge, joining any other Lodge in this grand

jurisdiction, Fairmount Lodge shall return to him the amount paid for
such life membership, less the amount of $1.00 for each month he has
been a member since paying for such life membership.
That these brethren be permitted individually to apply in writing to
Fairmount Lodge for certificates of good standing wbeneyer they may desire to apply to any other Lodge for admission to membership, and that
upon their election into any other Lodge, the usual dimit will be granted
by Fairmount Lodge.
And Be It Further Resolved : That the Grand Master is hereby requested to return to Fred Abbott Watkins, Master of Fairmount Lodge,
the charter of the Lodge, together with th8 necessary instructions for the
resumption of full .activities. It being understood that the restoration is
temporary, and that at the next annual communication of Grand Lodge the
charter may be permanently cancelled, providing a satisfactory showing
cannot be made that peace and harmony have been fully restored.

By-Laws Committee of the Grand Lodge, . being a member of that committee at the time of his death.

"There must be something after death
Behind the toil of man,
There must exist a God divine
Who's working out a plan.
And this brief journey that we know
As life, must really be
The gateway to a finer world
That some day we shall see."
Life would scarcely be worth the living if death were the end of all.
The Great Architect sets us to find out this plan, and work out as much
of it as possible in our short· year; and when our day is done, we feel
sure that He will not let it be the end.
"There is a mystic borderland that lies
Just past the limits of this work day world:
And it is peopled with those we met
And loved, a year, a month, a week, a day,
And parted from with aching hearts, yet knew
That through the distance we must lose the hold
Of hand with hand, and only clasp the thread
Of memory. But still so close we feel this land,
So sure we are that these same hearts are true,
That when in waking dreams there comes a call
That sets the threads of memory aglow,
We know that just by reaching out our hand
In written words of love, or book or flower,
The waiting hand will clasp our own once more
Across the silence in the same old way."
WM. H . PARCELS,
MAX A. PLUMB,
WILLIAM H . HOLBROOK,

Committee;
Song, "Crossing the Bar."

The virtues of good Masons who have answered the call of the Great
Architect leave us sweet memories and an inheritance of good examples.
These are among the most precious treasures of our Institution.
Man's life is too short to allow his full development in this earthly
life. Materially, he buds and blooms, and bears his fruit, but his soul
and spirit must require more time than this short span of life for its
fruition. Is it conceivable that this brief period ends all, and that our
lives then fade into nothingness?

Eulogy in Memoriam George Mairs. Perine
By Harry K. Wolff, Past Master, Pacific Lodge No. 136
Most Worshipful Gr.and Master of Masons of California, 0 fficer s and
Members of Grand Lodge, and Visiting Brothers:
In obedience to the command of this honorable body, this memorial
hour has been appropriately set aside during the present convocation as a
Masonic monument of respect and honor to the memory of our dearly
beloved brother, Past Grand Master George M. Perine, whose mortal
being passed from this earthly sphere on October 6, 1933. His entire life
was ever devoted to the promotion of the welfare and best interests of the
craft. May his soul rest in peace.
·
A great scholar in Masonry admonishes us :
"Death is the great teacher-stern, cold, irresistible-whom the collected might of the world cannot stay or ward off. The breath that, parting
from the lips of king or beggar, scarcely stirs the hushed air, cannot be
bought, or brought ·back for a moment, with the wealth of empires. What
a lesson is this, teaching our frailty and feebleness, and an Infinite Power
beyond us! It is a fearful lesson that never becomes familiar. It walks
through the earth in dread mystery, and lays its hands upon all. It is a
universal lesson that is read everywhere and by all men. Its message comes
every year and every day. The past years are crowded with its sad and
solemn mementoes; and death's finger traces its handwriting upon the
walls of every human habitation.
"It teaches us duty; to act our part well; to fulfill the work assigned
us. When one is dying, and after he is dead, there is but one question :
Has he lived well? There is no evil in death but that which life makes."
It is both fitting and wholesome that we, the living, should fondly and
reverently recall to mind the life and nobleness of character of our friend
and brother who has been called to his eternal reward. We would that the
world may see his good works and glorify not him but the Great Architect
of the Universe whose instrument he was. Imbued with this spirit, may
we translate into our own lives his exemplary character and exalted friendship, which should prove to us a nourishing source of strength, constantly
purifying ·our minds and inspiring the heart to nobler living and diviner
thinking.
Our beloved brother, Past Grand Master George M. Perine, rang
down the curtain of mortal existence at the mellow age of 81 years,
having lived a full and honorable life, truly·squared by the ideal tenets of
Freemasonry. He was raised to the sublime degree of a Master Mason
on June 25th, 1889, in Pacific Lodge No. 136, Free and Accepted Masons
of California. In the year 1892 he graced the Oriental Chair of his
mother Lodge, and served with dignity and honor to himself and to the

659

fraternity. Thereafter and in the month of October, 1907, he ornamented
this august body by officiating as Grand Master of the Masons of California, the highest honor that can be conferred upon any man at any time
by our fratern ity, and the obligations and responsibilities of which he fully
and admirably carried out in a true Masonic spirit. Subsequently, and in
the month of October, 1913, in recognition of the extraordinary and
valuable services rendered by him to the Masonic Fraternity, and to
Scottish Rite Masonry, in particular, and humanity in general he was
selected by the Supreme Council of the 33° for the Southern Jurisdiction
of the United States for the honorable degree of Knight Commander of
the Court of Honor, and on December 11th, 1915, he was crowned Honorary 33° member of the order.
Our friend and brother had many ennobling and lovable characteristics which, when viewed through the mirror of truth, prove that he lived
according to the pattern of the prophet of old who said, "I carry the
world in my heart." Brother Perine had the refreshing touch of a kindly
heart. He was imbued with a high sense of public duty, and was ardently
patriotic. He was not without a fair share of self-assertion, and yet he
was one of the most unselfish of men. He was by nature warm-hearted
and magnanimous. He exemplified the characteristics of a true Mason by
constantly abstaining from all profanity; he was temperate in all things;
. he dealt honestly with all men, and was always ready, willing and anxious
to help the distressed whithersoever dispersed-a true lover of his fellowman. He was a loyal and devoted husband, and a true friend.
More cannot, aye, more need not be said of any man. Let us who
are living emulate him.
Members of the craft:
Again our line has been broken ; again the vacant chair;
Again a true and loyal brother has left us for service over there.
Again we bow in sorrow1 but let us not despair,
For we shall meet-Tomorrow--0ur brother 'over there.
Yes, 'twill be but Tomorrow, and e'er we are aware
Till we shall all be leaving for servic~ over there. '
Oh, in that great Tomorrow, if for it we prepare,
We'll meet our absent brother and greet him over there!
Then farewell, friend and brother, your qualities so rare
Have fitted you for Heaven, and service over there.
You have the life immortal, we have the vacant chair;
Your heritage the richer, for God is over there.
With God and Heaven, and free from pain and care,
Who would not leave this mortal life for service over there?
So good-bye our dear, absent brother,
P: · G.' · M: · George M. Perine ; our sorrow we must bear
Until the grand reunion which awaits us over there.

Eulogy in Memoriam Wallace Rider Farrington
By Herbert S. Bowen, Master, Lodge le Progres de l'Oceanie No. 371

Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
It has become my sad duty to review briefly for you the life of our
friend and brother, Wallace Rider Farrington, who on October 5, 1933,
was raised to the celestial Lodge above.
Wallace Rider Farrington was born in Orono, Maine, May 3, 1871.
He was educated in the public schools and was graduated from the University of Maine in 1891 with the degree of Bachelor of Science.
In 1894 he went to Hawaii as managing editor of the Pacific Commercial Advertiser. He later affiliated with the Evening Bulletin as its editor
and subsequently became publisher of the present Honolulu Star Bulletin.
Wallace Rider Farrington was appoint&d Governor .of Hawaii by
President Hard.ing in June, 1921. He served in the highe~t office of the
Territory µntil 1929, when he was retired at his own request.
Governor Farrington's record of accomplishments is so brilliant that
time does not permit a complete review of them. Governor Farrington
was a civic minded, tireless worker for the good of the community in which
he lived. The Territory of Hawaii had a strong friend in Wallace Rider
Farrington, and he did much for the Territory; as Governor he was able
to get federal aid for his Territory, and he was instrumental in having
Congress acknowledge the intent of the Kuhio, which meant rehabilitation
for the Hawaiian race through homestead help.
The educational facilities of the Territory were also greatly increased
during the Farrington regime, and it was largely due to his efforts that
the College of Hawaii was raised to the standard of a university.
The present territorial budget system, the territorial retirement and
pensions systems are due directly to Brother Farrington's efforts.
The outside contacts of the territorial government were also greatly
developed under Governor Farrington, and it was during his regime that
Hawaii became the center of many of the outstanding affairs of the
Pacific in the way of international conferences, trade meetings and educational gatherings. As an honorary officer of the Pan-Pacific Union he did
much to encourage pleasant relations and promote better understanding
among the peoples of the Pacific.
To us, of course, his Masonic activities are particularly brilliant and
outstanding. He was a Past Master of Lodge le Progres de l'Oceanie
No. 371, and at his death an officer of the Grand Lodge of California.
Governor Farrington was a deep student of the history of Masonry in
Hawaii and its progress there. He had an intimate personal knowledge
of most of the outstanding Masons of Hawaii and their Masonic activities.

AFTERN90N SESSION
Wednesday, October 11, 1933.
Grand Lodge was called on at 2 o'clock, the Grand Master presiding.
REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC
EDUCATION
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California7
At our last communication the Grand Master was authorized to appo~t
a committee "To study the question of Masonic education and to report its
conclusions at the next communication."
The undersigned committee was appointed by our Grand Master pur.
suant thereto and respectfully presents herewith its report.
The conunittee begs to call your attention to the fact that all o.f its
e bers have had opportunity to consider the elements of an educational
;r;ram both from a theoretical and practical standpoint, by reason of the
fact that all of them have at one time or another been members of former
educational committees.
The committee has approached the study of the question of Masonic
educat.ion in the light of the experience of its members and also by reason
of contacts with members of our order during the past . several mo.nths.
The committee has likewise e.x amined programs of educat10nal comm.1tt~es
in other jurisdictions. We find very little in the programs of othe~ JUr~s­
dictions which differs from those heretofore in operation in Cahfo~ma.
By reason of the intimate contact which the men:ibers of .this committee
have had with educational programs in the past, this co~1ttee feels th~t
it may safely draw certain deductions from such observation and ex~n­
ence, and these deductions now represent the conclusions of the comm!ttee
on the question involved.
They are as follows :
.
1. The existing members probably do not desire to expend any considerable amount of time on educational programs as such.
2. The members are willing to receive information but, ~ith the exception
of intermitte~t groups, are not anxious to work for tt.
3. The officers, generally speaking, have enthusiastic intention~ with respect to an educational program but apparently do not follow it through.

663

4. When Grand Lodge or Grand Lodge officers lead or direct with respect
to the programs, the subordinate Lodge officers follow the same.
5. Notwithstanding the probable attitude of present membership above
referred to, it does not follow that nothing should be done by Grand
Lodge and that all programs of educational activity should be left to
the Lodge; on the contrary, it would appear that although certain types
of programs, such as the presentation of papers and of speakers, may
be left to the Lodges, in the matter of the type of program which might
well be used by every Lodge such program should be required by Grand
Lodge.
6. The candidate is the logical individual with whom to start and through
whom, .i n the course of years to come, to build up a more extensively
informed body of members. This committee feels that instruction and
information in addition to and in elaboration of the present instruction
and information furnished by the ritual is desirable.
7. A program of instruction to candidates would succeed if:
a. It were made a prerequisite for the candidates' advancement.
b. By direction of Grand Lodge, the Grand Lecturer and through him
the Inspectors and Masters were made no less responsible for the
program than they ~re for other of their present duties.
8. Such a program need entail no considerable expense, if indeed any at
all.
·
Your committee, of course, is aware of the many other phases of an
educational program but feels that all such phases other than that of
instruction to candidates should be left to the individual Lodges.
The foregoing represents the "conclusions" of this committee, based
upon its study, observation and experience. For the purpose, however, of
presenting the matter for action by Grand Lodge, your committee recommffi~:
·
a. Adopting the principle of voluntary action by subordinate Lodges on
. all phases of an educational program except that of instruction to
candidates.
b. Adopting the principle of a program of instruction to candidates, and
authorizing and d·i recting the Grand Master to appoint a committee to
formulate and promulgate such program:
1. Making the use of such program compulsory and requiring proficiency as a prerequisite to advancement.
2. Charging the Grand Lecturer, Inspectors and Masters with the
duty of instituting and executing the program.
c. That no program as to candidates dependent on voluntary execution by
subordinate Lodges be adopted, and hence

664

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF. CALIFORNIA

d. Unless the compulsory method be adopted, no action be taken as to
such compulsory program; and
e. If · the compulsory method as to candidates be approved, then appropriate legislation with respect to amendments to the proper sections
of our constitution be adopted.
Respectfully submitted,
.

IRVING MAGNES,
IRA F. THOMPSON,
JESSE M . WHITED,

LEE T . MULLEN,
A. HEBER WINDER,
Committee.

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CLANDESTINE
MASONRY
To the M. ·. w. ·. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Clandestine Masonry begs leave to report as
follows:
In our report of 1932, your committee enumerated ten central organizations pretending to be Masonic.
We have not obsered much activity among the Filipino Lodges. Their
members are largely transient at their places of residence, and consequently
their Lodges may be very active at one time and at another dormant.
The clandestine negro Grand Lodge called "M.'. W .'. Hiram of
Tyre,'; which was formerly M.'. w:. R. J. Fletcher Grand Lodge, is
practically dead. We have been unable to discover any signs of its activity.
The other negro Grand Lodge known as the "M.' · W.' · Sovereign
Grand Lodge, F. & A. M.,'' also known as "Prince Hall Masons,'' has
maintained its existence, held its annual communication, though many of
its Lodges are in precarious condition.
The largest body of clandestine Masons in California heretofore reported as "Rito Nacional Mejicano" has had great difficulty in holding
its Lodges together. A number of its subordinate Lodges have passed out
of existence, and we are informed that an attempted reorganization is
being brought about. It is said that this Rite has yielded up its charter
from the Grand Orient of Mexico City and is attempting to organize a
purely independent Rite in California. The former Inspector General,
Professor Cristobal Aguillon, has resigned. His successor is one Isaac
Romero of Tia Juana and San Diego. We are further informed that

666

Professor Aguillon is urging the reorganization of these Mexican Lodges
into an independent American Rite and that they have held a meeting in
the City of Los Angeles on October 6th and 7th for this purpose. We
have no advice as yet as to the result.
Much fragmentary information has come to your committee, but we
have been unable to get very much that is concrete and specific of the
activity of certain isolated Masonic bodies. For instance, we are informed
that a clandestine body is operating in Los Angeles known as "University
Lodge, F. & A. M. No. 106."
Also, a negro Lodge known as "Sunset No. 26" is operating in Los
Angeles. · We have been unable to learn its affiliation, but it is probably
active in the neighborhood of San Diego.
A benefit certificate issued by a M.'. W.'. King Solomon Grand Lodge
of Ancient and Accepted York Masons of the State of California has
been handed to your committee. This is said to be operative in the City
of Oakland, and the beneficiary certificate bears date, September 13, 1926.
This Lodge may not now be operative.
The Co-Masonic Lodges have continued to be quite active. A district
meeting of all of their organizations was held in Ojai, April 23rd. The
Ojai Lodge of this order was organized in 1926, and the present Master
is Mrs. Mary Goldy, with Mrs. Susan Cooper as Senior Warden. and
Mrs. Diana Gillespie as Junior Warden. A chapter of Rose Croix is
headed by Mrs. Grace Hall. Mr. John Royne of Ojai is the District
Deputy over all the Lodges of sout~ern California.
While most of the clandestine Lodges heretofore reported upon are
dormant at the present time, an improvement in economic conditions will
undoubtedly revive their activity. Therefore, we believe that your committee should be continued and further watchfulness maintained.
WILLIAM A. SCHREIDER,

Chairman;
]OHN APERS.

The report and recommendation to continue the committee were adopted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETURNS
To the M:. w:: Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Returns herewith submits its annual report:
In the report of the Very Worshipful Grand Secretary will be found
the complete statistics of the gains and losses for the year. The gains in
membership by initiation, by affiliation and by restoration to membership
have decreased very much, while there have been increases in the numbers
lost by withdrawals and by suspension for non-payment of dues.
The membership, as of July 31, 1933, is 136,694, which shows loss

a

~~~~~

.

We would draw attention to the fact that 1,110 withdrew from membership and only 618 affiliated from California Lodges, showing that 492
h~ve dropped their membership.
· We would also point out that the report for the year 1932 shows 3,173
members were suspended for non-payment of dues, while this year's report
shows only 302 were restored to membership; less than 10 per cent. This
may be one of the results of mass production. Whatever the cause, the
figures are worthy of serious consideration.
It is to be noted that while the net loss of membership for the year
.
1s 3,942, the loss from suspension for non-payment of dues is 3 992 which
is 50 more than the total net loss. This is a tremendous wasta~e a~d furnishes grave food for thought.
. Lodge members are still feeling the effects of the depression, as
shown by 7,904 having had their dues remitted. But it shows charity is
not dead. There is hope.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON CHANGING
SYSTEM OF PAY OF MEMBERS
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California :
At the eighty-third annual communication, the Grand Master was
"authorized to appoint a committee ·of five to study the matter of an equitable system of pay of members in attendance of Grand Lodge, to report ·
at the next annual communication."
·
Your committee has carefully studied and considered several plans
offered as a substitute for our now existing system, and is thoroughly convinced that our present system, from the viewpoint of Grand Lodge, the
constituent Lodges, and the delegates, is the most equitable that can be
devised.
We therefore offer the following resolution, and move its adoption.
Resolved: That no change be made in our present system of pay of
members.
SIDNEY K. LEHMAN,
Chairman;
HOMER E. VEDDER,

w. J. STEWART,
FRED R. p ARDEE,
FRANK G. FALLOON.

Report and resolution adopted.

TO REDU CE EXPE NSE OF PROCEEDINGS
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of Califorwia:
Your Committee on Finance, in casting around for ways and means
of reducing expenses of Grand Lodge, has come to the conclusion that a
material saving can be effected in the cost of printing and distributing the
Proceedings of Grand Lodge.
The report of the Grand Secretary disclosed that this cost for the
year 1932 was $3,213.95. In addition to this cost is the expense of mailing,
which will be less if the size of the copy is reduced .
In the Proceedings is included the complete reports of all committees.
Many reports contain statistical information which it is desirable to have
placed before Grand Lodge and is helpful to committees and members in
their deliberations, yet which it is believed could be eliminated from the
printed report without taking away fr om those Proceedings but little, if
any, value and ·interest. A casual study of the 1932 copy seems to indicate
that at least one hundred pages or about one-sixth of the volume could be
dispensed with in this manner. Like the reports of other committees, the
complete report of the Committee on Correspondence is included. F or the
preparation of this report Grand Lodge pays $500, and in the 1932 Proceedings its printing required 141 pages, or one-quarter of the entire
volume. There is also printed 800 advance copies of the report for distribution at Grand Lodge during the session.
Your Fi~ance Committee is of the opinion that Grand Lodge should
g·ive consideration to the entire elimination of the correspondence report,
thereby saving the expense of preparation as well as of printing and distributing, a total saving of probably $1,000.
It has been the policy to mail to each Lodge two copies of the Proceedings. It would seem to this committee that one copy would suffice,
thereby saving the cost of about six hundred copies.
Your committee recognizes that all of these items are matters of policy
for this Grand Lodge to determine.
It therefore is bringing in this preliminary report, with the recommendation it be referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
w. P. JEFFRIES,
F.

c. R UPPEL,

ARTHUR

s. CRITES,

JOSEPH M. ARGABRITE,

G. A. H U TAFF,

Committu.

Referred to the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, which committee subsequently reported, approving
the recommendation of the Finance Committee, and it w as

RESOLUTION TO REDUCE SALARIES
Resolved, that the maximum compensation to be received by the Grand
Secretary, from all sources, shall not exceed $5,000 per annum; that the
maximum compensation to be received by the Assistant Grand Secretary,
from all sources, shall not exceed $2,400 per annum ; that the maximum
compensation to ·be received by the Grand Lecturer shall not exceed $3,600
per annum; that the maximum compensation to be received by each of the
two employees in the Grand Secretary's office shall not exceed $1,200; and
be it further resolved, that the Most Worshipful Grand Master is hereby
authorized to appoint a special committee for the purpose of conducting a
survey of the salaries received by the employees of the Decoto and Covina
Homes, and that such committee is hereby authorized to make such reductions in any or all salaries received by these employees as it may deem just
and proper.

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of Coliiornia:
In presenting its annual report to Grand Locjge in accordance with the
provisions of Article VIII-A of the Constitution, the Board of Control
desires to express its appreciation ~f the helpfulness, the co-operation, and
the sympathetic understanding of our' Grand Master, which have contributed so materially to whatever measure of success and accomplishment
your board is able to report at the close of this trying year. Our Grand
Master has attended our meetings;. he has demonstrated a marked interest
in our proceedings and our problems ; and he has -promptly responded to
our appeals. His many courtesies and his helpful suggestions have made
a pleasant duty of .what otherwise might have been an arduous task.
His splendid indorsement in his annual message gives evidence of
understanding and approval of the work of the Board of Control.
Our Deputy Grand Master, our Grand Secretary, and other grand
officers have been helpful and co-operative.
Our Boards of Relief, through their Secretades and officers, generally,
have acted in' greater harmony and accord with the Board of Control than
ever before. During the 1932 communication of Grand Lodge, conferences of 'the Secretaries of Boards of Relief and the Board of Control were
held at Oakland. At that time, and long before N. R. A. had ever been
heard of, our Boards of Relief established a code of ethics and procedure
with which they have religiously complied ever since. Another conference
has been held this year which has been equally beneficial.
The Board of Control's difficulties, if it has had any, are no longer
with the Boards of Relief. They are complying with the provisions of the
Constitution and the regulations of the Board of Control, with very few
exceptions. If there be lack of understanding and co-operation in the
matter of administering relief, it is now with the Lodges and their officers.
It must be admitted, however, that the Board of Control and Grand Lodge
are not and have not been generally approached to relieve their burdens.
The Lodges in most cases assume their supposed rsponsibility without
question and discharge it without appeal. This is genero~s and magnanimous, but it should not be.
Born of the practices that were instituted in the days of old ; because
of the prosperous conditions that then prevailed; because Lodge finances
have been ever at the command of the membership when relief appeals
have been presented, our Lodges, governed by the principle that "Masonry
takes care of its own," have administered charity without let or hindrance,
regardless of whether the applicant was of the California or a foreign
jurisdiction; regardless of authorization or d-i rection; and often, regardless
of the brother's standing in his own Lodge.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

685

The time has come, however, when our Lodges cannot, ,at least should
not continue these practices. More and more of our sister jurisdictions are
declaring that they will not make reimbursement for relief extended without express authorization. Our Board of Control during the year 1931,
wjth the consent and approval of Grand Master Ross, issued a warning to
all Lodges and Boards of Relief to grant only nominal relief and no extended relief to any applicant without first notifying the brother's Lodge,
and receiving instruction and authorization before further relief is granted.
But still this unauthorized and often unwarranted relief work goes on.
In many cases, Lodges make no effort to recover ; to be reimbursed. Perhaps it is all very well for us to say that if the Lodges do not care to protect
themselves it should not be our concern. But we should not say it. How
best can we safeguard our Lodges is then the question. The Board of
Control recommends that it be done through education; that some questions
on, Masonic relief be made a part of the examination of the Master-elect
each year; that we secure the co-operation of our Inspectors through their
district officers' associations.
Few of us realize the full extent of our Masonic relief expenditures.
The Board of Control has made a compilation of the yearly expenditures
for the ten-year period from 1924 to 1933, inclusive. The total reaches an
enormous figure. In that ten-year period the seventeen Boards of Relief
expended the total sum of $960,5li. And it must be noted that only eight
of these boards have been in existence for the full ten-year period ; two
have been in existence for nine years ; one for seven years,; one for six
years; one for five years; two for two years, and two for one year each.
One Board of Relief, Los Angeles, has expended $354,834 in the tenyear time. San Francisco paid out $221,550, and East Bay $156,970 in the
same period.
But this does not take into consideration the moneys paid out for relief
by the many Lodges within and without the Boards of Relief. Each and
every Lodge in the jurisdiction is called upon each and every year to contribute its funds for charity. Without laborious effort it is not possible to
know what this total sum for relief amounts to, but it is safe to say that
it reaches into the thousands-perhaps hundreds of thousands of dollars.
A table showing the total amount of Board of Relief expenditures for
relief alone is appended to and made a part of this report.
Reimbursements
The Board of Control is pleased to report that the amount of money
which Grand Lodge is called upon to pay to reimburse Lodges for relief
extended and for which no reimbursement has been made by foreign
jurisdiction Lodges, is Jess this year than it was the preceding year. The
amount has been lower each succeeding year since the Board of Control
has been in existence. The total amount this year is $2,091.67.

There is not much probability of further reduction. There will always
be certain Lodges in our sister jurisdictions that will not reimburse our
Boards of Relief, and there will always be Lodges in our own jurisdiction
whose ·finances are such that they cannot make provision for their own
brethren and, therefore, cannot reimburse others who do care for them.
In this connection, we desire to again impress upon Boards of Relief,
and Lodges as well, the necessity and importance of reporting to the Board
of Control, without delay, all cases in which there is difficulty of whatever
nature, in securing reimbursement. If the Board of Control is to be of
ser~ice to a Lodge or Board of Relief it must have the case, with all its
details and correspondence, at the earliest .possible moment. The Board
of Control, within the past few weeks, has received a case from a California Board of Relief, in which the board was authorized by the Grand
Secretary of New York two years ago, to care for and ship the remains
of a brother to his New York City Lodge. The claim amounted to $200.
The duty was discharged, but the claim was never presented. The fault,
however, is not with the present officers of the board. Now comes the
Board of. Relief to the Board of Control, appealing for reimbursement.
Imagine the consternation of the New York Lodge, which, perhaps, has
been under the impression all the time, that the California Board of Relief
was generously assuming the expense. Grand Secretary Kenworthy, who
authorized the expense, is dead.
The officers of the Lodge have changed. No one connected with the
case is on duty. The particulars of the case have been forgotten. .The
California Board may receive reimbursement from New York; if it does,

it will be long delayed. The new Grand Secretary of New York knows
nothing of it, but he assured our representative at the Cincinnati meeting
that he would give the case immediate attention. Of course, our Grand
Lodge cannot reimburse the Board of Relief under such circumstances.
Grand Lodge has approved our recommendation that Boards of Relief
refer all such cases to the Board of Control at once, but some of our boards
still hold them to the end of the year. .
Meetings
Your Board of Control has held five meetings during this year. These
meetings have seemed necessary to dispose of controversial matters that
have arisen, of business that has accumulated during the year. The first
was held at San Francisco, November 19, 1932; the second at Los Angeles,
February 18, 1933; the third at San Francisco on May 20th; the fourth
at San Francisco, August 19th, and the fifth during this session of Grand
Lodge in San Francisco. At each of these meetings conferences have been
held with representatives of the respective Boards of Relief, who have
come to the meetings to seek guidance and information. We believe that
with ·the work of the Boards of Relief so splendidly co-ordinated and
standardized, it will not be necessary to hold as many meetings next year.
But the meetings do not tell the ·s tory of the work of the Board of Control.
With the exception ·of the Homes Board, the Board of Control is the only
continuing committee of Grand Lodge.
Every day brings to the Board some new problem to consider. The
correspondence connected with it is voluminous. Up to the end of the year
114 cases had been turned over to the board by Lodges and Boards of
Relief. Each of these cases has required from five to twenty letters. The
Grand Master, sensing the situation, directed and authorized the board to
secure the services of a part-time stenographer. Each case is filed and
all correspondence kept together. T he chairman has briefed each one of
· the 114 cases and has furnished copies of same to the members of the
board and t~ the grand officers.
Withdrawals From Boards of Relief
Notwithstanding the constitutional amendment enacted in 1929, which
provided (Sec. 37) "that the Board of Control shall, with the consent and
by direction of the Grand Master, have power to compel any Lodge within
this grand jurisdiction to become a member of the Board of Relief nearest
its place of meeting," and Sec. 83, amended in 1928, which prescribed the
same requirement in connection with all concurrent jurisdiction Lodges,
two Lodges in this jurisdiction this year have adopted resolutions providing
for resignation and withdrawal from their respective . Boards of Relief.
In each case, the Board of Control, after thorough investigation, has
expressed its disapproval ; and the Grand Master, after ascertaining all the

688

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF · CALIFORNIA

facts, has sustained the Board of Control and has directed the Lodge to
continue its affiliation with the Board of Relief, quoting the Constitution
and declaring:
"May I respectfully call your attention to Section 370 of our Constitution and suggest that in view of the construction of said section
I feel unwilling at this time to approve the withdrawal of your Lodge
from the San Diego Board of Relief. I can appreciate the fact that in
these times of economic stress, situations arise which are extremely
difficult and embarrassing, but I feel that because of this we should all
put forth more strenuous effort to work together in a spirit of cooperation and harmony, to the end that the ideals and objectives of our
Institution may be preserved intact so far as possible."
Disagreement With Uniform Compact :ind By-Laws
In the Grand Lodge communication of 1929, the Board of Control
presented and recommended the adoption of a uniform compact and
by-laws for the government of all Boards of Relief. Grand Lodge unanimously adopted that report and recommendation. Boards of Relief are
now generally working under the uniform compact and by-laws. Nevertheless, in two instances, certain Lodges, members of Boards of Relief,
have refused to accept or to be parties to the said uniform compact and
by-laws. In the first case, the Board of Control sought opinion from the
chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee, who, referring to the recommendation and decision, stated:
"I construe this as meaning that the uniform compact must be
adopted by all Boards of Relief except Los Angeles and San Francisco. It therefore requires affirmative action by the several Lodges
of a Board of Relief, or such action is mandatory. I believe that under
this legislation the ·several Lodges in a Board of Relief must enter into
this uniform compact."
Masonic Relief Association of United States and Canada
By direction and authorization of our Most Worshipful Grand Master, the chairman of the Board of Control was afforded the opportunity
and privilege of attending the sessions of the Masonic Relief Association
of the United States and Canada, which were held in Cincinnati, October 4,
5, and 6, 1933. It was a privilege and an experience well worth while, not
alone for the chairman, who came into intimate contact with the relief
administration of this country and Canada, but for our Board of Control
and for our Grand Lodge as well, because, by reason of those contacts,
we believe we have established a better understanding, a closer affiliation,
and a relationship between our jurisdiction and our sister jurisdictions that
will be of permane~t benefit.
The personnel of the convention exceeded our highest anticipations.
Here were gathered the representatives of more than twenty grand juris-

689

dictions; men prominently identified with the relief and with relief proc·edure of their organizations for many years; veterans of the order, who
have grown gray in relief service, and among them four Grand Masters
eight Grand Secretaries, a number of Past Grand Secretaries, a Sovereig~
Grand Commander of the Scottish Rite and chairman of Boards of Relief
including the head of the oldest Masonic relief organization in the United
States, Master of Louisiana Relief Lodge No. 1, founded in 1848. Your
chairman was impressed with the sincerity and purposefulness of these
men; the· seriousness and the dignity of the proceedings. Theirs was no
joy ride or pleasure junket, etc.; there were no parties or reunions or
entertainments. The delegates were there to get the most out of their
meeting. It was a business convention. The chairman of your Board of
Control was accorded the courtesy of presenting a paper on the relief work
of California and the history of the Board of Control. This afforded us
the opportunity of recounting the work that has been done by our relief
organizations since the founding of our first Board of Relief in 1856, and
of the organization procedure and purposes of our Board of Control.
Particularly did we stress the problems in relief that confront our
Lodges and Boards of Relief ; the problem of the transient Mason, or
rather, of the thousands of them who came to our jurisdiction without
means of support and then come to us for relief; the problem of our too
frequent inability and failure to secure response to our communications by
our sister jurisdictions, as well as the refusal or ignoring of our requests
for reimbursement; in many cases after authorizing our Lodges or Boards
of Relief to extend relief.
It is worthy of note that the presentation of our situation and our
problems met with a responsive reception. It is quite evident that our
eastern jurisdictions, engrossed with their own troubles and problems, have
given little attention and less concern to our problems. Certainly, we do
not desire to annoy them with our problems, only in so far as those problems concern the unfortunate brethren Of their own jurisdictions to whom
our Lodges and Boards of Relief extend aid and relief. Then do we
demand and insist that they give consideration and response. We conferred with the representatives present of those jurisdictions with which
our Boards of Relief and our Board of Control have had unsatisfactory
negotiations during the past year. In every case, we found them sympathetic, willing to co-operate with California. They deplored the lack of
Masonic courtesy; the denial of responsibilities by many of the respective
Lodges, and gave us assurance that they would investigate and endeavor to
·
bring about more and better co-operation.
As a result of our appeal, we were able to present, through M.", W.".
Walter Stockwell of North Dakota, who is a great friend of California
Masonry, and to secure the unanimous adoption of the following resolu"
tion:

690

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"Resolved, that it is the sense of this meeting that it is the duty of each
Lodge of Masons to take care of its own members and, as well, of their
widows and orphans in distress, wherever they be may ; and that in case
of its inability so to do, this duty devolves upon the Grand Lodge from
which it holds its charter, provided that the Lodges furnishing relief shall
in no case go beyond actual necessities, without the expressed authority
from the Lodge to be charged."
That our Eastern brethren have a high appreciation and regard for
California Masonry is evidenced by the following excerpt from the annual
address of M.". w:. Brother Nash, Grand Master of Masons of Ohio,
which will be presented at the annual communication of the Ohio Grand
Lodge in session this week, a copy of which was presented to us at the
convention.' It reads: ·
"On the 12th day of March, 1933, the daily press carried the news of
a disaste.r in and about Los Altgeles, and particularly Long Beach, California. Not knowing the extent of the suffering, and real.izing that. at all
times there are many sojourning Masons in that locality, on the next day
I wired the Grand Secretary of California as follows:
"'The Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of Ohio, desiring to do its part in
relief of distressed Masons of southern California, we will send to you
as soon as banking conditions permit, in a few days, one thousand .dollars
for your relief fund. More will be available if necessary. Request advice
as to necessities of the situation.'
"I promptly received a wire from M.". w:. Brother Frank W . Mixter, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California, as
follows:
" 'Deeply thankful for ·proffered assistance, but so far no outside
money needed. If further survey develops demand for aid we will advise
you. Damage at Los Angeles mainly from broken glass. Long Beach
damage very heavy.'
"Later on I received from M.". w:. Brother Frank W. Mixter,
Grand Master of California, a copy of the report of the loss of the
Masonic Fraternity, which was considerable, but for which no outside aid
was accepted. I here again express the sympathy which the Masons of
Ohio had for our California brethren in this disaster, and add that we
honor them in their desire and ability to meet and care for their own
problems. I recall to you the fact, which is recorded in our Proceedings,
that the beginning of our present emergency fund was a fund returned to
us, from contributions made ·by the Grand Lodge of Ohio, at the time of
the San Francisco fire in 1906 to the Grand Lodge of California for relief.
After meticulously accounting for all receipts and expenditures, the Grand
Lodge of California returned to the Grand Lodge of Ohio $2,184.60. Grand
Master Lewis P. Schaus reported this to the Grand Lodge of Ohio (Pro.

691

1906, page 31 ) , and recommended the establishment of an emergency fund
by the Grand Lodge of Ohio; and following that recommendation our
emergency fund was established in that year in the sum of $2,184.60."
. The~e two inc_idents, the careful accounting by the Grand Lodge of
Cahforma at the time of the San Francisco fire, and the desire today of
the Grand Lodge of California to meet its own problems is indicative of
the character of California Masonry. The Grand Lod~e of Ohio here

and auto insurance are carried. One automobile is used.

of board, and 219 by Funeral Committee. Total number of funerals, 251.
