Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred trial record
.No. 787, tried by Live Oak Lodge No. 61, begs leave to report as follows:
The accused, one E. L. P., was charged with un-Masonic conduct, as
set forth in seven specifications. He was found guilty on each of these
specifications, also found guilty of the charge of un-Masonic conduct, and
the penalty was fixed at suspension. The accused has appealed.

712

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

This record, and the points raised on appeal, present some very troublesome questions. In order to adequately present these questions to you it will
be necessary to present the matter in some detail.
The first specification alleges that the accused addressed a circular
letter generally to the members of George Washington Lodge. This letter
reads as follows :
.
"San Francisco, September 2, 1932.
"To the Members of Geo. Washington Lodge.
"Dear Sir and Brother :
"There are three proposed amendments to the charter of the City
and County of San Francisco governing municipal employment, now
being circulated for signature, which, among other things, would
drastically and permanently cut wages and salaries and seriously affect
the pension system.
"The following members of Geo. Washington Lodge No. 525,
F. & A . M., are city employees whose incomes would be seriously
affected should these amendments take effect :
"Thomas M. May,
Paul F. Kiesow,
Maurice N. McCreary,
Thomas B. Johnson,
Geo. F. Staff,
Cleveland Sturke,
}. J. Burns,
Eugene L. Packard,
John Johnson,
Thomas Patterson.
"In addition to the abave, it is estimated that there are 1500 to
2000 Master Masons in the service of the City and County of San
Francisco.
"Aside from the injury to these brothers, there are other important objections to the proposed amendments.
"In the first place, the amendments will undoubtedly delay the
return of prosperity to San Francisco because every wage cut means
reduced purchasing power. Business needs increased not decreased
purchasing power in order to revive.
"Secondly, these amendments propose permanently to reduce the
standard of living of 13,500 families to a level fixed on the basis of
the worst depression in our history and will make that lower standard
the excuse for still further lowering of wages and salaries paid in
all fields of private employment.
"Thirdly, these amendments will not save any money to the taxpayer. If any amendment is carried to reduce the wages of municipal

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

713

employees, it will automatically stop the voluntary contribution of
$1,500,000 now being given by them to the Unemployed Relief Fund.
The burden of making up that $1,500,000 will then fall directly upon
the shoulders of the taxpayer . .
"This is a request that you refuse to sign or support in any way
·any petition for charter amendments affecting municipal employment;
and, in the event you have already signed petitions for these amendments, that you kindly write to the Registrar of Voters, City Hall,
withdrawing your name from such petitions.
"Sincerely and fraternally yours,
"(Signed) EUGENE PACKARD,
"Office Phone WE st 0191."
The accused freely and frankly admits the mailing of this letter to
the members of his Lodge. The finding of guilty, therefore, of the facts
alleged in the first specification is correct. This does not determine, however, that these facts constitute un-Masonic conduct.
The second specification reads as follows :
"Second. That the charter amendments referred to in said letter
were, at the time of the issuance of said letter, a matter of controversial politics engaging the attention of the citizens of the City and
County of San Francisco, State of California."
The evidence with reference to these proposed charter amendm~nts is
to the effect that petitions were being circulated for the purpose of having
same placed on the ballot; the proposed amendments were never placed
on the ballot and were not submitted to the electorate of San Francisco.
A copy of the proposed amendments was not placed in evidence at the trial
and is not incorporated in the record.
The gist thereof may, however, ·be inferred from the letter above
quoted. By the finding of guilty under the second specification the trial
commission held that these proposed charter amendments were matters of
"controversial politics."
The third specification alleges that by the issuance of said letter the
accused sought to influence the political action and discretion of the members of his Lodge by an appeal to the selfish interest of said members, and
that the accused sought to promote the selfish interest of himself and such
other members by an appeal to the members of his Lodge.
No direct evidence was introduced in support of this specificatiqn. The
letter sent out by the accused to the members of his Lodge, of course
speaks for itself, and undoubtedly makes clear the purpose which inspired
its mailing.
The fourth specification charges that the accused in issuing said
letter, used the official roster of the Lodge for the purpose of obtaining a

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

list of the names and addresses of the members of the Lodge to whom
the letter was sent. The accused admits this to be the fact, and the finding
of guilty of the facts alleged in the fourth specification was therefore
entirely proper. This, also, does not amount to a determination that such
use constituted tin-Masonic conduct.
The fifth &pecification charges that the issuance of said letter tended
to bring controversy into said Lodge and the Masonic Fraternity into
disrepute.
The accuser introduced no evidence to directly support this specification and left the determination thereof to such inferences as the trial commission might draw from the nature and character of the letter itself and
the matters therein referred to. On the other hand, there was direct
evidence introduced by the accused by several members of the Lodge to
the effect that the sending of the letter did not create any controversy
within the Lodge or among its members. The trial commission, nevertheless, found the accused also guilty of this specification.
The sixth specification is quite long, somewhat involved and charges
several different matters, in substance that concurrently with the issuance
of the letter above quoted, similar letters were sent to members of two
other Lodges by a member in each of said Lodges and which said letters
differed in form only, that the names specified in the letters were in each
instance the names of the members of the Lodge in which the respective
senders held membership. It further alleges that the accused and the other
two Masons sending out such letters were active in promoting the issuance
thereof. The sixth specification then alleges that the then Grand Master
summoned the accused, together with the other two brothers, to jointly
appear before him on the 6th day of October for the purpose of investigation by the Grand Master of the issuance of the letters and the numbers
and names of the Lodges in which similar letters had been circulated. It is
then charged that the accused conspired with the other two brothers to
evade appearance in response to the summons by postponing the date of
appearance to a date after the expiration of the term of office of the then
Grand Master, to the end that it would not be possible for the then Grand
Master to take action upon the matter. Of this entire specification the
accused was found guilty.
In order to properly present the matter it is necessary to review in
some detail the facts which occurred. The Grand Master did issue a summons to the three brothers involved, to appear at his office on October 6th.
In response to the summons the accused addressed a: letter to the then
Grand Master in which the accused asserted that it was impossible . for
him to absent himself from his office at the time mentioned, and suggesting
a date one week later, the letter ending with the phrase, "Trusting this
will not inconvenience you in any way and assuring you that my presence is

yours to command I am sincerely yours, E. L. P." The other two brothers
also summoned ~fore the then Grand Master sent letters to him, in one
of which it was asserted that the brother summoned would be out of the
city on city business on the date mentioned, and in which the other set
forth that he had certain reports which had to be completed by the 12th
of the month and that by reason thereof he could not attend at the hour
fixed by the Grand Master.
·
It is vigorously urged by counsel for the accused that no authority
rests in the Grand Master to issue a summons directing a Mas!er Mason
to appear at his office. Your committee feels that it
unnec_essary for
Grand Lodge to determine here this particular question. Thi~, for the ·
reason that it appears that the then Grand Master, after receipt of the
letter from accused by telephone arranged for the accused to call at
5 :15 p. m. of October 6th, instead of at 2 p. m. This appointment ":as
kept by the accused, as well as by one of the other. brothers involved with
whom a similar arrangement had been made. In view of the fact that _the
Grand Master who issued the summons arranged .and agreed to the appointment at the later hour we are of the opinion that this constituted a retraction of the summons'. at least as to the hour named therein, and that
accused having kept the later appointment cannot now be held to have
refused to obey the summons.
The other matter of importance alleged in specification six, relates
to the alleged conspiracy to avoid appearance in response to the summons.
While the accused freely stated that he had talked with one of the other
brothers involved with reference to the receipt of the summons from the
then Grand Master, it was vigorously denied that there was any conspiracy
or any attempt to evade appearance in response thereto. The accused
likewise vigorously denies that he had in mind that th~ then Grand "¥aster
would go out of office within a short time. There 1s no other evidence
supporting the conspiracy.
In view of the foregoing facts we feel that the finding of guilty under
the sixth specification cannot be sustained.
The seventh specification alleges that between the 30th of September
and the 14th of October the then Grand Master requested the accused on
several occasions to iss~e a letter to the members of 'the Lodge to whom
the previous letter had been sent, reciting the impropriety of the former
Jetter and that the accused persistently declined so to do.
The then Grand Master propcised that the letter to be sent out to the
members of George Washington ' Lodge by the accused, should be in the
following form :

714

715

!s

"To the Members of George Washington Lodge:
"We recently caused to be issued to the members of the Lodge
a letter requesting them to oppose three proposed amendments to the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

San Francisco Charter, upon the ground that their adoption would
reduce the salaries of members of George Washington Lodge whose
names were listed in the letter, and salaries of other San Francisco
Masons, as well as for other reasons stated in the letter.
"We ar·e advised that this was grossly improper, both because of
its attempt to use Lodge membershi>p and the Lodge roster to promote
the financial interest of individual members, and also because of the
political character of the circular; We issued the circular without
authority from the Lodge, and take this means of apologizing to the
Lodge and its members for having engaged in the activity; Masonic
affiliation should not influence their action in such matters.
"Fraternally yours, .. ."
In response to this, the accused, in November, wrote a reply of great
length in which he tOC'Jk the position that the letter proposed by the Grand
Master, and who in the meantime had become a Past Grand Master, made
him confess that the letter sent out by him was of a political character,
whereas he had consistently taken a contrary position. In this letter the
accused points out that he had consulted various prominent Masons, among
them a. Past Grand Master, who concurred in his views· that the original
letter was non-political in character. He further stated that he felt it
would be un-Masonic for him to admit guilt where he felt there was
none. He, however, proposed to publish in his Lodge bulletin a statement
as follows:
"I was advised by Grand Master Gaylord that the letter I mailed
to the members of George Washington Lodge was ill advised and
improper, but I do not agree that I have committed any un-Masonic
act in sending out this letter which was to protect those members of
George Washington Lodge employed by the city from a reduction of
wages for all time, and also to protect their pension when they had
reached the age of 70. Inasmuch as it has created a controversy, I am
sorry I sent it out, and I trust the brethren will understand my position."
He closed the letter by stating as follows: "I would submit to such fair
modification of this · letter that you might suggest, but .beyond this I
cannot go."
Your committee is of the opinion that the accused should have been
found not guilty of the seventh specification, because we can see no
Masonic offense involved therein. The sending of the letter of retraction
or apology was proposed by the Grand Master for the purpose of correcting the harm which he conceived had been done; in which event, undoubtedly, the matter would have been permitted to drop; in fact, the Grand
Master so indicated. If the accused desired to stand upon the position

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

717

which he had taken and declined to make a retraction except in the form
proposed by him, we feel that he had a right to do so, and that the
question of whether he had then been guilty of any un-Masonic conduct in
the first instance could accordingly be determined,
U Grand Lodge concurs in the views which we have heretofore expressed, this matter then narrows itself to a consideration of the questions
as to whether there was un-Masonic conduct on the part of the accused
in sending to the members of his Lodge the letter above quoted, and in
using the Lodge roster in so doing. The gist of the entire matter is involved
in these two questions.
There may well be a diversity of op1mon as to whether the letter
sent by accused fo the members of his Lodge involved a matter of controversial politics. To define what is and what is not political in character
involves many and varied difficulties. The line of demarcation between
things political in character and matters merely of civic interest, is not at
all well defined. The accused has consistently maintained that his letter
did not involve a matter of controversial politics, but that it related only
to a matter of civic interesL In support of his position he pointed out in
his letter to the Grand Master that Grand Lodge had heretofore approved
the policy of a prior Grand Master wherein he proclaimed the belief that
there is no higher duty devolving upon us as Masons than t>he duty we owe
the State as citizens; " ... and taking a part in politics-not political in
that sense of artful and dishonest efforts to secure the success of party
schemes ... but politics in that broader and larger sense."
The accused has further shown that prior to sending out the letter in
question he consulted with various Masons as to the propriety thereof,
among whom was included the Master of his Lodge. In each instance the
letter was approved. In this the accused is fully corroborated. Unfortunately, most, but not all of the Masons so consulted were city employees
whO' would be directly affected by the charter amendments referred to in
the letter.
Your committee is thoroughly convinced that the accused acted in the
best of faith, and that he is sincere in the position, consistently maintained,
that he has ·not violated any of the laws of Masonry. Our conclusion in
this respect is verified by the · fact that it was stipulated before the trial
commission that the accused had no intention of violating any of the
laws of Masonry.
As previously pointed out, we feel that the finding of guilt in failing
to respond to the summons cannot be sustained. It impresses us that it is
quite probable that this was viewed by the trial commission as the most
serious offense charged. We are exceedingly doubtful if they had found
the accused not guilty of this charge, as they should have done whether
the penalty in any event would have been more than a reprimand.

719

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

718

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

We are in accord with the attitude of the then Grand Master that the
act of the accused in sending out a letter of this sort addressed generally
to all oI the members of his Lodge was ill advised and that there were
improprieties in his so doing. We also feel that when doubt exists as to
whether a matter is or is not political or controversial in character, the
doubt should be resolved against intermingling such a matter with
Masonry. We recognize the right of every Mason to address his brethren
individually on any proper subject, political or otherwise, but feel that
matters controversial in character should not be brought so intimately in
contact with our Lodges, or their membership as a whole, that the peace
and quiet thereof and the good-fellowship of Masonry may be disturbed.
In this particular case, we must consider the unquestioned good faith
of the accused; the fact, unquestioned and stipulated, that the accused had
no intention of violating any Masonic law; the fact that the accused sought
and obtained advice before sending out the letter, and the further fact that
from ·the record, the matter does not seem to have created any dissension
or discord in the Lodge. Viewing these several facts, we are of the
opinion that suspension is not at all warranted. We also feel that when
the then Grand Master very forcibly pointed out to the accused the improprieties of his act and the accused expressed his" regret and sorrow,
therefor all was accomplished in this case which the circumstances
required.
We therefore offer the following resolution and move its adoption:
Be It R esolved, that the finding of guilt of the accused in the above
matter, and the fixing of the penalty at suspension, be, and the same is
hereby reversed.

Adopted as read.

REPORTS OF THE COMMITTEE ON POLICY
AND GENERAL PURPOSES
Past Grand Master Hervey, chairman of the Committee
on Policy and General Purposes, reported verbally that no
report would be made this year relative to Masonry in other
countries.
Grand Master's Recommendations
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has considered the
recommendations numbered 1 to 6, contained in the message of the Grand
Master, and with regard thereto respectfully reports as follows:
1. The proposal that the uniform code of by-laws be amended by
requiring the appointment of a Budget Committee, whose duty it shall
be to prepare a budget on approved forms, was made because of well
founded complaints that the financial affairs of some of the subordinate
Lodges are managed .very poorly and inefficiently.
Your committee is informed that it is the practice of the Lodges to
receive and act upon the reports of the Secretary· and Treasurer rendered
annually in December and in some Lodges rendered semi-annually, .and
that such reports reflect the transactions of the Lodge, and advise the
members thereof. At the stated meetings of the Lodges, .bills are approved
by vote of the members for disbursements of the preceding month, and
in this way those members who attend Lodge are kept somewhat conversant
with its running expenses. The proposed budget, however, is intended to
reflect the financial requirements for the future and the revenues which
would satisfy those requirements.
The items for the salaries of the Secretary, Tyler and Organist, for
rent, light, heat and similar expenses, are fairly fixed and are necessary
expenses whether stipulated in a budget or not. The remainder of the
Lodge expenses, cqnsisting of Grand Lodge dues, charity disbursements,
and unexpected and non-recurring expenses, are not certain and can only
be guessed at. The matter of revenues is also speculative and, if placed in
a budget, must necessarily be the result of a guess or a hope. No Lodge
can foresee the amount of fees that would be received during the year
from candidates for the degrees, nor the amount of dues that will be paid
by the members. It seems unwise to require by law the setting up of a
budget unless such -budget can be relied upon as showing an approximation
of expense and income. We think that instead of having such a fixed law, ·
that the situation would be better met by leaving to the Lodges the responsibility of the management of its financial affairs, with the earnest recommendation that the Master himself, or through a Budget Committee or
otherwise, make up an estimate of ex11enditures and revenue, and endeavor

721

to· manage the financial affairs of his . Lodge as nearly in conformity to
such estim:rtes as may be practicable and expedient. T his is a businesslike
method of procedure. The Inspector of the district has the power to investigate the action of the Master in regard to this matter, and to report
to the Grand Master any laxity or inattention to the business of the Lodge.
Your Committee also is of the opinion that in the event the law required the making of a budget, it should go further and require that the
Lodge conform to the budget prepared and adopted, for it would seem
nugatory to require a budget if it could be cast aside and made inoperative.
It would be unwise to require by law adherence to a budget which admittedly must be speculative, both as to expense and income.
It has been repeatedly held that all of the funds of a Lodge are charity
funds, and as such can be used in the same manner as income, if the calls
for charity demands such use. Yet it would be improper to set up all the
assets of the Lodge in a budget as proper resources with which to discharge
the expenses shown in the budget.
Your committee also strongly recommends to every Lodge in the
jurisdiction that at the annual meetings in December of this year, when
we are entering upon another year which may be lean and beset with much
financial distress, that the items of fixed expenditures, such as the Secretary's salary, T iler's salary, Organist's salary, rent, etc., be carefully
reviewed and that the same be divorced from sentiment and placed upon
a businesslike basis for the financial good of the Lodge and its members.

Adopted.

6. The Grand Master recommends that the uniform code of by-laws
be amended to limit the Secretary's salary to 10 cents per member per
month. The reason for this recommendation doubtless is that some of the
Lodges are paying excessive salaries to the Secretaries. In such cases, the
Lodges should carefully consider the subject matter and should reduce
the salary to meet the necessities of the situation. A Lodge should not pay
more than its resources and income will reasonably permit for the services
of its Secretary, but at the same time it should recognize the right of the
Secretary ·to be reasonably compensated for his services. It is difficult,
if not impossible, to fix a just rule for a salary scale to apply to the Secretaries of 580 Lodges. These Lodges range from a small body, with probably an unpaid Secretary, to Lodges having more than one thousand mem~
hers. The services of a Secretary fall under three general heads:
First : He is to attend the meetings of his Lodge, record its transactions, make up reports for the Lodge, and prepare and transmit reports
to the Grand Secretary, and otherwise act as the recording officer of the
Lodge.
Second: He is the cashier and fiscal agent of his Lodge, collecting
dues of the members and keeping accounts thereof, issuing receipts, ordering supplies and paying the bills of the Lodge. In this capacity he is a
bookkeeper, auditor, a receiving teller, a paying teller and the financial
agent of the Lodge.
Third : The Secretary is the right hand of the Master in the performance of his administrative duties. He should be active in the relief
work of the Lodge, the contact man with the membership, an invaluable •
special aid to the Master, and if the Lodge holds property or outside
interests, he will find tenants, collect r entals, and other wise render indispensable services.

We are in sympathy with the opinion of the committee that the ritualistic instruction to the candidate should be supplemented by other forms
of instruction. There are many ways by which the candidate can be enlightened as he learns his ritual. However, we cannot agree that such
instruction should be made compulsory and a condition precedent to
advancement in the several degrees. There are many sides to Masonic
education. There is the symbolism which could be explained outside the
ritual. The historical side of Masonry is very important. A study of o\ir
form of organization and our Constitution is well worth while, and the
philosophical side of Masonry should not be ignored. These and many
other phases could well be used in instructing the candidate. The same
candidate might not be interested in all of them, just as many of us are
not interested in all phases of Masonry.
We are not asked to approve the adoption of any particular system
of education, but merely to approve the principle of compulsory instruction.
We do not favor the adoption of any compulsory plan. Once in the Constitution it would be practically as unchangeable as our ritual, and we do
not believe that Grand Lodge is ready to adopt an innovation which is at
variance with our established custom. We believe that any educational
plan adopted should be voluntary and adapted fo the individual need of
the candidate.
However, your committee does not believe that the subject of further
instruction for candidates should be dropped by Grand Lodge. We believe
that it is a very vital question and that much can be done in the way of
supplemental instruction at present, when the Lodges have more time to
give to their candidates. This, however, ·should be voluntary on the part
of the Lodge and the candidate. A coach who is well grounded in the
history and philosophy of Masonry should have no difficulty in giving
instruction suited to the needs of the individual candidate. There should
be a committee appointed by Grand Lodge to which a Lodge could turn
for assistance in this work.
We therefore propose the following resolution and move its adoption :
Resolved, that the committee to study the question of Masonic education be continued during the coming year. That that committee consider
the means and methods of supplementing the ritualistic instruction now
given the candidate. That it consider only such methods as may be adopted
voluntarily by the Lodge and the candidate, attempting to arrive at some
standard practice which can be used by all Lodges desiring to adopt the
plan. That this committee be instructed to report at the next annual
communication.

from Grand Lodge per capita tax at other stated meetings in addition to
the July stated meeting, as at present provided for.
Brother Hughes has stated to·tne committee that his object in proposing this resolution is to give the Lodges greater leeway in remissions
without forcing them to pay the per capita tax. He has given instances in
which he feels injustice has been-done in the collection of the per capita
tax when the remrssion should have been given at other periods, had the
law so provided.
Your committee is of the opinion that the law never was intended· to
relieve the Lodges entirely of the per capita tax in cases of remission of
dues. One standard time for the remission of dues is provided for-the
July stated meeting. This is the logical time for such remissions becau9e it
is the last date on which the Lodge can remit and secure exemption from
the per capita tax in the current year. In other words, Grand. Lodge has
adopted the most advantageous time for the Lodges to take advantage of
their privilege to secure exemption from the per capita tax by remission of
dues. There are of course certain borderline cases which eannot be covered
and in these cases Lodges must pay the per capita tax.
Your committee is of the opinion that the change proposed would make
the procedure more confusing and would not result in any widespread
advantages to the Lodges. It might result in the remission of dues which
are actually collectible and cause a consequent loss to Grand Lodge in per
capita tax.
Fmthermore', its adoption would open the way for· a possible conflict
with Section 128 of our Constitution, which provides that dues shall not
be remitted in advance.
Because of the law forbidding remission of dues in advance the legal
effect of a remission made at any stated meeting prior to July would place
the member whose dues were so· remitted in the position of owing dues at
tile time of the annual report and would impose upon the Lodge the per
capita tax.
We believe that the law as it stands is simple and understandable and
affords ample protection to the Lodges.
We therefore recommend that the proposed amendment be not adopted.

Report adopted.

Form of Dues Receipt
Brother Daniel M. Goulter, Master o.f Argonaut Lodge No. 461, has
submitted to the Grand Secretar;y a suggestion that Grand Lodge consider
the "advisability of changing our dues r.eceipt form to require tha:t the
age, weight, height and color of eyes and hair of member be shown thereon
in much ·the same manner as on a passport or hunting .and fishing license."
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes ·has had the foregoing under consideration, and respectfully reports as follows :
The purpose of the suggestion is to aid in the perfection of identification either for visitation or relief. The adoption of such a plan, however,
would involve a great deal of additional labor on the ·part of secretar·ies
and the maintenance of records of the physical peculiarities of members.
While frau dulent identification is possible under our present receipt
form, and probably would be possible under any form we might devise,
your committee is reminded that the possession of a receipt for ·dues does
not constitute the sole test for Masonic recognition, the requirements of
which, particularly for purposes of visitation, are set forth in Section 124
of the Constitution. Officers of our Boards of Relief are thoroughly
experienced, and alert in the detection of imposters. While an unqualified
applicant may, in rare instances, have obtained relief, it is certain that very
little abuse of this sort has been permitted. The adoption by our Grand
Lodge of the form of receipt suggested would afford us no protection
against an imposter coming from other jurisdictions using the ordinary
forms. Finally, your committee has consulted officials actively 'interested
in our relief work, who express the belief that the suggested change is
unnecessary and ·not advisable.
Your committee therefore recommends that no change be made in our
dues receipt form at this time.

Adopted.

Proposals to Print Decisions in Advance
Mount Vernon Lodge No. 517 submits a proposed new provision to
be added to Section 43, Article 1, Part 2, of the Constitution, relative to
the powers of the Grand Master. The proposed provision appears at page
529 of these Proceedings.
Wesley Kergan and others propose that Section 216 of the Constitution, relative to the presentation of amendments thereto, be rewritten.
This section now provides that proposed amendments to the Constitution
be presented at the Annual Communication. The rewritten draft prepared
by said brethren appears in earlier pages of these Proceedings.
While the foregoing proposals relate to different sections of the
Constitution, they have, in fact, a single purpose, which is to provide
Lodges and the officers thereof with more ample notice than is now available respecting matters which are to be brought before and considered by
Grand Lodge. They indicate that healthy and helpful interest in our legislation which is so prevalent throughout the jurisdiction. They have, therefore, been given very close consideration by your Committee on Policy
and General Purposes, which herewith reports as follows:
While ~he ends sought to be attained by the foregoing proposed
amendments command our sympathetic interest, we believe the working
conditions of Grand Lodge and the offices of Grand Master and Grand
Secretary are such as to detract from the practicability of these measures.
The Grand Master, busy with the discharge of his manifold duties as well
as with his numerous fraternal visitations, does not ordinarily review his
work and prepare his recommendations until the latter days of his term.
· His decisions, of course, are made from time to time and could, if necessary, be made available. They are, however, printed in his annual address,
which is distributed on the opening day of Grand Lodge. They are not
acted upon until the second day following, after review by the Committee
on Jurisprudence. It would seem, therefore, that all members of Grand
Lodge have ample opportunity to study these matters, together with the
Grand Master's recommendations, before being called upon to legislate
thereon.
With particular respect to the suggestion that proposed amendments
be first submitted to our constituent Lodges, your committee feels that
Grand Lodge, being a supreme body, would be unwise in limiting its own
power to take legislative action. Grand Lodge, according to Section 3 of
its Constitution, is composed of its own officers and past officers, together
with Past Masters of this jurisdiction, and the Masters and Wardens of
the several chartered and duly constituted Lodges, or the representatives
thereof duly elected. Constituent Lodges, as such, are not members of
Grand Lodge. They are represented, however, by the officers above mentioned, who are the only members of Grand Lodge and who alone exercise

legislative authority. Lodges may, however, instruct their officers or representatives relative to vo~ing. (Sec. 79.)
The additional suggestion that proposed amendments not submitted
to constituent Lodges by August 25th, may · subsequently be offered .bY
written consent of the Grand Master or by majortiy vote of Grand Lodge,
would, in the opinion of your committee, tend to nullify in practice the
entire plan. Neither the Grand Master nor Grand Lodge would be apt to
deny to any Brother the privilege of introducing a proposed constitutional
amendment ; and since it is a strong tendency of mankind to procrastinate,
we believe the bulk of proposed legislation would continue to be introduced
approximately at the opening of our Annual Communications, as at present.
For the foregoing reasons your committee recommends that the
amendments offered by Mount Vernon Lodge, through Brother Charles
R. Berm~!, its Master, and by Brothers Wesley W. Kergan, Max A. Plumb
and W . R. Ralston, be not approved.
In closing this report it may be stated that our discussions with the
foregoing and other brethren have impressed us with the conviction that
numerous members of Grand Lodge feel, at times, that an improved method
of procedure should be adopted whereby members might be acquainted more
in advance with matters which are to be brought before them. Some
brethren feel that they do not have sufficient opportunity to prepare themselves for the exercise of settled judgment respecting those measures
which may be complicated or controversial. It is, we are sure, much to be
desired that the fullest measure of information be supplied, and while a
number of conditions militate against the end we all have in view, it
nevertheless is possible that procedural improvement can be accomplished.
Accordingly, Past Grand Master W illiam Rhodes Hervey, chairman of
our committee, has engaged to take up a study along these lines in concert
with the Grand Master, Grand Secretary and chairman of other committees
in the hope that some practical and helpful suggestions may be forthcoming
· for consideration at our next ensuing Annual Communication.

Report adopted.
Serving of Beer at Masonic Gatherings
On the 10th day of June, 1933, in response to numerous inquiries, our
M.". W:. Grand Master forwarded a letter to all Lodges within the
jurisdiction directing that until Grand Lodge had passed upon the matter
at our present communication, the serving, dispensing or use of 3.2 per cent
beer be forbidden "in any Masonic hall, or the dining, banquet, refreshments or other rooms connected therewith, or at any Masonic gatherings."
On August 2nd, at its stated meeting, Bay City Lodge No. 526
adopted a resolution which, after reciting its adherence to the Grand
Master's direction, concluded as follows:

732

"Be it resolved, that this Lodge respectfulty petition Grand Lodge to
refrain from adopting the order of the M.". w:. Grand Master."
At its stated. meeting held September 1, Military Service Lodge No.
570 adopted a resolution identical w.ith that of Bay City Lodge.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had the foregoing mattero under consideration- and reports with respect thereto as
follows:
At our fifty-ninth annual communication" in 1908, Grand Lodge
adopted· a resorution by Past Grand Master Motley H. Flint, as follows:
"Resolved, that no spirituous,. malt or fermented liquors shall be
served at any Masonic banquet or gathering."
't'his policy was at that time· incor.po11ated into our law in the form of
a. proviso attached to Section. 89,. governing expenditures of Looge funds
for social purposes, the express language being as follows :
"Provided, that no expenditure whatever shall be made for spirituous,
malt,, or fermented liqUDrs,. nor shall any such liquors be used or served at
any Masonic banquet or gathering."
The foregoing law remained in our Constitution until the adoption of
national. pI'ohibition 1 when it was dropped, being superseded by the provisiol'ls of the Federatl Constitution. It exp11essed a policy adopted by
Grand· Lodge as the result of many years of experience and observation,
and was acce~ed, apparently with general satisfaction; by the craft
throughcmt the jur.isdietion. For a quarter of a century Masonry has
ftourished and prosl)er-ed in California, in conformity, first with its own
law and· latterly with the federal law.
The repeal of the eighteenth amendment of the Constitution of the
United States appears now to be imminent, after which the several States
will again make and enforce their own laws for the control of the sale and
use of l~quors and akoholic beverages of all kinds. It is- presumed that
henceforth the individua.l citizen of California wilt· be enabled legally to
purchase and consume liquors of either high or low alcoholic content.
Your committee, however, sees no reason to justify the abandonment of a
policy and practice applied by our Lodges for twenty-five years. We
believe that our Lodges shoutd continue to operate upon the highest plane
oi manifest propriety, thus observing the admonition so solemnly imparted
to every Master Mason: "To preserve unsullied the reputation of the
fraternity ought to be your constant care" ; and also -the injunction laid
upon every Master at his installation : "To avert the shadow of any scandal
or reproach. against the fraternity."
Regardless of the fact that 3.2 per cent beer is now legalized and that
high-content liquors will soon become legal, it should be remembered that
t;h(: introduction of alcoholic beverages into our assemblies would offend

the feeli~gs· of many thousands of our brethren and thus unnecessa.ril'y
establish causes· of discord and div,ision, and militate aga-inst that harmony
which is the strength and support of our society.
\four committ!ee therefore recommends; first,. that the action of the
Grand Master, as expressed by his. letter of June 10th, be approved, a~d,
secontl that in order to ensure the continued effect of our present practice
so Ion~ a.nd firmly established and so generally accepted by Masons, not
only of this jurisdiction but by those of our sister jurisdictions through?ut

thereto the proviso formerly included, that "no· expenditure· whatever shall
be made for spirituous, malt or fermented liquors, nor shall any such

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE
Right of Member.s to Attend Masonic Trials
To the M.".

w.:. Gram! Lodge of CaUfo1'nJi.a:

Your Committee on Jurisprudence, t'o wliom, at our last annual communic-ation wmr referred· the report of tire Committee- on Grievances, with
respect to ;he right of Masons generally to attend Masonic trials ('Ret>ott
of' Proceedings, 1932, pp. J1Q:3H) gave the matter somewhat cursory
consideration at that annual communication (Report of Proceedings, 1932,
p. 3ij.Z)', but' suggested that it go over un~il this ~ear for d~finite a~tion.
fo this behalf we desire to call attention to an obvious error m the prmt'ed
record. Instead of the language actually appearing therein on page 34J2,
the committee intended to say and report that:
"It is· the unanimous opinion· of. this committee that it is contrary to
the spirit of our institution to declare, as a matter of law, that trials in a

736

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Masonic Lodge may be conducted in secret, and that properly avouched
Masons should not be admitted." The error lay in the unintentional omission of the word "not."
With the foregoing declaration we are still in complete concurrence.
That it may find reflection in our law, we now recommend that Section 202
of the Constitution of the Gran~ Lodge be amended by adding thereto at
the end thereof the following words :
"Any Master Mason in good standing may tie present at such trial;
provided, that the Master may, for good cause and in the interest of justice,
exclude from attendance any person whose presence is not necessary to the
actual conduct of the trial."
That possible abuse of this right, of the sort adverted to in the report
of the Committee on Grievances above referred to, may be avoided, we
also recommend that Section 200 be amended .by adding thereto, after the
word "trial" in the first sentence thereof, the words: "And see to it that
the trial is conducted in all respects · with due order and propriety."
In this behalf, further, we at'e constrained to suggest to the Grand
Lodge that certain requirements appearing in our trial procedure, originally
enacted when trials were usually held in the Lodges in which the charges
were preferred, under the system of transfer now frequently made use of
have become obsolete and unnecessary, and to simplify the procedure we
recommend that the following additional amendments to the Constitution
in reference to trial procedure be had:
Amend Section 205 by eliminating therefrom the entire sentence
beginning with the words "When the trial is concluded" and substituting
therefor the words: "Such record, so made, showing the result of the
actual vote had and rendered upon the various matters to be determined,
as above stated, shall thereupon be signed by the Commissioners there
present, duly attested by the Secretary and delivered to the Master for filing
for safe keeping in the archives of the Lodge. The Master shall thereupon
order the meeting opened for the entry of those lawfully entitled to admission and desirous of attending. And, they being admitted, the Master shall
read the record so prepared and signed. And at the next stated meeting
of the Lodge the Master shall announce the result and the Secretary shall
record the same as the judgment of the Lodge and file the record among
its archives."
These amendments do nothing other than make possible the announcement of the commission's determination immediately after the completion
of its labors and the elimination of the requirement that the announcement
of the result of the trial made in open Lodge shall be in the presence of
the members of the Lodge only.
We believe that the result of the trial should be communicated to those
interested as soon as possible and, that being done, there is no longer reason

for limiting the attendance in the Lodge to members of the Lodge, when
the announcement and entry of the judgment of the Lodge is made.

734

Report and recommendation adopted, · and Sections 200,_
202 and 205 were declared amended by a five-sixths vote.
Proficiency of Senior Deacons
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referred the decision
of the M." . w:. Grand Master and his recommendation in connection
therewith, ·relating to the proficiency of Senior Deacons, have had the
same under consideration, and report as follows:
The Grand Master was undoubtedly correct in his action in causing
the suspenskm of a Senior Deacon who was not qualified, especially as
this Grand Lodge adopted the policy at its last communication that "such
officer should have the certificate of the Inspector of his district as to
his proficiency."
As the resolution adopting this policy at the last communication
reached this committee too late for consideration and action, we now present for your consideration the legislation necessary to make it operative.
We therefore propose the following amendments to our Constitution
and move their adoption:
That after the words "in the work and lectures," in Section 54, the
following be inserted :
"And also to examine Senior Deacons as to their proficiency, and
in particular as to the lecture of the second degree."
And that the following provision be added at the end of Section 137:
"No Senior Deacon appointed shall be installed until he shall have
produced to the installing officer the certificate o1 the Grand Lecturer
or the Inspector of the district in which his Lodge is situated, certifying that he has examined such Senior Deacon appointed, and that he
is duly qualified to give his work, and in particular the lecture of the
second degree."

Grand Lodge concurred in the report and recommendations, and Sections 54 and 137 of the Constitution were
accordingly amended by a five-sixths vote.

of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes, recommending the

Rights of Members of Arrested Lodge
There have been submitted to your Committee on Jurisprudence two
resolutions prepared by the Grand Master's special committee on the affairs
of Fairmount Lodge No. 435, both of which we believe should be adopted.
We therefore recommend that Section 165 of the Constitution, as submitted
by said special committee, be amended by adding thereto the following: "Provided, however, that a member of a Lodge whose .charter
has been revoked, or who shall take his dimit while the charter of his
Lodge is under arrest, may keep himself in standing by making application for membership to a Lodge within the jurisdiction, and by
depositing, in addition to the affiliation fee, if any, required by such
Lodge, a suni equivalent to six months' dues therein, and if re}ected
the affiliation fee paid by him shall be -returned, and the amount paid
as dues shall be remitted to the Grand /Lodge and shall become the
property of the Grand Lodge; and he ·may then apply for membership

737

GRAND LODGE OF CALIJmRNIA

as a non-affiliated Master Mason to any Lodge within the jurisdiction
before the expiration of six months from the date of his prior application upon the same terms as above set forth, and, if necessary, may
continue to so apply at intervals not greater than six months."

Gra~d Lodge concurred, and Section 165 of the Constitution was amend~d as above set out by unanimous vote.
Suspension of Lodge Defined
Y.our -Commitree on Jurisprudence recommends that paragraph one of
Section 229 of the Constitution be amended to read as follows :
"Sec. 229. The suspension of a Lodge is an arrest of its charter
and a temporary prohibition to assemble or work as a legal Lodge,
until the charter is restored by competent authority, excepting that,
with the consent of the Grand Master and after notice to the brethren
who were members of -the Lodge at the time of the suspension, meetings o.f such brethren may be held for the purpose of granting relief,
paying bills or other obligations of the Lodge, granting dimits, or for
such other purposes as may be authorized by the Grand Master. The
places and stations of the officers at any such meeting shall be filled
by members of the Lodge designated by the Grand Master, and upon
the completion of the business for the transaction of which the meeting
was called, the brother acting as Secretary shall prepare and forward
to the Grand Master a statement setting forth the giving of the notice
of the meeting and the action of the members on the matter or matters
presented. On the approval of the proceedings by the Grand Master,
the regular Secretary of the Lodge is then authorized to draw such
warrants as are so approved, and upon the order of the Master, the
Treasurer shall pay .the same from the assets of the Lodge, and the
Secretary is also directed to issue such dimits, certificates or other
documents as may be authorized at such meeting, and so approved.

REPORTS OF COMMITTEE ON FINANCE
Expenses of Grand Lodge

To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
This part of the report of your committee has to do with those two
resolutions presented in Grand Lodge---one by Thayer B. Thomas, Master
of King Solomon Lodge No. 260 of San Francisco, and the other signed
jointly by George M. Donovan, Master of South Gate Lodge No. 320;
Thomas H. Ewers, Senior Warden of Golden State Lodge No. 358, and
Carl Peters, Senior Warden of Arlington Lodge No. 414, all of Los
Angeles, both which resolutions deal with expenses of Grand Lodge and
contain mention of specific items and both which were referred to this
committee for report.
Every item mentioned in these two resolutions have had serious consideration by this committee, and long before the receipt of these two
resolutions, and every item will be dealt with in the general report of this
committee which follows.
It is to be commented that the items of expense to the reduction of
which these two resolutions are aimed, are the result of many years of
previous legislation of this Grand Lodge and that many of these items
were reported against at the time by this committee.
Your committee is of the opinion that expressions of this nature are
to be welcomed. They bring to Grand Lodge a better understanding of the

'

.739

burdens now being felt by our Lodges and brethren, a realization to the
various spending agencies of Grand Lodge of the need of the strictest
economy in the expenditure of . its funds, an opportunity to the various
spending agencies to present to Grand Lodge the justification of the items,
a better understanding of ·au of the efforts and services being performed
and the quieting of criticisms and rumors.
It is believed that a thorough discussion will bring to all a better
understanding of the institutions of Masonry and a greater pride in your
membership in the Order.

Adopted.

Masonic Clubs of the University of California at Berkeley and Los
Angeles
10. Your Committee on Finance has reviewed the reports of the
trustees of these club houses and their request for funds for maintenance
during the fiscal year 1933-1934.
Your Committee on Finance is very much pleased with the manner in
which these clubs are being conducted, and we feel they are operated on
an economic basis. Both of these institutions closed the year with a small
cash balance, and when the funds now on hand (approximately $13,000),
one-half of which will go to each club house, has been transmitted by
the Grand Secretary they will have sufficient money to meet their expenses
until the next annual communication of Grand Lodge.
Your committee, in an effort to reduce the per capita tax levied on
subordinate Lodges, will not this year recommend any tax for the support
of the club houses, but will at the next session of. Grand Lodge appropriate
sufficient funds to maintain them for .the year 1934-1935.

Adopted.

Masonic Homes
21. The report of the Trustees of our Masonic Homes has occupied
many hours of the time of your Finance Committee. This activity of
Masonry in California is the greatest manifestation of its generosities and
the largest justification of its worth, as well as making the greatest call
for its funds.
Realizing that if any reduction was to be made in per capita assessment, the greatest possibility lay in its largest item of expense-operation
and the maintenance of the Homes are calling for 70 per cent of the
revenue of Grand Lodge. The members of your committee have analyzed
~nd ?igested every item of expense-salaries, number of employes, food,
its kmd and. cost, -clothing, medical care, outside relief, costs of operating
the farms-m fact, no part of this activity has escaped their attention and
examination. They have also discussed with 'the Trustees of the Homes
ways and means of reducing the costs to Grand Lodge.
. Al~ this ana!~s'.s and examination have failed to disclose a single item
of _iust1fiable criticism. The Trustees are fully a:live to the need of the
strictest economy in operation.
Among the items given most consideration is the item of outside relie[
1:he Homes report shows this expense the past year was $44,802.33. Much
d1scussi?n was had with the Trustees over this item, and particulady a
suggestion that a maximum allowance to any one person-and considerably
below the average now being allowed-be fixed by resolution. I't appears
~at ali:iost without exception ihese are cases where some exceptional care
is reqmred, due to some malady, and in every case only the barest requirements are granted by the Trustees.
The result of all this effort is the conclusion of your commhtee that
the Homes are care.fully and economically administered.
. Your committee has also discussed with the Trustees the employment,
either by the Grand Master or by this committee, of some outside agency

to make an analysis of all features pertaining to the Homes. The Trustees
assure us .that .they will welcome such an analysis.
For the guidance of future committees, a statement of estimated
income for the coming year of the Homes is included in !his report. It is
as follows .:

Friday, October 13, 1933.
Grand Lodge was called on at 1 :15 o'clock, the Grand
Master presiding.

ANNUAL ELECTION OF OFFICERS

Grand Marshal, Henry G. Mathewson of Argonne Lodge
No. 514.
Grand Standard Bearer, Percy King of Yount Lodge
No. 12.
Grand Sword Bearer, Walter C. Shields of Hawaiian
Lodge No. 21.

The Grand Master declared that the annual election of
officers was now in order. Tellers were appointed, and the
result of the election was a15 follows:

Grand Bible Bearer, Harry Horne of Redlands Lodge
No. 300.

The R.'. W.'. James B. Gist of Pentalpha Lodge No. 202
was elected Grand Master.

Senior Grand Deacon, Sidney K. Lehman of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42.

The R.'. W.'. Randolph V. Whiting of King Solomon's
Lodge No. 260 was elected Deputy Grand Master.

Junior Grand Deacon, Theodore T. Spurgeon of Pentalpha Lodge No. 202.

The W.'. Earl Warren of Sequoia Lodge No. 349 was
elected ·Senior Grand Warden.

Senior Grand Steward, Ralph Merriam of Pasadena
Lodge No. 272.

The W.'. Rollie W. Miller of Sunset Lodge No. 352 was
elected Junior Grand Warden.

Junior Grand Steward, Walter D. Adriance of King
David's Lodge No. 2o<J.

The V.'. W.'. William P. Filmer of King Solomon's
Lodge No. 260 was re-elected Grand Treasurer.

Grand Pursuivant, Warren D. Gill of San Gabriel Lodge
No. 546.

The V.'. W.'. John Whicher of King David's Lodge
No. 209 was re-elected Grand Secretary.

Grand Organist, Charles E. Anderson of Jewel Lodge
No. 374.

The V.'. W.'. Thomas J. Baker of Union Lodge No. 58
was re-elected Grand Lecturer.

Grand Tiler, Frank G. Watson of Pr_e sidio Lodge No. 354.

The Grand Master-elect caused to be read the names of
the appointive officers as follows:
Grand Chaplain, Rev. Herbert P. Shaw of Ingleside
Lodge No. 630.

The M.'. W.'. Dana R. Weller, Past Grand Master, was
appointed Master of Ceremonies, and the officers-elect and
appointed, excepting the Senior Grand Warden, the Grand
'1 'reasurer, Grand Sword Bearer and the Grand Marshal,
were installed by the retiring Grand Master in d1fe and
ancient form,

796

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Past Grand Master Wm. Rhodes Hervey, speaking for
Pentalpha Lodge No. 202, then presented to Grand Master
Gist a gavel in the form of a pentagon, fashioned from wood
grown on the grounds of the Masonic Home at Decoto.
Inspector John A. Madden of Honolulu, in behalf of the
brethren of · the Hawaiian Islands, invested the retiring
Grand Master with two royal leis, with the aloha of his
brethren.
Inspector Edwin S. Lawson of the 64th Masonic district
presented the retiring Grand Master, in the name of the
Grand Lodge, a set of silverware.
The Grand Master then clothed his predecessor with the
apron of a Past Grand Master, and also invested him with
a diamond-studded lapel button indicative of his present
rank.
The usual interchange of lapel buttons was had, and
after the announcement of the appointment of Chas. Albert
Adams as Trustee of the Masonic Homes, vice self term
expired, at 5 :25 o'clock p. m., all business being now completed, Grand Lodge was closed in am pie form.
JAMES B. GIST,
Grand Master.
JOHN WHICHER,
Grand Secretary.

Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California, 1933
REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
CORRESPONDENCE
October, 1933
BY JESSE M. WHITED

.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Master, Officers, Members of the
Grand Lodge of California, and Brethren of this Jurisdiction:
Herewith is submitted my Thirteenth Report as Chairman of the
Correspondence Committee. As usual, the views expressed under the
various topics are the individual ideas of the Chairman.
No matters of unusual importance to the Fraternity appear to
have occupied the attention of the various Grand Lodges during .the
past year. In treating the various Topics, and expressing our opinions,
we trust that we may be in the position of a Speaker who often appeared upon the public rostrum. Being invited to fulfill an engagement in a city where he remembered he had spoken once before, he
wrote to a friend, asking if he could recall the subject of his address
at that time and a general idea of what he had said. The candid
friend replied that he had interviewed a number of persons, whom he
remembered had been present at the time in question. They had
uniformly replied that they did not remember the Speaker or anything that he had said, so consequently he was safe in discussing any
subject he pleased.
Some of the Topics or conditions that are of general interest and
find space in the various Proceedings, but which are not treated in the
general body of this Report, may be briefly summarized as follows:
BULLETINS-GRAND LODGE: Some Jurisdictions issue
Bulletins or publications at regular intervals, setting forth items of
general interest to the Craft. They have either a limited circulation
or are sent to all members. In both cases satisfactory results are
reported. The question of expense in the larger Jurisdictions has
been found to make the practice prohibitive.
One Jurisdiction issued a regular publication financed by voluntary subscriptions. It was found that this was not satisfactory, and
the Grand Lodge decided to furnish the paper to all members, meeting
the expense out of the per capita tax paid by the constituent Lodges.
This seems to be the only way to reach all the members, provided the
finances of a Jurisdiction are sufficient to take care of it.
DUAL MEMBERSHIP : Continued consideration and education along the line of Dual Membership has ·caused additional
Jurisdictions to adopt the plan.

The establishment of Lodges of Research, organized for the

EDUCATION-MASONIC: During the past years practically
every Grand Lodge, in one form ~r another, has endeavore? to handle
the question of Masonic Education. Many have be~ome dis~eartened
with the lack ofinterest and dropped the matter entrrely, while others
continue their search for a satisfactory solution. We believe it is now
generally conceded that a large proportion of the. Fraternity are. not
interested in Masonic Education, either along special or general lines.
The method that seems to be producing the most sa~isfacto~y resu.lts
is one designed to educate the candidate during the time he 1_s receiving his Degrees or immediately thereafter. It ~as · the advanta~e of
supplying information when needed and . most hkely to be retained.
Even if this plan is not adopted we beheve that perhaps the same

This instruction would be in addition to the "coaching work" as
required by present regulations.
FUNERALS: J. Edward Allen, Chairman of the Correspondence Committee of North Carolina, says: "The business of revising
the Masonic burial service is a popular indoor sport." No Ritual has
yet been adopted which seems to be generally satisfactor~, even .to
the Jurisdiction adopting it. Secretary Clandy of the Masonic Service
Association has recently prepared a Digest of all of the Funeral
Rituals, segregating it by sections, subjects and topi~s. This sh?uld
be of material assistance in helping prepare a satisfactory Ritual
along the lines of present day ideas.
LIFE MEMBERSHIP: Some of the Jurisdictions have allowed constituent Lodges to award Life Memberships to Brethren
who have been on the rolls for a prescribed number of years, or to
those who have or were supposed to perform conspicuous se_rvice.
The result has been that in a number of instances the Lodges found
themselves in serious financial difficulties, and Grand Lodges are
tightening up on the practice.
The suggested Oregon plan of allowing Life Membership to be
paid for on a graduated scale does not seem to have received favorable
consideration. Undoubtedly the safest method from a financial standpoint is the one requiring payment of a sufficient amount to produce
annually, at the current rate of interest, an amount equal to the dues
of the Lodge.

LODGES-CONSTITUENT: We believe the following extract
from the Correspondence Report of Chairman J. Edward Allen of
North Carolina covers the situation entirely:
"All members of our Lodges may be divided into three classes- .
those who are attracted by the Masonic Ritual, those who will attend
Lodge and take part in its activities because they find other modes
than the Ritual, of satisfaction therein; and those who do not take
part in any Lodge activity, nor will they. We think these three groups
include just about all of our members. Let us see, taking the second
class first.
"There are in these latter days many thousands of Masons who
want no more of degree work. It is not inspiring, stimulating or
satisfying to them. They shun it. But they see in the beauties of
Masonry, its philosophical background, its social philosophy, that
which appeals to ·them. They love Masonry in spite of its Ritual, its
lectures, its circnmambulations, its dialogue, its addresses and readings. To them, many who enjoy the Ritual of certain degrees s~em
to border on Sadism-enjoy seeing the candidate "put through."
There are in existence today certain organizations making good standing as a Master Mason a prerequisite, which number in their membership many Masonic leaders, which have Rituals of their own but
very frankly never use them-they appeal to those who have borne
the burden and the heat of the day in degree work and desire to lie
down in the pastures green of philosophy, pure and applied. For these
Masonry hqs a beautiful field. One sees few of them taking dimits or
going via the N. P. D. route-it is only those who have tired of Ritual
without finding its consummation in philosophy and Masonic living,
who depart from us voluntarily.
"We must always depend on Masons who love a beautiful Ritual
beautifully exemplified. To these, all honor! ·We have a profound
vote of gratitude to those fellows who really feel that the biggest
thing in Masonry is to make the very best, deepest and most profound
impression on the candidate in the ceremonies. We must help them
in their chosen field. We must help them to expand the great vision,
so that if at last they weary of this work, they will proceed to the
other group of those who delve in the philosophy and the applications
of Masonry's teachings. Many thousands of these good ritualists
have withdrawn from us because they have not been, in the midst of
their work, drawn into its applications. We have not yet found one
who had learned in the fullness of things the true secrets of a Master
Mason, who saw fit to throw them overboard. It takes untold patience
to be a real Master Mason. This scribe has, at one time or another
in his Masonic career, been buffeted about, traded around, thwarted,
disappointed, enough to sour one who thought the secrets of a Master
Mason consisted in certain syllables in an unknown tongue, beyond
hope of any desire for further contacts with Masonry; but we pride

ourselves in the belief that Masonry is bigger than this sort of
things. Some days ago this writer accidentally remarked in the course
of an address that he had at sundry times in the course of a quarter
of a century of public service as a teacher, been threatened with horse. whippings, shotguns, personal violence and a museum full of other
things. Being asked what happened as the results of these events, we
had to answer that nothing had happened except that so far as we
could remember, all who uttered. such threats are now dead. He who
is outside the circle of true Masonry will eventually be lost to true
Masonry or become known for what he is.
"The name of 'Freemasonry' is indeed a talisman to many. We
are persuaded that of the tens of thousands who flocked into our
Lodges around 1918-1920, many there were who were attracted by
that talisman. We know that there are many on our rolls today who
keep their names on the books because of the prestige of that name.
We could name to you many such in the bat of an eye-men who have
not attended a meeting in a decade, who have no notion of t?e real
meaning of .Masonry in theory or in practice, but who pay their dues
as promptly as anybody. To them Masonry is satisfying ~ecause the
magic of the name is something with which they do not desire to part;
that was what they sought in the beginning, and that leaves no cause
for complaint. Try to enlist one such in the work of the Lodge, and
he finds it necessary to do something else. He pays his dues and
assessments, but his voluntary contributions ~e likely to be s~ll.
Of the philosophy of Masonry he knows nothing. When,. a finan~1al
pinch comes and he has to dispense with some of the thmgs which
lend respectability to life, he throws Masonry overboard."
Whether Masonry is best served by the large Lodge or the
small one, is also a debatable question. In the day of "Big Business"
a Lodge with a large membership seems to be the one best fitted to
cope with the financial demands. A sm?ll :1-?dge, however, doe.s serve
a purpose, as it furnishes a means for ind1v1dual contact that is la~k­
ing in the large Lodge. Many of the Grand Masters are advocating
consolidation of small Lodges, which in a number of cases should
be done.

MASONRY'S OBJECTIVE: We believe that the following
from the Message of the Grand Master of Illinois, presents in a very
able manner the idea that the future of Masonry depends upon the
individual:
"For many years that have passed, we have gone along on the
crest of the waves, happy in our prosperity and thoughtless as to the
future, with the spirit of 'Eat and be merry.' We have carried on,
thinking that such prosperity was perpetual and everlasting and that
it would continue forever. Then came the change, and Lodge after
Lodge, being caught in bank failures or loss of investments, have
faced embarrassing financial situations. Along with the unfortunate
change have come multiplied calls for charity from their membership
and, the Lodge not being able to cope with these calls, constant and
repeated pleas have been made to the Grand Lodge for relief. Masonry, in its inception, had for its fundamental principle a personal
responsibility. A member, becoming sick or in need, made an appeal,
and his Brother in Masonry, recognizing the call as a personal one,
hastened to relieve his wants. But as time went on our membership
drifted away from the principle and took the more modern way of
'letting George do it.' When calls came the Lodge hired someone
to sit up with the sick Brother, or a check was sent to relieve his
distress. In that way we have wandered away from the real, personal
obligations which we all accepted and which say, ' I will aid and
assist' and 'I will ever go on foot and out of my way to assist,' and
our Institution has been greatly weakened in the good it could do.
We must return to this fundamental and, recognizing our individual
responsibility, we will find that a great many of our financial problems
will be solved and Masonry will take upon itself a new awakening."
If Masonry is to revert to its original idea of being a Fraternity
rather than a Philosophy or Institution, the character of the Individual, his conception of Masonry and how he must exemplify it in
his daily and Masonic life, will be the best method of changing the
viewpoint of a great many as to the real purpose of our Institution.'
PROCEEDINGS-GRAND LODGE ~ The necessity for economy in general business as far as Masonry is concerned is reflected
in the publication of the Proceedings of the various Grand Lodges.
Some of the Jurisdictions, wedded to the idea that it is necessary to
publish a complete roster of all their members, have omitted them.
Detailed statistics have been omitted. Committee Reports and Addresses have been shortened or not published, and other economies
of a like nature adopted.
Some have even gone so far as to eliminate the Report on Foreign
Correspondence, or limit the space· allotted to it. We are, of course,
prejudiced, but do believe that this Report is of value to the Members.
While it may not reach all of them through the published Proceedings,

RECORDS: As "Coming Events cast their shadows before,"
so Grand Masters are urging the collection and preservation of old
records and interesting documents touching upon the early history
of the Fraternity in their respective Communities. One Jurisdiction
requires that the Charter of the Lodge remain with the Grand Secretary, duplicate or photostatic copy being delivered to the Lodge.
The agitation for the publication of Masonic histories and the
establishment of Museums is receiving increased attention. The.
increase in the number of recommendations along this line and interest
in it generally, speaks well for the future.
RELIEF: Existing economic conditions, as far as Masonic relief
is concerned, may be a blessing in disguise. We believe it is bringing
home to the members that the Fraternity is not a Beneficial or Insurance organization. As one Grand Master stated, it has helped dispel
the erroneous idea that Masonry does not assume the full responsibility and care, not only of its members in distress, but also their
ancestors and descendants. Perhaps Masonry as a whole is not
entirely free from blame in creating this impression. The establishment of Homes, both for the aged and young, are the most promine'nt
symbols of Masonic activities presented to the public. Their thought
as to the ultimate aim of the Fraternity, as far as its members are
concerned, is based upon this evidence.
The Talmud says in effect, that he who makes a gift only after
his death gives Copper; he who gives while ill in the hope of reward
through recovery gives Silver; but he who gives while well and
enjoying the many blessings and opportunities of life gives Gold.
YOUNGER GENERATION: In Western Australia the Grand
Master has power to grant ·a dispensation to initiate petitioners between the ages of 18 and 21 years, provided such petitioners are the
sons of Masons. One time in France this custom was followed, the
petitioner being known as a "Lewis." There are numerous theories
as to why this term was adopted. Following the builder's art, it may
perhaps be traced to the name of the Mason's aid that is used in
moving large building stones. The Acacia Fraternity, an organization
restricting its membership to Masons attending colleges and universities, has lately changed its requirement so that sons of Master
Masons are _eligible.
The Order of De Molay, while not a Masonic organization or
a part of the Masonic system, but having its advice and co-operation,
is endeavoring to train young men between 16 and 21 to maintain the
ideals of clean speaking, clean thinking and clean living. That this
thought appeals to the youth of today is evidenced by the fact that

ATTENDANCE
Existing conditions have had a tendency to increase Attendance
at Lodge meetings, and particularly so where leadership in a Lodge
has developed a program of interest. In seeking entertainment the
average man has been compelled to economize, and perhaps his desire
to talk his troubles over with someone else has caused him to seek
a place where he can find a sympathetic listener.
The mere conferring of degrees has ceased to have very great
attraction. Even the finest drama, opera or other form of entertainment is very rarely witnessed a second time by the same person,
and this is particularly true of subordinating the purpose of the Lodge
to only conferring of degrees.
There must be leadership capable of advancing something for
. the Members who are not interested in mere routine. If the Fraternity
and Lodge is to prosper it must furnish something in which all of the
members can participate and not endeavor to confine activities to
only. one phase of our Institution, and that the most uninteresting.
Canada (1932):
{Grand Master): My attention has frequently been called to the time
that is unnecessarily wasted in the Lodge room. At the hour appointed
for opening the Lodge the Master and his officers should be in their
respective chairs and the members in their seats. There is a tendency
among some members to linger in the ante-room and enjoy a smoke or
a visit with their friends and complaint has been made to me that some
have so far forgotten their duty as to indulge in a game of bridge or
billiards while the Lodge was in session.
The recreation rooms are not provided for any such purposes. When
the Master's gavel calls the Brethr~n to order every member except the
Tyler should be in the Lodge room unless he has had some special duty
assigned to him by the Master or Junior Warden which calls for his
presence else~here. The rules of order should be strictly observed. While
no attempt should be made to stifle a full and free discussion of any
question under consideration, the Master should see to it that there is
no idle repetition and that the Brethren adhere to the rules laid down
for their guidance. It frequently occurs that a Brother moves a resolution
which meets with the general approval of all present, yet there is a
painful interval before a seconder is secured. This could be very easily
overcome by having a general understanding that th«; Senior or Junior
Warden assume that duty if it be not promptly seconded by some other
Brother present. Masters have been known to engage in conversation
with others sitting in the East. While this may be ent\taining to those

In ancient times and. up until the opening of the Twentieth Century,
the atmosphere surroundmg a Lodge meeting was entirely different from
what it is now. The members were glad to come from far and wide in
ord.er to see ~nd converse with each other. For many that was almost
their ~nly social c~ntact and the post-Lodge gatherings were the bright
spots m an otherwise drab and dreary routine. E ven in the larger com-

munities there was not much to draw the members away from Lodge
interests, but those days have gone forever.
The Masonic Fraternity, founded in antiquity and steeped in reverence for the ancient ways, has found it painfully difficult to adapt itself
to the modern "high powered" conditions. Philosophic and abstract teachings, no matter how beautiful, do not in themselves attract large numbers
of people in these days. Men no longer gather in taverns and coffee rooms
to discuss philosophy, science, literature and life. Things are moving too
fast. When we learn how to combine the beauty and moral ·value of
our teachings with attractive entertainment, the problem of attendance
will be solved.
Ohio (1932):
· (Grand Master}: Good of the Order: Open Lodge at the appointed
time. Conduct the business of the Lodge in a dignified, orderly manner,
then close. The Brethren who care to visit may do so with more freedom
and less disturbance after Lodge than in it. Those who want to go home
may go.
Past Masters should be frequently seen (in the Lodge), but not too
often heard.
The quickest and surest way to ruin a good Lodge is to continue
the same Brethren in office from year to year. The best talent is frequently on the side lines.
If your Lodge officers persist and insist on banking Lodge funds
with their own, put them under bond. You and they will be embarrassed
sooner or later. The bond will protect against financial loss.
The Grand Lodge will give permission to smoke in Lodge to all
Brethren who smoke in their church. All others must refrain.
The little things as well as the big ones make Freemasonry different.
The big things force recognition and obedience. Neglect of the little
ones will bring your Lodge to the level of just another meeting.
Are you a Freemason or just a member of the Lodge?
