CANDIDATES
The present loss of members has been attributed to the influx
during the war and the boom times following. We believe these are
not the main causes. It can be ascribed rather to lack of interest by
reason of not furnishing what the average member .wants. One of
the most serious problems before the FraternitY is building for the
future. We think the question may properly be asked if when we
return to normal times the same desire for Numbers rather than
Selection will not ultimately produce the same condition. Lodges who
have suffered financially will either consciously or unconsciously
consider candidates from the viewpoint of quantity rather than quality. There is only one way that this can be prevented and that is by
positive legislation.
We have heretofore advanced the idea that a candidate and those
recommending him should appear before the Officers of the Lodge
for a personal examination before his application is received. This
should precede the formal reference to an Investigating Committee.
The candidate should be impressed with the purposes of Masonry
through a system such as is used in some of the other Jurisdictions,
outlining just what Masonry is and what part he is to play in it. A
time .limit should be fixed between each degree sufficiently long to
allow the candidate, with proper instruction, to understand the significance af what he is receiving or is about to receive. We have
had our period of inflation, and to try the other extreme might be of
benefit.
District of Columbia (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee}: We still find in the Proceedings many cases where dispensations are issued for shortening the
time between degrees. Sometimes reasons are given and sometimes they
are not, but this writer regrets to see a growing tendency along this line.
If we have a rule we ought to stick to it, and even if it proves to be a
bad one we ought to stick to it until it is changed.
One of the things that first impressed this writer about Masonry was
the extreme deliberation with which he was compelled to await his degrees, and the thoroughness with which it was impressed upon . him that
ample time should be allowed for a candidate to become proficient. We
are feeling the effects today of the almost total disregard for time between
degrees that was indulged in during the recent days of world upheaval,
and this writer had hoped that by this time a lesson had been learned.
Certainly it is calculated to appeal to a candidate's sense of personal
importance to know that the law had been set aside in his case, and likely

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): So far as we know, all
-Grand Lodges provide that the names of applicants for the degrees shall
be presented to the entire membership of the Lodge, which, of course,
entails the necessity of bulletins or notices at regular intervals. If ~ent
under seal as first-class mail there is only a remote possibility of these
names falling into the hands of anyone not entitled to know them, but
several cases are recorded during the past year where postal cards were
used, indicating that the Masters so sending them out had no sense of their
responsibility in the matter.
We sometimes seriously doubt if the practice of sending out these
names, even in a sealed cover, is either necessary or advisable, though
of course it must be admitted that every Brother is entitled to know who
is applying to his Lodge. But even under the present plan it is often the
case tha.t some Brother wonders how some other Brother got into his
Lodge, all unmindful of the fact that he could have kept him out if he
had any legitimate reason, had he only read his bulletin.
The right way to find out who is applying to your Lodge is to attend
the communications of your Lodge and hear the petitions read, but if it
should ever happen that all the members of a Lodge came to a communication it would no doubt cause the Master's death from heai:t failure, so
we shall probably be obliged to struggle along under the present plan till
some better one can be devised.

* * * * *

(Chairma11 Correspondence Committee): In spite of the profound
respect in which the ba1lot is held by Masons, it is the occasional cause
of no little trouble. While its purpose is primarily to protect the West
Gate from the intrusion of improper persons, it is sometimes used for
private purposes, and its complete inviolability often results in injustice
to a candidate, although be it said of Grand Masters that when any such
injustice is discovered it is quickly righted.
In the opinion of this writer the ballot box is one of the most important pieces of furniture in a Lodge, because it is through the ballot
that the personnel is selected, and a collective selection of men for
Masonry is not always wise. Suppose it does take a little time to vote
on candidates individually. It is time well spent, and calculated to prevent
many regrets at a later day. This writer is not now nor ever has been
in favor of the collective ballot for Lodges.
As an example of how carefully the ballot should be guarded, a very
unusual occurrence is recorded in the proceedings of one Grand Lodge.

Maine (1933):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Here is a "ruling" of Grand
Master Sykes of Louisiana which never would have been considered with
us, much less referred to a Grand Master. "A man desirous of being a
.Mason states his birth was illegitimate, but the man is living a respectable
life. Is the man eligible? Answer: We cannot accept the application of
a man who is of illegitimate birth." We have rubbed our eyes several
times since reading that answer, in order to be sure we had read it aright.
The first reading put us back in the "dark ages" of history, the second
reading reminded us that last summer, at The Hague in Holland, we saw
a score of instruments of torture, thumb-screws, stocks, ropes for drawing
and quartering, and such like ehgineery of pain. And the third reading
reminded us that this was the year of our Lord and his Divine Grace,
1933. The church of today would not do that cruel, heartless thing, make
a good man suffer by denying membership in its fellowship and communion. This correspondent has often thought that in strictest biological
truth there is no such thing as an illegitimate child; plenty of illegitimate
fathers and mothers, but every child arrives by the natural laws of birth,
and why stigmatize and brand an innocent child, especially after he has
reached man's estate and is living a respectable life, with a term of almost
vindictive 'reproach, and why should our Institution take that attitude if
our principles and obligations mean what we believe they do? Now it
may well be that the Code or Constitution of an honored sister jurisdiction compels that attitude, and if so-while in one sense it is none of our
business-in another and altogether higher sense, common humanity must
speak out in the name of fairness and in the spirit of the Great Light,
and say that Code and Constitution needs amending in the light of that
word from Galilee, "Judge not." Perhaps we have been carried a little
too far in this matter, but we deeply feel the inhumanity of the situation.
As we read of the splendid philanthropies, the Hospital for Crippled
Children and the Children's Home we are certain that this is not the real
spirit of Masonry in Louisiana which has always challenged our respect
and veneration.

the fact that it is, in a large measure, due to the lack of comprehension
of the philosophy of Freemasonry. In our Lodges, time should be found
for an explanation of the meaning of many things which every Freemason
should know, and, because so many have no chance to participate in the
ritualistic work, they become indifferent and remain away. No one who
has any comprehensive conception of Freemasonry ever loses interest,
but, on the other hand, as his knowledge progresses his interest grows.

South Australia (1933):
(Grand Master): The duty and responsibility which devolves upon
every Freemason is to use his vote to guard the portals, and to keep without
those who are not worthy to participate in our privileges. But the other side
of the moral obligation is that the privilege of the vote should not be used
to deliberately or thoughtlessly and undeservedly, yet irrevocably, besmirch
the reputation of another. A black ball in the hand of a conscientious member, who considers the question and nothing but the question whether the
candidate will justify the trust of the Brethren, may be the safety device
for preventing a subsequent Masonic disappointment. But a black ball cast
by one . who is actuated by unworthy motives, or influenced by envy or
spleen, is a weapon of merciless power and oppression: "Oh, it is excellent
to have a giant's strength; but it is tyranno'us to use it like a giant."
It must be understood that it is quite as constitutional to cast a black
ball as a white one, and that the Brother who exercises this privilege
conscientiously and righteously is entitled to be protected from suspicion
and abuse. But it cannot be too forcibly impressed on Brethren that the
right of voting upon the election of a candidate is a serious responsibility,
and that any Brother who abuses that sacred trust for the gratification of
a personal grudge, or by way of unjust retaliation, is debasing himself,
and that his actions reflect on his own moral sense. It is a mean and
contemptible action, unworthy of a member of the Fraternity.
Western Australia (1932):
{Chairman Correspondence Committee): One notices in the Grand
Master's address a gentle reminder to Lodge officers which seems applicable to others besides those in the Vermont Jurisdiction. Speaking of his
refusal of many requests to shorten the intervals between degrees, the
Grand Master said it seemed to him that Lodge officers ought to realize
that the policy of Grand Lodge was strictly against the hurry-up process
in degree work. The Western Australian reviewer trusts he may be
permitted to concur. Only too often does this hustling spasm attack Lodges
in. the different parts of the world, and its cause may be diagnosed in a
failure on the part of Lodge officers to realize that leisured advancement
is more likely to impress our candidates. All said and done, if it took even
a twelvemonth before the Third Degree was taken, the candidate would
be better off than his Brethren in some European Continental Jurisdictions,
where the two intervals between the First and Third Degrees approximate
two years.

CO-ORDINATE BODIES
The struggle for existence of every organization at the present
time is working to reduce the number of organizations having as a
requirement membership in the Masonic Fraternity. It also has had
the effect of curtailing some activities that in the past have been
open to criticism.
In a Communist demonstr~tion in New York some time ago one
of the banners carried the following sentence: "Let's be· pleasant to
each other; we are all having a dreadful time." This thought may
also perhaps be applicable to existing conditions.
District of- Columbia (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Some Grand Masters think
they are, and some do not, depending, perhaps, on just what is the extent
of their connection with some particular organization. At any rate, the
matter has drawn considerable attention lately, and the consensus of
opinion seems to be that organizations seeking to exploit the Lodges for
members should first obtain the consent of Grand Lodge, and thus, with
an authoritative sponsor, they would be likely to violate fewer of the
tenets of Masonry. It is a large question, certainly, and one not likely to
come to a complete understanding all at once.' But it is a fact that many
Masons who are members of these extraneous organizations apparently
think the Grand Lodge has no control over them, which leads them into
many extravagant malpractices, such as attempting to visit a Lodge without
wearing an apron because the apron would detract from the beauty of
their uniforms, or sitting in open Lodge towed with some fantastic headdress, or attempting to take their own pleasure as to the manner in· which
the great lights are to be·saluted.
·
A Lodge is a place where all Brethren must conform to the same rules,
and a Mason is subject to the rules of the Grand Lodge no matter how
many other Bodies he may belong to. Disregard for the rules for Masonic
conduct, particularly on public occasions, has brought a number of these
outside organizations into disrepute with Grand Lodges, and Masonry into
disrepute with certain easily-prejudiced Classes of the general public. These
organizations a1t have something good about them, as this writer has found
from membership in several, but until they come to a realization that after
all they are Masons first; unpleasant incidents will continue to crop up, and
much of the_attention they will get from Grand Lodges will be unfavorable.
Missouri (1932):
(Grand Master): The Masonic barque is so covered with the barnacles
of extraneous societies that ofttimes one wonders whether the ship may

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

19

land or whether it will sink. Societies and commercial associations; which,
under ordinary circumstances, could scarcely pay expenses, limit ·their
membership to Masonic families, or to Masons only, and immediately
become successful businesses.
The conduct of the membership of many of these societies is not such
as to support the dignity of the Masonic character, and the day is rapidly
approaching when our Fraternity must use a strong hand in dealing with
them. Lotteries, side shows, street carnivals, drunken pilgrimages, and
conduct such as to disgrace the name of the Fraternity, destroys every
vestige of their right for Masonic support. If extraneous organizations
continue to persist in basing their membership on Masonic connection or
membership, then they must expect to be held to account for infraction of
the ordinary rules of conduct. The Grand Lodge of Missouri knows no
Masonry but the Ancient Craft Masonry of the three degrees. Because of
the dignity and the educational influence of the York and Scottish Rites
and the splendid manner in which these Rites have kept themselves free
from censure and reproach, toleration has been accorded them.
For the past two years we have read in the metropolitan press, accounts
of rows, trials, and counter-trials which have arisen in what has ·been
wrongly termed "adoptive Masonry." A prominent official of that association assures me, that in practically all of their troubles, there has 'been
a man at the bottom of the trouble. Red-blooded men will find plenty to
occupy their time and mind if they confine their activities to a man's
Fraternity.
The Lodge in Missouri affords every opportunity for fellowship and
social intercourse, and there is no reason why the . membership need go
elsewhere, searchi,ng for the pot of gold.

CORNER STONES
The ceremony of laying comer stones of public buildings under
Masonic auspices during the past year has often been criticized and
objected to by those opposed to the Fraternity. In practically every
instance it was without effect. The controversy, however, generally
serves the. useful purpose of informing the public of the antiquity of
the ceremonies, emphasizes that it is entirely "Symbolic," and has no
ulterior motive.
Florida (1933):
(Grand Master): Being unable to be present at the corner stone laying
Brother
.of the new Government Building in Miami, I directed R:.
William Sydow to act as my proxy.
This corner stone laying had been planned for many months previous
and it was thought that all difficulties in connection therewith had been
satisfactorily arranged, but I quote from Brother Sydow's report to me,
as follows:
"Outside influences tended to prevent the laying of the stone by the
Masonic Fraternity. A few days before the ceremony the Postmaster
received a telegram from Washington stating it 'was preferable to the
Department for the ceremonies to be in charge of some civic organization.'
We got around this by inviting the presidents of each civic club to be
present, 28 in all. Also invited 53 city, county and local state officials;
a Catholic Judge, a Jewish Rabbi, consuls of various foreign countries;
and about 25 officials from Tallahassee and Washington. Another hitch
occurred when the building contractor, who had not been very warm, demanded at 5 o'clock the day before May 14, that we place insurance in
case of accident to those on the platform. There was no time to arrange
this nor money to pay the premium, but I fixed it up by giving releases
personally in writing. The Stone Mason's Union furnished their men to
handle the stone; and in order to comply with their rules they made me a
member of the Union, so I could legitimately and correctly (I hope)
spread the cement, and work in the same crew with the Union men."
I have been advised there was a certain amount of sentiment attached
to the laying of this corner stone by Union men. They were all Union
Masons and all members of the Masonic Fraternity.

ENDOWMENT FUNDS
If the Masonic Home system is to be maintained there can only
be one practical way of makinK it permanent. That is by the creation
of an endowment fund, the interest from which will be sufficient to
maintain the Homes. To establish such a reserve calls for education,
not only among the members but also among those of the general
public who are desirous of contributing to institutions that work for
humanitarian purposes. This program will, of course, require time
and constructive effort.
The Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania is an example. Their Proceedings shows that they have received donations and bequests not
only from the members but the general public, which at the present
time totals approximately sixt~en million dollars.

(Chairman Correspo11Jence Committee): Despite economic conditions,
the Grand Master seems optimistic on Masonic well-being. He calls atten-

tion to the Endowment Fund for the Masonic Home and urges all to

Illinois (1932):
(Grand Master): All thinking Masons realize, as never before, the
necessity of making ample provision for the future of our homes.
For many years this particular work of Masonry has been carried
on without thought of any plan being formulated, such as an endowment
fund where the principal could not be touched, but a sufficient amount be
raised that the interest would carry on the work through the years, But
now we face this task and with this in mind, I bring this subject before
this Grand Lodge to urge everyone to do their part in a tangible way for
the benefit of these children who will be the men and women of the future,
for the benefit of those men and women of our Masonic family who,
through the turn of fortune's wheel, have been unable to accumulate a
surplus of worldly goods.
And so I appeal to the Masons of Illinois for the Endowment Fund
which we start this year and which, in the future, will become the greatest
outstanding monument to the liberality and goodness of those who give.
It will show that you appreciate Masonry in deed and in fact, a living,
throbbing, vital .institution. You will find that the real joy of life is
enhanced many times by giving. In giving money, we give sunshine to
the heart that is clouded with sorrow, hope to the boy and girl who have
been bereft of a father, and above.and beyond all in such giving, we will
enjoy the glory and happiness of knowing that we have done what we
could to make this world a haven of peace and have made the unfortunate
of our Fraternity rich in the knowledge that they have not been forgotten.

EDUCATION-PUBLIC
There is a growing demand that Masonry should adopt some constructive program, and we have always maintained that interest in the
public schools would be one of the greatest activities to which the
Fraternity could devote its time and energies. It is not one that permits of a great deal of ballyhoo, but yet the interest shown in the
Public Schools Week of our Jurisdiction demonstrates what can be
accomplished in this field.
Aristotle said, "The main object of education should be to prepare
men for the right use of leisure." The first step in carrying that out
necessarily has to do with the youth of today. Benjamin Franklin
also said, "A Bible and .a newspaper in every house, a good school in
every district-all studied and appreciated as they merit-are the
principle support of fraternity, morality and civil liberty." Perhaps

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The prime object of an

we were before. The educated man is not he who knows all things, even

the tools with which the wise man works. Too much education, with no
incentive to use it, is often a detriment to society. That fact is being
demonstrated every day by the educated incompetents that are turned out
from our institutions of learning. The only education that is worth much
to society is that which a man gets for himself. It only gives the mean
man an opportunity to become meaner; the cruel man a means of being
more cruel, and the good man the opportunity for him to enlarge his means
of usefulness.
ENTERTAINMENT
The absence of degree work necessarily calls for the adoption of
a program that will attract and hold the interest of the members.
While the object of Masonry is not primarily to amuse or entertain,
still the adage that "All work and no play makes Jack a dull boy" is
just as true in our Fraternity as in others. We cannot change human
nature, and the attendance at Masonic entertainments or banquets is
evidence that the so-called "Fourth Degree" still remains popular.
Massachusetts (1932):
(Grand Master): It is only a few years ago that a Lodge offering
its members a quartet on the night it worked a Third Degree, and afterwards providing a modest buffet supper of sandwiches, ice cream, and
coffee, would be considered as having met all the requirements of the
occasion. Little by little during the World War, when conservation of
food was in order, many Lodges arranged a six o'clock dinner, sometimes
paid for by the Lodge and more often, perhaps, paid for either wholly
or in part by the members themselves. Another reason for this dinner

was to secure a larger attendance of members at the meeting ·of the
Lodge, since through this arrangement the Brethren were able to come

of remaining there rather than go out again to the meeting.
At the dinners, a quartet would occasionally render pleasing ·and
appropriate musical numbers for the entertainment of those present.
As this offering began to pall,. Masters commenced to look about for
other attractive forms of entertainment, and invited speakers to their
dinners, and sometimes lecturers with or without a stereopticon. Then
followed motion picture shows, often with films showing little care in

and even wrestling bouts and boxing matches have found their way ·into

in relation to the festive board. No musical items should be called for,
or smoking permitted, until after those Grand Officers whose names are

No item should be permitted in the .refectory which is not in complete
harmony with the instruction given in the Lodge or which may tend in
any way to burlesque the seriousne~s of that instruction. Such items as
parodies on the Working Tools are objectionable in the latter way. The
Board expects that Masters of Lodges in particular and the Brethren
generally will see that the proceedings in the refectories are maintained
in proper tone, and that nothing is introduced to which exception can be
taken by any Brother.

Your Grand Master is most reluctant to consider the inauguration of
a censorship or oversight of entertainments offered in connection with
the exemplification of Masonic Degrees, preferring that it be left to the
good judgment of the Masters themselves to determine what is appropriate and fitting to offer their Brethren on such occasions, if indeed anything should be offered at all.
But this may be said, in all sincerity, that the tone of such entertainments as are offered must definitely be raised to a far higher level, and I
am confident my Brethren will see the propriety of my comments and that
there will be no occasion to speak of this again.
This brings me back to my opening words on the subject that money
spent on elaborate and inappropriate programs of entertainment may much
better be diverted to the care of worthy Brethren in need of the common
necessities of life, and in making up the shortage in Lodge exp~nse accounts
caused by a more generous and fraternal attitude in the matter of nonpayment of dues and suspensions therefor.

FINANCES
This question still continues to be an acute one in practically all
of the Jurisdictions. In order to conserve funds, one Grand Lodge
eliminated its annual session; another one required the members to
pay their own mileage. Drastic cuts have been made in per capita
taxes, salaries and other activities. While the experience has not been
pleasant, it has impressed upon those in authority the fact that they
must cut their garment according to the amount of cloth they possess.
The other evening we heard a statement made by a well informed
man that one of the Chinese war lords had collected taxes in his
province fifty-seven years in advance. The present sales tax in California is bringing home to the taxpayer the hard lesson that expenditures, either extravagant or otl).erwise, must be ultimately paid. This
same principle must apply in the financial handling of Lodges.
Arizona (1932):
(Grand Master}: A survey of the business affairs and financfal undertakings of our Lodges has brought me to believe that these things should
undergo a radical change. Apparently most Lodges do not even try to
live WITHIN their income, but rather to live ait least up to their income.
And their plans, if they have any worthy the name, are made in the most
optimistic spirit of the most prosperous year, with seemingly never a
thought of possible adversity.

* * * * *

In recent years, particularly in the heyday of a few years ago, many
of our Lodges have undertaken to acquire homes. A commodious and
elegant home is a fine thing, and to possess such a laudable ambition, but
if . secured only with the accompaniment of a burdensome debt, and everpresent worry and a constant handicap, 'twere better that a Lodge should
live .in more modest quarters, though rented, yet able to carry on.
Some Lodges in the days of prosperity undertook the financing of
temples, entailing debts which now threaten the very existence of those
Lodges. Some have erected or purchased business buildings, figuring that
rentals would pay off the debts incurred, only to find now, perhaps, empty
store rooms converted into liabilities instead of assets, for taxes, insurance
·
and repairs go right on.

Arkansas (1932):
(Grand Master}: We had our years of plenty from 1920 to 1928;
it was a period marked by rapid growth numerically and financially by this
Grand Lodge. Our physical expansion was paralleled by an extension of
our activities; we increased the work of the Orphan's Home SO per cent ;
the scope of the Pension Fund was enlarged several hundred per cent.
Many of our Lodges entered upon similar programs of expansion; imbued
with a commendable desire to have proper quarters in which to meet and
to do work fitting the character of Masonry, they started building programs, to provide themselves halls of their own. Such things were justifiable; progress must be the watchword of every worthwhile institution;
to stagnate is to die in Masonry as in every other form of life.
But the seven years of plenty in anoient Egypt had their corresponding
years of famine, years in which the lean cattle ate up the fat ones. No
Joseph arose to point this out to us, or if he did, we heeded him not. It
has been hard for us now to realize the necessity of adjusting 'our ideas
and our actions to the limitations of reduced incomes.
There are two sources of Lodge revenue--dues and fees from degrees.
We have witnessed a steadily decreasing number of degrees conferred, ·and
this year will show the fewest of any in the recent history of the Grand
Lodge. This is not a disturbing factor, however, for we know that economic conditions will eventually improve, and will bring with such improvement an increasing number of applicants for Masonry.
Florida (1933):
(Grand Maste1·): I approved amendment, which amendment made the
fee for initiation $45, for passing $2.50 and for raising $2.50. The question may be raised that I have nullified Regulation 325, which prevents a
Lodge from requiring a candidate for initiation to present with his petition
advance fees for the Fellowcraft and Master Mason Degrees. There is a
psychology about this maximum initiation fee, with a minimum for the
other two, which I felt was worth experimenting with. The abnormal
number of Entered Apprentices who go no further, cannot be because of
disappointment in Masonry, but from some other cause, and I ha~e
always felt, personally, that it was embarrassment, or rather an inferiority
complex created in the minds of men of maturity when the knowledge
reached them that it would be necessary to memorize a ritualistic ceremony, with its necessary effort, and felt, in approving this by-law that
if there was as much money involved as would be necessary f~r his
Entered Apprentice Degree and the small amounts for subsequent degrees,
that he would make an additional effort to familiarize himself for the
necessary examination.

New Mexico (1933):
(Grand Master): Possibly the greatest loss sustained by Lodges of
the Jurisdiction is occasioned by the lax methods in the collection of
dues. The practice of allowing "further time" is prevalent, and although
the membership believe that they are doing the Brother a favor, in reality
they are actually doing him an injustice. If a year's dues cannot be collected, it follows without question that a greater amount will not be
forthcoming. We are only adding- to the amount of loss which sooner or
later must be absorbed when suspension actually occurs. And during the
interim, the Lodge has been paying the per capita to sustain the Grand
Lodge in its activities. The whole plan is unfair to all concerned.
In many cases the evil is abetted by the manner in which Secretaries
pursue the collection of dues. Too many of these officers allow the year
to come to a close without an effort being made to place the matter before
the membership. I have urged the plan of individual contact early in the
year, and followed at least quarterly. Experience has taught us that ability
to take care of financial obligations is seasonal, depending upon the occupation of the Brother, and it is imperative that we realize this fact, if we are
to keep this account to a minimum.
North Carolina (1933):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Lodges are the craziest
financial institutions on earth. They are like the mule in the story, when
it comes to a sound financial structure: A certain mule wrecked a buggy
on a tree, and when the negro driver was asked whether the mule was
blind, to do so unn~cessary a thing as this, he answered, "Naw suh, he just
don't give a damn." Lodges more often than otherwise do not have a
budget, or if they do, ignore it; some noisy spellbinder gets up and exhorts,
and the timid members, unwilling to say nay to him, cheerfully give away
or spend all they have; an ambitious member with the building itch makes
a stirring speech and buttonholes some members, and they go in debt to
build a house which there is no hope of ever paying for. Many never
stop to ascertain whether dues are high enough to meet fixed charges.
Other Lodges pay excessively high percentage to Secretaries, salaries to
Treasurers. Still others,_ in most respects sane, vote to excuse every Master
on his retirement from office, from the payment of his dues for the rest
of days. They vote to remit dues of people in arrears indiscriminately,
never remembering that per capita tax goes on indefinitely on each, and
piles up against them mighty soon. The number of fraternal officials who
have stolen moneys collected by them or held in trust for the Lodges,
has of late become a scandal ; and the fault lies largely with Lodges which
never have any legally acceptable accounting of such things. Sometimes,
too, the crowd gets hungry and just feel that they have got to have a

feed-the majority of those present, or all of them usually, vote to have
such an event and make the Lodge pay for it-result, the Lodge eats up
its savings. And so on ad infinitum.

GRAND LODGE
It is a mooted question as to what the Governor of North Carolina said to the 9overnor of South Carolina, but what the Past Grand
Master of North Carolina said to the Grand Master of South Carolina,
as far as Grand Lodge communications are concerned, is not only
interesting but true. He very graphically summarized it as follows:
"The Grand Master puts on his stove-pipe hat, literally and
sometimes figuratively as well, and reads his report. What does it
include? Dispensations, decisions, nine-tenths of which are unnecessary; discipline, necrology, with fulsome eulogy of dead Brethren, a
great deal of it undeserved, accompanied with the world's worst
poetry. I have heard more bad poetry in Masonry, and especially
in Grand Lodge, than in all other places put together. If that sort
of poetry is read over my body, I'll haunt the man who does it. Then
the Grand Master goes on to the State of the Craft, statistics, new
Lodges established, and so on, and finally winds up with a grand
burst of eloquence. After that the distinguished visitors are introduced, and they arise and strut. I have seen some who could sit
down and strut. They extend compliments, and say usually nothing
net. The address of the Grand Master of Georgia tonight was a
refreshing change from the usual address of a distinguished visitor
at Grand Lodge.
"Then the committees report--on Ritual, finance, appeals, etc.
The Superintendent of the Home asks for a little more money; new
officers are elected, appear to be very much surprised and get up
and make the same identical speech that they have been making for
the ·last hundred and fifty years: 'With the help of you Brethren and
your co-operation I will endeavor to discharge the duties of my office
to the best of my ability.' Meanwhile the Past Grand Masters sit
all ready to pounce on anything new and alive; and everybody has a
grand time fraternizing and eating big meals at the expense of somebody else."

Maine· (1933):
(Grand Master): The Grand Lodge of Maine is one of the largest
corporations in this state. It has 42,152 stockholders, with 675 directors.
E,very member of the Grand Lodge is a director of this corporation, and
every Master Mason in the state who is a member of a subordinate Lodge
is a stockholder. No stockholder of this corporation can hold more · than
one share of common stock. This stock is without par value. Every
certificate of stock is issued on the same basis. The fundamental and
underlying principle is the belief in a Supreme Being. Every stockholder
is supposed to be a man of good moral character, at least of average
ability and a good citizen. No two shares of stock are of exactly the
same value. Each share is measured by the ability and efforts of the
respective stockholder. There is no stock market report which you can
examine to determine its value.

Vermont (1933):

(Grand Master): Electioneering, so far as I am able to ascertain
has never received any attention in the addresses of any of my predeces~

I have spent some time looking up and reading what has been said
about this matter in other Jurisdictions, and I find that many Grand Masters have had occasion to comment on it. In some Jurisdictions it has
been a subject of resolution. In all cases it has been held without question

has been indulged.
I unhesitatingly say that such practice is not Masonic and should never
be countenanced. A Masonic office should come as an award for merit

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master of Idaho
signed as Past Grand Master, a little previously we should say, although

and let someone else pick it up. We have noticed here at home that every
Grand Master elected is anxious to get started and in most .cases is just

and just about as glad to get out again.

I would have a few take notice of the following paragraph from
Grand Master Middleton's (of Connecticut) address: "It has been my
pleasure to meet with the Past Grand Master's Association during the
year. I have found their counsel and suggestions very helpful, and I wish
at this time to express my appreciation of the many courtesies and acts of
kindness shown me during the year."
We have a Past Grand Masters' Association, and some of our
Brethren hold the mistaken idea that it is a political and dictatorial Body,
which it is neither one nor the other.

* * * * *

·As was the case last year, there were no decisions to be reported by
the Grand Master of Delaware. Just think of it : 207 Masters and over
43,000 Masons and no decisions for two years! It either shows that the
members of Grand Lodge have made the laws and regulations so plain
that there can be no doubt as to the meaning, or that the principal officers
of the Lodges have posted themselves so well that their handling of the
business was such as to merit the approbation of all their members.

HISTORY-DEBUNKING
. A number of statements made regarding Masonry, its origin,
history, etc., would be highly interesting if true. Unfortunately, a
large number of these misleading statements are made by those in
the Fraternity who should know better. In a number of cases they
are absolutely unfounded, and are productive of criticism and ridicule.
Someone has said that the history of civilization is the history of the
displacement of old conceptions by new ones more conformable to
facts. Masonic history should be along this line. Too often it is
along the line of:
"A rural orator, when extolling the manifold virtues of his favorite
congressman, and asking an endorsement by the dear 'peepul,' said:
'He is the greatest man in the country. He is the greatest man in the
state. He is the greatest man in the United States. Yes, fellow-citizens,
he is the greatest man in the universe.' Whereupon one of his audience
gave a prolonged whistle. Nothing daunted, the orator, with accession
of heat, exclaimed: 'Well, if he ain't, he ought to be!'"
Maryland (1932):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): In the Address of Welcome
in the Grand Lodge of Oklahoma we find certain hysterical utterances
caused in part by the "wish being father to the thought" and also by
the fact that the orator of the occasion had not posted himself on the latest
Masonic researches. He is one of those who wish to believe that these
United States became a nation by Masonic means or, as he states, "because
it (Masonry) is largely responsible for the formation of this great gov-

ernment." And he goes on to say, "Masons formed the Continental
Congress, Masons wrote and signed the Declaration of Independence,
Masons kept alive the embers of patriotism throughout the war; and as
this country has grown and blossomed, Masons have guided and will
continue to guide her to the great goal she is destined to attain."
The following statement has recently appeared in a little pamphlet
issued under the authority of the Grand Lodge of New York:
"Of the Presidents of the United States it is known that 11 have
become members of the Craft. It is believed others have been raised, but
to date proof is lacking. . . . Of the 56 Signers of the Declaration of
Independence, the records show that 13 were Brethren: Benjamin Franklin, Lyman Hall, John Hancock, Joseph Hewes, William Hooper, Thomas
McKean, Thomas Nelson, Jr., Robert Treat Paine, John Penn, Roger
Sherman, Richard Stockton, Matthew Thornton, George Walton, William
Whipple, and John Witherspoon."
Also the Shawnee Brother might refer to William L. Boyden's·
"Masonic Presidents, Vice-Presidents and Signers," wherein he might
find matter that would make him correct his above statements, or, at
least, some of them.
'
And again he must remember that there were as many and as good
Freemasons who were Loyalists as there were Revolutionists-and again
let him remember that Freemasonry was the creation of English thought
and that the principles of freedom and .liberty of the English colonist
were those principles first enunciated in the .Magna Charta of King John
(June 15, 1215) and were the precious heritage of the population of the
Thirteen Colonies at the time of the Revolution.
We are afraid, if the Brother who made the above referred to address were taken seriously, Masonry would come in (and properly so)
for very severe criticism when he states that Masons have guided this
country and will continue to do so.
Allow us to say, that (and we apologize for the use of slang) this
is pure "bunk." The speaker implies that Freemasonry runs this government and that what it now is, is due to •the Order. Even if . this were
true (which, of course, it is ·not) would Freemasonry wish to assume the
burden of the evils the citizen is suffering today by reason of the failure
of those whom the electorate have placed in power to act for the good
of the individual and the protection of the rights and . liberties of the
people? · In addition to the above, it must be remembered that Freemasonry
is not a political machine but a mighty force for good, and instead of
claiming mighty political power it would be better to view things as they
are and to strive, by the teachings of our profession in a firm, but humble,
spirit, for the amelioration of the frightful !Jlisgovernment now oppressing
these United States.

43

Let us put aside the spirit of Chauvinism and, uninfluenced by the
hysteria of the moment engendered by a larg.e crowd, let us read some
well-authenticated history and call attention to the need of the electorate
to apply their intelligence to the protection of the few rights th~y .have
left and to the restoration cif the rights and liberties they have blmdly
relinquished. '
As Grand Orator, Brother Gayle of Louisiana gives a wonderful
display of the science of hermeneutics when he says :
"We do know that in the struggle for human liberty, while leading
the Continental Army through its years of hardship and trial and suffering to final victory, he surrounded _himself with trusted aides ~nd
officers who were bound to him by the ties of Masonry. Even the foreign
heroes, Marquis de Lafayette, the Frenchman, and Baron de Steuben, the
German, were Masons, and in time of crisis, when· everything depended
upon faithfulness and patriotism, devotion to duty and inte~rity, ,he pas~ed
the word to his aides and generals, 'Let none but Amermms, meamng
Masons, 'be placed on gtKird'."
This is indeed writing history (?) with a vengeance!
Upon what does 'the Grand Orator base his statement except upon
the fact that George Washington was a Mason and ~ad a high regard
for the Fraternity. This surely is far from the establishment of the
conclusion that as General he would give an order with such a concealed
meaning; and from Washington's character, if he had meant any such
thing as that only American Masons be put on guard, he would have been
very apt to give the order as Brother Quayle would have liked it to have
been given. Besides all this it may as well be understood that Freemasonry
as such did not establish this government, and while a number of prominent
Colonials were Masons, yet equally prominent men of that day were
Loyalists and Masons, also. Again it must be remembered that there
were comparatively few of the Colonial forces that were members of the
Order, and it would have been hardly advisable for Washington to have
endeavored to lead his mixed body of troops making his army a Masonic
army to establish a Masonic government. If Freemasonry is respons~ble
for the establishment of this government (which it is not) , then certainly
the Craft have been sadly derelict in guiding the ship of state for many
years; for if Patrick Henry of Revolutionary fame complained at the
present day of the abuses he attacked he would be regarded with wonder,
since the citizen of these U nited States today has to suffer greater abuses
of power than the fiery orator of the Virginia Houses of Burgesses could
well imagine outside of an Eastern despotism.
Grand Orators as well as Reviewers should be careful in their expressions when dealing with matters of history and of Masonry, since their
utterances go over the world and are subject to the careful scrutiny of
students outside of the Fraternity as well as of it.

New York (1932):
(Chafrman Correspondence Committee): Loose talk about "Latin
Freemasonry" among uninformed Brethren has done grave injustice to the
great majority of the Grand Lodges in countries where a Latin language
is spoken. Just because the Grand Orient and the Grand Lodge of France
and the Grand Orient of Spain are active politically and in anti-clerical
lines, antagonists of the Craft have made it appear that all others were
of the same character. Masonic writers and speakers have allowed themselves to fall into the trap and refer to "Latin Masonry" as if it were an
entity and one characterized by irreligiousness and politics. The truth is
that with only three or four exceptions, the Latin American Jurisdictions
observe the Landmarks quite as strictly as our Grand Lodges do. Their
Constitutions declare definitely that religious and political discussions and
line-ups are forbidden. Of course, when placed on the defensive by
unscrupulous or misinformed anti-Masonic agitators, they talk back to
reassure the general public of their neutral stand in all matters of religious
and political controversy. There is no such thing as "Latin Freemasonry."
Each Grand Lodge is independent of every other and must be judged by
itself. The reviews given above are intended as a help toward that end.
Utah (1933):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): In the last two or three
decades much has been accomplished in the matter of "debunking" history-Masonic and "profane." That this work could go forward in either
case without being overdone, would be too much to expect. Place a hammer
in the hands of a thoroughgoing iconoclast and one cannot be certain that
he will always enter the house of Dagon, or exercise discrimination once
he is inside.
•
And what a multitude of idols have fallen! Why, we are not permitted even to retain that pretty little story about Franklin's suggestion
in the Constitutional Convention that resort be had to prayer when there
·appeared to be a real "jam," and delegates were on the point of returning
to their homes. For one, we are not satisfied with the substitution of
Hamilton's alleged remark to the effect that the situation was not sufficiently serious to call for "foreign" aid.
But to come to the matter in mind. The reader of Masonic history
hardly needs to be told that the name of Rev. James Anderson is usually
associated with the names of William Preston and Dr. Ge()rge Oliver, as
having made too free a use of the imaginatiQn when writ!ng on the early
history of organized Freemasonry, ,and that .consequently Anderson's
account of what transpired in the formative period from 1716 to June 24,
1723, "the date when the premier Grand Lodge installed its first Secretary," must be taken with more than the proverbial grain of salt. For this

LEGISLATION
The great indoor sport in our national, state and municipal legislative bodies is that of passing laws, and some Grand Lodges show
that this custom is still prevalent. Someone has expressed the thought
that at the present date thousands of laws are made, hundreds understand them and a few individuals live by them. Too mucli legislation
tends to weaken an individual or an organization. In those Jurisdictions requiring amendments or changes to lay over for one year, and
be discussed in the Lodges, it is noticeable that a majority are not
adopted. Those that are acted upon favorably generally seem necessary.
England (1933):
(Board of Great Britain): In ·view of the large number of amendments which have been made to this Book of Constitutions since the last
edition was issued in 1926, the Board feels that a new edition should be
issued as soon as possible. There are many Rules, however, which require
redrafting, and the Board proposes to undertake a general revision as soon
as practicable. This will involve very extensive consideration, and the
Board would appreciate the assistance of the Craft. It hopes that any
Brother who has any suggestion to make in amendment of any of the
existing Rules, will forward such suggestion to the Grand Secretary for
consideration in due l=ourse.

(Chairma1i Correspondence Committee): Burdensome and vexatious
taxation, sumptuary laws and regulations imposed on the individual,
troublesome and intricate rules for the government of every private and
corporate business have made present-day conditions a nightmare.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Illinois is one of the Grand

in consequence we are not surprised when we read of various amendments
to the "CODE" and proposed amendments to same. We are indeed glad
that Freemasonry in Maryland follows the "Common Law System" rather
than the ideas of "Code Legislation."

Nevada (1933):
(Grand Master): Brethren, it is with a great deal of regret that I
bring you any recommendations whatsoever. It is my belief that we have
enough laws and regulations in our Masonic Code as it is, and I think you
will agree with me the condition of the Masonic Fraternity in Nevada is
something to be proud of, when the Grand Master is not called upon for
any decisions. It also tells you of the caliber of the men who direct the
affairs of the Order throughout the state. This also speaks well of the
wisdom of the Pioneers who framed our Code.

* * * * *

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The amount of Masonic
legislation that has been enacted and repealed is probably more than we
have in our Masonic Codes now. Every Masonic statute that is passed
should be worded in good homely language and stated in such a plain
manner as to leave no doubt as to the meaning intended by its authors;
and also in such a way there could be no technicality. to get around it to
fit an occasion.
Utah (1933):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A correspondent seeks an
explanation of the voluminous "Decisions and Opinions" which cover vast
areas of white paper that come labeled "Proceedings." He wondered
whether the law (Masonic) in some Jurisdictions is faulty or inadequate,
or were they due to a penchant on the part of certain Grand Masters.
Our opinion is that responsibility lies at the "door of Grand Masters,
and for this reason, and to illustrate: We have in mind a series of
"Decisions," sixty or seventy in number, each consisting of two or more
long paragraphs, the first of which presents the question submitted with
all the attendant circumstances, and details, followed by a lengthy discussion of the matter; a formal pronouncement, or "decision," and closing
with words to this effect: "This subject is fully covered by section so and
so of the Code of this Grand Lodge !"

Florida (1932):
(Grand Ma.st er): The close of the Masonic year is almost with us,
with its most important problems, delinquency lists and the election of
officers. Delinquency is all important in this period of depression, a depression used by many as an excuse for the non-payment of obligations.
Personal investigations and contacts should be made in all delinquent
cases, that no injustice may be done to worthy Brothers, delinquent
through misfortune. Where this personal contact has been employed
by particular Lodges it has developed an opportunity for education of the
delinquents as to our .activities, both local and Grand Lodge. It has
developed the reasons for non-attendance--lack of fraternalism, personal
irritation, and many others possible of correction, and it has developed the
worthy cases of delinquency (a very small percentage).
Not less important the election of officers. Too frequently officership
is the reward of attendance, not ability, and a hesitancy on the part of the
membership to drop one who supposedly ranks on the appointive list of
officers. Out of respect to this consideration on the part of the membership, each officer who is eligible for promotion· according to the custom
of your particular Lodge should make a complete analysis of himself
-and the duty which he owes to the Booy that has already honored him by
its recognition. He should ask of himself a few pertinent questions:
Have I both the ritualistic and business ability to successfully administer the affairs of my Lodge?
Will I have the time to devote to the proper administration of its
affairs?
Am I broad enough to forget my personal feelings in this administration?
Is my own moral deportment of such a character that I not only
will be respected by my membership but the community as well?
These are a few of the questions which the Brother who is possibly
<h.te promotion by service should ask of himself, and if he cannot answer
them as a true Mason should answer, his announcement should be on
election night that ''I do .not c_hoose to serve."
Maine (1933):

LODGE OFFICERS
A Lodge looks to its officers for leadership and inspiration. They
must possess ability, experience and knowledge. To furnish these,
the officers, from the \Vorshipful Master down to the Junior Steward,

(Grand Master): Lodges must be more careful in selecting their
officers, because the question of leadership determines the interest in the
Lodge work. Many Lodges seem to feel if a man is started at the foot of

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

the line that he must be advanced until he is Master of the Lodge. This
is a great error. If a man shows that he has not the qualities to make a
good officer, nor the qualities of leadership, then he should not be advanced.
Lack of competent leadership means smaller attendance, lack of interest
and finally suspension or demits among the members.

formed, the ballot is always dark. You could not blame the members of
the Lodge-the Brother refused to learn the work of the office he held,
and when approached as to what he would do if advanced to a higher
station, answered that he would not learn the work of that office. Now he
is a "sour member" and nothing is done right.
A Grand Master of a certain Jurisdiction would like to stop the
popular habit of the Brethren from rushing out the moment a Brother
is raised because they are afraid they will have to listen to the lectures:
the lectures which the Worshipful Master and his officers have worked
hard to perfect and which mean so much to the candidate who is seeking
further light. Have we any Masons of this kind in this Jurisdiction?
The saddest thing that can be said about any Mason is that he is a
"has been." The more he has done the more he should do. Unwise is that
Past Master who, when he steps down from the Master's chair, feels and·
acts as though his responsibility has ceased and he is through. Past
Masters do not step down, but up. His experience should make him more
useful to the Craft, and he still has duties to perform and advice to give,
that the Lodge may function properly and not go off on a tangent. The
Past Master should be the counselor of his Lodge, not only because of
his ability to do so, but because he owes it to what he himself has already
put into Masonry.

North Carolina (1933):
(Chairnum Correspondence Committee): Cases where the Secretary
and the Deacon run things are just plain illustrations of Masonic cussedness on the part of somebody else ·who is willing to let these two do it.
We have seen such cases-more than once. We see all sorts of cases of
indifference in high places, where somebody else has to shoulder the
situation vicariously and keep things going. Sometimes the Secretary is
a Past Master and is not at all unwilling to do his full share-in fact, he
may be a bit too ready. But there is too much disposition to condemn
people hastily in such things. He is a wise leader who puts his men to
work, gives them training, prepares for the future, even keeps himself in
the background while acting as leader. God save us from those folks who
are always wanting to be spectacular, who are anxious to get the credit
for something, who make one big mistake. In only one case is noise the
equivalent of health-we've got one of those at our house, and it's the
year-old namesake, son and heir of the writer. In all other cases, excessive
noise is scarcely compatible with the most healthy of conditions, and the
post of leader is no exception.
Wyoming (1932)
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A member who accepts a
station in his Lodge should strive to be a real officer. No matter what
his station may be, he should thoroughly acquaint himself with the duties
of that office, and then proceed to make himself proficient in the work
of the officer above him. If the Worshipful Master is ~areless in his
work, what can be expected from the other officers and the members?
Everyone likes to see his Lodge conducted in a creditable manner, for
it is a pleasure to each member to sit in a Lodge where the officers are
thoroughly acquainted with their duties.
The Grand Lodge requires the officers of its Subordinate Lodges to
be proficient in their respective duties, otherwise the members lose interest,
·attendance drops off, and the work is not well done.
Of all the pests with which Masonry is afflicted, none is worse than
the "sour member," the fellow who is always dissatisfied. He spreads
discomfort wherever he is, and it is too bad he cannot confine his grumbling
to himself. I know of a member who became "sour" because the Lodge
did not advance him · in the chairs; and since that time, I have been in-

NEWS FLASHES
Under this heading we have listed unusual or outstanding events
that have taken place in the Masonic world in the past year. They
may serve to show that it is often the unusual that will attract
attention.
Arizona (1933):
(Grand Master}: I was greatly interested in remarks made by Past
Grand Master Walter L. Stockwell of North Dakota, relative the practice
in his Jurisdiction of Subordinate Lodges having what is termed "Grand
Lodge Night," when business and activities of the Grand Lodge is reported
upon and discussed, thus enabling the membership to become conversant
with action had on various matters at the Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge.
In my opinion much good will result from Subordinate Lodges in
this Jurisdiction adopting a similar practice, such meetings to be held
immediately after proceedings of the Annual Communication are available.

Massachusetts (1933):
(Grand Master): I desire to bring . to the attention of Grand Lodge
an act of Masonic service rendered by three California Brethren which
is so outstanding an example of brotherly love that it well may serve as
an· inspiration to every Mason.
Brother Samuel Duncan, a member of Sojourners Lodge, of Cristobal,
. Canal Zone, under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, and residing in
San Bruno, California, became dangerously ill and was expected to live
but a few hours.
Worshipful Brother Arthur T. Weed, Master of Francis Drake
Lodge No. 376, of South San Francisco, when informed of the situation,
communicated immediately with the physician in charge of the case, from
whom he learned that Brother Duncan was almost certain to die within
a very few hours, but there was a slight possibility that his life might
be prolonged and perhaps saved through a blood transfusion. Worshipful
Brother Weed immediately submitted to a blood test, and it being found
suitable, he gave of his blood to this unknown ·Brother whom he had
never seen before, whereupon two of his officers, Brother Richard M.
Zemke, Senior Warden, and Brother Carl ·A. E. Peterson, Senior Steward,
also submitted to the operation of transfusion. Brother Duncan rallied
under this treatment, but later succumbed to his infirmities and passed
away. This, however, did not in the least detract from the generous and
unselfish act of the three Brethren of Francis Drake Lodge, and I deem
this outstanding service on the part of these Brethren sufficient to merit
bringing the matter to your attention.

:M:ontana (1932):

(Chairman Co1-respondence Committee):. The Traveling Trowel appeared on the scene, and Maritime Lodge (Oregon) staged a performance
with K. S., H. A., H. T., Craftsmen, etc., as actors, and the scene was laid
at K. S. Temple, Mount Moriah. How the trowel, a "replica" of the

we wind it and then start in to turn the hands to set it, and think to the
right and lo! we find them moving to the left. The traveling trowel did
some tall jumping over centuries and centuries. We trust that Brother
Mason will pardon our levity ; we cannot help it; it appeals to us so
childish; the "replica" has no historic or histrionic value, and the entire
proceedings seem to us ridiculous ; perchance we are not attuned to the

side of the particular "replica"; by the way, "replica" we find to be defined
in our small Webster's New Standard Dictionary, to be "a copy of an
original picture or statue executed by the same artist or sculptor" ; but we
have written enough and really mean no offense, and trust that Rufus
Cheney will shake hands with us next time we see him and not feel sore at
our cruel effort to shatter an Oregon idol.

New :M:exico (1933):
(Grand Master): Early last year, the State Tax Commission ordered
assessors in all counties to place Masonic properties on the tax roll.
Temple Lodge No. 6, Albuquerque, instituted suit to force the assessor
of Bernalillo County to remove the assessment of their property from the
tax roll. In the trial, judgment was entered against the Lodge and the
case was promptly appealed to the Supreme Court. After due consideration, the higher court found that Freemasonry is an educational institution
and, as such, was exempt by statute from taxation.
This case has caused much interest among the Craft, and in many
instances the imposition of a tax would place a great burden upon Lodges

OFFENSES
Masons, being human, must err. One of the disagreeable sections
of the Grand Lodge Proceedings is that of Masonic trials. When
every Mason realizes that the Masonic Fraternity is judged by his
individual actions the standard will be raised. It has been truly stated
that Freemasonry that cannot be seen does not count for much.
Lamps do not talk-they shine; a lighthouse sounds no drum, it beats
no gong, but over the water its cheering light is seen by the mariner.
Our sister state, Nevada, has a plan which could well be followed.
They have what is known as the Cognizance Committee. Whenever
by general knowledge or special charge it is found that a Mason is
departing from the precepts and practices of Masonry, an investigation is made, he is summoned to appear before the Committee and
the entire matter threshed out. An opportunity is given to remove
the cause for complaint, but if persisted in, charges are preferred.
Often this counsel and advice is more effective than drastic action.
It starts the individual on the right road and removes a condition
that ultimately would result in undesirable publicity through a Masonic
trial.

•• • • •

(Gra-nd Master): Most of us who have given the matter serious
thought, realize that during the prosperous times in the period after the
'Yar, a certain laxness crept into our organization, as in all others-a tendency towards disrespect of law and high standards. These were all right
·for the other fellow to live up to, but not for the individual himself·
in fact, a leading criminal lawyer in this country said, "No man should
be forced to obey any law that he did not like."

From the moment I was installed as your Grand Master, I determined
to enlist the Masonic Order in this state, in the fight against any such
doctrine, and against dishonesty, which is the basic cause of our present
world situation.
Believing that our own conduct as "just and upright men and Masons"
should be just what that statement implies, in any gathering, whether it
be in the Blue Lodge or in any affiliated branch of the Order, you will
remember that I made this statement at the installation one year ago:
"That any act of intemperance that will bring discredit to the reputation
and teachings of this Fraternity will be looked after by the proper officers."
Further than that, I also told you that no record of this action would go
into any of the proceedings " if I could help it."
Brethren, I had hoped that this warning would be sufficient to correct
what little trouble we were having along these lines. However, it became
necessary upon receiving information as to the conduct of a Brother to
take action in this matter, and as it is the duty of your Grand Master to
report his actions during his year of service, it becomes necessary to
make this part of his report.
My action in this case was as follows : I instructed the Worshipful
Master of the Blue Lodge in which this Brother held member.ship, to
have him brought before the Cognizance Committee, an investigation made,
and if the evidence warranted, to proceed in the usual manner and file
charges for un-Masonic conduct.
After many consultations with the Master and· Cognizance Committee,
it was deemed best to take the following action, for which your Grand
Master assumes all responsibility. These charges were to be held in abeyance, pending the future conduct of this Brother. If no further complaint
was made, the charges would not be pressed. In fact, the solution of the
problem was placed in the Brother's own hands. I am very glad to say
that during the past eleven months there has been no further complaint
in this particular case, nor has there been any meeting or gathering of
Masons in any organir.ition of which criticism could be made-what wonderful co-operation, and what a record for Nevada Masonry.

(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : Missouri has a piece of law
which seems to us to be bad. If a Missouri Mason, one of the one hundred
and ten thousand run-of-the-mine, goes to another state, as some twelve
thousand are doing by the law of averages, and if he there does things
un-Masonic, as folks away from the restraints of home-ties sometimes do;
and if he gets into Masonic disrepute by so doing; and if the Lodge
near by where he is, which he has visited, takes notice of the fact that
he has brought Masonry into disrepute there and tries him and suspends
or expels him-after all of these things, Missouri refuses to recognize that
he has received Masonic discipline, but says he must be tried by a Missouri
Lodge. In the first place, we hold that this contravenes the Masonic common law. In the next place, it is wholly beyond the pale of common sense.
In this book, for instance, is the case of a Missouri Mason living in
Colorado who put out five hundred dollars to save himself Masonically in
a Lodge trial back home in Missouri. Then, too, the bringing of evidence
to a place remote from the scene of a man's activities suggests the possibility, at least, of preventing the presentation of the full force of the
charges against him.

South Australia (1933):
(Provincial Grand Master): I have been asked by the Board of General Purposes to refer to a matter that has caused them some anxiety. It
arises out of an address recently delivered in one of our Lodges, and
subsequently forwarded for publication in "The S. A. Freemason." As
this address was published, it appears to be neither more nor less than a
chapter extracted from "The Builders," by Brother Fort Newton. The
incident is regrettable from every point of view. I suppose that we must
admit that there are very few-if, indeed, any of us-who can claim the
ability to produce original work. It is a great and rare achievement to
present new thought, and all that most of us can hope for is to present, in
our own way, what we have collected, as the bee gathers honey.
There is no harm in a paper that consists of passages and quotations
culled from different sources, and we should be grateful to any Brother
who is prepared to go to the trouble of finding, and introducing us to,
anything that is worthy of our attention. But the common understanding,
if one is consciously adopting the very language as well as the thought of
another, is that this shrn.1ld not be d{me without acknowledging the source
from which it is taken. In the case of which I am speaking, I should make
it clear that I am not concerned with the address as it was delivered in the
Lodge. If it was delivered in the same form without any acknowledgment
of the source from which it was taken, I regard that as a matter of good
taste, which concerns the lecturer and the Lodge in question. But I regard
the action of forwarding the report for publication in "The Freemason,"
under the guise of an original work, as a matter that concerns this Grand
Lodge as the custodians of the honor of the Craft in South Australia.
There may have been-I hope that there was-some misunderstanding
or some inadvertence which would explain the matter, but the fact remains
that the Editor of "The Freemason" has been induced to publish what
might well be charged as a breach of copyright. The least that we can dD
is to express our regret for what has occurred, and I sincerely trust that
nothing of the sort will ever occur again.
South Carolina (1932):
The laws of South Carolina prohibit the granting of a divorce. A
South Carolina Mason secured a divorce in Georgia, and later married in
New York, after which he returned to his former home in South Carolina.
The Grand Master was called on to know if the Brother was not living
in adultery and subject to Masonic trial. The Grand Master replied that
"since we must recognize the laws of Georgia and New York," the Brother
was not a bigamist and was not subject to Masonic trial.

1933--Recent Rulings:
Masons in a number of Jurisdictjons are asking what the Masonic
attitude is going to be toward the sale of 3~2 beer. Grand Masters of Ohio
and Illinois have recently:,i_s1med statem.ents for the guidance of Brethren

"Section 58 of the Masonic Code of the Grand Lodge of Ohio reads
as follows:
" 'To engage in the selling of intoxicating liquors for beverage purposes is a Masonic offense and should subject any Brother so offending to
charges and expulsion; it should also be a disqualification for initiation or
affiliation in a Masonic Lodge.'
"The present legislation concerning 3.2 per cent beer has caused many
inquiries to be sent to me, and in order to avoid confusion, the status of
this legislation not having been determined by the court, I am announcing
certain principles to govern the Craft until the Annual Communication in
October:
· "So long as the present legislation is effective, my ruling ·is that beer
which complies with that legislation will have to be held. to be nonintoxicating, and therefore it will not be a Masonic offense to sell it. Any
Brother so engaging, however, must expect to cease. such business and
conform to the Masonic Code if the courts hereafter invalidate this
legislation.
"Our Masonic duty to circumscribe our desires requires that I direct
that such 3.2 per cent beer be not sold or used in any Masonic Temple,
either at festivities or any restaurants conducted therein.
" The Masonic Code sti'll requires Masons to properly conduct themselves. Any Mason engaged in any business, who suffers disorderly or
any other conduct in connection therewith, which would tend to cast
disrepute upon the Fraternity, will always be guilty of un-Masonic
conduct.''

POLITICS
A king of old propounded the question to his wise men, "What
is Truth?" As far as Masonry is concerned the same question might
be asked as to politics. Considering the term in the broadest sense
as questions affecting government, we b_elieve a Masonic Lodge can
very properly discuss, without taking a positive stand or attempting
to legislate for others, conditions which are of vital interest in our
present day life. While there might not be a meeting of the minds,
and there will always be difference of opinion, we believe with Voltaire
when he stated that, while he did not agree with the ideas of his
opponent, still he would oppose to the end any attempt to limit his
right to express his views.
President James Madison said: " A popular government without
popular information or the means of acquiring it is but a prologue to
a farce or tragedy, or perhaps both. Knowledge will forever govern
ignorance; and a people who mean to be their own governors must
arm themselves with the power that knowledge brings."
Where could be a better place to secure such knowledge than
in ·il gathering of men actuated by the highest ideals and following
the "Charges" given in a Masonic Lodge?
Connecticut (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : We do not object to the
livest interest and action in political, religious and like matters on the
part of the individual. Indeed, we ·ardently advocate it. At times we
ourself are an ardent partisan. Yet we would never think of introducing
such· matters into Lodge. We still object to bringing into our Lodges any
question which inevitably evokes hot discussion, pro and con, as political,
religious and other subjects, even those meritorious intrinsically always
will. According to all accounts, this has been the bane of Masonry.

North Carolina (1933):

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A member of a certain
Lodge in Florida was a candidate for political office to succeed himself,
and in the campaign a certain newspaper published an article charging him
with having misappropriated eight thousand dollars. He asked of the
Master of his- Lodge permission to explain to the Lodge the facts, which
was granted, and he satisfied the Lodge as to his innocence. But things
were hot thereabouts and some accused the Master of that Lodge of letting
politics get into the Lodge. He asked the Grand Master whether he had
made a mistake, and the reply of Grand Master Pasco is as follows, duly
approved by the Grand Lodge:
"You are not only acting within your rights, but you did the proper
Masonic thing in giving the Brother an opportunity to clear himself of the
charge of misappropriating money. Personal and partisan politics should,
?f course, be ~ept entirely out of the Lodge, but if a member of a Lodge
is charged with such a serious offense as this he would be subject to
charges and discipline at the hands of his Brethren; and if he requested an
opportunity to convince them of his innocence he should be accorded that
privilege, and the mere fact that he happened to be running for- political
office should not deprive him of this benefit of Masonry;"

PUBLICITY
As Will Rogers aptly says, "All we know is what we read in the
papers." The custom of broadcasting to the world the affairs of a
Lodge has left little to the imagination. The Masonic and public
press are not the only means where. censorship could be exercised.
Too often the intimate affairs of a Lodge are thoughtlessly revealed
by the members to those who have no connection with the. Fraternity.
If the outside .world must have information as to the aims, objectS
and· purposes of the Fraternity, perhaps no better means could be
employed than that adopted by one of the .Jurisdictions, of a weekly
broadcast, treating Masonry from a historical and educational standpoint. It has the advantage of being .treated by well informed speakers
who know the extent to which they can go.
Alberta (1932):
(Grand Master): Having noticed more than once in the public press,
extended notices concerning certain entertainments sponsored by members
of the Craft under the auspices of Masonic Lodges, I instituted inquiries
into the natur:e of these public performances. I found they were travesties
or caricatures of Masonry or its ceremonies, tending to bring ridicule on
our Fraternity, and I have expressed my strong disapproval of such forms
of entertainment being sponsored by Lodges and put on by Masons as
such, and in one case refused my consent to a proposed performance of this
nature. Many members o~ our Institution would, I believe, after witnessing
such exhibitions feel that the seriousness and solemnity of our rites had
lost for them s~mething that was v"ital a~d sacred. Our Masonic ceremonies are c:if such a nature that they should be carefully guarded at all
times from the slightest suggestion of ridicule or mockery.

New South Wales (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee) : We have often wondered
just what it was in the Institution of Masonry that made some of its
leaders to appear to believe that no man not a member, or a woman, should
ever participate in any Lodge function, even to cooking the food. Masonry's
principles are ideal; these deal with men and women in the outer world
as well as those in the fold, and their kin. Masonry has passed through
the stone age, it would seem to us. It may be stated in passing that we
have noticed that those most strict and severe in matters of this kind will
not only advocate but actually take part in other phases of Masonic work
with all sorts of freedom; in other words, strain at a gnat and swallow
a camel.
New York (1933):
(Grand Master): I believe, Brethren, that an installation, united in
