RITUAL
With the radio, the movie and service clubs the attempt to function only through the Ritual is losing· force. The tendency to subor~inate the true purpose of a Lodge to the mere conferring of degrees
is the greatest handicap in the Masonic world today.
Again referring to what the Past Grand Master of North Carolina
said to the Grand Master of South Carolina, we quote from his address
as follows:

72

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

"Then we get the ritualist. His interest is confined to ritualistic
work. He is a useful Mason, and yet how he does love to bedeck
himself in robes and titles and magnificence I If you could just see me
dressed up as Cyrus, King of Persia I I am glad my wife can't ever
see me. I put on the first section at a recent Shrine ceremonial in
New Bern, dressed up in gorgeous robes, and with a long black beard.
One candidate said: 'That man with_all that rig is some sort of Turk,
ain't he?' He was told: 'Yes, he's a 'l,'urk. We had to pay him
$5,000.00 to come over here and confer this degree _today.' The candidate said: 'Yes, I knew dam' well he won't no American.'
"We have the ritualist, and he is useful, if we can wake him up
to the fact that Ritual is only the beginning. Men of all sorts come
to us. What are we doing about it? Here is Masonry's opportunity
for the regeneration of society through the regeneration of the individual members of it. All too often we merely grind the sausage-mill,
and say to the Brother, after he has finished his Third Degree:
'You will now have a seat with the Brethren,' and there he sits and
sits and sits, and finally does what he might be expected to doexchanges mental vacuum for mental oblivion and slides sweetly off
to sleep.
"I tell you the time has come when we must say to the newlymade Master Mason, not, 'You will now have a seat with the Brethren,' but 'You will now take your stand with your Brethren/ and
seek to equip him to go forth carrying the banner and the message
of . the Fraternity to the world."
Alberta (1932) :
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master of -North
Dakota has been in favor for some time of a revision of the Ritual. He
has·advocated that the penalties should be changed, that some claims t o a.
very ancient history should be eliminated, and that for the Middle Chamber
Lecture there be substituted a lecture on citizenship from "the Ancient
Charges" concerning "the Civil Magistrate, Supreme and Subordinate."
The report, however, of the Custodians of the Work points out that probably the thing that appeals to most men in the Ritual is its antiquity.
There is an aroma of the past in its language and diction; One cannot
rewrite Shakespeare, nor can one rewrite the Ritual. The purpose of
Preston's Middle Chamber Lecture was not so much to present scientific,
mathematical accuracy, but to direct the attention of the Craftsman to his
need of knowledge and education, and give him a bird's-eye view of the
then known field of knowledge. The Custodians thought it would be
destructive to remove that l~ture from the work.

Connecticut (1933):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The question sometimes
arises as to whether conscientious objectors may be allowed to affirm when
taking a Masonic obligation. To us, this is a trivial technicality. In
courts, witnesses are allowed to either swear or affirm at pleasure, but
false testimony enl:ails punishment for perjury in either case. Does not
this parallel hold true in Masonry?

.. ..
.-

(Chairman Correspondence Committee): A decision, disapproved by
a Grand Lodge, involved the case of a Mason who had joined the 0. E. S.
before he had "proved up," which we presume means that he had not
passed examination as to proficiency in the Master Mason Degree. For
obvious reasons, we consider such a man a full-fledged Mason, and believe
any regulation requiring shown proficiency before he can acquire full
membership, as a blow to fundamentals. If he is so short-sighted as to
neglect proficiency, the loss is mainly his own.
District of Columbia (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): We do not know the requirements in all Grand Lodges as to proficiency in the Third Degree, but
it may be reasonably presumed most of them require the same standard
of proficiency in the Third Degree that is required in the other two. Every
once in a while we find some Grand Master advocating that a Brother's
good standing card be withheld until such a time as he shall become proficient in the Third Degree, but we do not believe this would be right,
because after a Brother has signed the by-laws and paid his dues he is in
good standing and is entitled to a certificate to that effect, sb that some
other remedy for lack of such proficiency must ·be found.
In the opinion of this writer, it is just as much the duty of a Worshipful Master to see that a Brother is proficient in the Third Degree as
in the others, but, as our old friend Pepys would say, "How to do it?"
We have no sure remedy to. offer, but believe that if the same stress was
laid on the necessity for proficiency in the Third as in the other two
degrees, if the candidate could be convinced when he started out that it
_was necessary to learn all three, the idea would be in his mind and he
would approach the matter with less reluctance.
However, that is another of the questions concerning the Craft that
probably will never be answered to everybody's satisfaction, so why worry
about it? There are plenty of good Ma~ons who will never learn the
Third Degree the same as they did the _First and Second, and we do not
believe they should be especially penalized for that.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Sometimes we wonder whether this sort of action, standing naked and
alone, is worth while. For one thing, how is it going to be enforced?
There is no penalty provided for failure; no reward for performance is
promised, other than that which would be found without legislation.

• • • • •
(Chairman Correspondence Committee); For another thing, rot~
memory work is very elementary education and psychologically fits best
into the eighth to twelfth year of a normal person's life-rote memory
for adults is oftentimes a chore rather than a satisfying experience.
Moreover, rote memory is not the experience which will chalknge the
best that is in the sort .of men that Masonry today really needs. One
hears on every hand the .cry, "}4asonry needs the interest and the efforts
of worthwhile men-men of affairs-men of the sort who do things big!"
We feel that if we could require some rote memory work to start with,
and then make this the starter for a course in reading, we could get
somewhere. We are not advertising , anything, and don't believe in some
things which proceed along the lines which we here suggest; but nevertheless we suggest that if we had to pick out a set of worthwhile "higher
degrees," we should make them really higher and higher in the intellectual
sphere-bigger and bigger in bigness . of heart-more advanced in advancing, as Robert Browning put it in the immortal "Rabbi Ben Ezra,"
the immortal soul on that journey which it must travel divested of body
and things material. We know something about, and have in our possession the rituals of, something more than four hundred degrees which
are in some sort of way "Masonic" degrees-and . out of that library, we
could pick a very good Order of Masonic Thinkers which would be a
better Rite than any of which we know at this time. Then, when we
wrote our name, and tied on after it, "Umpty steenth degree, Master of
the Secret of Living,'' this would mean something; ~nd not to the fellow
who paid his money or the fellow who was a shrewd politician or the
fellow who by artful ways ingratiated himself with his associates, would
the degrees go--perhaps they would not be so much coveted as some of
the baubles of the Masonic. world-but to him who in deed and in truth
had earned the right in heart, soul and mind to be called "Master of the
Secret of Living, Ultimate Degree." It i$ trite to say that there's much
fool snobbishness because baubles· and vital things get a trifle mixed
sometimes. We have been received into the circle of the most exclusive,
and do not sneer at them' ; but we do realize that the Masonic world
really has a crying need for some .things that it has not in these days.
Vermont (1933):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): The Grand Master of Indiana granted eleven dispensations for interstate visitations, Indiana Lodges
entertaining Lodges from other states which visited and worked degrees
by their own Ritual, and Indiana Lodges visiting and working in other

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

77

Grand Jurisdictions in six instances. The custom is growing, and we
believe it to be a good one. Yet some G~and Lodges do not yet allow such
friendly interchange of visits, probably fearing that their own Ritual will
be imperiled if their officers hear the work of other Grand Lodges. We
believe the fear is not well grounded.

Washington (1932):
(Chairman Correspondence Committee): Tinkering with the Ritual
seems to be epidemic with a certain class of Masons, and especially with
those who have come into the institution after having joined other organizations and had their ideals formed upon a different basis from that which
underlies the Masonic organization.
While legislation may be changed by Grarid Lodges to suit the conditions, and use such methods for the betterment of their members as may
be deemed wise, yet even such changes should be made only after careful
investigation and due deliberation, for most of our customs have been
adopted after long trial and are backed up by a wisdom that it is not
wise to reject.

Western Australia (1932):
Many years ago, gocid old Brother Shryock, Maryland's record Grand
Master in point of service, declared that as a Mason he was a Fundamentalist, and found no relish in Masonic modernism. This, especially,
in relation to the Ritual. Well, Grand Master . Starke, of North Dakota,
seems to ·be at the other end as regards some parts of the Ritual. He
would have the penalties changed, some of our claims to a very ancient
history eliminated, and, as a substitute for the second T. B. lecture, "a
lecture on citizenship from the Ancient Charges concerning the civil
magistrate, supreme and subordinate." But why? If the form of the
penalties seems archaic to the reforming spirit, and likely to injure a
Brother's respect for the Order, whose fault is it? Not the fault of the
words used. May not the fault be traceable to the lack of knowledge
on the part of the Worshipful Master, the absence of any desire on his
part to grasp the full intent and meaning of the words or their historic
ancestry? In many Grand Jurisdictions prodigious emphasis is laid upon
ritualistic letter-perfectness as a prerequisite for the highest office in the
Lodge, when it is of much greater importance that there should be the
possession of at least elementary knowledge of our laws, customs, usages
and symbolism, and the ability to explain them to the Brethren. Preachers,
not parrots, are needed. Again, what is wrong with the Middle Chamber
lecture? Or with our claims to a very ancient history. The lecture is in
strict conformity with the symbolic intent of the F. C. D., and as to our
historical claims, at least quite as much can be said in their favor as against
them~ Personally, I prefer the Fundamentalism of my late Most Worshipful Brother of Maryland.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE

Minnesota:
After Grand Lodge was formally opened the Grand Chaplain, Brother
Very Rev. John Snape, conducted brief, interesting and instructive devotional services, and a beautiful tribute to George Washington was given
by Brother Albert E. Boynton, P. G. M.

,..

.. . .

A very lengthy address was presented by the Grand Master. He had
many perplexing problems to deal with and displayed diplomacy,' courage,
executive ability and sound judgment in solving them, instilling the Craft
with renewed hope, inspiration and determination to carry on and keep
pure and clean the high principles of true Masonry.

• • • • •

89

The Jurisprudence Committee report was also carefully prepared, and
it was likewise adopted in its entirety.

•••••

Brother Jesse Whited presents his twelfth correspondence report.
He has an excellent style all his own, and he does not overlook anything of any importance. His comments on the several topics should be
published in separate form so more would have a chance to read-it. It is
a relief to pick up Jesse Whited's report, because we know it is going to
be different and painstakingly correct.

• ••••

The Grand Orator, Brother James F . Fraser, delivered an unusually
fine address.

New Hampshire :
So big is this Grand Lodge, so important are its affairs, that four .days
are used to hold their Annual Communications.

A very exhaustive and interesting report was given by the Trustees
· of the Masonic Homes.

One of the first things done was to hear a fine tribute paid to Washington.

It is impossible in the space at our disposal to do adequate .justice
to a review of this wonderful volume portraying and reciting the doings
of the Grand Lodge of California at its eighty-third annual communication. We commend it to the careful perusal of all our Brethren.

There are many pages used to report decisions. These are ever interesting. to one who likes to know how the law is being interpreted.

• •• • •
•• • • •

Nevada:
The Grand Master condemned, in no uncertain terms, the issuance of
some circular letters to some San Francisco Lodges, wherein the Lodge
roster was used to- address the membership on some pending municipal
legislation.
He also had to use a whole lot of space to dispose of the Shrine
Lottery business.
He reported that the Sciots had fallen in line with the ideas of Grand
Lodge and that any break had been properly healed.
He also pays fine tribute to the Grand Officers who served under him.
Especially to our good fri!!nds John Whicher and Tom Baker.

• •• • •

Worthy Brother James T. Frazer, Grand Orator, delivered a very
illuminating address.
The Committee on Clandestine Masonry presented an exhaustive report, giving names of Lodges and individuals, and the basis of their operations.

• • • • •

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes presented a well prepared report covering a large range of subjects. It was so well written and
the sentiment was so properly stated that each paragraph was adopted.

• • * ••

• * * * *

•••••

Page after page is devot!!d to lottery schemes. It is all square and
virile-calling names and hitting heads in homely fashion. The discussion
dodged nothing, but sought to turn sunlight upon the projects.

• • * * •
They had a splendid oration. In it these words loom large: "Masonry
is a battle and not a dream."

* * * * *
The Committee on Grievances had fifty-nine cases before it. It would
be a grievance to us to be compelled to serve on that committee.

·- • • • *
Arriving at the correspondence, we stayed with it a long time, studying
its make-up, as a scheme. The longer we looked at it, the more sure
minded we became that we shall never try to do it in that way. It is of
the topical variety-encyclopedic in its arrangement. As a document for
reference, for some special thing, it is convenient and attractive, and of
course the work of preparing is ideally executed.
New Jersey:
Grand Master Gaylord's address covers seventy-seven pages and treats
of many things.

The report of the Committee on Correspondence is prepared by

interesting and helpful material.

The systems of Freemasonry practiced in the United States are
generally known as the York Rite and the Scottish Rite. Properly
speaking, they should be termed the American Rite and the Scottish
Rite, for the one commonly called York is peculiar. in its organized
proceedings only to the United States.
The American Rite embraces the Symbolic, the Capitular, the
Cryptic and the Templar Degrees.
The Symbolic Degrees are conferred in a Lodge and are the
Entered Apprentice, the Fellow Craft and the Master Mason. They
are called Symbolic because their prominent mode of instruction is
by symbols.
The Capitular Degrees are conferred in a Chapter and are the
Mark Master, the Past Master, the Most Excellent Master and the
Royal Arch. The supplemental and honorary degree of High Priesthood is conferred in a Council of High Priests upon those who have
been regularly elected to preside over a Chapter of Royal Arch
Masons. They are called Capitular because they are conferred in a
Chapter, the word "Capitular" meaning "done in a Chapter."
The Cryptic Degrees are conferred in a Council. They are the
Royal Master, the Select Master and the Super-Excellent Master.
They are called "Cryptic" because the word "cript" means a secret
vault or underground passage.
The Templar Degrees are conferred in a Commandery and are
the Red Cross, the Temple and the Malta. The name Knight Templar comes from the efforts of the Christian Knights to take the
temple at Jerusalem from the Mohammedans.
The Scottish Rite embraces the degrees from the 4th to the
33rd, inclusive. In the Southern Jurisdiction of the United States
(which includes all territory south of the Ohio River and west of
the Mississippi ·River) the organization of the different Bodies, and
the degrees conferred by them, are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 ° to 14 •,
inclusive; Chapter Rose Croix, 15° to 18°; Council of Kadosh, 19°
to 30°; Consistory, 31° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.
In the Northern Jurisdiction (which includes all states north of
the Ohio River and east of the Mississippi River) the degrees conferred are: Lodge of Perfection, 4 • to 14 °, inclusive; Council Princes
of Jerusalem, 15° and 16° ; Chapter Rose Croix, 17° and 18°; Consistory, 19° to 32°; Supreme Council, 33°.

MASONIC CALENDAR
Ancient Craft .Masons-Commence their era with the creation of
the world, calling it Anno Lucis (A. L.), "in the year of light."
Add 4000 years to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 4~5923.
Scottish Rite--Same as Ancient Craft, except the Jewish chronology is used. Anno Mundi (A. M.), "in the year of the world."
Add 3760 to the common era. Thus: 1923 and 3760-5683. After
September add another year.
Royal Arch Masons-Date from the year the second temple was
commenced by Zerubbabel, Anno lnventionis. (A. Inv.), "in the year
of discovery."
Add 530 years to the vulgar era. Thus: 1923 and 530-2453.
. Royal . and Select Masters-Date from the year in which the
Temple of Solomon was completed, Anno Depositionis (A. Dep.),
"in the year of the deposit."
Add 1000 to the common time. Thus: 1923 and 1000-2923.
Knights Templar-Commence their era with the organization of
their Order. Anno Ordinis (A. 0.), "in the year of the Order."
From the Christian era take 1118. Thus: 1118 from 1923--805.
Order of High Priesthood-Dates from the year of the blessing
of Abraham by the High Priest Melchizedek, Anno Benedictionis
(A. B.), "in the year of the blessing."
To the Christian era add 1913, the year of blessing. Thus: 1923
and 1913-3836.

GREAT BRITAIN AND IRELAND

Acacia Fraternity ···-----------··-·-···-·-·-·····-··-·-····-·····--·-·-·····-····-····....,.-·..........,. 6
American Freemasonry
l)J , 95

Page
There is no possibility of determining the number of members affiliated at the present time with the Lodges of England, Scotland, and
Ireland.
"Multiple membership" was taken advantage of by English Brethren
to an extraordinary extent in days gone by. When the difficult times
came and many were not able to maintain all their connections, the majority retained membership in one Lodge only, while others dropped out
altogether.
With Scotland there is the additional difficulty of life-memberships
which usually are forgotten after the holder leaves the country; he may
become identified with some Lodge elsewhere, or he may die, without
his Mother Lodge knowing anything about it.
In Ireland, too, there has been an appreciable decline m numbers,
during the past three years.
Probably 400,000 is a. liberal estimate of the aggregate of Brethren
identified with the three Grand Lodges at the present time.
